1\. A company collects data for temperature, humidity, and atmospheric pressure in cities across multiple continents.  
The average volume of data that the company collects from each site daily is 500 GB. Each site has a high-speed Internet connection.  
The company wants to aggregate the data from all these global sites as quickly as possible in a single Amazon S3 bucket. The solution must minimize operational complexity.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination S3 bucket. Use multipart uploads to directly upload site data to the destination S3 bucket.  
B. Upload the data from each site to an S3 bucket in the closest Region. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy objects to the destination S3 bucket. Then remove the data from the origin S3 bucket.  
C. Schedule AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device jobs daily to transfer data from each site to the closest Region. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy objects to the destination S3 bucket.  
D. Upload the data from each site to an Amazon EC2 instance in the closest Region. Store the data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. At regular intervals, take an EBS snapshot and copy it to the Region that contains the destination S3 bucket. Restore the EBS volume in that Region.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The sites have fast links, so physical transport isn't needed — what's needed is to speed up the actual upload over the internet into a single bucket. S3 Transfer Acceleration routes data to the nearest edge location, from where it travels to the bucket over the AWS backbone, and multipart upload parallelizes the transfer of large files. This is configured with a single switch on the bucket — there's almost no operational complexity.  
Why B is not selected: The approach works, but it adds extra buckets, replication rules, and cleanup of the source objects: operational complexity is noticeably higher for the same result.  
Why C is not selected: Shipping Snowball devices daily contradicts the "as quickly as possible" requirement: delivery takes days, and the links are already fast.  
Why D is not selected: Instances, volumes, snapshots, and restoration in another Region are the most complex and expensive construction of the options listed, and the data still ends up having to be placed in S3 anyway.

---

2\. A company needs the ability to analyze the log files of its proprietary application. The logs are stored in JSON format in an Amazon S3 bucket. Queries will be simple and will run on-demand. A solutions architect needs to perform the analysis with minimal changes to the existing architecture.  
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?  
A. Use Amazon Redshift to load all the content into one place and run the SQL queries as needed.  
B. Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs to store the logs. Run SQL queries as needed from the Amazon CloudWatch console.  
C. Use Amazon Athena directly with Amazon S3 to run the queries as needed.  
D. Use AWS Glue to catalog the logs. Use a transient Apache Spark cluster on Amazon EMR to run the SQL queries as needed.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The data is already in S3, and the queries are simple and run on demand. Amazon Athena reads objects directly from the bucket, understands the JSON format, and is billed by bytes scanned — no cluster, no data loading, and no changes to the architecture.  
Why A is not selected: Loading the entire volume into Redshift means a separate data store, a loading pipeline, and a permanently running cluster.  
Why B is not selected: The logs are already in S3, and moving them into CloudWatch Logs is an architecture change and more expensive storage.  
Why D is not selected: A Glue catalog plus a transient EMR cluster solve the task, but they require setup and paying for nodes where a single service is enough.

---

3\. A company uses AWS Organizations to manage multiple AWS accounts for different departments. The management account has an Amazon S3 bucket that contains project reports. The company wants to limit access to this S3 bucket to only users of accounts within the organization in AWS Organizations.  
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?  
A. Add the aws PrincipalOrgID global condition key with a reference to the organization ID to the S3 bucket policy.  
B. Create an organizational unit (OU) for each department. Add the aws:PrincipalOrgPaths global condition key to the S3 bucket policy.  
C. Use AWS CloudTrail to monitor the CreateAccount, InviteAccountToOrganization, LeaveOrganization, and RemoveAccountFromOrganization events. Update the S3 bucket policy accordingly.  
D. Tag each user that needs access to the S3 bucket. Add the aws:PrincipalTag global condition key to the S3 bucket policy.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The company needs to admit anyone who belongs to the organization, without rewriting the policy every time a new account is added. That's exactly what the aws:PrincipalOrgID global condition key is for: the bucket policy specifies the organization ID (o-xxxx), and the request succeeds only if the calling principal belongs to an account within that organization. Add an account and access appears automatically; remove it and access disappears. Nothing needs to be enumerated or maintained, hence the LEAST operational overhead.  
Why B is not selected: aws:PrincipalOrgPaths restricts access to specific organizational units and requires enumerating OU paths and maintaining them through reorganizations. The task, however, is to admit the entire organization.  
Why C is not selected: Watching organization events and then updating the policy is a homegrown synchronization of the account list: code, delay, and risk of error where a ready-made condition already exists.  
Why D is not selected: Tags on users mean someone has to apply and remove those tags in every account. Organization membership is checked automatically.

---

4\. An application runs on an Amazon EC2 instance in a VPC. The application processes logs that are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The EC2 instance needs to access the S3 bucket without connectivity to the internet.  
Which solution will provide private network connectivity to Amazon S3?  
A. Create a gateway VPC endpoint to the S3 bucket.  
B. Stream the logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Export the logs to the S3 bucket.  
C. Create an instance profile on Amazon EC2 to allow S3 access.  
D. Create an Amazon API Gateway API with a private link to access the S3 endpoint.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Private connectivity to S3 from a VPC is provided by a gateway endpoint: a route to the service's prefix list is added to the subnet's route table, and requests to the bucket travel within the AWS network without going out to the internet. There's no charge for the endpoint itself.  
Why B is not selected: Streaming to CloudWatch Logs and then exporting is a rework of how logs are handled, not a networking solution, and accessing S3 will still require a route.  
Why C is not selected: An instance profile grants access permissions, but the route stays the same: without an endpoint, traffic will still go over the internet.  
Why D is not selected: There's no such thing as private access to S3 through API Gateway: that's not how this mechanism works.

---

5\. A company is hosting a web application on AWS using a single Amazon EC2 instance that stores user-uploaded documents in an Amazon EBS volume. For better scalability and availability, the company duplicated the architecture and created a second EC2 instance and EBS volume in another Availability Zone, placing both behind an Application Load Balancer. After completing this change, users reported that, each time they refreshed the website, they could see one subset of their documents or the other, but never all of the documents at the same time.  
What should a solutions architect propose to ensure users see all of their documents at once?  
A. Copy the data so both EBS volumes contain all the documents  
B. Configure the Application Load Balancer to direct a user to the server with the documents  
C. Copy the data from both EBS volumes to Amazon EFS. Modify the application to save new documents to Amazon EFS  
D. Configure the Application Load Balancer to send the request to both servers. Return each document from the correct server  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The symptom has a simple explanation: an EBS volume attaches to a single instance, so each machine has its own set of documents, and the load balancer shows one set or the other depending on where the request lands. What's needed is shared storage accessible to both machines at the same time — Amazon EFS mounts over NFS on all instances across all Availability Zones simultaneously. The existing files are copied to EFS, the application starts writing there, and the user sees the full list regardless of which instance the request reaches.  
Why A is not selected: A one-time copy synchronizes the volumes only at the moment of copying: the very next uploaded document will again end up on just one machine.  
Why B is not selected: Pinning a user to "their" server doesn't help: a single user's documents are already split across two volumes, and if that server fails, access to its files disappears.  
Why D is not selected: The load balancer sends a request to exactly one target. It can't split a request and stitch together the responses.

---

6\. A company uses NFS to store large video files in on-premises network attached storage. Each video file ranges in size from 1 MB to 500 GB. The total storage is 70 TB and is no longer growing. The company decides to migrate the video files to Amazon S3. The company must migrate the video files as soon as possible while using the least possible network bandwidth.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create an S3 bucket. Create an IAM role that has permissions to write to the S3 bucket. Use the AWS CLI to copy all files locally to the S3 bucket.  
B. Create an AWS Snowball Edge job. Receive a Snowball Edge device on premises. Use the Snowball Edge client to transfer data to the device. Return the device so that AWS can import the data into Amazon S3.  
C. Deploy an S3 File Gateway on premises. Create a public service endpoint to connect to the S3 File Gateway. Create an S3 bucket. Create a new NFS file share on the S3 File Gateway. Point the new file share to the S3 bucket. Transfer the data from the existing NFS file share to the S3 File Gateway.  
D. Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection between the on-premises network and AWS. Deploy an S3 File Gateway on premises. Create a public virtual interface (VIF) to connect to the S3 File Gateway. Create an S3 bucket. Create a new NFS file share on the S3 File Gateway. Point the new file share to the S3 bucket. Transfer the data from the existing NFS file share to the S3 File Gateway.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Two constraints apply: migrate as quickly as possible and use as little network bandwidth as possible. The second one directly rules out any network transfer, so the 70 TB travels offline — on an AWS Snowball Edge device (about 80 TB of usable capacity, i.e., a single order). Data is copied to the device locally, the device is shipped back to AWS, and the data lands in S3. A useful rule of thumb: 1 Gbps ≈ 10 TB per day, so 70 TB over the network would take a week with a fully free gigabit link, which isn't the case here.  
Why A is not selected: Copying via the CLI goes over the company's internet connection: the requirement to minimize bandwidth use is violated completely.  
Why C is not selected: S3 File Gateway is designed for ongoing hybrid access, not a one-time migration, and it still transfers data over that same network.  
Why D is not selected: Direct Connect takes months to set up and still transfers data over the link. It doesn't fit a one-time "as quickly as possible" transfer of 70 TB.

---

7\. A company has an application that ingests incoming messages. Dozens of other applications and microservices then quickly consume these messages. The number of messages varies drastically and sometimes increases suddenly to 100,000 each second. The company wants to decouple the solution and increase scalability.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Persist the messages to Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics. Configure the consumer applications to read and process the messages.  
B. Deploy the ingestion application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group to scale the number of EC2 instances based on CPU metrics.  
C. Write the messages to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with a single shard. Use an AWS Lambda function to preprocess messages and store them in Amazon DynamoDB. Configure the consumer applications to read from DynamoDB to process the messages.  
D. Publish the messages to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic with multiple Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SOS) subscriptions. Configure the consumer applications to process the messages from the queues.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Dozens of independent applications consume the messages, and each needs its own copy. An SNS topic fans the message out to all subscribers, while an SQS queue for each consumer smooths out spikes up to a hundred thousand messages per second and lets each consumer process at its own pace. This is the classic fan-out pattern.  
Why A is not selected: Kinesis Data Analytics processes streams with queries; it doesn't store messages for dozens of independent consumers.  
Why B is not selected: Scaling instances based on CPU load doesn't decouple the producer from the consumers and can't keep up with sudden spikes.  
Why C is not selected: A single Kinesis shard is limited to roughly a thousand records per second — far short of a hundred thousand — and the intermediate table adds complexity without benefit.

---

8\. A company is migrating a distributed application to AWS. The application serves variable workloads. The legacy platform consists of a primary server that coordinates jobs across multiple compute nodes. The company wants to modernize the application with a solution that maximizes resiliency and scalability.  
How should a solutions architect design the architecture to meet these requirements?  
A. Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as a destination for the jobs. Implement the compute nodes with Amazon EC2 instances that are managed in an Auto Scaling group. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling to use scheduled scaling.  
B. Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as a destination for the jobs. Implement the compute nodes with Amazon EC2 instances that are managed in an Auto Scaling group. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling based on the size of the queue.  
C. Implement the primary server and the compute nodes with Amazon EC2 instances that are managed in an Auto Scaling group. Configure AWS CloudTrail as a destination for the jobs. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling based on the load on the primary server.  
D. Implement the primary server and the compute nodes with Amazon EC2 instances that are managed in an Auto Scaling group. Configure Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) as a destination for the jobs. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling based on the load on the compute nodes.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The job coordinator is a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Jobs are placed into an SQS queue, and the compute nodes run in an Auto Scaling group whose size is driven by the queue length. This way the system reacts to the actual amount of work and survives the failure of any node.  
Why A is not selected: Scheduled scaling doesn't respond to the variable load stated directly in the requirements.  
Why C is not selected: CloudTrail records API calls and can't act as a destination for jobs, and keeping the primary server leaves a single point of failure.  
Why D is not selected: EventBridge routes events but doesn't hold a job queue, and the primary server remains in the design.

---

9\. A company is running an SMB file server in its data center. The file server stores large files that are accessed frequently for the first few days after the files are created. After 7 days the files are rarely accessed.  
The total data size is increasing and is close to the company's total storage capacity. A solutions architect must increase the company's available storage space without losing low-latency access to the most recently accessed files. The solutions architect must also provide file lifecycle management to avoid future storage issues.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS DataSync to copy data that is older than 7 days from the SMB file server to AWS.  
B. Create an Amazon S3 File Gateway to extend the company's storage space. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days.  
C. Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system to extend the company's storage space.  
D. Install a utility on each user's computer to access Amazon S3. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the data to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 7 days.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: There are three requirements: add storage space, keep low latency for recently accessed files, and get lifecycle management. Amazon S3 File Gateway presents an SMB share to local clients, stores the data in S3, and keeps recently used files in a local cache — hence the low latency for fresh data. A lifecycle rule transitions objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after seven days, which addresses the growth in cost and volume.  
Why A is not selected: DataSync copies data but doesn't leave local applications with transparent SMB access to what has already moved, and it doesn't manage lifecycle itself.  
Why C is not selected: FSx for Windows File Server provides space and the SMB protocol, but it's fully paid file storage with no automatic transition to cheaper archive storage classes.  
Why D is not selected: A utility on every user's computer means changing workflows and giving up the familiar network share, and S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval is more expensive than Deep Archive for the same requirements.

---

10\. A company is building an ecommerce web application on AWS. The application sends information about new orders to an Amazon API Gateway REST API to process. The company wants to ensure that orders are processed in the order that they are received.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use an API Gateway integration to publish a message to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic when the application receives an order. Subscribe an AWS Lambda function to the topic to perform processing.  
B. Use an API Gateway integration to send a message to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue when the application receives an order. Configure the SQS FIFO queue to invoke an AWS Lambda function for processing.  
C. Use an API Gateway authorizer to block any requests while the application processes an order.  
D. Use an API Gateway integration to send a message to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue when the application receives an order. Configure the SQS standard queue to invoke an AWS Lambda function for processing.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Only an SQS FIFO queue guarantees the order in which orders are processed: it preserves sequence within a message group and guarantees exactly-once processing. API Gateway puts the order into such a queue, and a Lambda function reads it and processes orders in order.  
Why A is not selected: SNS doesn't guarantee delivery order: messages can reach a subscriber in any sequence.  
Why C is not selected: Blocking all requests while one order is being processed would destroy the application's throughput.  
Why D is not selected: A standard SQS queue works on a best-effort ordering basis, but reordering is allowed: it doesn't provide strict sequencing.

---

11\. A company has an application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances and uses an Amazon Aurora database. The EC2 instances connect to the database by using user names and passwords that are stored locally in a file. The company wants to minimize the operational overhead of credential management.  
What should a solutions architect do to accomplish this goal?  
A. Use AWS Secrets Manager. Turn on automatic rotation.  
B. Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Turn on automatic rotation.  
C. Create an Amazon S3 bucket to store objects that are encrypted with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption key. Migrate the credential file to the S3 bucket. Point the application to the S3 bucket.  
D. Create an encrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume for each EC2 instance. Attach the new EBS volume to each EC2 instance. Migrate the credential file to the new EBS volume. Point the application to the new EBS volume.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The password sits in a file on the instance, which means someone has to distribute it, change it on every machine, and make sure it doesn't leak along with the image. AWS Secrets Manager removes all of that: the secret is stored encrypted with a KMS key, the application retrieves it via API under the instance role's identity, and built-in rotation changes the password in both the Aurora database and the secret itself, using a ready-made function for supported databases. No code needs to be written — hence "minimize the operational overhead". The key difference from Parameter Store: only Secrets Manager has rotation built in out of the box.  
Why B is not selected: Parameter Store can store the password as a SecureString, but it has no built-in automatic rotation — it can't be turned on with a checkbox; you'd have to write and maintain your own function.  
Why C is not selected: A file in an encrypted bucket is still the same file: the password in the database and in the object would still have to be changed manually or with your own code.  
Why D is not selected: An encrypted EBS volume protects data at rest but doesn't solve anything in credential management: there's no rotation, and now the file exists on every instance.

---

12\. A global company hosts its web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB).  
The web application has static data and dynamic data. The company stores its static data in an Amazon S3 bucket.  
The company wants to improve performance and reduce latency for the static data and dynamic data. The company is using its own domain name registered with Amazon Route 53.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that has the S3 bucket and the ALB as origins. Configure Route 53 to route traffic to the CloudFront distribution.  
B. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that has the ALB as an origin. Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator that has the S3 bucket as an endpoint Configure Route 53 to route traffic to the CloudFront distribution.  
C. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that has the S3 bucket as an origin. Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator that has the ALB and the CloudFront distribution as endpoints. Create a custom domain name that points to the accelerator DNS name. Use the custom domain name as an endpoint for the web application.  
D. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that has the ALB as an origin. Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator that has the S3 bucket as an endpoint. Create two domain names. Point one domain name to the CloudFront DNS name for dynamic content. Point the other domain name to the accelerator DNS name for static content. Use the domain names as endpoints for the web application.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The same service accelerates both static and dynamic content: CloudFront can have multiple origins and route requests by path-based behaviors — static files are served from the S3 bucket, dynamic requests are proxied to the load balancer. Dynamic content benefits not from caching but from TLS being terminated at the nearest edge location, after which the request travels over the AWS backbone. Route 53 points the company's domain at the distribution with an alias record.  
Why B is not selected: Global Accelerator doesn't support S3 as an endpoint: it works with ALB, NLB, EC2, and Elastic IP addresses. This design doesn't work.  
Why C is not selected: Putting an accelerator in front of CloudFront makes no sense: both services already provide a global network, and the design becomes more complex with no benefit.  
Why D is not selected: Two separate domains for static and dynamic content complicate the application, and S3 still can't be a Global Accelerator endpoint.

---

13\. A company performs monthly maintenance on its AWS infrastructure. During these maintenance activities, the company needs to rotate the credentials for its Amazon RDS for MySQL databases across multiple AWS Regions.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Store the credentials as secrets in AWS Secrets Manager. Use multi-Region secret replication for the required Regions. Configure Secrets Manager to rotate the secrets on a schedule.  
B. Store the credentials as secrets in AWS Systems Manager by creating a secure string parameter. Use multi- Region secret replication for the required Regions. Configure Systems Manager to rotate the secrets on a schedule.  
C. Store the credentials in an Amazon S3 bucket that has server-side encryption (SSE) enabled. Use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) to invoke an AWS Lambda function to rotate the credentials.  
D. Encrypt the credentials as secrets by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) multi-Region customer managed keys. Store the secrets in an Amazon DynamoDB global table. Use an AWS Lambda function to retrieve the secrets from DynamoDB. Use the RDS API to rotate the secrets.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Two requirements: the same credentials are needed in multiple Regions, and they must change on a schedule, with a minimum of manual work. Secrets Manager has exactly both mechanisms: multi-Region secret replication keeps replicas of the secret in the required Regions and updates them automatically whenever the primary changes, and built-in rotation for RDS changes the password on a schedule using a ready-made AWS function. The application in each Region reads the local replica, with no latency from cross-Region calls.  
Why B is not selected: Systems Manager Parameter Store has neither cross-Region parameter replication nor built-in rotation. Both mechanisms would have to be built from scratch.  
Why C is not selected: A file in a bucket plus a custom EventBridge-triggered function means writing your own code for what Secrets Manager does with a configuration setting, and there's no cross-Region replication out of the box.  
Why D is not selected: The design with multi-Region KMS keys, a DynamoDB global table, and a custom rotation function works, but it's three services and a hand-built process instead of a single configuration.

---

14\. A company runs an ecommerce application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The instances run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. The Auto Scaling group scales based on CPU utilization metrics. The ecommerce application stores the transaction data in a MySQL 8.0 database that is hosted on a large EC2 instance.  
The database's performance degrades quickly as application load increases. The application handles more read requests than write transactions. The company wants a solution that will automatically scale the database to meet the demand of unpredictable read workloads while maintaining high availability.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use Amazon Redshift with a single node for leader and compute functionality.  
B. Use Amazon RDS with a Single-AZ deployment Configure Amazon RDS to add reader instances in a different Availability Zone.  
C. Use Amazon Aurora with a Multi-AZ deployment. Configure Aurora Auto Scaling with Aurora Replicas.  
D. Use Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with EC2 Spot Instances.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Reads significantly outnumber writes, the load is unpredictable, and high availability is required. Aurora MySQL is compatible with the existing database, deploys across multiple Availability Zones, and can automatically add and remove read replicas based on load through Aurora Auto Scaling. The application switches to the reader endpoint without rewriting any queries.  
Why A is not selected: Redshift is an analytical data warehouse for complex queries over large datasets, not a transactional database for an online store, and a single node provides no high availability.  
Why B is not selected: A Single-AZ configuration contradicts the high-availability requirement, and RDS read replicas aren't added automatically based on load.  
Why D is not selected: Memcached is a cache with no data persistence and no replication; it isn't a database, and Spot Instances are unacceptable for a data store.

---

15\. A company recently migrated to AWS and wants to implement a solution to protect the traffic that flows in and out of the production VPC. The company had an inspection server in its on-premises data center. The inspection server performed specific operations such as traffic flow inspection and traffic filtering. The company wants to have the same functionalities in the AWS Cloud.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use Amazon GuardDuty for traffic inspection and traffic filtering in the production VPC.  
B. Use Traffic Mirroring to mirror traffic from the production VPC for traffic inspection and filtering.  
C. Use AWS Network Firewall to create the required rules for traffic inspection and traffic filtering for the production VPC.  
D. Use AWS Firewall Manager to create the required rules for traffic inspection and traffic filtering for the production VPC.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The on-premises inspection server did two things: examined traffic and filtered it. In AWS, that maps to AWS Network Firewall — a managed, stateful VPC-level firewall with Suricata-compatible rules, domain filtering, and deep protocol inspection. It's deployed in a dedicated subnet, and VPC traffic is routed through its endpoint. Distinction: Network Firewall filters traffic, WAF protects HTTP applications, Firewall Manager centrally manages policies, and GuardDuty only detects.  
Why A is not selected: GuardDuty analyzes logs and reports suspicious activity. It doesn't block anything and doesn't filter traffic.  
Why B is not selected: Traffic Mirroring copies traffic to an analyzer, but on its own it doesn't filter or block anything — it's an observability tool.  
Why D is not selected: Firewall Manager manages WAF, Shield, and Network Firewall policies across many accounts, but it doesn't perform inspection itself: it needs an underlying service, which is Network Firewall.

---

16\. A company hosts a data lake on AWS. The data lake consists of data in Amazon S3 and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The company needs a reporting solution that provides data visualization and includes all the data sources within the data lake. Only the company's management team should have full access to all the visualizations. The rest of the company should have only limited access.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create an analysis in Amazon QuickSight. Connect all the data sources and create new datasets. Publish dashboards to visualize the data. Share the dashboards with the appropriate IAM roles.  
B. Create an analysis in Amazon QuickSight. Connect all the data sources and create new datasets. Publish dashboards to visualize the data. Share the dashboards with the appropriate users and groups.  
C. Create an AWS Glue table and crawler for the data in Amazon S3. Create an AWS Glue extract, transform, and load (ETL) job to produce reports. Publish the reports to Amazon S3. Use S3 bucket policies to limit access to the reports.  
D. Create an AWS Glue table and crawler for the data in Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena Federated Query to access data within Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. Generate reports by using Amazon Athena. Publish the reports to Amazon S3. Use S3 bucket policies to limit access to the reports.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: What's needed is visualization across multiple sources (S3 and RDS) with access segmentation: full access for management, limited access for everyone else. Amazon QuickSight connects to S3 through Athena and to RDS directly, and published dashboards are shared with QuickSight's own users and groups — the service has its own user and group model. This is exactly what distinguishes the correct option from the similar one: a dashboard can't be shared with an IAM role.  
Why A is not selected: QuickSight dashboards are published to QuickSight users and groups, not to IAM roles. Roles control the service's own access to data sources, not the visibility of a dashboard.  
Why C is not selected: Glue jobs produce report files, but that's not interactive visualization, and access control through bucket policies is coarser than dashboard-level permissions.  
Why D is not selected: Athena Federated Query solves the data-access problem, but it still produces tables and files rather than visualizations. The requirement for dashboards isn't met.

---

17\. A company is implementing a new business application. The application runs on two Amazon EC2 instances and uses an Amazon S3 bucket for document storage. A solutions architect needs to ensure that the EC2 instances can access the S3 bucket.  
What should the solutions architect do to meet this requirement?  
A. Create an IAM role that grants access to the S3 bucket. Attach the role to the EC2 instances.  
B. Create an IAM policy that grants access to the S3 bucket. Attach the policy to the EC2 instances.  
C. Create an IAM group that grants access to the S3 bucket. Attach the group to the EC2 instances.  
D. Create an IAM user that grants access to the S3 bucket. Attach the user account to the EC2 instances.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: An EC2 instance can be granted permissions only one way — through an IAM role attached to the instance (technically, via an instance profile). The application obtains temporary credentials from the instance metadata, they refresh automatically, and no keys ever end up in files or environment variables. Policies, meanwhile, attach to the role, not to the instance; groups exist only for users.  
Why B is not selected: A policy can't be attached to an instance: policies attach to users, groups, and roles. The instance gets a role, and the role in turn carries the policy.  
Why C is not selected: An IAM group is a container for users. An instance can't be attached to one.  
Why D is not selected: An IAM user is long-lived credentials for a person or an external system. A user can't be attached to an instance, and placing its keys on disk is an anti-pattern.

---

18\. An application development team is designing a microservice that will convert large images to smaller, compressed images. When a user uploads an image through the web interface, the microservice should store the image in an Amazon S3 bucket, process and compress the image with an AWS Lambda function, and store the image in its compressed form in a different S3 bucket.  
A solutions architect needs to design a solution that uses durable, stateless components to process the images automatically.  
Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure the S3 bucket to send a notification to the SQS queue when an image is uploaded to the S3 bucket.  
B. Configure the Lambda function to use the Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as the invocation source. When the SQS message is successfully processed, delete the message in the queue.  
C. Configure the Lambda function to monitor the S3 bucket for new uploads. When an uploaded image is detected, write the file name to a text file in memory and use the text file to keep track of the images that were processed.  
D. Launch an Amazon EC2 instance to monitor an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. When items are added to the queue, log the file name in a text file on the EC2 instance and invoke the Lambda function.  
E. Configure an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) event to monitor the S3 bucket. When an image is uploaded, send an alert to an Amazon ample Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic with the application owner's email address for further processing.  
Answer: AB  
Explanation: Durable, stateless components are required. The S3 notification on upload places a message in an SQS queue, so the file details are stored reliably and survive a failure (A). The queue serves as the invocation source for the Lambda function, and the message is deleted after successful processing; on failure it returns to the queue and is retried (B).  
Why C is not selected: A text file in the function's memory is state that disappears along with the execution environment, and the function has no built-in way to poll the bucket itself.  
Why D is not selected: An EC2 instance with a log file adds both state and infrastructure to maintain.  
Why E is not selected: An email to the application owner is a notification to a person, not automated image processing.

---

19\. A company has a three-tier web application that is deployed on AWS. The web servers are deployed in a public subnet in a VPC. The application servers and database servers are deployed in private subnets in the same VPC.  
The company has deployed a third-party virtual firewall appliance from AWS Marketplace in an inspection VPC.  
The appliance is configured with an IP interface that can accept IP packets.  
A solutions architect needs to integrate the web application with the appliance to inspect all traffic to the application before the traffic reaches the web server.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create a Network Load Balancer in the public subnet of the application's VPC to route the traffic to the appliance for packet inspection.  
B. Create an Application Load Balancer in the public subnet of the application's VPC to route the traffic to the appliance for packet inspection.  
C. Deploy a transit gateway in the inspection VPConfigure route tables to route the incoming packets through the transit gateway.  
D. Deploy a Gateway Load Balancer in the inspection VPC. Create a Gateway Load Balancer endpoint to receive the incoming packets and forward the packets to the appliance.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The third-party inspection appliance accepts packets at the IP level — AWS has a purpose-built service for exactly this scenario. Gateway Load Balancer is deployed in the inspection VPC in front of the appliances, and a Gateway Load Balancer endpoint is created in the application's VPC: traffic is routed to the endpoint, passes transparently to the appliance over GENEVE, and returns the same way. Source addresses are preserved, and the load balancer takes care of scaling and health checks for the appliances — minimal operational overhead.  
Why A is not selected: A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and changes the connection's destination: it doesn't provide transparent inspection of the full flow, and the return path for packets would have to be built manually.  
Why B is not selected: An Application Load Balancer parses HTTP and terminates the connection itself, whereas the appliance expects raw IP packets.  
Why C is not selected: A transit gateway connects networks, but on its own it doesn't forward traffic to an inspection appliance or load-balance across multiple appliance instances. Routes would have to be maintained by hand.

---

20\. A company wants to improve its ability to clone large amounts of production data into a test environment in the same AWS Region. The data is stored in Amazon EC2 instances on Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. Modifications to the cloned data must not affect the production environment. The software that accesses this data requires consistently high I/O performance.  
A solutions architect needs to minimize the time that is required to clone the production data into the test environment.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Restore the snapshots onto EC2 instance store volumes in the test environment.  
B. Configure the production EBS volumes to use the EBS Multi-Attach feature. Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Attach the production EBS volumes to the EC2 instances in the test environment.  
C. Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Create and initialize new EBS volumes. Attach the new EBS volumes to EC2 instances in the test environment before restoring the volumes from the production EBS snapshots.  
D. Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Turn on the EBS fast snapshot restore feature on the EBS snapshots. Restore the snapshots into new EBS volumes. Attach the new EBS volumes to EC2 instances in the test environment.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: A volume restored from a snapshot is typically slow until blocks are lazily loaded from S3 on first access. Fast snapshot restore removes this behavior: volumes created from a snapshot with the feature enabled deliver full performance immediately. So the sequence is: take a snapshot, enable the feature, create new volumes from it, and attach them to the test instances — the copy is independent, and high performance is available from the first second.  
Why A is not selected: A snapshot cannot be restored to an instance store: an instance's local disks are not created from EBS snapshots.  
Why B is not selected: Multi-Attach connects the same volume to multiple instances, meaning the test environment would be writing to production data — a direct violation of the requirement.  
Why C is not selected: Manually initializing a volume by reading every block takes a long time, and time is exactly what needs to be minimized. The wording also reorders the steps.

---

21\. An ecommerce company wants to launch a one-deal-a-day website on AWS. Each day will feature exactly one product on sale for a period of 24 hours. The company wants to be able to handle millions of requests each hour with millisecond latency during peak hours.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use Amazon S3 to host the full website in different S3 buckets. Add Amazon CloudFront distributions. Set the S3 buckets as origins for the distributions. Store the order data in Amazon S3.  
B. Deploy the full website on Amazon EC2 instances that run in Auto Scaling groups across multiple Availability Zones. Add an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to distribute the website traffic. Add another ALB for the backend APIs. Store the data in Amazon RDS for MySQL.  
C. Migrate the full application to run in containers. Host the containers on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Use the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler to increase and decrease the number of pods to process bursts in traffic. Store the data in Amazon RDS for MySQL.  
D. Use an Amazon S3 bucket to host the website's static content. Deploy an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Set the S3 bucket as the origin. Use Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda functions for the backend APIs. Store the data in Amazon DynamoDB.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Millions of requests per hour, millisecond-level response times, and minimal operational overhead point to a serverless architecture. Static content lives in S3 and is served through CloudFront with caching at edge locations, dynamic calls are handled by API Gateway and Lambda, and order data is stored in DynamoDB with single-digit-millisecond response times. Everything scales automatically, and there are no servers to manage.  
Why A is not selected: A fully static site can't handle purchases, and storing order data in S3 won't work: transactions and fast key-based access are needed.  
Why B is not selected: A fleet of instances, two load balancers, and an RDS database represent the most operational overhead and require manually configuring scaling for the peak.  
Why C is not selected: An EKS cluster means managing nodes and autoscaling settings, and RDS remains a bottleneck at peak load.

---

22\. A solutions architect is using Amazon S3 to design the storage architecture of a new digital media application. The media files must be resilient to the loss of an Availability Zone. Some files are accessed frequently while other files are rarely accessed in an unpredictable pattern. The solutions architect must minimize the costs of storing and retrieving the media files.  
Which storage option meets these requirements?  
A. S3 Standard  
B. S3 Intelligent-Tiering  
C. S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA)  
D. S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA)  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Two requirements work together here. "Resilient to the loss of an Availability Zone" rules out anything that lives in a single zone, i.e., One Zone-IA. "Unpredictable pattern" rules out classes that charge retrieval fees: if you don't know when a file will be needed, every unguessed access to an IA class costs money. That leaves S3 Intelligent-Tiering: it automatically moves objects between tiers based on actual access, charges no retrieval fee, and stores copies across three zones. Exam rule of thumb: "unpredictable access" almost always points to Intelligent-Tiering.  
Why A is not selected: S3 Standard does survive the loss of a zone, but it doesn't solve the other half of the problem: you pay the full rate for rarely accessed files. The requirement to minimize costs isn't met.  
Why C is not selected: Standard-IA is cheaper to store, but it charges a fee for every gigabyte retrieved and bills a minimum 30-day storage period. With unpredictable access, these fees easily eat up the savings.  
Why D is not selected: One Zone-IA stores data in a single Availability Zone. The very first requirement — surviving the loss of a zone — isn't met.

---

23\. A company is storing backup files by using Amazon S3 Standard storage. The files are accessed frequently for 1 month. However, the files are not accessed after 1 month. The company must keep the files indefinitely.  
Which storage solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Configure S3 Intelligent-Tiering to automatically migrate objects.  
B. Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 month.  
C. Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 1 month.  
D. Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) after 1 month.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The access pattern here is known precisely: one month of active use, after which the files are never read again but must be kept forever. When the pattern is known, an explicit Lifecycle rule is the cheapest option, and the target class is chosen based on the required retrieval speed — which isn't specified in the question at all. So the cheapest archive tier, S3 Glacier Deep Archive, is the pick: roughly a dollar per terabyte per month against twenty-three for Standard. Compare with {{q:126}}, where part of the data must remain instantly accessible, and the answer changes.  
Why A is not selected: Intelligent-Tiering charges a per-object monthly monitoring fee and moves data based on actual access. When the schedule is already known, that's extra cost and extra uncertainty compared with a straightforward Lifecycle rule.  
Why C is not selected: Standard-IA costs roughly an order of magnitude more than Deep Archive. It's used when data is still read and instant access is needed, but here the files aren't accessed at all after the first month.  
Why D is not selected: One Zone-IA is cheaper than Standard-IA but still far more expensive than Deep Archive, and it also stores only a single copy in one Availability Zone — a poor trade-off for indefinite backups.

---

24\. A company observes an increase in Amazon EC2 costs in its most recent bill. The billing team notices unwanted vertical scaling of instance types for a couple of EC2 instances. A solutions architect needs to create a graph comparing the last 2 months of EC2 costs and perform an in-depth analysis to identify the root cause of the vertical scaling.  
How should the solutions architect generate the information with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use AWS Budgets to create a budget report and compare EC2 costs based on instance types.  
B. Use Cost Explorer's granular filtering feature to perform an in-depth analysis of EC2 costs based on instance types.  
C. Use graphs from the AWS Billing and Cost Management dashboard to compare EC2 costs based on instance types for the last 2 months.  
D. Use AWS Cost and Usage Reports to create a report and send it to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon QuickSight with Amazon S3 as a source to generate an interactive graph based on instance types.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: A two-month graph and root-cause analysis are needed with minimal effort. Cost Explorer provides both out of the box: ready-made graphs by period, filtering and grouping by service, instance type, tag, account, and Region, plus daily and hourly granularity. Nothing needs to be exported or built. Service boundaries: Cost Explorer is for interactive cost analysis, Budgets is for thresholds and alerts, CUR is raw data for custom analytics.  
Why A is not selected: AWS Budgets tracks thresholds and notifies when they're exceeded. It isn't a tool for analyzing why costs increased.  
Why C is not selected: The Billing dashboard shows summary totals without flexible filtering by instance type and without period-over-period comparison at the needed level of detail.  
Why D is not selected: The combination of CUR, S3, and QuickSight offers maximum flexibility, but it requires setting up the export, a catalog, and a dashboard. For a one-off analysis, that's unnecessary work.

---

25\. A company is designing an application. The application uses an AWS Lambda function to receive information through Amazon API Gateway and to store the information in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database.  
During the proof-of-concept stage, the company has to increase the Lambda quotas significantly to handle the high volumes of data that the company needs to load into the database. A solutions architect must recommend a new design to improve scalability and minimize the configuration effort.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Refactor the Lambda function code to Apache Tomcat code that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. Connect the database by using native Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) drivers.  
B. Change the platform from Aurora to Amazon DynamoDProvision a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster. Use the DAX client SDK to point the existing DynamoDB API calls at the DAX cluster.  
C. Set up two Lambda functions. Configure one function to receive the information. Configure the other function to load the information into the database. Integrate the Lambda functions by using Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS).  
D. Set up two Lambda functions. Configure one function to receive the information. Configure the other function to load the information into the database. Integrate the Lambda functions by using an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The problem is that during a traffic spike, the number of concurrent function invocations hits the quota, and the database can't keep up with the writes. The right fix is to decouple ingestion from writing using a queue: one function receives the data and places a message in SQS, and another function reads the queue and writes to the database at a controlled rate. The queue absorbs the spikes, nothing is lost, and there's almost nothing to configure.  
Why A is not selected: Rewriting to Tomcat on EC2 instances is both a large amount of work and a step back to managing servers.  
Why B is not selected: Switching the database to DynamoDB with a DAX cluster means reworking the data model and every query, and the phrase about "existing DynamoDB API calls" contradicts the requirement, since the database here is Aurora.  
Why C is not selected: SNS delivers messages to subscribers immediately and does not buffer them: during a spike, the second function would hit the exact same overload, and failed deliveries would be lost.

---

26\. A company needs to review its AWS Cloud deployment to ensure that its Amazon S3 buckets do not have unauthorized configuration changes.  
What should a solutions architect do to accomplish this goal?  
A. Turn on AWS Config with the appropriate rules.  
B. Turn on AWS Trusted Advisor with the appropriate checks.  
C. Turn on Amazon Inspector with the appropriate assessment template.  
D. Turn on Amazon S3 server access logging. Configure Amazon EventBridge (Amazon Cloud Watch Events).  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The task is to detect unauthorized configuration changes on the buckets. That's a job for AWS Config: it captures a resource's configuration on every change, keeps a history, and evaluates it against managed rules (s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited, s3-bucket-versioning-enabled, s3-bucket-ssl-requests-only, and others). On noncompliance, it can notify or auto-remediate. Distinguish: Config is state and compliance, CloudTrail is who called which API, GuardDuty is threats.  
Why B is not selected: Trusted Advisor gives periodic recommendations across a limited set of checks. It doesn't provide continuous configuration monitoring or a change history.  
Why C is not selected: Amazon Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities; it doesn't check bucket configuration.  
Why D is not selected: Object access logs show data access, not changes to bucket settings.

---

27\. A company is launching a new application and will display application metrics on an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard. The company's product manager needs to access this dashboard periodically. The product manager does not have an AWS account. A solutions architect must provide access to the product manager by following the principle of least privilege.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Share the dashboard from the CloudWatch console. Enter the product manager's email address, and complete the sharing steps. Provide a shareable link for the dashboard to the product manager.  
B. Create an IAM user specifically for the product manager. Attach the CloudWatchReadOnlyAccess AWS managed policy to the user. Share the new login credentials with the product manager. Share the browser URL of the correct dashboard with the product manager.  
C. Create an IAM user for the company's employees. Attach the ViewOnlyAccess AWS managed policy to the IAM user. Share the new login credentials with the product manager. Ask the product manager to navigate to the CloudWatch console and locate the dashboard by name in the Dashboards section.  
D. Deploy a bastion server in a public subnet. When the product manager requires access to the dashboard, start the server and share the RDP credentials. On the bastion server, ensure that the browser is configured to open the dashboard URL with cached AWS credentials that have appropriate permissions to view the dashboard.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The person has no AWS account, and creating one just to view a single dashboard isn't necessary: CloudWatch can share a dashboard externally. In the console you choose "Share dashboard," enter the email address, and the service creates separate credentials scoped to viewing just that dashboard and sends a link. Access is limited to a single resource and read-only — this is least privilege in its purest form.  
Why B is not selected: An IAM user with the CloudWatchReadOnlyAccess policy opens up every metric, log, and dashboard in the account, not just the one needed. It also creates long-lived credentials for an outside person.  
Why C is not selected: ViewOnlyAccess grants read access to resources across every service in the account — that's even broader and far from least privilege.  
Why D is not selected: A bastion host with cached credentials in the browser is both insecure and labor-intensive: the server has to be stood up, torn down, and access to it granted over RDP.

---

28\. A company is migrating applications to AWS. The applications are deployed in different accounts. The company manages the accounts centrally by using AWS Organizations. The company's security team needs a single sign-on (SSO) solution across all the company's accounts. The company must continue managing the users and groups in its on-premises self-managed Microsoft Active Directory.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Enable AWS Single Sign-On (AWS SSO) from the AWS SSO console. Create a one-way forest trust or a one- way domain trust to connect the company's self-managed Microsoft Active Directory with AWS SSO by using AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory.  
B. Enable AWS Single Sign-On (AWS SSO) from the AWS SSO console. Create a two-way forest trust to connect the company's self-managed Microsoft Active Directory with AWS SSO by using AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory.  
C. Use AWS Directory Service. Create a two-way trust relationship with the company's self-managed Microsoft Active Directory.  
D. Deploy an identity provider (IdP) on premises. Enable AWS Single Sign-On (AWS SSO) from the AWS SSO console.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Users and groups stay in the on-premises Active Directory, and sign-in is needed across every account in the organization. The standard setup: turn on IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO), deploy AWS Managed Microsoft AD, and establish a trust with the on-premises forest. The requirement being tested here: this integration needs a two-way forest trust — Identity Center must both find users and authenticate them, and a one-way trust won't achieve that. A trust-free alternative would be AD Connector or an external SAML provider, but neither appears among the options.  
Why A is not selected: A one-way trust isn't enough to integrate Identity Center with a self-managed Active Directory: the documentation specifically requires a two-way forest trust.  
Why C is not selected: Directory Service on its own provides a directory, but not single sign-on into the organization's accounts — assigning account access is Identity Center's job.  
Why D is not selected: Deploying an on-premises identity provider of your own is possible, but the requirement is to keep managing users in the existing Active Directory, not build a new sign-in system.

---

29\. A company provides a Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) service that uses UDP connections. The service consists of Amazon EC2 instances that run in an Auto Scaling group. The company has deployments across multiple AWS Regions.  
The company needs to route users to the Region with the lowest latency. The company also needs automated failover between Regions.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) and an associated target group. Associate the target group with the Auto Scaling group. Use the NLB as an AWS Global Accelerator endpoint in each Region.  
B. Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and an associated target group. Associate the target group with the Auto Scaling group. Use the ALB as an AWS Global Accelerator endpoint in each Region.  
C. Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) and an associated target group. Associate the target group with the Auto Scaling group. Create an Amazon Route 53 latency record that points to aliases for each NLB. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the latency record as an origin.  
D. Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and an associated target group. Associate the target group with the Auto Scaling group. Create an Amazon Route 53 weighted record that points to aliases for each ALB. Deploy an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the weighted record as an origin.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: UDP traffic rules out both CloudFront and Application Load Balancer — both work over HTTP. That leaves a Network Load Balancer in each Region, fronted by AWS Global Accelerator: it provides static anycast IP addresses, routes users to the Region with the lowest latency over the AWS backbone, and automatically shifts traffic if a regional endpoint group fails. The failover happens within seconds and doesn't depend on client-side DNS caching — an important advantage over Route 53-based routing.  
Why B is not selected: An Application Load Balancer only handles HTTP and HTTPS, but the service runs over UDP.  
Why C is not selected: CloudFront doesn't support UDP and can't use a Route 53 record as an origin for that kind of traffic. DNS-based failover also depends on TTL and resolver caching.  
Why D is not selected: Both the load balancer choice is wrong, and weighted routing doesn't select the Region with the lowest latency — and CloudFront is again inapplicable to UDP.

---

30\. A development team runs monthly resource-intensive tests on its general purpose Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with Performance Insights enabled. The testing lasts for 48 hours once a month and is the only process that uses the database. The team wants to reduce the cost of running the tests without reducing the compute and memory attributes of the DB instance.  
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Stop the DB instance when tests are completed. Restart the DB instance when required.  
B. Use an Auto Scaling policy with the DB instance to automatically scale when tests are completed.  
C. Create a snapshot when tests are completed. Terminate the DB instance and restore the snapshot when required.  
D. Modify the DB instance to a low-capacity instance when tests are completed. Modify the DB instance again when required.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The database is needed for 48 hours a month, and the instance class can't be changed. The key detail: a stopped RDS instance restarts automatically after seven days, so simply "stopping it" for a month won't work. It's cheaper to take a snapshot, delete the instance, and restore from the snapshot before the next round of tests — you only pay for snapshot storage.  
Why A is not selected: Stopping only helps for seven days: after that AWS starts the instance back up on its own, and billing resumes.  
Why B is not selected: RDS has no automatic scaling for compute, and storage only scales upward.  
Why D is not selected: Downsizing the instance class is explicitly forbidden by the requirement: the compute attributes must not be touched.

---

31\. A company that hosts its web application on AWS wants to ensure all Amazon EC2 instances. Amazon RDS DB instances. and Amazon Redshift clusters are configured with tags. The company wants to minimize the effort of configuring and operating this check.  
What should a solutions architect do to accomplish this?  
A. Use AWS Config rules to define and detect resources that are not properly tagged.  
B. Use Cost Explorer to display resources that are not properly tagged. Tag those resources manually.  
C. Write API calls to check all resources for proper tag allocation. Periodically run the code on an EC2 instance.  
D. Write API calls to check all resources for proper tag allocation. Schedule an AWS Lambda function through Amazon CloudWatch to periodically run the code.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Checking that all resources carry the required tags should be the job of a managed service, not custom code. The AWS Config required-tags rule specifies which tag keys are mandatory and for which resource types, evaluates them on every change, and keeps a compliance history. If desired, the rule can trigger automatic remediation through SSM Automation. Setup takes minutes and runs on its own after that.  
Why B is not selected: Cost Explorer shows spending and can group by tag, but it isn't an inventory tool for untagged resources, and manually tagging resources afterward doesn't scale.  
Why C is not selected: Custom code on an always-running instance means both development work and an extra machine to operate.  
Why D is not selected: A scheduled function removes the instance, but the code is still yours to maintain: pagination, new resource types, error handling. A ready-made Config rule does this without any development.

---

32\. A development team needs to host a website that will be accessed by other teams. The website contents consist of HTML, CSS, client-side JavaScript, and images.  
Which method is the MOST cost-effective for hosting the website?  
A. Containerize the website and host it in AWS Fargate.  
B. Create an Amazon S3 bucket and host the website there.  
C. Deploy a web server on an Amazon EC2 instance to host the website.  
D. Configure an Application Load Balancer with an AWS Lambda target that uses the Express.js framework.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The content is entirely static: HTML, CSS, client-side JavaScript, and images. A site like this can be hosted directly in an S3 bucket with static website hosting enabled — you pay only for storage and requests, there are no servers at all, and the service itself handles scaling.  
Why A is not selected: Containers on Fargate are billed for task run time around the clock, even though there's nothing for them to do.  
Why C is not selected: A web server on an EC2 instance means a constant hourly charge plus patching and monitoring.  
Why D is not selected: A load balancer with a Lambda function to serve static content means both an hourly charge for the load balancer and charges per invocation, where a bucket alone would suffice.

---

33\. A company runs an online marketplace web application on AWS. The application serves hundreds of thousands of users during peak hours. The company needs a scalable, near-real-time solution to share the details of millions of financial transactions with several other internal applications. Transactions also need to be processed to remove sensitive data before being stored in a document database for low-latency retrieval.  
What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?  
A. Store the transactions data into Amazon DynamoDB. Set up a rule in DynamoDB to remove sensitive data from every transaction upon write. Use DynamoDB Streams to share the transactions data with other applications.  
B. Stream the transactions data into Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to store data in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3. Use AWS Lambda integration with Kinesis Data Firehose to remove sensitive data. Other applications can consume the data stored in Amazon S3.  
C. Stream the transactions data into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use AWS Lambda integration to remove sensitive data from every transaction and then store the transactions data in Amazon DynamoDB. Other applications can consume the transactions data off the Kinesis data stream.  
D. Store the batched transactions data in Amazon S3 as files. Use AWS Lambda to process every file and remove sensitive data before updating the files in Amazon S3. The Lambda function then stores the data in Amazon DynamoDB. Other applications can consume transaction files stored in Amazon S3.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Scalable, near-real-time ingestion is required, along with removing sensitive data and distributing it to several internal applications. Kinesis Data Streams ingests the transactions and retains them, a Lambda function strips the sensitive fields and writes the result to DynamoDB for fast access, and other applications read the same stream independently, each at its own position.  
Why A is not selected: DynamoDB has no rules that transform data on write, and table streams aren't designed for dozens of independent consumers of historical data.  
Why B is not selected: Firehose delivers data with tens of seconds of buffering and doesn't let multiple applications read the stream concurrently from their own positions.  
Why D is not selected: Batch-writing files to S3 isn't near-real-time, and rewriting files introduces a risk of inconsistency.

---

34\. A company hosts its multi-tier applications on AWS. For compliance, governance, auditing, and security, the company must track configuration changes on its AWS resources and record a history of API calls made to these resources.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS CloudTrail to track configuration changes and AWS Config to record API calls.  
B. Use AWS Config to track configuration changes and AWS CloudTrail to record API calls.  
C. Use AWS Config to track configuration changes and Amazon CloudWatch to record API calls.  
D. Use AWS CloudTrail to track configuration changes and Amazon CloudWatch to record API calls.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Two different questions call for two different services. AWS Config tracks configuration changes on resources: it keeps a history of state and lets you see what changed and when. AWS CloudTrail keeps a history of API calls: who performed which action, and from where.  
Why A is not selected: The services are swapped: CloudTrail doesn't keep a configuration history, and Config doesn't log API calls.  
Why C is not selected: Config is the right choice, but CloudWatch collects metrics and logs, not a history of API calls.  
Why D is not selected: Both halves here are wrong.

---

35\. A company is preparing to launch a public-facing web application in the AWS Cloud. The architecture consists of Amazon EC2 instances within a VPC behind an Elastic Load Balancer (ELB). A third-party service is used for the DNS. The company's solutions architect must recommend a solution to detect and protect against large-scale DDoS attacks.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Enable Amazon GuardDuty on the account.  
B. Enable Amazon Inspector on the EC2 instances.  
C. Enable AWS Shield and assign Amazon Route 53 to it.  
D. Enable AWS Shield Advanced and assign the ELB to it.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: AWS provides two tiers of protection against large-scale DDoS attacks. Shield Standard is enabled for everyone at no cost and mitigates common network- and transport-layer attacks. Shield Advanced is a paid subscription that adds protection against sophisticated attacks, 24/7 support from the DDoS Response Team, cost protection for scaling during an attack, and detailed attack diagnostics; the resources to protect (here, the load balancer) must be explicitly added to the subscription. Since DNS is handled by a third-party provider, Route 53 is not part of this architecture — it is the load balancer that needs to be protected.  
Why A is not selected: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity from logs, but it does not absorb or mitigate DDoS traffic.  
Why B is not selected: Inspector scans instances for vulnerabilities. It has nothing to do with protecting against availability attacks.  
Why C is not selected: Route 53 is not in use here — DNS is served by a third-party service, so it is the ELB that needs protection. Also, Shield Standard is already enabled by default and does not require assigning any resources to it.

---

36\. A company is building an application in the AWS Cloud. The application will store data in Amazon S3 buckets in two AWS Regions. The company must use an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key to encrypt all data that is stored in the S3 buckets. The data in both S3 buckets must be encrypted and decrypted with the same KMS key. The data and the key must be stored in each of the two Regions.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create an S3 bucket in each Region. Configure the S3 buckets to use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Configure replication between the S3 buckets.  
B. Create a customer managed multi-Region KMS key. Create an S3 bucket in each Region. Configure replication between the S3 buckets. Configure the application to use the KMS key with client-side encryption.  
C. Create a customer managed KMS key and an S3 bucket in each Region. Configure the S3 buckets to use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Configure replication between the S3 buckets.  
D. Create a customer managed KMS key and an S3 bucket in each Region. Configure the S3 buckets to use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). Configure replication between the S3 buckets.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirement that rules everything else out is: "both S3 buckets must be encrypted and decrypted with the same KMS key," and the key must physically exist in both Regions. A regular KMS key is scoped to its own Region, and an object replicated to another Region is re-encrypted there with a different key. The only mechanism that provides the same key (same key ID and key material) across multiple Regions is a multi-Region KMS key. Of the options given, only B uses one. The ideal solution would combine a multi-Region key with SSE-KMS, but that option isn't offered, so we pick the one that satisfies the core requirement.  
Why A is not selected: SSE-S3 encrypts with keys that S3 itself manages. The requirement to use a customer managed KMS key is not met at all.  
Why C is not selected: A KMS key is created, but the buckets are configured for SSE-S3, so the created key is never actually used. The option contradicts itself.  
Why D is not selected: SSE-KMS is configured correctly, but there are two separate keys — one per Region. During cross-Region replication the object is decrypted with the source key and re-encrypted with the destination key, while the requirement calls for the same key throughout.

---

37\. A company recently launched a variety of new workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in its AWS account. The company needs to create a strategy to access and administer the instances remotely and securely. The company needs to implement a repeatable process that works with native AWS services and follows the AWS Well- Architected Framework.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use the EC2 serial console to directly access the terminal interface of each instance for administration.  
B. Attach the appropriate IAM role to each existing instance and new instance. Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to establish a remote SSH session.  
C. Create an administrative SSH key pair. Load the public key into each EC2 instance. Deploy a bastion host in a public subnet to provide a tunnel for administration of each instance.  
D. Establish an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection. Instruct administrators to use their local on-premises machines to connect directly to the instances by using SSH keys across the VPN tunnel.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The company needs a repeatable, secure way to administer instances using native AWS services. AWS Systems Manager Session Manager delivers exactly that: the agent on the instance makes an outbound connection to the service, so no open ports, bastion host, or SSH keys are needed; access is granted through IAM policies, and the entire session is logged and can be streamed to CloudWatch Logs or S3. The instance just needs a role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy attached — that's the "appropriate IAM role" the answer refers to.  
Why A is not selected: The EC2 serial console is an emergency tool for troubleshooting boot issues, not a day-to-day way to administer a fleet.  
Why C is not selected: A bastion host with a shared SSH key means an open port to the internet, key management overhead, and yet another server to operate. The Well-Architected Framework explicitly recommends moving away from this pattern.  
Why D is not selected: A VPN to every administrator plus direct SSH connections means building infrastructure and distributing keys instead of managing access through IAM policies.

---

38\. A company is hosting a static website on Amazon S3 and is using Amazon Route 53 for DNS. The website is experiencing increased demand from around the world. The company must decrease latency for users who access the website.  
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Replicate the S3 bucket that contains the website to all AWS Regions. Add Route 53 geolocation routing entries.  
B. Provision accelerators in AWS Global Accelerator. Associate the supplied IP addresses with the S3 bucket. Edit the Route 53 entries to point to the IP addresses of the accelerators.  
C. Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket. Edit the Route 53 entries to point to the CloudFront distribution.  
D. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket. Edit the Route 53 entries to point to the new endpoint.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The site is static and hosted in S3, so it's enough to put CloudFront in front of the bucket: content is cached at edge locations worldwide, latency drops, and data transfer out of CloudFront is cheaper than serving directly from S3. A Route 53 alias record points the domain at the distribution. This is the standard, and cheapest, pattern for delivering static content globally.  
Why A is not selected: Copies of the bucket in every Region mean paying for storage multiple times over plus constant synchronization, and geolocation routing doesn't guarantee proximity.  
Why B is not selected: Global Accelerator doesn't support S3 as an endpoint and is designed to accelerate TCP and UDP applications, not to serve static content.  
Why D is not selected: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploading objects into the bucket through edge locations — it doesn't serve the site to end users, and it adds extra charges.

---

39\. A company maintains a searchable repository of items on its website. The data is stored in an Amazon RDS for MySQL database table that contains more than 10 million rows. The database has 2 TB of General Purpose SSD storage. There are millions of updates against this data every day through the company's website.  
The company has noticed that some insert operations are taking 10 seconds or longer. The company has determined that the database storage performance is the problem.  
Which solution addresses this performance issue?  
A. Change the storage type to Provisioned IOPS SSD.  
B. Change the DB instance to a memory optimized instance class.
