C. Change the DB instance to a burstable performance instance class.  
D. Enable Multi-AZ RDS read replicas with MySQL native asynchronous replication.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The bottleneck is stated directly: storage performance under heavy write load. At this data volume, a General Purpose SSD volume runs into its I/O limit, whereas Provisioned IOPS SSD storage lets you specify a guaranteed number of IOPS independent of volume size and delivers consistently low latency.  
Why B is not selected: More memory helps with read caching, but inserts are bottlenecked on disk, not memory.  
Why C is not selected: A burstable instance class delivers even less sustained performance — once the burst credits run out, things only get worse.  
Why D is not selected: Read replicas offload read queries, but the problem is with insert operations on the primary instance.

---

40\. A company has thousands of edge devices that collectively generate 1 TB of status alerts each day. Each alert is approximately 2 KB in size. A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to ingest and store the alerts for future analysis.  
The company wants a highly available solution. However, the company needs to minimize costs and does not want to manage additional infrastructure. Additionally, the company wants to keep 14 days of data available for immediate analysis and archive any data older than 14 days.  
What is the MOST operationally efficient solution that meets these requirements?  
A. Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream to ingest the alerts. Configure the Kinesis Data Firehose stream to deliver the alerts to an Amazon S3 bucket. Set up an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition data to Amazon S3 Glacier after 14 days.  
B. Launch Amazon EC2 instances across two Availability Zones and place them behind an Elastic Load Balancer to ingest the alerts. Create a script on the EC2 instances that will store the alerts in an Amazon S3 bucket. Set up an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition data to Amazon S3 Glacier after 14 days.  
C. Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream to ingest the alerts. Configure the Kinesis Data Firehose stream to deliver the alerts to an Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) cluster. Set up the Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) cluster to take manual snapshots every day and delete data from the cluster that is older than 14 days.  
D. Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue to ingest the alerts, and set the message retention period to 14 days. Configure consumers to poll the SQS queue, check the age of the message, and analyze the message data as needed. If the message is 14 days old, the consumer should copy the message to an Amazon S3 bucket and delete the message from the SQS queue.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: One terabyte of small alerts per day, no infrastructure of its own to manage, and minimal cost. Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose ingests the stream, scales automatically, and delivers the data to S3 without a single server to run, while an S3 Lifecycle rule transitions objects to Glacier after 14 days. Data from the last two weeks stays available for immediate analysis directly in S3.  
Why B is not selected: A fleet of instances behind a load balancer running custom scripts is exactly the extra infrastructure the requirements rule out.  
Why C is not selected: An OpenSearch cluster has to be administered and paid for continuously, and taking manual snapshots every day is manual work.  
Why D is not selected: An SQS queue isn't a storage layer for analysis, and having consumers check message age and act on it is both awkward and unreliable.

---

41\. A company's application integrates with multiple software-as-a-service (SaaS) sources for data collection. The company runs Amazon EC2 instances to receive the data and to upload the data to an Amazon S3 bucket for analysis. The same EC2 instance that receives and uploads the data also sends a notification to the user when an upload is complete. The company has noticed slow application performance and wants to improve the performance as much as possible.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create an Auto Scaling group so that EC2 instances can scale out. Configure an S3 event notification to send events to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic when the upload to the S3 bucket is complete.  
B. Create an Amazon AppFlow flow to transfer data between each SaaS source and the S3 bucket. Configure an S3 event notification to send events to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic when the upload to the S3 bucket is complete.  
C. Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rule for each SaaS source to send output data. Configure the S3 bucket as the rule's target. Create a second EventBridge (Cloud Watch Events) rule to send events when the upload to the S3 bucket is complete. Configure an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic as the second rule's target.  
D. Create a Docker container to use instead of an EC2 instance. Host the containerized application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Configure Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights to send events to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic when the upload to the S3 bucket is complete.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The instances are doing three jobs at once: pulling data from external SaaS sources, uploading it to S3, and sending notifications. Amazon AppFlow is a managed integration service for SaaS sources: it pulls the data and delivers it to the bucket without a single server involved. The completion notification comes from a native S3 event sent to an SNS topic. The instances disappear entirely.  
Why A is not selected: An Auto Scaling group speeds things up, but the instances and their upkeep remain — the operational burden isn't reduced.  
Why C is not selected: EventBridge can't write data directly into an S3 bucket as a rule target, and it doesn't handle ingesting data from arbitrary SaaS sources.  
Why D is not selected: Containers are still a compute environment you have to manage yourself, and Container Insights collects metrics — it doesn't notify on S3 upload completion.

---

42\. A company runs a highly available image-processing application on Amazon EC2 instances in a single VPC. The EC2 instances run inside several subnets across multiple Availability Zones. The EC2 instances do not communicate with each other. However, the EC2 instances download images from Amazon S3 and upload images to Amazon S3 through a single NAT gateway. The company is concerned about data transfer charges.  
What is the MOST cost-effective way for the company to avoid Regional data transfer charges?  
A. Launch the NAT gateway in each Availability Zone.  
B. Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance.  
C. Deploy a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3.  
D. Provision an EC2 Dedicated Host to run the EC2 instances.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: As long as traffic to S3 flows through the NAT gateway, the company pays twice: for every gigabyte the gateway processes and for the hours it runs. A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 eliminates both charges: it adds a route to the S3 prefix directly in the route tables, traffic travels over the AWS internal network, and there's no charge for the endpoint itself or for the data passing through it. Traffic to S3 in the same Region via the endpoint isn't billed as data transfer at all. The same technique appears in {{q:91,497,612}}.  
Why A is not selected: A NAT gateway in every AZ eliminates cross-AZ transfer but keeps the main cost drivers — hourly charges per gateway and per-gigabyte processing charges. More gateways means more cost, not less.  
Why B is not selected: A NAT instance replaces the managed gateway with a regular machine: you pay for the instance and its traffic, and you're now responsible for its fault tolerance and throughput yourself.  
Why D is not selected: A Dedicated Host is a physical server reserved for your instances — a licensing and isolation concern. It has nothing to do with data transfer cost.

---

43\. A company has an on-premises application that generates a large amount of time-sensitive data that is backed up to Amazon S3. The application has grown and there are user complaints about internet bandwidth limitations. A solutions architect needs to design a long-term solution that allows for both timely backups to Amazon S3 and with minimal impact on internet connectivity for internal users.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Establish AWS VPN connections and proxy all traffic through a VPC gateway endpoint.  
B. Establish a new AWS Direct Connect connection and direct backup traffic through this new connection.  
C. Order daily AWS Snowball devices. Load the data onto the Snowball devices and return the devices to AWS each day.  
D. Submit a support ticket through the AWS Management Console. Request the removal of S3 service limits from the account.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Complaints about internal users' internet bandwidth mean backup traffic and office traffic are competing for the same connection. The long-term fix is a dedicated AWS Direct Connect connection carrying only backup traffic: bandwidth becomes predictable, latency stays stable, and the internet connection is freed up for people. It also lowers the cost of outbound data transfer.  
Why A is not selected: A VPN still runs over the same internet connection: bandwidth doesn't increase, and encryption adds overhead. A gateway endpoint is also reachable only from inside the VPC.  
Why C is not selected: Shipping Snowball devices daily doesn't fit with data being described as time-sensitive — delivery takes days.  
Why D is not selected: There's no S3 limit at play here; the bottleneck is the company's own connection. A support ticket won't change that.

---

44\. A company has an Amazon S3 bucket that contains critical data. The company must protect the data from accidental deletion.  
Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Enable versioning on the S3 bucket.  
B. Enable MFA Delete on the S3 bucket.  
C. Create a bucket policy on the S3 bucket.  
D. Enable default encryption on the S3 bucket.  
E. Create a lifecycle policy for the objects in the S3 bucket.  
Answer: AB  
Explanation: Protection against accidental deletion in S3 is built from two layers. Versioning (A) makes deletion reversible: instead of erasing the object, a delete marker is created and the prior version stays in place. MFA Delete (B) adds a second factor to irreversible operations — permanently deleting an object version and disabling versioning — so that not even the root owner can do this by mistake, and a compromised credential can't do it either. Versioning has to come first: MFA Delete can only be enabled on a versioned bucket.  
Why C is not selected: A bucket policy controls who is allowed to call which API actions. It doesn't protect against a mistake by someone who legitimately has delete permission, and it can't restore something already deleted.  
Why D is not selected: Default encryption protects the content from unauthorized eyes. It has nothing to do with the likelihood of an object being deleted.  
Why E is not selected: A lifecycle rule deletes objects on a schedule automatically — the exact opposite of what's needed here.

---

45\. A company has a data ingestion workflow that consists of the following:  
• An Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic for notifications about new data deliveries  
• An AWS Lambda function to process the data and record metadata The company observes that the ingestion workflow fails occasionally because of network connectivity issues.  
When such a failure occurs, the Lambda function does not ingest the corresponding data unless the company manually reruns the job.  
Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to ensure that the Lambda function ingests all data in the future? (Choose two.)  
A. Deploy the Lambda function in multiple Availability Zones.  
B. Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue, and subscribe it to the SNS topic.  
C. Increase the CPU and memory that are allocated to the Lambda function.  
D. Increase provisioned throughput for the Lambda function.  
E. Modify the Lambda function to read from an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue.  
Answer: BE  
Explanation: An SNS topic delivers a message immediately and, after a few failed delivery attempts, drops it. To make sure nothing is lost, an SQS queue is placed between SNS and the function: it subscribes to the topic (B), and the function reads from the queue instead (E). A message stays in the queue until it's successfully processed, and repeated failures route it to a dead-letter queue.  
Why A is not selected: Lambda functions already run across multiple Availability Zones by default — no configuration is needed, and this has nothing to do with lost messages.  
Why C is not selected: More CPU and memory speed up execution, but a message is still lost when a network failure occurs.  
Why D is not selected: Provisioned concurrency reserves pre-warmed execution environments and doesn't add anything to delivery reliability.

---

46\. A company has an application that provides marketing services to stores. The services are based on previous purchases by store customers. The stores upload transaction data to the company through SFTP, and the data is processed and analyzed to generate new marketing offers. Some of the files can exceed 200 GB in size.  
Recently, the company discovered that some of the stores have uploaded files that contain personally identifiable information (PII) that should not have been included. The company wants administrators to be alerted if PII is shared again. The company also wants to automate remediation.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?  
A. Use an Amazon S3 bucket as a secure transfer point. Use Amazon Inspector to scan the objects in the bucket. If objects contain PII, trigger an S3 Lifecycle policy to remove the objects that contain PII.  
B. Use an Amazon S3 bucket as a secure transfer point. Use Amazon Macie to scan the objects in the bucket. If objects contain PII, use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to trigger a notification to the administrators to remove the objects that contain PII.  
C. Implement custom scanning algorithms in an AWS Lambda function. Trigger the function when objects are loaded into the bucket. If objects contain PII, use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to trigger a notification to the administrators to remove the objects that contain PII.  
D. Implement custom scanning algorithms in an AWS Lambda function. Trigger the function when objects are loaded into the bucket. If objects contain PII, use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to trigger a notification to the administrators and trigger an S3 Lifecycle policy to remove the meats that contain PII.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirement is to find personally identifiable information in uploaded files without writing custom detection code. Amazon Macie is purpose-built to find PII in S3 objects: it classifies the data, reports findings with the type and location of the PII, and publishes them to EventBridge, from which it's easy to trigger an SNS notification or automated remediation. There's no need to build custom search logic — hence the LEAST development effort.  
Why A is not selected: Inspector looks for vulnerabilities in workloads and doesn't analyze object content. A Lifecycle rule also can't delete objects based on a scan result.  
Why C is not selected: Writing a custom algorithm to detect PII in a function is the most labor-intensive part of this task — exactly what Macie already handles as a managed service.  
Why D is not selected: The same custom detection algorithm, plus trying to delete objects with a Lifecycle rule, which acts on age and prefix, not on content.

---

47\. A company needs guaranteed Amazon EC2 capacity in three specific Availability Zones in a specific AWS Region for an upcoming event that will last 1 week.  
What should the company do to guarantee the EC2 capacity?  
A. Purchase Reserved Instances that specify the Region needed.  
B. Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation that specifies the Region needed.  
C. Purchase Reserved Instances that specify the Region and three Availability Zones needed.  
D. Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation that specifies the Region and three Availability Zones needed.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Guaranteed EC2 capacity is what an On-Demand Capacity Reservation provides, and a reservation is always made for a specific Availability Zone. So the company creates a reservation in each of the three required zones: the capacity is held for the entire duration of the event regardless of overall Regional demand.  
Why A is not selected: Reserved Instances are a financial commitment made in exchange for a discount; they don't guarantee capacity unless tied to a specific zone.  
Why B is not selected: A Capacity Reservation can't be created "for a Region" — it always applies to a specific Availability Zone.  
Why C is not selected: Even zonal Reserved Instances are meant for a long-term commitment of one or three years, which is disproportionate to a one-week event.

---

48\. A company's website uses an Amazon EC2 instance store for its catalog of items. The company wants to make sure that the catalog is highly available and that the catalog is stored in a durable location.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Move the catalog to Amazon ElastiCache for Redis.  
B. Deploy a larger EC2 instance with a larger instance store.  
C. Move the catalog from the instance store to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.  
D. Move the catalog to an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: An instance store is ephemeral storage: the data disappears when the instance stops, so there is no durability at all. The catalog needs to move to storage that survives an instance failure and is accessible from multiple machines at once — that's Amazon EFS: the file system replicates across Availability Zones and can be mounted on all the web servers.  
Why A is not selected: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache. It is not durable storage: restarting the cluster without persistence enabled loses the data.  
Why B is not selected: A larger instance just means more ephemeral space — the problem isn't capacity, it's that the data disappears along with the instance.  
Why C is not selected: Glacier Deep Archive is an archive with a retrieval time measured in hours. A site catalog that's read on every request can't live there.

---

49\. A company stores call transcript files on a monthly basis. Users access the files randomly within 1 year of the call, but users access the files infrequently after 1 year. The company wants to optimize its solution by giving users the ability to query and retrieve files that are less than 1-year-old as quickly as possible. A delay in retrieving older files is acceptable.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Store individual files with tags in Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval. Query the tags to retrieve the files from S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.  
B. Store individual files in Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Use S3 Lifecycle policies to move the files to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 1 year. Query and retrieve the files that are in Amazon S3 by using Amazon Athena. Query and retrieve the files that are in S3 Glacier by using S3 Glacier Select.  
C. Store individual files with tags in Amazon S3 Standard storage. Store search metadata for each archive in Amazon S3 Standard storage. Use S3 Lifecycle policies to move the files to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 1 year. Query and retrieve the files by searching for metadata from Amazon S3.  
D. Store individual files in Amazon S3 Standard storage. Use S3 Lifecycle policies to move the files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year. Store search metadata in Amazon RDS. Query the files from Amazon RDS. Retrieve the files from S3 Glacier Deep Archive.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: For the first year files are read irregularly, after that almost never, and both cost and fast access to recent files matter. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between tiers based on actual access patterns with no retrieval fee, and after a year a lifecycle rule moves them to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, where the retrieval delay is acceptable. Querying recent data is handled by Athena, and archived data by S3 Glacier Select.  
Why A is not selected: Glacier Instant Retrieval costs more to store than archival tiers, and searching by tags isn't a mechanism for querying content.  
Why C is not selected: S3 Standard storage costs more than Intelligent-Tiering throughout the first year given irregular access, and metadata stored in the same S3 bucket doesn't provide convenient search.  
Why D is not selected: Deep Archive takes hours to retrieve objects, and a separate RDS database just for metadata adds unnecessary cost and operational overhead.

---

50\. A company has a production workload that runs on 1,000 Amazon EC2 Linux instances. The workload is powered by third-party software. The company needs to patch the third-party software on all EC2 instances as quickly as possible to remediate a critical security vulnerability.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Create an AWS Lambda function to apply the patch to all EC2 instances.  
B. Configure AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to apply the patch to all EC2 instances.  
C. Schedule an AWS Systems Manager maintenance window to apply the patch to all EC2 instances.  
D. Use AWS Systems Manager Run Command to run a custom command that applies the patch to all EC2 instances.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The software is third-party, so standard baseline patch sets won't cover it — a custom command needs to be run instead. AWS Systems Manager Run Command executes it immediately across all selected instances with no SSH connection and no third-party agents required, which is exactly what's needed to close a vulnerability quickly.  
Why A is not selected: A Lambda function doesn't execute anything on the instances itself — it would still need a mechanism like Run Command.  
Why B is not selected: Patch Manager works with operating system updates and supported packages, not arbitrary third-party software.  
Why C is not selected: A maintenance window defers execution to a scheduled time, but the vulnerability needs to be closed as quickly as possible.

---

51\. A company is developing an application that provides order shipping statistics for retrieval by a REST API. The company wants to extract the shipping statistics, organize the data into an easy-to-read HTML format, and send the report to several email addresses at the same time every morning.  
Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Configure the application to send the data to Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose.  
B. Use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to format the data and to send the report by email.  
C. Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) scheduled event that invokes an AWS Glue job to query the application's API for the data.  
D. Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) scheduled event that invokes an AWS Lambda function to query the application's API for the data.  
E. Store the application data in Amazon S3. Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic as an S3 event destination to send the report by email.  
Answer: BD  
Explanation: The task comes down to two steps. A scheduled EventBridge rule invokes a Lambda function once a day, and the function calls the application's API to retrieve the data (D). The function then formats the data as an HTML report and sends it to multiple recipients through Amazon SES (B).  
Why A is not selected: Firehose delivers streaming data into storage destinations and has nothing to do with generating a daily report.  
Why C is not selected: AWS Glue is an ETL service for processing datasets, not a tool for calling an application's REST API.  
Why E is not selected: SNS sends notifications as plain text, not HTML-formatted email, and an S3 event isn't tied to a daily schedule.

---

52\. A company wants to migrate its on-premises application to AWS. The application produces output files that vary in size from tens of gigabytes to hundreds of terabytes. The application data must be stored in a standard file system structure. The company wants a solution that scales automatically. is highly available, and requires minimum operational overhead.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Migrate the application to run as containers on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Use Amazon S3 for storage.  
B. Migrate the application to run as containers on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) for storage.  
C. Migrate the application to Amazon EC2 instances in a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group. Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) for storage.  
D. Migrate the application to Amazon EC2 instances in a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group. Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) for storage.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The defining requirement is a "standard file system structure" plus automatic scaling and high availability with minimal operations. Amazon EFS grows and shrinks automatically, stores data across multiple Availability Zones, and mounts over NFS to every instance in the Auto Scaling group. Volumes ranging from tens of gigabytes to hundreds of terabytes are not a problem for it.  
Why A is not selected: S3 is object storage: it lacks the familiar directory hierarchy and file operations, so the application would have to be rewritten.  
Why B is not selected: An EBS volume attaches to a single Availability Zone and, typically, to a single instance: there is no shared access and no automatic growth to hundreds of terabytes.  
Why D is not selected: The same problem as the previous option: EBS volumes are not shared between instances in the group and do not grow automatically.

---

53\. A company needs to store its accounting records in Amazon S3. The records must be immediately accessible for 1 year and then must be archived for an additional 9 years. No one at the company, including administrative users and root users, can be able to delete the records during the entire 10-year period. The records must be stored with maximum resiliency.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Store the records in S3 Glacier for the entire 10-year period. Use an access control policy to deny deletion of the records for a period of 10 years.  
B. Store the records by using S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Use an IAM policy to deny deletion of the records. After 10 years, change the IAM policy to allow deletion.  
C. Use an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the records from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year. Use S3 Object Lock in compliance mode for a period of 10 years.  
D. Use an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the records from S3 Standard to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) after 1 year. Use S3 Object Lock in governance mode for a period of 10 years.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Break this down by three requirements. First, one year of immediate access followed by nine years of archival: that calls for a Lifecycle rule moving objects from Standard for the first year to Glacier Deep Archive after that. Second, no one can delete the records, including administrators and root: only S3 Object Lock in compliance mode guarantees this, because governance mode can normally be bypassed by anyone holding the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission. Third, maximum resiliency: that means storage classes that keep copies across three Availability Zones, which rules out One Zone-IA. Meeting all three conditions points to option C.  
Why A is not selected: Storing everything in Glacier for the full period violates the requirement for immediate access in the first year, and an access policy is not real protection: whoever wrote it can also rewrite it.  
Why B is not selected: An administrator or root user can change an IAM policy at any time, so "no one can delete" is not actually guaranteed. Intelligent-Tiering by itself does not prohibit deletion either.  
Why D is not selected: Governance mode can be bypassed by a user with the bypass permission, and One Zone-IA stores a single copy in a single Availability Zone — both requirements are violated.

---

54\. A company runs multiple Windows workloads on AWS. The company's employees use Windows file shares that are hosted on two Amazon EC2 instances. The file shares synchronize data between themselves and maintain duplicate copies. The company wants a highly available and durable storage solution that preserves how users currently access the files.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Migrate all the data to Amazon S3. Set up IAM authentication for users to access files.  
B. Set up an Amazon S3 File Gateway. Mount the S3 File Gateway on the existing EC2 instances.  
C. Extend the file share environment to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with a Multi-AZ configuration. Migrate all the data to FSx for Windows File Server.  
D. Extend the file share environment to Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with a Multi-AZ configuration. Migrate all the data to Amazon EFS.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The key phrase is "preserves how users currently access the files": users work with Windows file shares over SMB, with NTFS permissions and typically Active Directory. Only Amazon FSx for Windows File Server preserves this access method, and a Multi-AZ configuration adds a synchronous replica in a second Availability Zone with automatic failover. The custom-built synchronization between the two instances goes away along with the instances themselves once they're retired.  
Why A is not selected: S3 is object storage accessed through an API: users would have to change how they work with files, and the familiar file shares would disappear.  
Why B is not selected: S3 File Gateway presents an SMB interface, but behind it are objects, not a Windows file system: lock semantics and NTFS permissions are lost. The instances and their maintenance also remain in place.  
Why D is not selected: EFS is a file system that uses the NFS protocol for Linux. Windows clients do not natively work with it.

---

55\. A solutions architect is developing a VPC architecture that includes multiple subnets. The architecture will host applications that use Amazon EC2 instances and Amazon RDS DB instances. The architecture consists of six subnets in two Availability Zones. Each Availability Zone includes a public subnet, a private subnet, and a dedicated subnet for databases. Only EC2 instances that run in the private subnets can have access to the RDS databases.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create a new route table that excludes the route to the public subnets' CIDR blocks. Associate the route table with the database subnets.  
B. Create a security group that denies inbound traffic from the security group that is assigned to instances in the public subnets. Attach the security group to the DB instances.  
C. Create a security group that allows inbound traffic from the security group that is assigned to instances in the private subnets. Attach the security group to the DB instances.  
D. Create a new peering connection between the public subnets and the private subnets. Create a different peering connection between the private subnets and the database subnets.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The principle of least privilege is implemented here through security groups: the inbound rule on the database allows only the security group assigned to instances in the private subnets. The rule references a security group rather than addresses, so it keeps working regardless of how the fleet's membership changes, and nothing but those instances can connect to the database.  
Why A is not selected: Removing the route to the public subnets' CIDR blocks accomplishes nothing: routing between subnets within a VPC always works through the local route, which cannot be deleted.  
Why B is not selected: Security groups do not support deny rules — they can only allow traffic. A rule like this cannot be created.  
Why D is not selected: Peering connections are created between VPCs, not between subnets within the same VPC: connectivity within the VPC already exists.

---

56\. A company has registered its domain name with Amazon Route 53. The company uses Amazon API Gateway in the ca-central-1 Region as a public interface for its backend microservice APIs. Third-party services consume the APIs securely. The company wants to design its API Gateway URL with the company's domain name and corresponding certificate so that the third-party services can use HTTPS.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create stage variables in API Gateway with Name="Endpoint-URL" and Value="Company Domain Name" to overwrite the default URL. Import the public certificate associated with the company's domain name into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM).  
B. Create Route 53 DNS records with the company's domain name. Point the alias record to the Regional API Gateway stage endpoint. Import the public certificate associated with the company's domain name into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the us-east-1 Region.  
C. Create a Regional API Gateway endpoint. Associate the API Gateway endpoint with the company's domain name. Import the public certificate associated with the company's domain name into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the same Region. Attach the certificate to the API Gateway endpoint. Configure Route 53 to route traffic to the API Gateway endpoint.  
D. Create a Regional API Gateway endpoint. Associate the API Gateway endpoint with the company's domain name. Import the public certificate associated with the company's domain name into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the us-east-1 Region. Attach the certificate to the API Gateway APIs. Create Route 53 DNS records with the company's domain name. Point an A record to the company's domain name.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: For the API to respond on the company's own domain over HTTPS, three things are needed: a custom domain name in API Gateway, a certificate for it, and a DNS record. The key detail is the certificate's Region: for a Regional endpoint, the ACM certificate must be issued in the same Region as the API (here, ca-central-1) — only for an edge-optimized endpoint does it need to be issued in us-east-1. Once the certificate is attached, a Route 53 alias record points the domain to the Regional API Gateway endpoint.  
Why A is not selected: Stage variables pass values into integrations and do not change the URL at which the API is reachable. A custom domain is configured as its own custom domain name resource.  
Why B is not selected: For a Regional endpoint, the certificate must be issued in the same Region, not in us-east-1, and without a configured custom domain there's nothing for an alias record to point to.  
Why D is not selected: The same mistake with the certificate's Region, plus the A record should point to the API Gateway endpoint, not "to the company's domain name."

---

57\. A company is running a popular social media website. The website gives users the ability to upload images to share with other users. The company wants to make sure that the images do not contain inappropriate content. The company needs a solution that minimizes development effort.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Use Amazon Comprehend to detect inappropriate content. Use human review for low-confidence predictions.  
B. Use Amazon Rekognition to detect inappropriate content. Use human review for low-confidence predictions.  
C. Use Amazon SageMaker to detect inappropriate content. Use ground truth to label low-confidence predictions.  
D. Use AWS Fargate to deploy a custom machine learning model to detect inappropriate content. Use ground truth to label low-confidence predictions.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The task is to identify inappropriate content in images with minimal development effort. Amazon Rekognition has a built-in content moderation feature, so there's nothing to train, and Amazon Augmented AI plugs in human review for low-confidence predictions.  
Why A is not selected: Comprehend analyzes text, not images.  
Why C is not selected: SageMaker means developing and training a custom model — the direct opposite of the requirement for minimal effort.  
Why D is not selected: A custom model on Fargate means even more development plus managing the underlying infrastructure.

---

58\. A company wants to run its critical applications in containers to meet requirements for scalability and availability.  
The company prefers to focus on maintenance of the critical applications. The company does not want to be responsible for provisioning and managing the underlying infrastructure that runs the containerized workload.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Use Amazon EC2 instances, and install Docker on the instances.  
B. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on Amazon EC2 worker nodes.  
C. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate.  
D. Use Amazon EC2 instances from an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS)-optimized Amazon Machine Image (AMI).  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The company wants to focus on its applications, not the infrastructure underneath the containers. ECS with the Fargate launch type removes the nodes entirely: you describe the task and the resources it needs, and AWS handles the compute, patching, and scaling.  
Why A is not selected: Instances with Docker installed manually — maximum maintenance.  
Why B is not selected: EC2 worker nodes in an ECS cluster still need to be patched, scaled, and monitored for health.  
Why D is not selected: An ECS-optimized AMI simplifies setup, but the instances themselves remain the company's responsibility to maintain.

---

59\. A company hosts more than 300 global websites and applications. The company requires a platform to analyze more than 30 TB of clickstream data each day.  
What should a solutions architect do to transmit and process the clickstream data?  
A. Design an AWS Data Pipeline to archive the data to an Amazon S3 bucket and run an Amazon EMR cluster with the data to generate analytics.  
B. Create an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances to process the data and send it to an Amazon S3 data lake for Amazon Redshift to use for analysis.  
C. Cache the data to Amazon CloudFront. Store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. When an object is added to the S3 bucket. run an AWS Lambda function to process the data for analysis.  
D. Collect the data from Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to transmit the data to an Amazon S3 data lake. Load the data in Amazon Redshift for analysis.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Thirty terabytes of clickstream data a day calls for streaming ingestion followed by analytics. Kinesis Data Streams ingests the stream, Kinesis Data Firehose delivers it to a data lake on S3 with no administration required, and Redshift loads the data for analytical queries. It's a standard pattern that scales with volume.  
Why A is not selected: AWS Data Pipeline is a legacy batch orchestrator, and an EMR cluster has to be provisioned and paid for — both more complex and more expensive.  
Why B is not selected: A custom fleet of instances to ingest the stream requires manual scaling, monitoring, and failure handling.  
Why C is not selected: CloudFront delivers content to users and is not a mechanism for ingesting clickstream data, and processing each object with a Lambda function is no substitute for a streaming pipeline.

---

60\. A company has a website hosted on AWS. The website is behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that is configured to handle HTTP and HTTPS separately. The company wants to forward all requests to the website so that the requests will use HTTPS.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?  
A. Update the ALB's network ACL to accept only HTTPS traffic.  
B. Create a rule that replaces the HTTP in the URL with HTTPS.  
C. Create a listener rule on the ALB to redirect HTTP traffic to HTTPS.  
D. Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer configured to use Server Name Indication (SNI).  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The Application Load Balancer can perform the redirect itself: on the listener at port 80 you create a rule with a redirect action to HTTPS, typically using a 301 status code. No application changes are needed, and all traffic ends up arriving over the secured protocol.  
Why A is not selected: A network ACL would simply drop HTTP traffic: users would get an error instead of a redirect.  
Why B is not selected: A rule that "replaces HTTP with HTTPS in the URL" describes the same redirect but without saying where it's configured; the standard mechanism for this is called a listener rule.  
Why D is not selected: A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and does not perform HTTP redirects.

---

61\. A company is developing a two-tier web application on AWS. The company's developers have deployed the application on an Amazon EC2 instance that connects directly to a backend Amazon RDS database. The company must not hardcode database credentials in the application. The company must also implement a solution to automatically rotate the database credentials on a regular basis.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Store the database credentials in the instance metadata. Use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rules to run a scheduled AWS Lambda function that updates the RDS credentials and instance metadata at the same time.  
B. Store the database credentials in a configuration file in an encrypted Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rules to run a scheduled AWS Lambda function that updates the RDS credentials and the credentials in the configuration file at the same time. Use S3 Versioning to ensure the ability to fall back to previous values.  
C. Store the database credentials as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager. Turn on automatic rotation for the secret. Attach the required permission to the EC2 role to grant access to the secret.  
D. Store the database credentials as encrypted parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Turn on automatic rotation for the encrypted parameters. Attach the required permission to the EC2 role to grant access to the encrypted parameters.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The requirements read almost like a literal description of Secrets Manager: don't hardcode the password in the code, and rotate it automatically on a schedule. The secret is stored encrypted, the instance retrieves it through its role (no keys embedded in the application), and rotation for RDS is handled by a built-in AWS function that updates the password in both the database and the secret. Note the architectural detail: access is granted to the EC2 role, not to a user, so the credentials retrieved are temporary.  
Why A is not selected: Instance metadata is accessible to any process on the machine and isn't meant for secrets, and you'd have to write the synchronous password update in RDS and in metadata yourself.  
Why B is not selected: A configuration file in a bucket plus a custom rotation function means code, a schedule, and error handling instead of a single setting. Versioning only lets you roll back to previous values — it doesn't eliminate the development work.  
Why D is not selected: Parameter Store holds encrypted parameters, but it has no "turn on automatic rotation" switch: rotation has to be written yourself.

---

62\. A company is deploying a new public web application to AWS. The application will run behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application needs to be encrypted at the edge with an SSL/TLS certificate that is issued by an external certificate authority (CA). The certificate must be rotated each year before the certificate expires.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to issue an SSL/TLS certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.  
B. Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to issue an SSL/TLS certificate. Import the key material from the certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALUse the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.  
C. Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) Private Certificate Authority to issue an SSL/TLS certificate from the root CA. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.  
D. Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to import an SSL/TLS certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) to send a notification when the certificate is nearing expiration. Rotate the certificate manually.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The certificate is issued by an external certificate authority, so ACM can only import it. ACM does not automatically renew imported certificates — that's the owner's responsibility. So the certificate is imported and attached to the load balancer, and an EventBridge rule triggered by the approaching-expiration event sends a notification so the certificate can be replaced manually.  
Why A is not selected: Managed renewal only works for certificates issued by ACM itself, and the requirement calls for a certificate from an external CA.  
Why B is not selected: You can't import "key material" into a certificate already issued by ACM: a certificate is either issued by ACM or imported in its entirety.  
Why C is not selected: A private certificate authority issues certificates that browsers don't trust: a public-facing web application would not work.

---

63\. A company runs its infrastructure on AWS and has a registered base of 700,000 users for its document management application. The company intends to create a product that converts large .pdf files to .jpg image files.  
The .pdf files average 5 MB in size. The company needs to store the original files and the converted files. A solutions architect must design a scalable solution to accommodate demand that will grow rapidly over time.  
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Save the .pdf files to Amazon S3. Configure an S3 PUT event to invoke an AWS Lambda function to convert the files to .jpg format and store them back in Amazon S3.  
B. Save the .pdf files to Amazon DynamoDUse the DynamoDB Streams feature to invoke an AWS Lambda function to convert the files to .jpg format and store them back in DynamoDB.  
C. Upload the .pdf files to an AWS Elastic Beanstalk application that includes Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage, and an Auto Scaling group. Use a program in the EC2 instances to convert the files to .jpg format. Save the .pdf files and the .jpg files in the EBS store.  
D. Upload the .pdf files to an AWS Elastic Beanstalk application that includes Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) storage, and an Auto Scaling group. Use a program in the EC2 instances to convert the file to .jpg format. Save the .pdf files and the .jpg files in the EBS store.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The workload is event-driven and uneven: a file gets uploaded, then gets converted. The most cost-effective option is to store both the originals and the results in S3, with an S3 PUT event triggering a Lambda function that performs the conversion. You pay only for the actual milliseconds of compute and for storage, there are no idle instances, and scaling as the user base grows happens automatically.  
Why B is not selected: DynamoDB isn't meant for storing files: the item size limit is 400 KB, while the average PDF is 5 MB. This design doesn't work.  
Why C is not selected: A fleet of instances with EBS storage is billed around the clock regardless of load, and EBS costs far more than S3 as the volume of files grows.  
Why D is not selected: The same problem: constantly running instances plus file storage cost more than the S3-and-Lambda combination, and the wording is even self-contradictory — it proposes storing the files in both EFS and EBS.

---

64\. A company has more than 5 TB of file data on Windows file servers that run on premises. Users and applications interact with the data each day.  
The company is moving its Windows workloads to AWS. As the company continues this process, the company requires access to AWS and on-premises file storage with minimum latency. The company needs a solution that minimizes operational overhead and requires no significant changes to the existing file access patterns. The company uses an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection for connectivity to AWS.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Deploy and configure Amazon FSx for Windows File Server on AWS. Move the on-premises file data to FSx for Windows File Server. Reconfigure the workloads to use FSx for Windows File Server on AWS.  
B. Deploy and configure an Amazon S3 File Gateway on premises. Move the on-premises file data to the S3 File Gateway. Reconfigure the on-premises workloads and the cloud workloads to use the S3 File Gateway.  
C. Deploy and configure an Amazon S3 File Gateway on premises. Move the on-premises file data to Amazon S3. Reconfigure the workloads to use either Amazon S3 directly or the S3 File Gateway. depending on each workload's location.  
D. Deploy and configure Amazon FSx for Windows File Server on AWS. Deploy and configure an Amazon FSx File Gateway on premises. Move the on-premises file data to the FSx File Gateway. Configure the cloud workloads to use FSx for Windows File Server on AWS. Configure the on-premises workloads to use the FSx File Gateway.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Three constraints apply at once: access from both the cloud and on premises with minimal latency, minimal administration, and "no significant changes to the existing file access patterns." That last one is decisive: the Windows workloads use SMB with NTFS permissions and Active Directory, so the target storage has to be FSx for Windows File Server, not object storage like S3. FSx File Gateway removes the on-premises latency over the VPN: it's deployed on site, caches hot files, and serves them over SMB, while the full copy lives in FSx in the cloud. That gives the pairing: FSx for Windows File Server in the cloud for cloud workloads, and FSx File Gateway on premises for on-premises workloads.  
Why A is not selected: FSx alone, with no gateway, means on-premises users reach the files over the Site-to-Site VPN. The requirement for minimal on-premises latency isn't met.  
Why B is not selected: S3 File Gateway presents an SMB interface, but behind it is object storage, not a Windows file system: NTFS ACLs, Active Directory integration, and lock semantics are lost. For Windows workloads that need to move without changes, that's a significant rework.  
Why C is not selected: Some workloads are moved to direct S3 access, meaning a rewrite to the object API. The requirement explicitly forbids significant changes to how files are accessed.

---

65\. A hospital recently deployed a RESTful API with Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. The hospital uses API Gateway and Lambda to upload reports that are in PDF format and JPEG format. The hospital needs to modify the Lambda code to identify protected health information (PHI) in the reports.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use existing Python libraries to extract the text from the reports and to identify the PHI from the extracted text.  
B. Use Amazon Textract to extract the text from the reports. Use Amazon SageMaker to identify the PHI from the extracted text.  
C. Use Amazon Textract to extract the text from the reports. Use Amazon Comprehend Medical to identify the PHI from the extracted text.  
D. Use Amazon Rekognition to extract the text from the reports. Use Amazon Comprehend Medical to identify the PHI from the extracted text.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Reports arrive as PDF and JPEG files, so the text must first be extracted and then scanned for protected health information. Amazon Textract recognizes text in documents and images, and Amazon Comprehend Medical has a built-in PHI detection feature. Nothing needs training — it's just two calls from the same function.  
Why A is not selected: Custom libraries mean developing and maintaining your own text extraction and detection logic — maximum effort.  
Why B is not selected: SageMaker would require training a custom model, whereas a managed service already knows how to find PHI.  
Why D is not selected: Rekognition recognizes text in images but doesn't parse multi-page PDF documents: those require Textract.

---

66\. A company has an application that generates a large number of files, each approximately 5 MB in size. The files are stored in Amazon S3. Company policy requires the files to be stored for 4 years before they can be deleted.  
Immediate accessibility is always required as the files contain critical business data that is not easy to reproduce.  
The files are frequently accessed in the first 30 days of the object creation but are rarely accessed after the first 30 days.  
Which storage solution is MOST cost-effective?  
A. Create an S3 bucket lifecycle policy to move files from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier 30 days from object creation. Delete the files 4 years after object creation.  
B. Create an S3 bucket lifecycle policy to move files from S3 Standard to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) 30 days from object creation. Delete the files 4 years after object creation.  
C. Create an S3 bucket lifecycle policy to move files from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) 30 days from object creation. Delete the files 4 years after object creation.  
D. Create an S3 bucket lifecycle policy to move files from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) 30 days from object creation. Move the files to S3 Glacier 4 years after object creation.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Break this down by requirement. "Immediate accessibility is always required" rules out Glacier Flexible Retrieval, where retrieval takes minutes to hours. "Not easy to reproduce" means the data can't be lost, which calls for a storage class that keeps copies across three Availability Zones — ruling out One Zone-IA. "Frequently accessed in the first 30 days, rarely after" is exactly the pattern a Lifecycle rule is built for: Standard for the first 30 days, then Standard-IA. And company policy requires deleting the files after 4 years, so the rule needs an expiration action too. Be sure to compare this with question {{q:890}}: the same scenario, but Glacier Instant Retrieval appears among the options there — and the correct answer changes to that.  
Why A is not selected: S3 Glacier (Flexible Retrieval) returns an object in minutes with expedited retrieval and in hours with standard retrieval. The requirement for constant, immediate accessibility is violated.  
Why B is not selected: One Zone-IA keeps a single copy in a single Availability Zone. For critical data that's hard to reproduce, that's an unacceptable risk, and the savings over Standard-IA are only about 20%.  
Why D is not selected: This rule moves the files to Glacier in year four instead of deleting them. Company policy allows deletion after 4 years, but here you'd keep paying for storage indefinitely.

---

67\. A company hosts an application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances. The application processes messages from an Amazon SQS queue, writes to an Amazon RDS table, and deletes the message from the queue. Occasional duplicate records are found in the RDS table. The SQS queue does not contain any duplicate messages.  
What should a solutions architect do to ensure messages are being processed once only?  
A. Use the CreateQueue API call to create a new queue.  
B. Use the AddPermission API call to add appropriate permissions.  
C. Use the ReceiveMessage API call to set an appropriate wait time.  
D. Use the ChangeMessageVisibility API call to increase the visibility timeout.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Duplicates in the database with no duplicates in the queue mean a message takes longer to process than the visibility timeout lasts: the message becomes visible again and gets picked up by another worker while the first one is still processing it. The fix is to increase the visibility timeout by calling ChangeMessageVisibility to a value greater than the processing time.  
Why A is not selected: A new queue doesn't change the underlying cause: the visibility timeout would stay the same.  
Why B is not selected: Permissions have nothing to do with duplicate processing.  
Why C is not selected: Long polling reduces the number of empty responses and the cost of requests, but it doesn't prevent a message from being redelivered.

---

68\. A solutions architect is designing a new hybrid architecture to extend a company's on-premises infrastructure to AWS. The company requires a highly available connection with consistent low latency to an AWS Region. The company needs to minimize costs and is willing to accept slower traffic if the primary connection fails.  
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection to a Region. Provision a VPN connection as a backup if the primary Direct Connect connection fails.  
B. Provision a VPN tunnel connection to a Region for private connectivity. Provision a second VPN tunnel for private connectivity and as a backup if the primary VPN connection fails.  
C. Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection to a Region. Provision a second Direct Connect connection to the same Region as a backup if the primary Direct Connect connection fails.  
D. Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection to a Region. Use the Direct Connect failover attribute from the AWS CLI to automatically create a backup connection if the primary Direct Connect connection fails.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The requirements are consistently low latency, high availability, and minimized cost, with slower traffic being acceptable if the primary connection fails. That points to Direct Connect as the primary link, with its predictable latency, and a VPN over the internet as the backup: it spins up quickly, costs very little, and only kicks in during an outage.  
Why B is not selected: VPN runs over the public internet, where latency is unpredictable, and the requirement calls for consistently low latency.  
Why C is not selected: A second Direct Connect connection is more reliable, but it doubles the port cost, while the requirement explicitly allows a slower backup.  
Why D is not selected: There is no such thing as a failover attribute for Direct Connect that automatically creates a backup connection.

---

69\. A company is running a business-critical web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The EC2 instances are in an Auto Scaling group. The application uses an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database that is deployed in a single Availability Zone. The company wants the application to be highly available with minimum downtime and minimum loss of data.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?  
A. Place the EC2 instances in different AWS Regions. Use Amazon Route 53 health checks to redirect traffic. Use Aurora PostgreSQL Cross-Region Replication.  
B. Configure the Auto Scaling group to use multiple Availability Zones. Configure the database as Multi-AZ. Configure an Amazon RDS Proxy instance for the database.  
C. Configure the Auto Scaling group to use one Availability Zone. Generate hourly snapshots of the database. Recover the database from the snapshots in the event of a failure.  
D. Configure the Auto Scaling group to use multiple AWS Regions. Write the data from the application to Amazon S3. Use S3 Event Notifications to launch an AWS Lambda function to write the data to the database.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: High availability with minimum downtime and minimum data loss is required, at the least operational effort. For the application, that means spreading the Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones; for the database, deploying Aurora with a standby replica in another zone (Multi-AZ), where failover happens automatically within seconds and no data is lost. RDS Proxy rounds out the design: it maintains a connection pool and speeds up the application's recovery after failover. All of this is configuration, not a ground-up architecture.  
Why A is not selected: A multi-Region setup with Route 53 health checks is noticeably more work and cost, and DNS-based failover is slower and depends on resolver caching. For a 'least operational effort' requirement, this is overkill.  
Why C is not selected: A single Availability Zone with hourly snapshots means downtime during recovery and data loss of up to an hour.  
Why D is not selected: Writing data to S3 and then loading it into the database via a function means rewriting the application, with noticeably worse consistency as a result.

---

70\. A company's HTTP application is behind a Network Load Balancer (NLB). The NLB's target group is configured to use an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group with multiple EC2 instances that run the web service.  
The company notices that the NLB is not detecting HTTP errors for the application. These errors require a manual restart of the EC2 instances that run the web service. The company needs to improve the application's availability without writing custom scripts or code.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Enable HTTP health checks on the NLB, supplying the URL of the company's application.  
B. Add a cron job to the EC2 instances to check the local application's logs once each minute. If HTTP errors are detected. the application will restart.  
C. Replace the NLB with an Application Load Balancer. Enable HTTP health checks by supplying the URL of the company's application. Configure an Auto Scaling action to replace unhealthy instances.  
D. Create an Amazon Cloud Watch alarm that monitors the UnhealthyHostCount metric for the NLB. Configure an Auto Scaling action to replace unhealthy instances when the alarm is in the ALARM state.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: A Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and knows nothing about HTTP response codes: its health check passes as long as the TCP connection opens. An Application Load Balancer can check a specific URL and expected response code, and an Auto Scaling group using the load balancer's health checks automatically replaces unhealthy instances — without a single line of custom code.  
Why A is not selected: The NLB does support HTTP health checks, but the requirement also calls for automatic instance replacement, which the NLB itself does not trigger; besides, an application-layer app is more naturally served behind an ALB.  
Why B is not selected: A cron job that restarts the app is exactly the kind of custom script the requirement rules out.  
Why D is not selected: The unhealthy host count alarm fires only once a Layer 4 health check declares an instance dead — it never sees HTTP errors.

---

71\. A company runs a shopping application that uses Amazon DynamoDB to store customer information. In case of data corruption, a solutions architect needs to design a solution that meets a recovery point objective (RPO) of 15 minutes and a recovery time objective (RTO) of 1 hour.  
What should the solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?  
A. Configure DynamoDB global tables. For RPO recovery, point the application to a different AWS Region.  
B. Configure DynamoDB point-in-time recovery. For RPO recovery, restore to the desired point in time.  
C. Export the DynamoDB data to Amazon S3 Glacier on a daily basis. For RPO recovery, import the data from S3 Glacier to DynamoDB.  
D. Schedule Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots for the DynamoDB table every 15 minutes. For RPO recovery, restore the DynamoDB table by using the EBS snapshot.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: This is about data corruption, not a Region failure, and losing up to fifteen minutes of data is acceptable. DynamoDB point-in-time recovery keeps continuous backups for the last 35 days and lets you restore the table to any second, accurate to the minute — enough to satisfy both the recovery point and the recovery time requirement.  
Why A is not selected: Global tables replicate data, including corrupted data: failing over to another Region would just return the same corrupted record.  
Why C is not selected: A daily export gives a recovery point of one day, far worse than the required fifteen minutes, and importing from the archive would take hours.  
Why D is not selected: DynamoDB is a managed service with no EBS volumes: there is no table volume to snapshot.

---

72\. A company runs a photo processing application that needs to frequently upload and download pictures from Amazon S3 buckets that are located in the same AWS Region. A solutions architect has noticed an increased cost in data transfer fees and needs to implement a solution to reduce these costs.  
How can the solutions architect meet this requirement?  
A. Deploy Amazon API Gateway into a public subnet and adjust the route table to route S3 calls through it.  
B. Deploy a NAT gateway into a public subnet and attach an endpoint policy that allows access to the S3 buckets.  
C. Deploy the application into a public subnet and allow it to route through an internet gateway to access the S3 buckets.  
D. Deploy an S3 VPC gateway endpoint into the VPC and attach an endpoint policy that allows access to the S3 buckets.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The data transfer charges arise because traffic to S3 travels through an internet gateway or a NAT gateway. An S3 gateway endpoint adds a route to the service's prefix, so traffic stays inside the AWS network and isn't charged, while the endpoint policy restricts access to the required buckets. Since the buckets are in the same Region, there's no cross-Region charge either.  
Why A is not selected: API Gateway isn't a networking device that requests to S3 can be routed through: there's no route table entry that could point to it.  
Why B is not selected: A NAT gateway charges for every gigabyte it processes — that would increase costs rather than reduce them, and it has no endpoint policies.  
Why C is not selected: A public subnet and internet gateway keep the same paid path over the internet and weaken security.

---

73\. A company recently launched Linux-based application instances on Amazon EC2 in a private subnet and launched a Linux-based bastion host on an Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet of a VPC. A solutions architect needs to connect from the on-premises network, through the company's internet connection, to the bastion host, and to the application servers. The solutions architect must make sure that the security groups of all the EC2 instances will allow that access.  
Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Replace the current security group of the bastion host with one that only allows inbound access from the application instances.  
B. Replace the current security group of the bastion host with one that only allows inbound access from the internal IP range for the company.  
C. Replace the current security group of the bastion host with one that only allows inbound access from the external IP range for the company.  
D. Replace the current security group of the application instances with one that allows inbound SSH access from only the private IP address of the bastion host.  
E. Replace the current security group of the application instances with one that allows inbound SSH access from only the public IP address of the bastion host.  
Answer: CD  
Explanation: Access comes from the corporate network over the internet, so the bastion must accept connections from the company's external IP range — that's what the inbound rule specifies (C). The application instances in the private subnet should accept SSH only from the bastion, and the bastion reaches them over its private address, so the rule references the bastion's private address (D).  
Why A is not selected: Allowing the bastion to accept inbound connections from the application instances makes no sense: the direction of the connection is reversed.  
Why B is not selected: The company's internal IP range gets translated on the way out to the internet: what reaches the bastion is the external address, so this rule would never match.  
Why E is not selected: The bastion reaches the private instances inside the VPC using its private address; its public address plays no part in that traffic.

---

74\. A solutions architect is designing a two-tier web application. The application consists of a public-facing web tier hosted on Amazon EC2 in public subnets. The database tier consists of Microsoft SQL Server running on Amazon EC2 in a private subnet. Security is a high priority for the company.  
How should security groups be configured in this situation? (Choose two.)  
A. Configure the security group for the web tier to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0.  
B. Configure the security group for the web tier to allow outbound traffic on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0.  
C. Configure the security group for the database tier to allow inbound traffic on port 1433 from the security group for the web tier.  
D. Configure the security group for the database tier to allow outbound traffic on ports 443 and 1433 to the security group for the web tier.  
E. Configure the security group for the database tier to allow inbound traffic on ports 443 and 1433 from the security group for the web tier.  
Answer: AC  
Explanation: The web tier is public-facing, so its security group accepts inbound traffic on port 443 from the internet (A). The SQL Server database accepts connections only from the web tier, so its inbound rule allows port 1433 referencing the web tier's security group (C).  
Why B is not selected: Security group outbound rules allow everything by default, and restricting the web tier's outbound traffic has nothing to do with this requirement.  
Why D is not selected: Security groups are stateful: the database's response traffic is allowed automatically, so no separate outbound rule is needed.  
Why E is not selected: The database doesn't need port 443 inbound: connections to SQL Server go over port 1433, and adding an unnecessary allowance violates the principle of least privilege.

---

75\. A company wants to move a multi-tiered application from on premises to the AWS Cloud to improve the application's performance. The application consists of application tiers that communicate with each other by way of RESTful services. Transactions are dropped when one tier becomes overloaded. A solutions architect must design a solution that resolves these issues and modernizes the application.  
Which solution meets these requirements and is the MOST operationally efficient?  
A. Use Amazon API Gateway and direct transactions to the AWS Lambda functions as the application layer. Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) as the communication layer between application services.  
B. Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to analyze the application performance history to determine the servers' peak utilization during the performance failures. Increase the size of the application server's Amazon EC2 instances to meet the peak requirements.  
C. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to handle the messaging between application servers running on Amazon EC2 in an Auto Scaling group. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the SNS queue length and scale up and down as required.  
D. Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to handle the messaging between application servers running on Amazon EC2 in an Auto Scaling group. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the SQS queue length and scale up when communication failures are detected.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Transactions are dropped whenever one tier becomes overloaded, so the tiers need to be decoupled with a buffer and freed from server management. API Gateway accepts requests, Lambda functions run the logic and scale automatically, and SQS queues between the services hold messages during spikes, so nothing gets lost.  
Why B is not selected: Sizing instances for peak load isn't modernization, it just postpones the problem, and you end up paying for peak capacity even during idle periods.  
Why C is not selected: SNS delivers messages immediately and doesn't form a queue: there's no buffering, and the topic simply has no queue-length metric.  
Why D is not selected: The queue choice is correct, but the EC2 instances still have to be managed, and scaling on 'detected communication failures' reacts only after data has already been lost.

---

76\. A company receives 10 TB of instrumentation data each day from several machines located at a single factory. The data consists of JSON files stored on a storage area network (SAN) in an on-premises data center located within the factory. The company wants to send this data to Amazon S3 where it can be accessed by several additional systems that provide critical near-real-time analytics. A secure transfer is important because the data is considered sensitive.  
Which solution offers the MOST reliable data transfer?  
A. AWS DataSync over public internet  
B. AWS DataSync over AWS Direct Connect  
C. AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) over public internet  
D. AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) over AWS Direct Connect  
Answer: B  
Explanation: What needs to move is files (JSON on a SAN), and it has to happen reliably and securely. AWS DataSync is a service built specifically for file transfer: it verifies integrity, automatically retries failed transfers, encrypts data in transit, and can run on a schedule. Running it over Direct Connect is more reliable and predictable than over the internet, and for 10 TB a day, consistent bandwidth is critical.  
Why A is not selected: The same DataSync, but over the public internet: bandwidth is shared with other traffic, latency fluctuates, and reliability is lower.  
Why C is not selected: DMS migrates databases, not files on network-attached storage. It's the wrong tool for JSON files.  
Why D is not selected: A dedicated connection doesn't fix the underlying problem: DMS still isn't designed to copy files from a SAN to S3.

---

77\. A company needs to configure a real-time data ingestion architecture for its application. The company needs an API, a process that transforms data as the data is streamed, and a storage solution for the data.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Deploy an Amazon EC2 instance to host an API that sends data to an Amazon Kinesis data stream. Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream that uses the Kinesis data stream as a data source. Use AWS Lambda functions to transform the data. Use the Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream to send the data to Amazon S3.  
B. Deploy an Amazon EC2 instance to host an API that sends data to AWS Glue. Stop source/destination checking on the EC2 instance. Use AWS Glue to transform the data and to send the data to Amazon S3.  
C. Configure an Amazon API Gateway API to send data to an Amazon Kinesis data stream. Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream that uses the Kinesis data stream as a data source. Use AWS Lambda functions to transform the data. Use the Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream to send the data to Amazon S3.  
D. Configure an Amazon API Gateway API to send data to AWS Glue. Use AWS Lambda functions to transform the data. Use AWS Glue to send the data to Amazon S3.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: What's needed is an API, on-the-fly data transformation, and storage — with minimal operational overhead. API Gateway accepts requests and writes directly into a Kinesis data stream, Firehose reads the stream, invokes a Lambda function to transform the data, and delivers the result to S3. There isn't a single server anywhere in this design.  
Why A is not selected: An EC2 instance acting as the API is a machine that has to be maintained and scaled.  
Why B is not selected: Again a self-managed instance, and Glue is a batch ETL service, not built to ingest a real-time stream.  
Why D is not selected: AWS Glue is not a destination for streaming data from API Gateway: no such integration exists.

---

78\. A company needs to keep user transaction data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The company must retain the data for 7 years.  
What is the MOST operationally efficient solution that meets these requirements?  
A. Use DynamoDB point-in-time recovery to back up the table continuously.  
B. Use AWS Backup to create backup schedules and retention policies for the table.  
C. Create an on-demand backup of the table by using the DynamoDB console. Store the backup in an Amazon S3 bucket. Set an S3 Lifecycle configuration for the S3 bucket.  
D. Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rule to invoke an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to back up the table and to store the backup in an Amazon S3 bucket. Set an S3 Lifecycle configuration for the S3 bucket.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Keeping copies of the table for seven years is easiest to manage centrally. AWS Backup supports DynamoDB, lets you set a schedule and retention period through policy, stores copies in its own managed storage, and shows job status — no scripts and no manual steps.  
Why A is not selected: Point-in-time recovery retains data for at most 35 days: the seven-year requirement isn't met.  
Why C is not selected: An on-demand backup created from the console is a manual action, and it isn't exported to a bucket as a file that lifecycle rules can manage.
