Why A is not selected: EBS volumes are tied to an Availability Zone and to an instance, are limited in size, and cost far more than S3. The option doesn't work for 900 TB.  
Why B is not selected: EFS solves the problem technically but costs considerably more per gigabyte than S3, and cost is stated as the deciding factor.  
Why C is not selected: OpenSearch is a search engine, not storage: keeping 900 TB of documents in it would be impractical and very expensive.

---

119\. A global company is using Amazon API Gateway to design REST APIs for its loyalty club users in the us-east-1 Region and the ap-southeast-2 Region. A solutions architect must design a solution to protect these API Gateway managed REST APIs across multiple accounts from SQL injection and cross-site scripting attacks.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of administrative effort?  
A. Set up AWS WAF in both Regions. Associate Regional web ACLs with an API stage.  
B. Set up AWS Firewall Manager in both Regions. Centrally configure AWS WAF rules.  
C. Set up AWS Shield in bath Regions. Associate Regional web ACLs with an API stage.  
D. Set up AWS Shield in one of the Regions. Associate Regional web ACLs with an API stage.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: SQL injection and cross-site scripting are filtered by AWS WAF, but the question asks about the least administrative effort across multiple accounts and Regions. AWS Firewall Manager lets you define a WAF policy once in the organization's admin account and have it applied automatically to all matching resources across every account, including newly created ones. The web ACLs themselves remain Regional, but they're managed centrally. Note: Firewall Manager requires AWS Organizations and delegated administration to be enabled.  
Why A is not selected: Configuring WAF manually in each Region and account is possible, but the rules then have to be maintained separately in every location — exactly the extra administrative effort being avoided.  
Why C is not selected: AWS Shield protects against DDoS and does not filter SQL injection or XSS. WAF is needed for that.  
Why D is not selected: Same mistake of using Shield, plus protecting only one Region leaves the other unfiltered.

---

120\. A company has implemented a self-managed DNS solution on three Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in the us-west-2 Region. Most of the company's users are located in the United States and Europe.  
The company wants to improve the performance and availability of the solution. The company launches and configures three EC2 instances in the eu-west-1 Region and adds the EC2 instances as targets for a new NLB.  
Which solution can the company use to route traffic to all the EC2 instances?  
A. Create an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy to route requests to one of the two NLBs. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Use the Route 53 record as the distribution’s origin.  
B. Create a standard accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator. Create endpoint groups in us-west-2 and eu-west- 1. Add the two NLBs as endpoints for the endpoint groups.  
C. Attach Elastic IP addresses to the six EC2 instances. Create an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy to route requests to one of the six EC2 instances. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Use the Route 53 record as the distribution's origin.  
D. Replace the two NLBs with two Application Load Balancers (ALBs). Create an Amazon Route 53 latency routing policy to route requests to one of the two ALBs. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Use the Route 53 record as the distribution’s origin.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The DNS service runs over UDP and sits behind a Network Load Balancer, so CloudFront cannot be used. What's needed is AWS Global Accelerator: it provides a pair of static anycast IP addresses, accepts traffic at the edge location closest to the user, and delivers it over the AWS backbone to the nearest healthy group of endpoints — in this case, either us-west-2 or eu-west-1. If a Region fails, traffic switches over automatically, without waiting for DNS record TTLs to expire.  
Why A is not selected: CloudFront does not serve UDP traffic and cannot use a DNS record as an origin for this kind of service.  
Why C is not selected: The scheme with Elastic IP addresses on six instances removes the load balancers and shifts fault tolerance onto DNS records, and CloudFront is still not applicable.  
Why D is not selected: Replacing the NLBs with ALBs won't work for DNS: an ALB only handles HTTP and HTTPS.

---

121\. A company is running an online transaction processing (OLTP) workload on AWS. This workload uses an unencrypted Amazon RDS DB instance in a Multi-AZ deployment. Daily database snapshots are taken from this instance.  
What should a solutions architect do to ensure the database and snapshots are always encrypted moving forward?  
A. Encrypt a copy of the latest DB snapshot. Replace existing DB instance by restoring the encrypted snapshot.  
B. Create a new encrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume and copy the snapshots to it. Enable encryption on the DB instance.  
C. Copy the snapshots and enable encryption using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) Restore encrypted snapshot to an existing DB instance.  
D. Copy the snapshots to an Amazon S3 bucket that is encrypted using server-side encryption with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) managed keys (SSE-KMS).  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The key thing to remember about RDS: you cannot turn on encryption for an existing unencrypted instance. There is only one path — take a snapshot, copy it with encryption enabled (specifying a KMS key at copy time), and restore a new instance from the encrypted copy, then cut the application over to it. All subsequent snapshots of the new instance inherit encryption automatically. The reverse is also impossible: an encrypted instance cannot be decrypted, only have its data exported.  
Why B is not selected: EBS volumes have nothing to do with RDS storage — the service manages it itself. And turning on encryption for an existing instance, as this option suggests, isn't possible.  
Why C is not selected: Restoring a snapshot always creates a new database instance. RDS has no way to restore a snapshot "into an existing instance."  
Why D is not selected: A copy of the snapshot in an encrypted bucket protects only that copy. The database itself and its regular snapshots remain unencrypted.

---

122\. A company wants to build a scalable key management infrastructure to support developers who need to encrypt data in their applications.  
What should a solutions architect do to reduce the operational burden?  
A. Use multi-factor authentication (MFA) to protect the encryption keys.  
B. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to protect the encryption keys.  
C. Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create, store, and assign the encryption keys.  
D. Use an IAM policy to limit the scope of users who have access permissions to protect the encryption keys.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The task is to give developers a managed key infrastructure without building it themselves. AWS KMS is built exactly for this: keys are stored in hardware modules, never leave the service in plaintext, access is described by the key policy and IAM policies, every use is logged to CloudTrail, and automatic rotation is a checkbox away. Applications work through envelope encryption: they request a data key, encrypt locally with it, and store an encrypted copy of that key alongside the data.  
Why A is not selected: Multi-factor authentication protects account sign-in. It is not a key management infrastructure and does not solve the problem of applications encrypting data.  
Why C is not selected: ACM issues and maintains TLS certificates for load balancers, CloudFront, and API Gateway. It does not handle keys for encrypting data inside applications.  
Why D is not selected: An IAM policy restricts access, but by itself it does not create, store, or rotate keys. It complements KMS rather than replacing it.

---

123\. A company has a dynamic web application hosted on two Amazon EC2 instances. The company has its own SSL certificate, which is on each instance to perform SSL termination.  
There has been an increase in traffic recently, and the operations team determined that SSL encryption and decryption is causing the compute capacity of the web servers to reach their maximum limit.  
What should a solutions architect do to increase the application's performance?  
A. Create a new SSL certificate using AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Install the ACM certificate on each instance.  
B. Create an Amazon S3 bucket Migrate the SSL certificate to the S3 bucket. Configure the EC2 instances to reference the bucket for SSL termination.  
C. Create another EC2 instance as a proxy server. Migrate the SSL certificate to the new instance and configure it to direct connections to the existing EC2 instances.  
D. Import the SSL certificate into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Create an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener that uses the SSL certificate from ACM.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The bottleneck is encryption on the web servers themselves. It can be offloaded by moving TLS termination to the Application Load Balancer: the company's own certificate is imported into ACM, and the HTTPS listener uses it. The load balancer decrypts traffic using its own resources, while the instances receive plain HTTP and free up CPU.  
Why A is not selected: Certificates issued by ACM cannot be exported and installed on instances, and more importantly, the encryption work would still stay on the servers.  
Why B is not selected: S3 is object storage; it plays no part in TLS termination. No such setup exists.  
Why C is not selected: A separate proxy instance would indeed take the load off, but it's a machine of its own — its own patching, scaling, and a new single point of failure in place of a managed service.

---

124\. A company has a highly dynamic batch processing job that uses many Amazon EC2 instances to complete it. The job is stateless in nature, can be started and stopped at any given time with no negative impact, and typically takes upwards of 60 minutes total to complete. The company has asked a solutions architect to design a scalable and cost-effective solution that meets the requirements of the job.  
What should the solutions architect recommend?  
A. Implement EC2 Spot Instances.  
B. Purchase EC2 Reserved Instances.  
C. Implement EC2 On-Demand Instances.  
D. Implement the processing on AWS Lambda.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The job is stateless, can be stopped and resumed at any time without consequences, and runs for over an hour. That's the ideal profile for interruptible instances: up to a 90 percent discount, and capacity reclamation causes no harm because the work can simply start over.  
Why B is not selected: Reserved Instances imply steady consumption over a one- or three-year term, and the workload is described as highly variable.  
Why C is not selected: On-Demand pricing is noticeably more expensive when interruptions are acceptable anyway.  
Why D is not selected: The job runs for more than an hour, while the Lambda function execution limit is fifteen minutes.

---

125\. A company runs its two-tier ecommerce website on AWS. The web tier consists of a load balancer that sends traffic to Amazon EC2 instances. The database tier uses an Amazon RDS DB instance. The EC2 instances and the RDS DB instance should not be exposed to the public internet. The EC2 instances require internet access to complete payment processing of orders through a third-party web service. The application must be highly available.  
Which combination of configuration options will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Use an Auto Scaling group to launch the EC2 instances in private subnets. Deploy an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance in private subnets.  
B. Configure a VPC with two private subnets and two NAT gateways across two Availability Zones. Deploy an Application Load Balancer in the private subnets.  
C. Use an Auto Scaling group to launch the EC2 instances in public subnets across two Availability Zones. Deploy an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance in private subnets.  
D. Configure a VPC with one public subnet, one private subnet, and two NAT gateways across two Availability Zones. Deploy an Application Load Balancer in the public subnet.  
E. Configure a VPC with two public subnets, two private subnets, and two NAT gateways across two Availability Zones. Deploy an Application Load Balancer in the public subnets.  
Answer: AE  
Explanation: The instances and the database must not be exposed to the internet, but the instances need outbound access to the payment service, and everything must survive an Availability Zone failure. So the Auto Scaling group launches instances in private subnets, and the RDS database in a Multi-AZ configuration also sits in private subnets (A). The network is built from two public subnets for the load balancer, two private subnets for the workload, and two NAT gateways — one per zone (E).  
Why B is not selected: An Application Load Balancer that's reachable from the internet must sit in public subnets: in private subnets it can't accept user traffic.  
Why C is not selected: Instances in public subnets are exposed to the internet — a direct violation of the requirement.  
Why D is not selected: One public and one private subnet mean a single Availability Zone for each tier: the load balancer needs subnets in at least two zones, so there's no high availability.

---

126\. A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to reduce a company's storage costs. All the company's data is in the Amazon S3 Standard storage class. The company must keep all data for at least 25 years. Data from the most recent 2 years must be highly available and immediately retrievable.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive immediately.  
B. Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years.  
C. Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Activate the archiving option to ensure that data is archived in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.  
D. Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) immediately and to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirement splits along a timeline: the most recent two years need high availability and instant retrieval, while everything older just needs to survive 25 years as cheaply as possible. That's literally a description of a Lifecycle rule transitioning to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years: recent data stays in Standard, and old data costs about a dollar per terabyte per month. Deep Archive returns an object within 12 hours under standard retrieval, but no speed requirement was set for data older than two years.  
Why A is not selected: Moving to Deep Archive immediately violates the core requirement: data from the last two years must be available instantly, and Deep Archive returns an object only after hours.  
Why C is not selected: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects to archive tiers based on lack of access (after 90 and 180 days), not on a fixed two-year age. An unused but recent object would be archived ahead of schedule, plus you'd pay monitoring charges per object for 25 years.  
Why D is not selected: S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single Availability Zone, while recent data is required to be highly available. The intermediate transition is also pointless here: it saves pennies at the cost of reduced fault tolerance.

---

127\. A media company is evaluating the possibility of moving its systems to the AWS Cloud. The company needs at least 10 TB of storage with the maximum possible I/O performance for video processing, 300 TB of very durable storage for storing media content, and 900 TB of storage to meet requirements for archival media that is not in use anymore.  
Which set of services should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?  
A. Amazon EBS for maximum performance, Amazon S3 for durable data storage, and Amazon S3 Glacier for archival storage  
B. Amazon EBS for maximum performance, Amazon EFS for durable data storage, and Amazon S3 Glacier for archival storage  
C. Amazon EC2 instance store for maximum performance, Amazon EFS for durable data storage, and Amazon S3 for archival storage  
D. Amazon EC2 instance store for maximum performance, Amazon S3 for durable data storage, and Amazon S3 Glacier for archival storage  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Three requirements, three different storage types. Maximum I/O performance for video processing calls for the instance's local NVMe disks (instance store), which outperform any network-attached volume; data loss risk isn't a concern here because it's just a processing scratch space. Durable storage for 300 TB of media content is S3, with eleven nines of durability. The 900 TB archive of content that's no longer accessed is S3 Glacier.  
Why A is not selected: EBS volumes are fast, but they fall short of the instance's local NVMe disks in performance, and the requirement calls for the maximum.  
Why B is not selected: Same performance shortfall here, plus EFS as durable storage for media content is noticeably more expensive than S3.  
Why C is not selected: Using EFS for 300 TB is more expensive than S3, and plain S3 for a 900 TB archive is more expensive than Glacier: both substitutions make the solution worse.

---

128\. A company wants to run applications in containers in the AWS Cloud. These applications are stateless and can tolerate disruptions within the underlying infrastructure. The company needs a solution that minimizes cost and operational overhead.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Use Spot Instances in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group to run the application containers.  
B. Use Spot Instances in an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) managed node group.  
C. Use On-Demand Instances in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group to run the application containers.  
D. Use On-Demand Instances in an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) managed node group.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The applications are stateless and tolerate disruptions, so interruptible instances fit — up to a 90 percent discount. Among the container options, an EKS managed node group takes node provisioning and patching off the team's plate and itself handles Spot interruption notices, replacing nodes as needed.  
Why A is not selected: An Auto Scaling group on Spot Instances is cheap, but the team would have to build container orchestration themselves — more operational overhead.  
Why C is not selected: On-Demand Instances are noticeably more expensive, while the requirement explicitly allows for interruptions.  
Why D is not selected: Managed node handling is convenient, but On-Demand pricing does not minimize cost.

---

129\. A company is running a multi-tier web application on premises. The web application is containerized and runs on a number of Linux hosts connected to a PostgreSQL database that contains user records. The operational overhead of maintaining the infrastructure and capacity planning is limiting the company's growth. A solutions architect must improve the application's infrastructure.  
Which combination of actions should the solutions architect take to accomplish this? (Choose two.)  
A. Migrate the PostgreSQL database to Amazon Aurora.  
B. Migrate the web application to be hosted on Amazon EC2 instances.  
C. Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the web application content.  
D. Set up Amazon ElastiCache between the web application and the PostgreSQL database.  
E. Migrate the web application to be hosted on AWS Fargate with Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS).  
Answer: AE  
Explanation: The problem is stated directly: infrastructure operations and capacity planning are holding back growth. So server management needs to go away. The containers move to AWS Fargate running on ECS — no nodes to manage at all (E) — and the PostgreSQL database moves to Aurora, where storage scales itself and AWS handles availability and backups (A).  
Why B is not selected: EC2 instances are the same servers with patching and capacity planning, just in the cloud: the original problem remains.  
Why C is not selected: CloudFront speeds up content delivery but does not remove the operational burden.  
Why D is not selected: A cache can help performance, but it does not solve the stated problem of infrastructure and capacity management.

---

130\. An application runs on Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zonas. The instances run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The application performs best when the CPU utilization of the EC2 instances is at or near 40%.  
What should a solutions architect do to maintain the desired performance across all instances in the group?  
A. Use a simple scaling policy to dynamically scale the Auto Scaling group.  
B. Use a target tracking policy to dynamically scale the Auto Scaling group.  
C. Use an AWS Lambda function ta update the desired Auto Scaling group capacity.  
D. Use scheduled scaling actions to scale up and scale down the Auto Scaling group.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirement sets a target value for a metric — roughly 40 percent CPU utilization. A target tracking policy is built exactly for this: it calculates on its own how many instances to add or remove to keep the average utilization at the specified level.  
Why A is not selected: A simple scaling policy fires on a threshold and adds a fixed number of instances rather than aiming to hold a specific value, and it requires a cooldown period between actions.  
Why C is not selected: A custom function that changes the desired capacity is code in place of a ready-made mechanism.  
Why D is not selected: A schedule does not react to actual load: it cannot hold utilization at 40 percent.

---

131\. A company is developing a file-sharing application that will use an Amazon S3 bucket for storage. The company wants to serve all the files through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The company does not want the files to be accessible through direct navigation to the S3 URL.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Write individual policies for each S3 bucket to grant read permission for only CloudFront access.  
B. Create an IAM user. Grant the user read permission to objects in the S3 bucket. Assign the user to CloudFront.  
C. Write an S3 bucket policy that assigns the CloudFront distribution ID as the Principal and assigns the target S3 bucket as the Amazon Resource Name (ARN).  
D. Create an origin access identity (OAI). Assign the OAI to the CloudFront distribution. Configure the S3 bucket permissions so that only the OAI has read permission.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The goal is to close off direct access to the bucket and leave a single door through CloudFront. To do that, the distribution is given a special identity: an origin access identity (in modern deployments, origin access control), which is specified as the principal in the bucket policy, after which only it is granted read access. Public access to the bucket is turned off entirely, and the direct S3 URL for the object stops working. Signed URLs can then be layered on top, as in {{q:542,313}}.  
Why A is not selected: "Individual policies for each bucket" doesn't describe a mechanism: what matters is not the number of policies but which principal they name. Without an OAI or OAC, there's nothing to name in the policy.  
Why B is not selected: An IAM user is not assigned to a CloudFront distribution: the service does not act on behalf of an IAM user. No such construct exists.  
Why C is not selected: A distribution ID is not an IAM principal and cannot be placed in the Principal field. The principal is the OAI, or for OAC, the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service with a condition on the distribution's ARN.

---

132\. A company’s website provides users with downloadable historical performance reports. The website needs a solution that will scale to meet the company’s website demands globally. The solution should be cost-effective, limit the provisioning of infrastructure resources, and provide the fastest possible response time.  
Which combination should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?  
A. Amazon CloudFront and Amazon S3  
B. AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB  
C. Application Load Balancer with Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling  
D. Amazon Route 53 with internal Application Load Balancers  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The reports are static files that users download from around the world. Storing them in S3 requires no servers at all and costs cents per gigabyte, while CloudFront caches the files at edge locations, delivering the fastest possible response time and lowering the cost of outbound traffic. The requirements to avoid provisioning infrastructure, keep costs low, and respond as fast as possible are all met at once.  
Why B is not selected: Lambda and DynamoDB are for dynamic logic and data, whereas here ready-made files are being served: extra calls and extra cost for nothing.  
Why C is not selected: A fleet of instances behind a load balancer means provisioning resources and paying for them continuously, which the requirement asks to avoid.  
Why D is not selected: Internal load balancers aren't reachable from the internet and don't solve the problem of serving files globally.

---

133\. A company runs an Oracle database on premises. As part of the company’s migration to AWS, the company wants to upgrade the database to the most recent available version. The company also wants to set up disaster recovery (DR) for the database. The company needs to minimize the operational overhead for normal operations and DR setup. The company also needs to maintain access to the database's underlying operating system.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Migrate the Oracle database to an Amazon EC2 instance. Set up database replication to a different AWS Region.  
B. Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. Activate Cross-Region automated backups to replicate the snapshots to another AWS Region.  
C. Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle. Create a read replica for the database in another AWS Region.  
D. Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. Create a standby database in another Availability Zone.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The key constraint is that access to the database's underlying operating system is required, which standard RDS does not provide. Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle keeps the managed benefits (patching, backups, replicas) while also opening up access to the underlying system. For disaster recovery, a read replica is created in another Region and promoted to primary if a disaster occurs.  
Why A is not selected: A database on an EC2 instance provides OS access, but all maintenance and replication setup then falls on the company.  
Why B is not selected: Standard RDS gives no OS access, and cross-Region automated backups yield a far larger recovery time than a replica does.  
Why D is not selected: There's still no OS access, and a standby instance in another Availability Zone is not a plan for a Region-level failure.

---

134\. A company wants to move its application to a serverless solution. The serverless solution needs to analyze existing and new data by using SL. The company stores the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The data requires encryption and must be replicated to a different AWS Region.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create a new S3 bucket. Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to replicate encrypted objects to an S3 bucket in another Region. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region kays (SSE-KMS). Use Amazon Athena to query the data.  
B. Create a new S3 bucket. Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to replicate encrypted objects to an S3 bucket in another Region. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region keys (SSE-KMS). Use Amazon RDS to query the data.  
C. Load the data into the existing S3 bucket. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to replicate encrypted objects to an S3 bucket in another Region. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Use Amazon Athena to query the data.  
D. Load the data into the existing S3 bucket. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to replicate encrypted objects to an S3 bucket in another Region. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Use Amazon RDS to query the data.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: There are three requirements: serverless SQL analysis of data in S3, encryption, and cross-Region replication. Amazon Athena is the only one of the given options that runs SQL directly against S3 objects in a serverless way, so the options with RDS drop out immediately. Next comes the choice of encryption scheme: replicating objects encrypted with a KMS key to another Region requires a key that's usable there too, and a multi-Region key solves this without re-encryption and without a second policy — one key with identical key material in both Regions. That leads to the combination "SSE-KMS with a multi-Region key plus CRR plus Athena."  
Why B is not selected: Amazon RDS is a database server that data has to be loaded into, while the requirement calls for a serverless solution over objects already sitting in S3.  
Why C is not selected: Athena is the right choice, but SSE-S3 means keys fully managed by the service, separately in each Region: there's no way to confirm or control the key used for the replica. When encryption and cross-Region replication appear together in the requirements, the exam expects multi-Region KMS keys.  
Why D is not selected: Two problems at once: RDS instead of a serverless analysis solution, and SSE-S3 instead of company-managed keys.

---

135\. A company runs workloads on AWS. The company needs to connect to a service from an external provider. The service is hosted in the provider's VPC. According to the company’s security team, the connectivity must be private and must be restricted to the target service. The connection must be initiated only from the company’s VPC.  
Which solution will mast these requirements?  
A. Create a VPC peering connection between the company's VPC and the provider's VPC. Update the route table to connect to the target service.  
B. Ask the provider to create a virtual private gateway in its VPC. Use AWS PrivateLink to connect to the target service.  
C. Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet of the company’s VPUpdate the route table to connect to the target service.  
D. Ask the provider to create a VPC endpoint for the target service. Use AWS PrivateLink to connect to the target service.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The connection must be private, restricted to a single target service, and initiated only from the company's side — that is exactly what AWS PrivateLink describes. The provider publishes its service as an endpoint service behind a Network Load Balancer, the company creates an interface endpoint in its own VPC, and reaches it over a private address. Only that one service is visible, not the provider's whole network, and connections cannot be initiated in the reverse direction.  
Why A is not selected: VPC peering connects entire networks: the route opens access to the provider's whole address space, and connections can go in either direction. The requirement to restrict access to a single service isn't met.  
Why B is not selected: A virtual private gateway is a VPN or Direct Connect attachment point; it has nothing to do with PrivateLink.  
Why C is not selected: A NAT gateway sends traffic out to the internet, meaning the connection stops being private.

---

136\. A company is migrating its on-premises PostgreSQL database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The on-premises database must remain online and accessible during the migration. The Aurora database must remain synchronized with the on-premises database.  
Which combination of actions must a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Create an ongoing replication task.  
B. Create a database backup of the on-premises database.  
C. Create an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) replication server.  
D. Convert the database schema by using the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT).  
E. Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rule to monitor the database synchronization.  
Answer: AC  
Explanation: Both the source and target are PostgreSQL, so there's no need to convert the schema. It's enough to stand up an AWS DMS replication server (C) and create a task with ongoing (continuous) replication (A): DMS first migrates the existing data, then reads the transaction log and applies the changes, so the source database stays available and both databases remain in sync.  
Why B is not selected: Restoring from a backup gives a point-in-time snapshot and doesn't keep the databases in sync, which would also require stopping the database.  
Why D is not selected: The Schema Conversion Tool is needed when the engine changes, for example Oracle to PostgreSQL. Here it's the same engine on both sides.  
Why E is not selected: An EventBridge rule is monitoring. It doesn't migrate or synchronize anything.

---

137\. A company uses AWS Organizations to create dedicated AWS accounts for each business unit to manage each business unit's account independently upon request. The root email recipient missed a notification that was sent to the root user email address of one account. The company wants to ensure that all future notifications are not missed. Future notifications must be limited to account administrators.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Configure the company’s email server to forward notification email messages that are sent to the AWS account root user email address to all users in the organization.  
B. Configure all AWS account root user email addresses as distribution lists that go to a few administrators who can respond to alerts. Configure AWS account alternate contacts in the AWS Organizations console or programmatically.  
C. Configure all AWS account root user email messages to be sent to one administrator who is responsible for monitoring alerts and forwarding those alerts to the appropriate groups.  
D. Configure all existing AWS accounts and all newly created accounts to use the same root user email address. Configure AWS account alternate contacts in the AWS Organizations console or programmatically.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Two parts to the requirement. Notifications must not be missed, which means each account's root address should not be a personal inbox but a distribution list that several administrators read (one person goes on vacation, the list remains). Notifications must reach only administrators, so the distribution list must be narrow, not company-wide. The second part is covered by alternate contacts: each account can have separate addresses for billing, operations, and security, and AWS sends category-specific notifications to those addresses directly. Related question — {{q:878}}.  
Why A is not selected: Forwarding root notifications to every employee in the organization is the opposite of the requirement to limit recipients to administrators.  
Why C is not selected: A single person as the sole recipient just recreates the original problem — that person is the one who missed the notification. Plus it adds manual forwarding to groups.  
Why D is not selected: Using the same root email address for every account means administrators of one business unit see notifications for other accounts, and accounts can no longer be separated by ownership.

---

138\. A company runs its ecommerce application on AWS. Every new order is published as a massage in a RabbitMQ queue that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance in a single Availability Zone. These messages are processed by a different application that runs on a separate EC2 instance. This application stores the details in a PostgreSQL database on another EC2 instance. All the EC2 instances are in the same Availability Zone.  
The company needs to redesign its architecture to provide the highest availability with the least operational overhead.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Migrate the queue to a redundant pair (active/standby) of RabbitMQ instances on Amazon MQ. Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application. Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the PostgreSQL database.  
B. Migrate the queue to a redundant pair (active/standby) of RabbitMQ instances on Amazon MQ. Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application. Migrate the database to run on a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.  
C. Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the RabbitMQ queue. Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application. Migrate the database to run on a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.  
D. Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the RabbitMQ queue. Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application. Create a third Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the PostgreSQL database  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Each component is replaced with a managed equivalent and stretched across two Availability Zones. The RabbitMQ queue moves to Amazon MQ in an active/standby broker configuration, the application runs in a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group, and the PostgreSQL database becomes an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance in a Multi-AZ deployment. This gives the least operational overhead and the highest availability.  
Why A is not selected: Running PostgreSQL in an EC2 Auto Scaling group doesn't work — the instances would have no shared data.  
Why C is not selected: Self-managed RabbitMQ brokers in an Auto Scaling group require manual cluster configuration and ongoing maintenance.  
Why D is not selected: This option has both a homegrown broker cluster and a database in an Auto Scaling group — both are either non-functional or high-effort.

---

139\. A reporting team receives files each day in an Amazon S3 bucket. The reporting team manually reviews and copies the files from this initial S3 bucket to an analysis S3 bucket each day at the same time to use with Amazon QuickSight. Additional teams are starting to send more files in larger sizes to the initial S3 bucket.  
The reporting team wants to move the files automatically analysis S3 bucket as the files enter the initial S3 bucket. The reporting team also wants to use AWS Lambda functions to run pattern-matching code on the copied data. In addition, the reporting team wants to send the data files to a pipeline in Amazon SageMaker Pipelines.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create a Lambda function to copy the files to the analysis S3 bucket. Create an S3 event notification for the analysis S3 bucket. Configure Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as destinations of the event notification. Configure s3:ObjectCreated:Put as the event type.  
B. Create a Lambda function to copy the files to the analysis S3 bucket. Configure the analysis S3 bucket to send event notifications to Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events). Configure an ObjectCreated rule in EventBridge (CloudWatch Events). Configure Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as targets for the rule.  
C. Configure S3 replication between the S3 buckets. Create an S3 event notification for the analysis S3 bucket. Configure Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as destinations of the event notification. Configure s3:ObjectCreated:Put as the event type.  
D. Configure S3 replication between the S3 buckets. Configure the analysis S3 bucket to send event notifications to Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events). Configure an ObjectCreated rule in EventBridge (CloudWatch Events). Configure Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as targets for the rule.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Copying between buckets is handled by native S3 replication — no custom function is needed for that. To have a single event fan out to two destinations at once (the Lambda function and the SageMaker Pipelines pipeline), notifications are routed through EventBridge: an ObjectCreated rule supports multiple targets, while a plain S3 event notification can only deliver an event to one destination per event type.  
Why A is not selected: A custom copy function is unnecessary code, and an S3 event notification can't send a single event to two different targets of this kind.  
Why B is not selected: EventBridge is the right choice here, but a custom copy function is redundant when replication already handles it.  
Why C is not selected: Replication is the right choice here, but plain S3 notifications can't target both a Lambda function and a SageMaker pipeline at the same time.

---

140\. A solutions architect needs to help a company optimize the cost of running an application on AWS. The application will use Amazon EC2 instances, AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda for compute within the architecture.  
The EC2 instances will run the data ingestion layer of the application. EC2 usage will be sporadic and unpredictable. Workloads that run on EC2 instances can be interrupted at any time. The application front end will run on Fargate, and Lambda will serve the API layer. The front-end utilization and API layer utilization will be predictable over the course of the next year.  
Which combination of purchasing options will provide the MOST cost-effective solution for hosting this application? (Choose two.)  
A. Use Spot Instances for the data ingestion layer  
B. Use On-Demand Instances for the data ingestion layer  
C. Purchase a 1-year Compute Savings Plan for the front end and API layer.  
D. Purchase 1-year All Upfront Reserved instances for the data ingestion layer.  
E. Purchase a 1-year EC2 instance Savings Plan for the front end and API layer.  
Answer: AC  
Explanation: Different layers call for different purchasing models. Data ingestion on EC2 instances is sporadic, unpredictable, and interruption-tolerant, which points to Spot Instances with up to a 90 percent discount (A). The Fargate front end and the Lambda API layer are predictable a year out, and the only way to cover both under a single commitment is a Compute Savings Plan, which applies across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda (C).  
Why B is not selected: On-Demand Instances for interruption-tolerant workloads is a significant overpay.  
Why D is not selected: Reserved Instances assume steady, ongoing usage, but data ingestion is described as sporadic and unpredictable.  
Why E is not selected: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan covers only EC2 instances and does not apply to Fargate or Lambda.

---

141\. A company runs a web-based portal that provides users with global breaking news, local alerts, and weather updates. The portal delivers each user a personalized view by using mixture of static and dynamic content. Content is served over HTTPS through an API server running on an Amazon EC2 instance behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The company wants the portal to provide this content to its users across the world as quickly as possible.  
How should a solutions architect design the application to ensure the LEAST amount of latency for all users?  
A. Deploy the application stack in a single AWS Region. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve all static and dynamic content by specifying the ALB as an origin.  
B. Deploy the application stack in two AWS Regions. Use an Amazon Route 53 latency routing policy to serve all content from the ALB in the closest Region.  
C. Deploy the application stack in a single AWS Region. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve the static content. Serve the dynamic content directly from the ALB.  
D. Deploy the application stack in two AWS Regions. Use an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy to serve all content from the ALB in the closest Region.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: CloudFront speeds up more than just cacheable static content. For personalized dynamic content, the gain comes from the user establishing their TLS connection with the nearest edge location, after which the request travels to the origin over AWS's optimized backbone with connections already warmed up — noticeably faster than crossing the public internet to a distant Region. So a single deployment plus CloudFront routing every path through the distribution delivers the lowest latency without duplicating the stack.  
Why B is not selected: Two copies of the stack in different Regions doubles both cost and complexity, and latency-based routing still sends the user across the public internet to reach the Region.  
Why C is not selected: Serving dynamic content directly from the load balancer leaves distant users without the AWS backbone speedup — and dynamic content is exactly what suffers most.  
Why D is not selected: A user's geographic location doesn't equal the lowest latency, and duplicating the stack again doubles the cost.

---

142\. A gaming company is designing a highly available architecture. The application runs on a modified Linux kernel and supports only UDP-based traffic. The company needs the front-end tier to provide the best possible user experience. That tier must have low latency, route traffic to the nearest edge location, and provide static IP addresses for entry into the application endpoints.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Configure Amazon Route 53 to forward requests to an Application Load Balancer. Use AWS Lambda for the application in AWS Application Auto Scaling.  
B. Configure Amazon CloudFront to forward requests to a Network Load Balancer. Use AWS Lambda for the application in an AWS Application Auto Scaling group.  
C. Configure AWS Global Accelerator to forward requests to a Network Load Balancer. Use Amazon EC2 instances for the application in an EC2 Auto Scaling group.  
D. Configure Amazon API Gateway to forward requests to an Application Load Balancer. Use Amazon EC2 instances for the application in an EC2 Auto Scaling group.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The three requirements point unambiguously to one service. UDP traffic rules out ALB and CloudFront. Static IP addresses for the entry point are provided only by AWS Global Accelerator (a pair of anycast addresses). Accepting traffic at the nearest edge location and carrying it over the AWS backbone delivers low latency. Behind the accelerator sits a Network Load Balancer, which operates at layer 4, plus an Auto Scaling group of instances, since the application needs a modified Linux kernel, which rules out any serverless option.  
Why A is not selected: ALB doesn't support UDP, and Lambda can't run an application with a modified kernel.  
Why B is not selected: CloudFront doesn't serve UDP traffic and doesn't provide static IP addresses, and Lambda again doesn't fit the modified-kernel requirement.  
Why D is not selected: API Gateway works with HTTP and WebSocket, not arbitrary UDP, and it doesn't provide static addresses.

---

143\. A company wants to migrate its existing on-premises monolithic application to AWS. The company wants to keep as much of the front-end code and the backend code as possible. However, the company wants to break the application into smaller applications. A different team will manage each application. The company needs a highly scalable solution that minimizes operational overhead.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Host the application on AWS Lambda. Integrate the application with Amazon API Gateway.  
B. Host the application with AWS Amplify. Connect the application to an Amazon API Gateway API that is integrated with AWS Lambda.  
C. Host the application on Amazon EC2 instances. Set up an Application Load Balancer with EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group as targets.  
D. Host the application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Set up an Application Load Balancer with Amazon ECS as the target.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The monolith needs to be split into several applications while keeping as much of the existing code as possible, and the result needs to scale with minimal operational overhead. Containers fit best here: the code carries over with almost no changes, each piece becomes its own ECS service owned by its own team, and an Application Load Balancer routes requests to the right service by path or header.  
Why A is not selected: Porting the monolith to Lambda requires substantial code rework and doesn't naturally support splitting the work across teams.  
Why B is not selected: Amplify is built for the front end, and pairing it with API Gateway and Lambda again means rewriting the backend.  
Why C is not selected: Instances behind a load balancer keep the monolith intact as a single unit and leave the company responsible for managing the servers.

---

144\. A company recently started using Amazon Aurora as the data store for its global ecommerce application. When large reports are run, developers report that the ecommerce application is performing poorly. After reviewing metrics in Amazon CloudWatch, a solutions architect finds that the ReadIOPS and CPUUtilizalion metrics are spiking when monthly reports run.  
What is the MOST cost-effective solution?  
A. Migrate the monthly reporting to Amazon Redshift.  
B. Migrate the monthly reporting to an Aurora Replica.  
C. Migrate the Aurora database to a larger instance class.  
D. Increase the Provisioned IOPS on the Aurora instance.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The reports create a heavy read load that interferes with the main application. The cheapest fix is to offload reporting to an Aurora Replica: it reads from the same shared storage, lags by milliseconds, and can be added with a single action. The primary instance is freed up, and the only added cost is one extra reader instance.  
Why A is not selected: Moving reporting to Redshift means a separate data store, a loading pipeline, and an always-on cluster — noticeably more expensive and more complex.  
Why C is not selected: Scaling the primary instance up to a larger class raises cost around the clock even though the spike only happens once a month, and it doesn't separate the workloads.  
Why D is not selected: Aurora has no Provisioned IOPS setting — its storage is shared and managed by the service itself.

---

145\. A company hosts a website analytics application on a single Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instance. The analytics software is written in PHP and uses a MySQL database. The analytics software, the web server that provides PHP, and the database server are all hosted on the EC2 instance. The application is showing signs of performance degradation during busy times and is presenting 5xx errors. The company needs to make the application scale seamlessly.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On-Demand Instance. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the load to each EC2 instance.  
B. Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On-Demand Instance. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted routing to distribute the load across the two EC2 instances.  
C. Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB instance. Create an AWS Lambda function to stop the EC2 instance and change the instance type. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to invoke the Lambda function when CPU utilization surpasses 75%.  
D. Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Apply the AMI to a launch template. Create an Auto Scaling group with the launch template Configure the launch template to use a Spot Fleet. Attach an Application Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The application is bottlenecked on a single instance hosting both the web server and the database. The cheapest fix is to separate the layers and make compute elastic: the database moves to a managed Aurora MySQL instance, the application image becomes a launch template, an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer adds and removes instances with load, and using Spot capacity within a fleet cuts compute cost by a large factor. For a stateless web tier, Spot interruptions are absorbed simply by replacing the instance.  
Why A is not selected: Two fixed-size On-Demand instances don't scale with peaks and cost more than an elastic Spot-backed group.  
Why B is not selected: DNS weighted routing doesn't check target health as responsively as a load balancer, and it doesn't scale capacity.  
Why C is not selected: Changing the instance type from a function triggered by an alarm is vertical scaling with a restart and downtime, not seamless scaling.

---

146\. A company runs a stateless web application in production on a group of Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The application experiences heavy usage during an 8-hour period each business day. Application usage is moderate and steady overnight. Application usage is low during weekends.  
The company wants to minimize its EC2 costs without affecting the availability of the application.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use Spot Instances for the entire workload.  
B. Use Reserved Instances for the baseline level of usage. Use Spot instances for any additional capacity that the application needs.  
C. Use On-Demand Instances for the baseline level of usage. Use Spot Instances for any additional capacity that the application needs.  
D. Use Dedicated Instances for the baseline level of usage. Use On-Demand Instances for any additional capacity that the application needs.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The load consists of a steady baseline (moderate overnight, high during the day) plus a variable overlay. The baseline is most cost-effective covered with discounted Reserved Instances, while the extra capacity during peaks is covered with Spot Instances: the application is stateless, so reclaiming some instances doesn't affect availability.  
Why A is not selected: Fully Spot capacity puts the baseline service level at risk — a mass interruption would leave the application unavailable.  
Why C is not selected: Paying full price for the baseline is an overpay when usage is predictable a year in advance.  
Why D is not selected: Dedicated Instances cost the most and are only needed for hardware isolation requirements, which aren't part of this scenario.

---

147\. A company needs to retain application log files for a critical application for 10 years. The application team regularly accesses logs from the past month for troubleshooting, but logs older than 1 month are rarely accessed.  
The application generates more than 10 TB of logs per month.  
Which storage option meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Store the logs in Amazon S3. Use AWS Backup to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.  
B. Store the logs in Amazon S3. Use S3 Lifecycle policies to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.  
C. Store the logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use AWS Backup to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.  
D. Store the logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use Amazon S3 Lifecycle policies to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: More than 10 TB of logs a month, kept for ten years: the cheapest approach is to store them as S3 objects and use a lifecycle rule to move anything older than a month into S3 Glacier Deep Archive, the cheapest storage class. The most recent month stays instantly accessible.  
Why A is not selected: AWS Backup doesn't manage storage classes for S3 objects — transitions between classes are handled by a lifecycle rule.  
Why C is not selected: Storing logs in CloudWatch Logs is noticeably more expensive than S3, and AWS Backup doesn't apply to CloudWatch Logs.  
Why D is not selected: S3 lifecycle rules don't act on logs sitting in CloudWatch Logs — they'd first need to be exported.

---

148\. A company has a data ingestion workflow that includes the following components:  
An Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic that receives notifications about new data deliveries An AWS Lambda function that processes and stores the data The ingestion workflow occasionally fails because of network connectivity issues. When failure occurs, the corresponding data is not ingested unless the company manually reruns the job.  
What should a solutions architect do to ensure that all notifications are eventually processed?  
A. Configure the Lambda function for deployment across multiple Availability Zones.  
B. Modify the Lambda function's configuration to increase the CPU and memory allocations for the function.  
C. Configure the SNS topic’s retry strategy to increase both the number of retries and the wait time between retries.  
D. Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as the on-failure destination. Modify the Lambda function to process messages in the queue.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Network failures cause the function invocation to fail, and the notification is lost. For asynchronous invocations, Lambda has a configurable destination for failures: an SQS queue is set as the on-failure destination, events that couldn't be processed land there, and the function picks them up later. Nothing gets lost.  
Why A is not selected: Lambda functions already run across multiple Availability Zones — there's nothing to configure there, and it doesn't protect against network failures.  
Why B is not selected: More memory and CPU don't affect events being lost during a connectivity failure.  
Why C is not selected: Increasing SNS retries lowers the chance of loss but doesn't guarantee it — once retries are exhausted, the message is still lost.

---

149\. A company has a service that produces event data. The company wants to use AWS to process the event data as it is received. The data is written in a specific order that must be maintained throughout processing. The company wants to implement a solution that minimizes operational overhead.  
How should a solutions architect accomplish this?  
A. Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue to hold messages. Set up an AWS Lambda function to process messages from the queue.  
B. Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to deliver notifications containing payloads to process. Configure an AWS Lambda function as a subscriber.  
C. Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue to hold messages. Set up an AWS Lambda function to process messages from the queue independently.  
D. Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to deliver notifications containing payloads to process. Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as a subscriber.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Processing order must be preserved, and operational overhead must be minimal. An SQS FIFO queue preserves order within a message group and guarantees exactly-once processing, and a Lambda function reads from it as an event source — no servers involved.  
Why B is not selected: SNS doesn't guarantee delivery order to subscribers.  
Why C is not selected: A standard queue can reorder messages, so strict ordering isn't guaranteed.  
Why D is not selected: A topic with a plain queue subscriber also doesn't preserve order, and the scenario doesn't even describe a processor for it.

---

150\. A company is migrating an application from on-premises servers to Amazon EC2 instances. As part of the migration design requirements, a solutions architect must implement infrastructure metric alarms. The company does not need to take action if CPU utilization increases to more than 50% for a short burst of time. However, if the CPU utilization increases to more than 50% and read IOPS on the disk are high at the same time, the company needs to act as soon as possible. The solutions architect also must reduce false alarms.  
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Create Amazon CloudWatch composite alarms where possible.  
B. Create Amazon CloudWatch dashboards to visualize the metrics and react to issues quickly.  
C. Create Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries to monitor the application and raise an alarm.  
D. Create single Amazon CloudWatch metric alarms with multiple metric thresholds where possible.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Action is only needed when two conditions hold at the same time — high CPU utilization and high disk read IOPS. A CloudWatch composite alarm combines multiple alarms with a logical expression and fires only when they coincide, which is exactly what eliminates false alarms from short spikes.  
Why B is not selected: Dashboards are useful for eyeballing metrics but don't create automatic notifications.  
Why C is not selected: Synthetics canaries check application endpoint availability from the outside and have nothing to do with instance metrics.  
Why D is not selected: A regular CloudWatch alarm tracks a single metric — you can't set a condition spanning two different metrics in one.

---

151\. A company wants to migrate its on-premises data center to AWS. According to the company's compliance requirements, the company can use only the ap-northeast-3 Region. Company administrators are not permitted to connect VPCs to the internet.  
Which solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Use AWS Control Tower to implement data residency guardrails to deny internet access and deny access to all AWS Regions except ap-northeast-3.  
B. Use rules in AWS WAF to prevent internet access. Deny access to all AWS Regions except ap-northeast-3 in the AWS account settings.  
C. Use AWS Organizations to configure service control policies (SCPS) that prevent VPCs from gaining internet access. Deny access to all AWS Regions except ap-northeast-3.  
D. Create an outbound rule for the network ACL in each VPC to deny all traffic from 0.0.0.0/0. Create an IAM policy for each user to prevent the use of any AWS Region other than ap-northeast-3.  
E. Use AWS Config to activate managed rules to detect and alert for internet gateways and to detect and alert for new resources deployed outside of ap-northeast-3.  
Answer: AC  
Explanation: There are two requirements: operate only in ap-northeast-3, and prevent VPCs from reaching the internet, and both must hold for everyone, including administrators. Both are met by preventive, organization-level guardrails. AWS Control Tower offers ready-made data residency guardrails that deny both resource creation in other Regions and attaching internet gateways (A). The same outcome can be built manually with service control policies (SCPs) in AWS Organizations — using the aws:RequestedRegion condition and denying creation of internet gateways and NAT (C). The key point: the requirement that "administrators are not permitted" is only satisfied by SCPs, because an administrator can rewrite an IAM policy on themselves.  
Why B is not selected: AWS WAF filters HTTP requests to applications and doesn't control VPC internet access. There's also no "deny Regions account-wide" setting.  
Why D is not selected: A network ACL can be changed back, and an administrator can rewrite an IAM policy on themselves. Neither is a preventive restriction that can't be bypassed from inside the account.  
Why E is not selected: AWS Config detects and alerts after the fact. The requirement is to prevent these resources from being created, not to find out about them afterward.

---

152\. A company uses a three-tier web application to provide training to new employees. The application is accessed for only 12 hours every day. The company is using an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance to store information and wants to minimize costs.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Configure an IAM policy for AWS Systems Manager Session Manager. Create an IAM role for the policy. Update the trust relationship of the role. Set up automatic start and stop for the DB instance.  
B. Create an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cache cluster that gives users the ability to access the data from the cache when the DB instance is stopped. Invalidate the cache after the DB instance is started.  
C. Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. Create an IAM role that grants access to Amazon RDS. Attach the role to the EC2 instance. Configure a cron job to start and stop the EC2 instance on the desired schedule.  
D. Create AWS Lambda functions to start and stop the DB instance. Create Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) scheduled rules to invoke the Lambda functions. Configure the Lambda functions as event targets for the rules.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The application is only accessed for 12 hours a day, so the database shouldn't be billed for the other 12. A stopped RDS instance isn't charged for compute (only storage and snapshots continue to accrue), and the question is really about what stops and starts it. The standard pairing is an EventBridge scheduled rule invoking a Lambda function that calls Stop and Start. Keep in mind RDS's limit: a stopped instance restarts automatically after 7 days, so the schedule needs to stop it regularly, which is exactly what happens here.  
Why A is not selected: Session Manager provides access to servers, not scheduling. The role and trust policy have nothing to do with stopping the database.  
Why B is not selected: A Redis cache doesn't replace the database — writes and ad hoc queries still need somewhere to go. It also adds another always-on service, increasing cost.  
Why C is not selected: A dedicated EC2 instance with cron just to make two API calls is a machine that still needs to be paid for and maintained. The serverless pairing is cheaper and more reliable.

---

153\. A company sells ringtones created from clips of popular songs. The files containing the ringtones are stored in Amazon S3 Standard and are at least 128 KB in size. The company has millions of files, but downloads are infrequent for ringtones older than 90 days. The company needs to save money on storage while keeping the most accessed files readily available for its users.  
Which action should the company take to meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Configure S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage for the initial storage tier of the objects.  
B. Move the files to S3 Intelligent-Tiering and configure it to move objects to a less expensive storage tier after 90 days.  
C. Configure S3 inventory to manage objects and move them to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard- 1A) after 90 days.  
D. Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy that moves the objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-1A) after 90 days.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The access pattern is known and tied to object age: heavily downloaded for the first 90 days, rarely after. A known pattern like this is most cheaply described with a Lifecycle rule, and the requirement to keep "the most accessed files readily available" means the target class must still serve files instantly — that's Standard-IA. The file size is mentioned for a reason: Standard-IA has a minimum billable object size of 128 KB, and the "at least 128 KB" condition confirms there's no small-object overcharge.  
Why A is not selected: Putting objects straight into Standard-IA is a bad deal — for the first 90 days they're downloaded heavily, and Standard-IA charges per gigabyte retrieved. There's also a 30-day minimum storage duration.  
Why B is not selected: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects after 30 days without access and its threshold can't be set to 90 days. Across millions of files it also adds a monthly monitoring charge per object.  
Why C is not selected: S3 Inventory is a CSV or Parquet report of bucket contents. It doesn't move anything itself — moving objects would still require a Lifecycle rule or Batch Operations.

---

154\. A company needs to save the results from a medical trial to an Amazon S3 repository. The repository must allow a few scientists to add new files and must restrict all other users to read-only access. No users can have the ability to modify or delete any files in the repository. The company must keep every file in the repository for a minimum of 1 year after its creation date.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a legal hold of 1 year.  
B. Use S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a retention period of 365 days.  
C. Use an IAM role to restrict all users from deleting or changing objects in the S3 bucket. Use an S3 bucket policy to only allow the IAM role.  
D. Configure the S3 bucket to invoke an AWS Lambda function every time an object is added. Configure the function to track the hash of the saved object so that modified objects can be marked accordingly.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Three requirements are handled by different mechanisms, but the decisive one is "no users can have the ability to modify or delete any files," with a minimum retention of one year from the creation date. The only guarantee that neither an administrator nor root can bypass is S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 365-day retention period. Write access for a few scientists and read-only access for everyone else is granted through an ordinary bucket policy — that part of the requirement is orthogonal and doesn't affect the choice of option. Also note the distinction: the retention period is tied to the object version's creation date, while a legal hold has no expiration date and is removed manually via a separate permission.  
Why A is not selected: Governance mode can routinely be bypassed with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission, and "a legal hold for one year" isn't a real construct: a legal hold has no duration and stays in place until it is removed.  
Why C is not selected: The role and bucket policy control who is allowed to do what. Whoever writes these policies can also rewrite them, so they don't provide immutability.  
Why D is not selected: A hash computed by the Lambda function only records that an object was changed, after the fact. The requirement is to prevent modification, not to detect it after it happens.

---

155\. A large media company hosts a web application on AWS. The company wants to start caching confidential media files so that users around the world will have reliable access to the files. The content is stored in Amazon S3 buckets. The company must deliver the content quickly, regardless of where the requests originate geographically.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS DataSync to connect the S3 buckets to the web application.  
B. Deploy AWS Global Accelerator to connect the S3 buckets to the web application.  
C. Deploy Amazon CloudFront to connect the S3 buckets to CloudFront edge servers.  
D. Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to connect the S3 buckets to the web application.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The goal is to deliver files quickly to users worldwide while keeping the content confidential. CloudFront caches objects at edge locations, so requests are served close to the user, and access to the bucket is locked down with origin access control: no one can reach S3 directly — files are served only through the distribution, where signed URLs or signed cookies can be enabled.  
Why A is not selected: DataSync copies data between storage systems and isn't a tool for delivering content to end users.  
Why B is not selected: Global Accelerator optimizes the network path to applications, but it doesn't cache objects and doesn't work with S3 as a content origin.  
Why D is not selected: SQS is a message queue and has nothing to do with delivering media files.

---

156\. A company produces batch data that comes from different databases. The company also produces live stream data from network sensors and application APIs. The company needs to consolidate all the data into one place for business analytics. The company needs to process the incoming data and then stage the data in different Amazon S3 buckets. Teams will later run one-time queries and import the data into a business intelligence tool to show key performance indicators (KPIs).  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)  
A. Use Amazon Athena for one-time queries. Use Amazon QuickSight to create dashboards for KPIs.  
B. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for one-time queries. Use Amazon QuickSight to create dashboards for KPIs.  
C. Create custom AWS Lambda functions to move the individual records from the databases to an Amazon Redshift cluster.  
D. Use an AWS Glue extract, transform, and load (ETL) job to convert the data into JSON format. Load the data into multiple Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) clusters.  
E. Use blueprints in AWS Lake Formation to identify the data that can be ingested into a data lake. Use AWS Glue to crawl the source, extract the data, and load the data into Amazon S3 in Apache Parquet format.  
Answer: AE  
Explanation: Data arrives both as batches from databases and as streams from sensors, and it all needs to land in one place with minimal effort. Blueprints in AWS Lake Formation describe common ingestion scenarios, and AWS Glue jobs crawl the sources and land the data in S3 in Apache Parquet format (E). One-time queries against that data are run with Athena, and QuickSight builds the KPI dashboards (A).  
Why B is not selected: Kinesis Data Analytics processes streams in real time — it doesn't run one-time queries against data already staged in S3.  
Why C is not selected: Custom functions for moving individual records mean code to write and maintain, and Redshift is overkill here.  
Why D is not selected: JSON loses to Parquet on query cost, and multiple OpenSearch clusters are unnecessary, expensive infrastructure.

---

157\. A company stores data in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster. The company must store all the data for 5 years and must delete all the data after 5 years. The company also must indefinitely keep audit logs of actions that are performed within the database. Currently, the company has automated backups configured for Aurora.  
Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Take a manual snapshot of the DB cluster.  
B. Create a lifecycle policy for the automated backups.  
C. Configure automated backup retention for 5 years.  
D. Configure an Amazon CloudWatch Logs export for the DB cluster.  
E. Use AWS Backup to take the backups and to keep the backups for 5 years.  
Answer: DE  
Explanation: There are two requirements. Storing data for five years and then deleting it: Aurora's automated backups are capped at 35 days, so AWS Backup is needed, with a plan and a five-year retention period (E). Indefinite audit logs of actions performed within the database: enable a CloudWatch Logs export for the cluster, where the log group's retention can be set to never expire (D).  
Why A is not selected: A manual snapshot is a single point-in-time capture, not a continuous five-year retention strategy.  
Why B is not selected: Aurora's automated backups have no lifecycle policy — their retention is capped at 35 days.  
Why C is not selected: Automated backups can't be configured with a five-year retention period — the limit is 35 days.

---

158\. A solutions architect is optimizing a website for an upcoming musical event. Videos of the performances will be streamed in real time and then will be available on demand. The event is expected to attract a global online audience.  
Which service will improve the performance of both the real-time and on-demand streaming?  
A. Amazon CloudFront  
B. AWS Global Accelerator  
C. Amazon Route 53  
D. Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration  
Answer: A  
Explanation: CloudFront speeds up both the live stream and the on-demand playback: video segments (HLS or DASH) are cached at edge locations, so thousands of viewers in a region get them locally instead of from the origin. For a live event this also protects the origin from a flood of requests for the same segments. The other services solve different problems: Global Accelerator speeds up TCP and UDP applications, Route 53 handles DNS routing, and S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads into S3.  
Why B is not selected: Global Accelerator optimizes the path to application endpoints, but it doesn't cache content, and caching is exactly what pays off when streaming video at scale.  
Why C is not selected: Route 53 only routes the client to the right resource and doesn't change the performance of the delivery itself.  
Why D is not selected: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploading files into a bucket, not delivering video to viewers.

---

159\. A company is running a publicly accessible serverless application that uses Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. The application’s traffic recently spiked due to fraudulent requests from botnets.  
Which steps should a solutions architect take to block requests from unauthorized users? (Choose two.)  
A. Create a usage plan with an API key that is shared with genuine users only.  
B. Integrate logic within the Lambda function to ignore the requests from fraudulent IP addresses.  
C. Implement an AWS WAF rule to target malicious requests and trigger actions to filter them out.  
D. Convert the existing public API to a private API. Update the DNS records to redirect users to the new API endpoint.  
E. Create an IAM role for each user attempting to access the API. A user will assume the role when making the API call.  
Answer: AC  
Explanation: The goal is to block requests from unauthorized parties at the entry point, before they reach Lambda, using two complementary controls. A usage plan with an API key (A) separates legitimate users from everyone else: without a key, API Gateway itself rejects the request, and this also enables quotas and throttling.
