The company hosts the API on three Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The API consists of static and dynamic front-end content along with backend workers that process sales requests asynchronously.  
The company is expecting a significant and sudden increase in the number of sales requests during events for the launch of new products.  
What should a solutions architect recommend to ensure that all the requests are processed successfully?  
A. Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the dynamic content. Increase the number of EC2 instances to handle the increase in traffic.  
B. Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the static content. Place the EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group to launch new instances based on network traffic.  
C. Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the dynamic content. Add an Amazon ElastiCache instance in front of the ALB to reduce traffic for the API to handle.  
D. Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the static content. Add an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to receive requests from the website for later processing by the EC2 instances.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: A sharp, sudden surge is expected, and every order must be processed. CloudFront takes the static content off the instances, and purchase requests are accepted into an SQS queue: the queue accepts them instantly and holds them until the processors work through them. This way no request is lost, even if the instances temporarily can't keep up.  
Why A is not selected: Manually adding instances can't keep up with a sudden spike, and caching dynamic content through CloudFront provides little benefit.  
Why B is not selected: An Auto Scaling group based on network traffic takes minutes to grow, and requests that arrived earlier would still be dropped during the overload.  
Why C is not selected: A cache in front of the load balancer doesn't help with writing orders, and CloudFront for dynamic content doesn't solve the problem of preserving them.

---

329\. A security audit reveals that Amazon EC2 instances are not being patched regularly. A solutions architect needs to provide a solution that will run regular security scans across a large fleet of EC2 instances. The solution should also patch the EC2 instances on a regular schedule and provide a report of each instance’s patch status.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Set up Amazon Macie to scan the EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities. Set up a cron job on each EC2 instance to patch the instance on a regular schedule.  
B. Turn on Amazon GuardDuty in the account. Configure GuardDuty to scan the EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities. Set up AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to patch the EC2 instances on a regular schedule.  
C. Set up Amazon Detective to scan the EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities. Set up an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule to patch the EC2 instances on a regular schedule.  
D. Turn on Amazon Inspector in the account. Configure Amazon Inspector to scan the EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities. Set up AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to patch the EC2 instances on a regular schedule.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: There are two requirements here, met by two different services. Vulnerability scanning is Amazon Inspector: continuous scanning of packages on the instances via the SSM agent, with prioritized findings. Regularly applying updates and reporting patch status is Patch Manager, part of Systems Manager: patch baselines, maintenance windows, and a compliance report per instance. Both parts are managed, with no custom code required.  
Why A is not selected: Macie analyzes data in S3, and a cron job on every instance is a manual scheme with no reporting or compliance tracking.  
Why B is not selected: GuardDuty doesn't scan packages for vulnerabilities, and Session Manager provides access to an instance but doesn't manage patching.  
Why C is not selected: Amazon Detective helps investigate incidents from logs rather than find vulnerabilities, and an EventBridge schedule by itself doesn't apply any patches.

---

330\. A company is planning to store data on Amazon RDS DB instances. The company must encrypt the data at rest.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?  
A. Create a key in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Enable encryption for the DB instances.  
B. Create an encryption key. Store the key in AWS Secrets Manager. Use the key to encrypt the DB instances.  
C. Generate a certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Enable SSL/TLS on the DB instances by using the certificate.  
D. Generate a certificate in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Enable SSL/TLS on the DB instances by using the certificate.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Encryption at rest in RDS is turned on when the instance is created (or when restoring from an encrypted snapshot copy) and relies on a KMS key — either your own customer managed key or the AWS default key. This simultaneously encrypts the data on disk, automated backups, snapshots, and read replicas. Don't confuse this with encryption in transit — that's handled by a TLS connection to the database, which is a separate matter.  
Why B is not selected: Secrets Manager stores secrets, such as database passwords. It doesn't provide keys for encrypting RDS storage — that's KMS's job.  
Why C is not selected: A certificate from ACM provides encryption for the connection, i.e., protection of data in transit. It doesn't encrypt the data on disk.  
Why D is not selected: Same issue, plus the IAM certificate store is a legacy mechanism that has since been replaced by ACM.

---

331\. A company must migrate 20 TB of data from a data center to the AWS Cloud within 30 days. The company’s network bandwidth is limited to 15 Mbps and cannot exceed 70% utilization.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS Snowball.  
B. Use AWS DataSync.  
C. Use a secure VPN connection.  
D. Use Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: This is solved with arithmetic. The available bandwidth is 70% of 15 Mbps, or about 10.5 Mbps, which works out to roughly 113 GB per day. At that rate, twenty terabytes would take about 180 days, but the deadline is 30. Any online method fails on time regardless of how convenient it is, so what's left is offline delivery: Snowball. Keep this rule of thumb in mind: 100 Mbps ≈ 1 TB per day, 1 Gbps ≈ 10 TB per day — enough to rule out online options in ten seconds.  
Why B is not selected: DataSync transfers data over the same link. It speeds up and verifies the transfer, but it doesn't change the underlying physics of 10.5 Mbps.  
Why C is not selected: A VPN is the same link plus the overhead of encryption. The deadline is even less achievable.  
Why D is not selected: Transfer Acceleration optimizes the route from an edge location to the bucket, but the bottleneck here is the data center's own uplink, which the acceleration can't reach.

---

332\. A company needs to provide its employees with secure access to confidential and sensitive files. The company wants to ensure that the files can be accessed only by authorized users. The files must be downloaded securely to the employees’ devices.  
The files are stored in an on-premises Windows file server. However, due to an increase in remote usage, the file server is running out of capacity.  
.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Migrate the file server to an Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet. Configure the security group to limit inbound traffic to the employees’ IP addresses.  
B. Migrate the files to an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. Integrate the Amazon FSx file system with the on-premises Active Directory. Configure AWS Client VPN.  
C. Migrate the files to Amazon S3, and create a private VPC endpoint. Create a signed URL to allow download.  
D. Migrate the files to Amazon S3, and create a public VPC endpoint. Allow employees to sign on with AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On).  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The files sit on a Windows share with domain-based permissions, space is running out, and employees work remotely. Migrating to FSx for Windows File Server preserves the familiar SMB protocol and NTFS permissions, integrating with the existing Active Directory preserves the same authorization, and Client VPN gives remote employees a secure channel into the VPC where the file system lives. Downloads then go over the encrypted tunnel rather than the open internet.  
Why A is not selected: A file server in a public subnet with an IP-based filter for employees means SMB exposed to the internet and manually maintaining an address list. It's both insecure and inconvenient for remote work.  
Why C is not selected: A private endpoint is reachable only from inside the VPC, and employees work from outside it, so they wouldn't be able to reach it. Moving to object storage also changes how people are used to working with files.  
Why D is not selected: A "public VPC endpoint" doesn't exist. And signing in through Identity Center doesn't solve the problem of securely delivering files to devices.

---

333\. A company’s application runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The instances run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. On the first day of every month at midnight, the application becomes much slower when the month-end financial calculation batch runs. This causes the CPU utilization of the EC2 instances to immediately peak to 100%, which disrupts the application.  
What should a solutions architect recommend to ensure the application is able to handle the workload and avoid downtime?  
A. Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the ALB.  
B. Configure an EC2 Auto Scaling simple scaling policy based on CPU utilization.  
C. Configure an EC2 Auto Scaling scheduled scaling policy based on the monthly schedule.  
D. Configure Amazon ElastiCache to remove some of the workload from the EC2 instances.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The spike is known in advance: midnight on the first of every month. That means the instances need to be scaled up before it starts, not reactively. A scheduled scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group ramps up capacity ahead of the known time and scales back down afterward, so CPU utilization never gets pinned at a hundred percent.  
Why A is not selected: CloudFront caches content for users, while the load is generated by a batch calculation inside the application.  
Why B is not selected: A simple CPU-based scaling policy triggers only after utilization has already hit a hundred percent: the application will be unavailable for the few minutes it takes new instances to launch.  
Why D is not selected: A cache offloads read traffic, but the peak load here comes from a computational task, not from data requests.

---

334\. A company wants to give a customer the ability to use on-premises Microsoft Active Directory to download files that are stored in Amazon S3. The customer’s application uses an SFTP client to download the files.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead and no changes to the customer’s application?  
A. Set up AWS Transfer Family with SFTP for Amazon S3. Configure integrated Active Directory authentication.  
B. Set up AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to synchronize the on-premises client with Amazon S3. Configure integrated Active Directory authentication.  
C. Set up AWS DataSync to synchronize between the on-premises location and the S3 location by using AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On).  
D. Set up a Windows Amazon EC2 instance with SFTP to connect the on-premises client with Amazon S3. Integrate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).  
Answer: A  
Explanation: There's an SFTP client that can't be changed, and a local Active Directory where the users live. AWS Transfer Family provides a managed SFTP endpoint directly on top of an S3 bucket and can authenticate users against an external directory, including Active Directory via AWS Managed Microsoft AD or a custom identity provider. The application keeps working over SFTP, with no infrastructure to run underneath it.  
Why B is not selected: AWS DMS migrates databases. It provides neither SFTP nor file synchronization.  
Why C is not selected: DataSync copies data on a schedule, but it doesn't give the client an SFTP endpoint for downloading files.  
Why D is not selected: A custom SFTP server on a Windows instance is a machine that has to be maintained, patched, and scaled. A managed service does the same thing without a server.

---

335\. A company is experiencing sudden increases in demand. The company needs to provision large Amazon EC2 instances from an Amazon Machine Image (AMI). The instances will run in an Auto Scaling group. The company needs a solution that provides minimum initialization latency to meet the demand.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Use the aws ec2 register-image command to create an AMI from a snapshot. Use AWS Step Functions to replace the AMI in the Auto Scaling group.  
B. Enable Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) fast snapshot restore on a snapshot. Provision an AMI by using the snapshot. Replace the AMI in the Auto Scaling group with the new AMI.  
C. Enable AMI creation and define lifecycle rules in Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (Amazon DLM). Create an AWS Lambda function that modifies the AMI in the Auto Scaling group.  
D. Use Amazon EventBridge to invoke AWS Backup lifecycle policies that provision AMIs. Configure Auto Scaling group capacity limits as an event source in EventBridge.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Startup latency when launching an instance from an image happens because the root volume's blocks are pulled from the snapshot on first access. Fast snapshot restore eliminates exactly that: volumes created from a snapshot with the feature enabled run at full performance immediately. An AMI is created from such a snapshot, and the Auto Scaling group is switched over to it.  
Why A is not selected: Registering an image from a snapshot by itself doesn't speed up initialization, and Step Functions only orchestrates the steps.  
Why C is not selected: Amazon DLM automates scheduled image creation, but it doesn't affect how fast the first launch is.  
Why D is not selected: AWS Backup manages backups, and Auto Scaling group capacity limits aren't an EventBridge event source.

---

336\. A company hosts a multi-tier web application that uses an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster for storage. The application tier is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances. The company’s IT security guidelines mandate that the database credentials be encrypted and rotated every 14 days.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement with the LEAST operational effort?  
A. Create a new AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption key. Use AWS Secrets Manager to create a new secret that uses the KMS key with the appropriate credentials. Associate the secret with the Aurora DB cluster. Configure a custom rotation period of 14 days.  
B. Create two parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: one for the user name as a string parameter and one that uses the SecureString type for the password. Select AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption for the password parameter, and load these parameters in the application tier. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the password every 14 days.  
C. Store a file that contains the credentials in an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encrypted Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the EFS file system in all EC2 instances of the application tier. Restrict the access to the file on the file system so that the application can read the file and that only super users can modify the file. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the key in Aurora every 14 days and writes new credentials into the file.  
D. Store a file that contains the credentials in an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encrypted Amazon S3 bucket that the application uses to load the credentials. Download the file to the application regularly to ensure that the correct credentials are used. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the Aurora credentials every 14 days and uploads these credentials to the file in the S3 bucket.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The requirement is to encrypt database credentials and rotate them every 14 days with the least operational effort. Secrets Manager does both through configuration: the secret is encrypted with a KMS key, associated with the Aurora cluster, and the rotation schedule is set to any number of days — 14 is set as a custom period. AWS itself provides the rotation function for supported databases, so there's no need to write one. Every other option proposes building the same result out of custom code.  
Why B is not selected: Parameter Store stores the password encrypted, but rotation would have to be implemented and maintained in a Lambda function yourself. That's noticeably more work than setting a rotation period in Secrets Manager.  
Why C is not selected: A file on a shared file system plus a custom rotation function adds development effort, file access permissions to manage, and the risk of the database and file getting out of sync.  
Why D is not selected: Downloading the password file from the bucket "regularly" means there's a window in which the application uses a stale password, and again, custom rotation code.

---

337\. A company has deployed a web application on AWS. The company hosts the backend database on Amazon RDS for MySQL with a primary DB instance and five read replicas to support scaling needs. The read replicas must lag no more than 1 second behind the primary DB instance. The database routinely runs scheduled stored procedures.  
As traffic on the website increases, the replicas experience additional lag during periods of peak load. A solutions architect must reduce the replication lag as much as possible. The solutions architect must minimize changes to the application code and must minimize ongoing operational overhead.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Migrate the database to Amazon Aurora MySQL. Replace the read replicas with Aurora Replicas, and configure Aurora Auto Scaling. Replace the stored procedures with Aurora MySQL native functions.  
B. Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster in front of the database. Modify the application to check the cache before the application queries the database. Replace the stored procedures with AWS Lambda functions.  
C. Migrate the database to a MySQL database that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. Choose large, compute optimized EC2 instances for all replica nodes. Maintain the stored procedures on the EC2 instances.  
D. Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB. Provision a large number of read capacity units (RCUs) to support the required throughput, and configure on-demand capacity scaling. Replace the stored procedures with DynamoDB streams.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Replica lag in RDS for MySQL grows under load because replication goes through the binary log and is applied on each replica independently. Aurora works differently: replicas read from the same shared storage, so lag is measured in milliseconds and is almost independent of load. Aurora Auto Scaling adds replicas as traffic grows, and stored procedures are replaced with native Aurora MySQL functions — the application changes minimally.  
Why B is not selected: A cache in front of the database requires reworking the application's logic and doesn't reduce lag on the replicas themselves.  
Why C is not selected: Self-managed MySQL instances mean the most operational overhead, while the replication mechanism stays the same, with the same lag.  
Why D is not selected: DynamoDB means rewriting the data model and the queries, and DynamoDB streams don't replace stored procedures.

---

338\. A solutions architect must create a disaster recovery (DR) plan for a high-volume software as a service (SaaS) platform. All data for the platform is stored in an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster.  
The DR plan must replicate data to a secondary AWS Region.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Use MySQL binary log replication to an Aurora cluster in the secondary Region. Provision one DB instance for the Aurora cluster in the secondary Region.  
B. Set up an Aurora global database for the DB cluster. When setup is complete, remove the DB instance from the secondary Region.  
C. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to continuously replicate data to an Aurora cluster in the secondary Region. Remove the DB instance from the secondary Region.  
D. Set up an Aurora global database for the DB cluster. Specify a minimum of one DB instance in the secondary Region.  
Answer: D  
Review status: Disputed key (alternative: B)  
Dispute note: AWS documents a headless configuration for Aurora Global Database: a secondary cluster with no instances replicates data at the storage level and costs less. Read literally, "MOST cost-effectively" favors option B; the case for key D is that without an instance, the secondary region isn't ready to take on load immediately  
Explanation: This is a disputed question. The dump's answer key is option D: an Aurora global database replicates data to the second Region at the storage level with about a one-second lag, and at least one instance is kept there so the Region is ready to take on load. A strong alternative is option B, a headless configuration: AWS explicitly documents a secondary cluster with no instances, which is cheaper because you only pay for storage and replication. Read literally, "most cost-effective" favors B; read as "the disaster recovery plan must be ready to work immediately," D wins.  
Why A is not selected: MySQL binary log replication as a way to replicate Aurora across Regions is slower and requires manual upkeep, whereas a global database does this at the storage level.  
Why B is not selected: Technically this configuration is valid and cheaper than the key's answer, which is why the question is flagged as disputed: the only objection to it is that a Region with no instance won't accept traffic immediately after a disaster.  
Why C is not selected: DMS is a migration tool, not Aurora's standard mechanism for ongoing cross-Region replication: an extra component that can itself fail.

---

339\. A company has a custom application with embedded credentials that retrieves information from an Amazon RDS MySQL DB instance. Management says the application must be made more secure with the least amount of programming effort.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to create keys. Configure the application to load the database credentials from AWS KMS. Enable automatic key rotation.  
B. Create credentials on the RDS for MySQL database for the application user and store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Secrets Manager. Create an AWS Lambda function that rotates the credentials in Secret Manager.  
C. Create credentials on the RDS for MySQL database for the application user and store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Secrets Manager. Set up a credentials rotation schedule for the application user in the RDS for MySQL database using Secrets Manager.  
D. Create credentials on the RDS for MySQL database for the application user and store the credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Parameter Store. Set up a credentials rotation schedule for the application user in the RDS for MySQL database using Parameter Store.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The constraint in the wording is "with the least amount of programming effort." Secrets Manager for RDS MySQL supports rotation out of the box: you turn on a schedule, and AWS provides the function that changes the password in the database and updates the secret. The application is left with a single GetSecretValue call instead of hardcoded credentials. This is exactly what distinguishes the correct option from the similar one where you're asked to write that same rotation yourself.  
Why A is not selected: KMS manages encryption keys, not database credentials. You can't load a username and password from it.  
Why B is not selected: The design is valid, but writing a custom rotation function is exactly the programming effort the question asked to avoid: it has to be written, tested, and maintained.  
Why D is not selected: Parameter Store has no built-in rotation mechanism, so "setting up a rotation schedule through Parameter Store" isn't possible.

---

340\. A media company hosts its website on AWS. The website application’s architecture includes a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and a database that is hosted on Amazon Aurora. The company’s cybersecurity team reports that the application is vulnerable to SQL injection.  
How should the company resolve this issue?  
A. Use AWS WAF in front of the ALB. Associate the appropriate web ACLs with AWS WAF.  
B. Create an ALB listener rule to reply to SQL injections with a fixed response.  
C. Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced to block all SQL injection attempts automatically.  
D. Set up Amazon Inspector to block all SQL injection attempts automatically.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: SQL injection is an attack at the HTTP request level, and it's filtered by AWS WAF in front of the application. A web ACL is attached to the Application Load Balancer, managed rule groups are enabled (in particular the SQL database rule set), and malicious requests are blocked before they reach the instances. This is a compensating control: in parallel, the code should be fixed to use parameterized queries, but the question's requirement is satisfied specifically by WAF.  
Why B is not selected: An ALB listener rule routes by path, host, headers, and method, but it doesn't inspect the request content for signs of injection.  
Why C is not selected: Shield Advanced defends against availability attacks and doesn't parse SQL injection.  
Why D is not selected: Inspector finds vulnerabilities and reports on them, but it doesn't filter traffic or block anything.

---

341\. A company has an Amazon S3 data lake that is governed by AWS Lake Formation. The company wants to create a visualization in Amazon QuickSight by joining the data in the data lake with operational data that is stored in an Amazon Aurora MySQL database. The company wants to enforce column-level authorization so that the company’s marketing team can access only a subset of columns in the database.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use Amazon EMR to ingest the data directly from the database to the QuickSight SPICE engine. Include only the required columns.  
B. Use AWS Glue Studio to ingest the data from the database to the S3 data lake. Attach an IAM policy to the QuickSight users to enforce column-level access control. Use Amazon S3 as the data source in QuickSight.  
C. Use AWS Glue Elastic Views to create a materialized view for the database in Amazon S3. Create an S3 bucket policy to enforce column-level access control for the QuickSight users. Use Amazon S3 as the data source in QuickSight.  
D. Use a Lake Formation blueprint to ingest the data from the database to the S3 data lake. Use Lake Formation to enforce column-level access control for the QuickSight users. Use Amazon Athena as the data source in QuickSight.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The key requirement is column-level access control with the least operational overhead. Lake Formation does exactly this: it maintains a catalog, grants permissions at the table, column, and row level, and propagates them to the engines that query it — primarily Athena. So data from Aurora is ingested into the lake through a Lake Formation blueprint, column-level permissions are configured there, and QuickSight connects through Athena and automatically sees only the permitted columns. No bucket policies, no separate datasets per team.  
Why A is not selected: EMR for data ingestion is heavy machinery, and it doesn't provide column-level access control — you would have to manually prepare separate extracts.  
Why B is not selected: An IAM policy can't restrict access to individual columns within S3 files — its granularity is objects and prefixes.  
Why C is not selected: A bucket policy is even less able to distinguish columns within objects. On top of that, Glue Elastic Views is a service that never reached general availability.

---

342\. A transaction processing company has weekly scripted batch jobs that run on Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances are in an Auto Scaling group. The number of transactions can vary, but the baseline CPU utilization that is noted on each run is at least 60%. The company needs to provision the capacity 30 minutes before the jobs run.  
Currently, engineers complete this task by manually modifying the Auto Scaling group parameters. The company does not have the resources to analyze the required capacity trends for the Auto Scaling group counts. The company needs an automated way to modify the Auto Scaling group’s desired capacity.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create a dynamic scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group. Configure the policy to scale based on the CPU utilization metric. Set the target value for the metric to 60%.  
B. Create a scheduled scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group. Set the appropriate desired capacity, minimum capacity, and maximum capacity. Set the recurrence to weekly. Set the start time to 30 minutes before the batch jobs run.  
C. Create a predictive scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group. Configure the policy to scale based on forecast. Set the scaling metric to CPU utilization. Set the target value for the metric to 60%. In the policy, set the instances to pre-launch 30 minutes before the jobs run.  
D. Create an Amazon EventBridge event to invoke an AWS Lambda function when the CPU utilization metric value for the Auto Scaling group reaches 60%. Configure the Lambda function to increase the Auto Scaling group’s desired capacity and maximum capacity by 20%.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The jobs run weekly, the baseline load is known (at least 60 percent), and there is no one to analyze the patterns manually. Predictive scaling does this automatically: it builds a forecast from the metric's history and pre-launches instances ahead of time, with the pre-launch lead time set explicitly — here, 30 minutes before the jobs start.  
Why A is not selected: A dynamic scaling policy reacts only after the load appears: it can't give you 30 minutes of lead time.  
Why B is not selected: Scheduled scaling works, but it requires someone to determine and maintain the required capacity manually, and the scenario states there are no resources for that analysis.  
Why D is not selected: A custom function triggered by an alarm is both extra code and a reaction after the fact, not proactive scale-out.

---

343\. A solutions architect is designing a company’s disaster recovery (DR) architecture. The company has a MySQL database that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance in a private subnet with scheduled backup. The DR design needs to include multiple AWS Regions.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Migrate the MySQL database to multiple EC2 instances. Configure a standby EC2 instance in the DR Region. Turn on replication.  
B. Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon RDS. Use a Multi-AZ deployment. Turn on read replication for the primary DB instance in the different Availability Zones.  
C. Migrate the MySQL database to an Amazon Aurora global database. Host the primary DB cluster in the primary Region. Host the secondary DB cluster in the DR Region.  
D. Store the scheduled backup of the MySQL database in an Amazon S3 bucket that is configured for S3 Cross- Region Replication (CRR). Use the data backup to restore the database in the DR Region.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The disaster recovery design must span multiple AWS Regions with the least operational overhead. Aurora Global Database does this natively: the primary DB cluster runs in the primary Region, the secondary cluster runs in the DR Region, replication happens at the storage layer with typically sub-second lag, and promoting the secondary cluster is a single operation. The self-managed MySQL setup, along with all its operational burden, goes away entirely.  
Why A is not selected: Self-managed instances with manually configured replication mean the most work and the most risk, and failover is manual too.  
Why B is not selected: Multi-AZ configuration and read replicas in different Availability Zones operate within a single Region: the multi-Region requirement isn't met.  
Why D is not selected: Restoring from a backup stored in a bucket takes hours and requires manual steps, and the data lags by the interval between backups.

---

344\. A company has a Java application that uses Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to parse messages. The application cannot parse messages that are larger than 256 KB in size. The company wants to implement a solution to give the application the ability to parse messages as large as 50 MB.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the FEWEST changes to the code?  
A. Use the Amazon SQS Extended Client Library for Java to host messages that are larger than 256 KB in Amazon S3.  
B. Use Amazon EventBridge to post large messages from the application instead of Amazon SQS.  
C. Change the limit in Amazon SQS to handle messages that are larger than 256 KB.  
D. Store messages that are larger than 256 KB in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS). Configure Amazon SQS to reference this location in the messages.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The 256 KB limit is a hard limit of the SQS service itself and can't be changed. The standard workaround is the Amazon SQS Extended Client Library for Java: the body of a large message is stored in S3, and only a reference to the object goes through the queue, with the library handling this transparently. The application code changes minimally — you just swap in the extended client.  
Why B is not selected: EventBridge has its own 256 KB event size limit, so it doesn't solve the problem, and it would mean changing the entire messaging model.  
Why C is not selected: The 256 KB limit is a hard service limit that can't be raised through configuration or a support request.  
Why D is not selected: Referencing files stored in EFS could work in principle, but you would have to write all the logic for writing, reading, and cleaning up files yourself, whereas the ready-made library does this for you.

---

345\. A company wants to restrict access to the content of one of its main web applications and to protect the content by using authorization techniques available on AWS. The company wants to implement a serverless architecture and an authentication solution for fewer than 100 users. The solution needs to integrate with the main web application and serve web content globally. The solution must also scale as the company's user base grows while providing the lowest login latency possible.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Use Amazon Cognito for authentication. Use [email protected] for authorization. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve the web application globally.  
B. Use AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory for authentication. Use AWS Lambda for authorization. Use an Application Load Balancer to serve the web application globally.  
C. Use Amazon Cognito for authentication. Use AWS Lambda for authorization. Use Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration to serve the web application globally.  
D. Use AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory for authentication. Use [email protected] for authorization. Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk to serve the web application globally.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Fewer than 100 users, a serverless architecture, global content delivery, and the lowest possible login latency. Cognito handles authentication (essentially free at this user count), CloudFront serves the application from edge locations, and token validation runs in Lambda@Edge — that is, at the same edge location the user connected to, without a round trip to the origin Region. That's exactly what minimizes login latency.  
Why B is not selected: AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a directory service billed hourly, overkill for a hundred users, and an ALB doesn't serve content globally.  
Why C is not selected: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads into a bucket, not the serving of a website, and a regular Lambda function runs in a single Region, which adds latency.  
Why D is not selected: The AD directory is again overkill and expensive, and Elastic Beanstalk means servers — a step away from a serverless architecture.

---

346\. A company has an aging network-attached storage (NAS) array in its data center. The NAS array presents SMB shares and NFS shares to client workstations. The company does not want to purchase a new NAS array. The company also does not want to incur the cost of renewing the NAS array’s support contract. Some of the data is accessed frequently, but much of the data is inactive.  
A solutions architect needs to implement a solution that migrates the data to Amazon S3, uses S3 Lifecycle policies, and maintains the same look and feel for the client workstations. The solutions architect has identified AWS Storage Gateway as part of the solution.  
Which type of storage gateway should the solutions architect provision to meet these requirements?  
A. Volume Gateway  
B. Tape Gateway  
C. Amazon FSx File Gateway  
D. Amazon S3 File Gateway  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Client workstations need to keep the same look and feel, and the data must move to S3 and fall under lifecycle rules. That's Amazon S3 File Gateway: it exposes NFS and SMB shares while storing each file as an object in a bucket, so lifecycle rules apply normally, frequently accessed data is cached locally, and the workstations notice no difference.  
Why A is not selected: Volume Gateway presents block volumes over iSCSI and stores data as snapshots rather than individual objects: lifecycle rules can't be applied to user files this way, and the workstations would lose their familiar shares.  
Why B is not selected: Tape Gateway emulates a virtual tape library for backup software; it has nothing to do with the workstations' network shares.  
Why C is not selected: FSx File Gateway caches access to FSx file systems, not S3, so there are no S3 lifecycle rules in this setup.

---

347\. A company has an application that is running on Amazon EC2 instances. A solutions architect has standardized the company on a particular instance family and various instance sizes based on the current needs of the company.  
The company wants to maximize cost savings for the application over the next 3 years. The company needs to be able to change the instance family and sizes in the next 6 months based on application popularity and usage.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Compute Savings Plan  
B. EC2 Instance Savings Plan  
C. Zonal Reserved Instances  
D. Standard Reserved Instances  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The commitment runs for three years, but the instance family and size may change within six months. A Compute Savings Plan gives up to a 66 percent discount and isn't tied to instance family, size, Region, or even service — the discount carries over when you move to different instances, Fargate, or Lambda.  
Why B is not selected: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan is tied to a specific instance family in a specific Region: changing the family voids the discount.  
Why C is not selected: Zonal Reserved Instances lock in a fixed instance type and Availability Zone.  
Why D is not selected: Standard Reserved Instances give the biggest discount but don't allow changing the instance family.

---

348\. A company collects data from a large number of participants who use wearable devices. The company stores the data in an Amazon DynamoDB table and uses applications to analyze the data. The data workload is constant and predictable. The company wants to stay at or below its forecasted budget for DynamoDB.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Use provisioned mode and DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA). Reserve capacity for the forecasted workload.  
B. Use provisioned mode. Specify the read capacity units (RCUs) and write capacity units (WCUs).  
C. Use on-demand mode. Set the read capacity units (RCUs) and write capacity units (WCUs) high enough to accommodate changes in the workload.  
D. Use on-demand mode. Specify the read capacity units (RCUs) and write capacity units (WCUs) with reserved capacity.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The workload is constant and predictable, and the budget needs to stay in check. Provisioned mode with defined read and write capacity units costs less than on-demand mode under a steady workload and produces a predictable bill: you pay for provisioned capacity rather than per request.  
Why A is not selected: The Standard-IA table class lowers storage cost but raises the cost of requests — not cost-effective under a steady workload — and "reserving capacity" is described imprecisely here anyway.  
Why C is not selected: On-demand mode doesn't let you set capacity units at all, and under a steady workload it costs more than provisioned mode.  
Why D is not selected: On-demand mode is incompatible with both specifying capacity units and reserving capacity — no such configuration exists.

---

349\. A company stores confidential data in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database in the ap-southeast-3 Region. The database is encrypted with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. The company was recently acquired and must securely share a backup of the database with the acquiring company’s AWS account in ap-southeast-3.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Create a database snapshot. Copy the snapshot to a new unencrypted snapshot. Share the new snapshot with the acquiring company’s AWS account.  
B. Create a database snapshot. Add the acquiring company’s AWS account to the KMS key policy. Share the snapshot with the acquiring company’s AWS account.  
C. Create a database snapshot that uses a different AWS managed KMS key. Add the acquiring company’s AWS account to the KMS key alias. Share the snapshot with the acquiring company's AWS account.  
D. Create a database snapshot. Download the database snapshot. Upload the database snapshot to an Amazon S3 bucket. Update the S3 bucket policy to allow access from the acquiring company’s AWS account.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The snapshot is encrypted with a KMS key, so sharing it again takes two steps: allow the other account to use the key (update the key policy, and a grant if needed) and explicitly share the snapshot itself with that account. The receiving side typically makes its own copy of the snapshot right away, re-encrypting it with its own key so it isn't dependent on yours. An important restriction that shows up often in exam questions: a snapshot encrypted with the default AWS-managed key (aws/rds) can't be shared at all — only one encrypted with a key you manage.  
Why A is not selected: You can't copy an encrypted snapshot into an unencrypted one in RDS — there's no way to decrypt the data that way. And for confidential data, that would also be a step down in protection.  
Why C is not selected: You can't share a snapshot encrypted with an AWS managed key, and a key alias is just a convenient name — it doesn't grant access to anyone.  
Why D is not selected: You can't download an RDS snapshot to disk — the service doesn't offer that option. The workaround through an S3 upload is more complex and less secure than sharing the snapshot directly.

---

350\. A company uses a 100 GB Amazon RDS for Microsoft SQL Server Single-AZ DB instance in the us-east-1 Region to store customer transactions. The company needs high availability and automatic recovery for the DB instance.  
The company must also run reports on the RDS database several times a year. The report process causes transactions to take longer than usual to post to the customers’ accounts. The company needs a solution that will improve the performance of the report process.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Modify the DB instance from a Single-AZ DB instance to a Multi-AZ deployment.  
B. Take a snapshot of the current DB instance. Restore the snapshot to a new RDS deployment in another Availability Zone.  
C. Create a read replica of the DB instance in a different Availability Zone. Point all requests for reports to the read replica.  
D. Migrate the database to RDS Custom.  
E. Use RDS Proxy to limit reporting requests to the maintenance window.  
Answer: AC  
Review status: Low-confidence audit  
Explanation: There are two requirements here. High availability with automatic recovery means converting the instance to a Multi-AZ deployment with synchronous replication and automatic failover (A). Speeding up reports without affecting transactions means a read replica in a different Availability Zone, with all report queries directed to it (C).  
Why B is not selected: Restoring from a snapshot creates an independent copy that starts going stale immediately, and it provides no automatic failover.  
Why D is not selected: RDS Custom is for cases where you need access to the underlying operating system; it has nothing to do with availability or reporting.  
Why E is not selected: RDS Proxy manages a connection pool and can't defer queries until a maintenance window.

---

351\. A company is moving its data management application to AWS. The company wants to transition to an event-driven architecture. The architecture needs to be more distributed and to use serverless concepts while performing the different aspects of the workflow. The company also wants to minimize operational overhead.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Build out the workflow in AWS Glue. Use AWS Glue to invoke AWS Lambda functions to process the workflow steps.  
B. Build out the workflow in AWS Step Functions. Deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances. Use Step Functions to invoke the workflow steps on the EC2 instances.  
C. Build out the workflow in Amazon EventBridge. Use EventBridge to invoke AWS Lambda functions on a schedule to process the workflow steps.  
D. Build out the workflow in AWS Step Functions. Use Step Functions to create a state machine. Use the state machine to invoke AWS Lambda functions to process the workflow steps.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The requirement is an event-driven, distributed architecture built on serverless components with the least operational overhead. AWS Step Functions describes the workflow as a state machine, invokes Lambda functions at each step, and handles errors, retries, and branching — all without a single server and without custom orchestration code.  
Why A is not selected: AWS Glue is an ETL service for processing data, not an orchestrator for arbitrary workflows.  
Why B is not selected: EC2 instances in the workflow steps bring back infrastructure that has to be maintained.  
Why C is not selected: EventBridge on a schedule means periodic invocation, not an event-driven workflow with state and branching.

---

352\. A company is designing the network for an online multi-player game. The game uses the UDP networking protocol and will be deployed in eight AWS Regions. The network architecture needs to minimize latency and packet loss to give end users a high-quality gaming experience.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Setup a transit gateway in each Region. Create inter-Region peering attachments between each transit gateway.  
B. Set up AWS Global Accelerator with UDP listeners and endpoint groups in each Region.  
C. Set up Amazon CloudFront with UDP turned on. Configure an origin in each Region.  
D. Set up a VPC peering mesh between each Region. Turn on UDP for each VPC.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: UDP across eight Regions, with the requirement to minimize latency and packet loss. Global Accelerator creates UDP listeners and endpoint groups in each Region: the player enters the AWS network at the nearest edge location and then travels over the AWS backbone, where loss and jitter are significantly lower than on the public internet. The anycast IP addresses stay static, and a failed Region is pulled out of rotation within seconds.  
Why A is not selected: Transit Gateway and inter-Region peering connect AWS networks to each other. They have no effect on the path from the player to the nearest Region.  
Why C is not selected: CloudFront has no UDP support: it serves HTTP and HTTPS only.  
Why D is not selected: VPC peering provides connectivity within AWS, not improved access for outside users. There is no such thing as "turning on UDP" for peering.

---

353\. A company hosts a three-tier web application on Amazon EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone. The web application uses a self-managed MySQL database that is hosted on an EC2 instance to store data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. The MySQL database currently uses a 1 TB Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) EBS volume. The company expects traffic of 1,000 IOPS for both reads and writes at peak traffic.  
The company wants to minimize any disruptions, stabilize performance, and reduce costs while retaining the capacity for double the IOPS. The company wants to move the database tier to a fully managed solution that is highly available and fault tolerant.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Use a Multi-AZ deployment of an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with an io2 Block Express EBS volume.  
B. Use a Multi-AZ deployment of an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with a General Purpose SSD (gp2) EBS volume.  
C. Use Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering access tiers.  
D. Use two large EC2 instances to host the database in active-passive mode.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Peak traffic of 1,000 IOPS with headroom for double that, so 2,000. A 1 TB gp2 volume delivers 3,000 IOPS based on the three-IOPS-per-GB formula, which covers that with margin, and it costs noticeably less than io2. The database also moves to managed RDS for MySQL in a Multi-AZ configuration, which provides fault tolerance and removes the administrative burden.  
Why A is not selected: io2 Block Express is built for tens of thousands of operations per second and is expensive: paying for it when you only need 2,000 IOPS is wasteful.  
Why C is not selected: S3 is object storage — it cannot serve as a database.  
Why D is not selected: Two large instances in active-passive mode is still a self-managed database, and the requirement calls for a fully managed solution.

---

354\. A company hosts a serverless application on AWS. The application uses Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, and an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database. The company notices an increase in application errors that result from database connection timeouts during times of peak traffic or unpredictable traffic. The company needs a solution that reduces the application failures with the least amount of change to the code.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Reduce the Lambda concurrency rate.  
B. Enable RDS Proxy on the RDS DB instance.  
C. Resize the RDS DB instance class to accept more connections.  
D. Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand scaling.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The errors stem from connections being exhausted: during a traffic spike, Lambda spins up many concurrent instances, and each one opens its own database connection. RDS Proxy maintains a connection pool and reuses connections, and the only code change needed is pointing to the proxy endpoint instead of the database endpoint.  
Why A is not selected: Lowering the function's allowed concurrency would limit the application's throughput and cause a different kind of failure.  
Why C is not selected: A larger instance class raises the connection limit, but the problem returns with unpredictable spikes, and you'd be paying for it continuously.  
Why D is not selected: Migrating to DynamoDB means rewriting the data model and the queries — the maximum possible amount of code change.

---

355\. A company is migrating an old application to AWS. The application runs a batch job every hour and is CPU intensive. The batch job takes 15 minutes on average with an on-premises server. The server has 64 virtual CPU (vCPU) and 512 GiB of memory.  
Which solution will run the batch job within 15 minutes with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use AWS Lambda with functional scaling.  
B. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate.  
C. Use Amazon Lightsail with AWS Auto Scaling.  
D. Use AWS Batch on Amazon EC2.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The job needs 64 vCPUs and 512 GiB of memory and runs for 15 minutes — well beyond Lambda's limits and too large for a typical Fargate task. AWS Batch on EC2 automatically picks an instance type that fits the job's requirements, launches it, runs the computation, and tears the capacity down afterward — the service handles queuing and scheduling for you.  
Why A is not selected: A Lambda function is capped at roughly 10 GB of memory and 15 minutes of execution time — the requirements don't fit.  
Why B is not selected: Fargate's maximum task size is far below 64 vCPUs and 512 GiB of memory.  
Why C is not selected: Lightsail offers small, fixed configurations and isn't built for this kind of workload.

---

356\. A company stores its data objects in Amazon S3 Standard storage. A solutions architect has found that 75% of the data is rarely accessed after 30 days. The company needs all the data to remain immediately accessible with the same high availability and resiliency, but the company wants to minimize storage costs.  
Which storage solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Move the data objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days.  
B. Move the data objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days.  
C. Move the data objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) after 30 days.  
D. Move the data objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) immediately.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The phrase "the same high availability and resiliency" fixes the choice to three Availability Zones and immediate access, so the decision comes down to Standard versus Standard-IA. Age then decides it: 75% of the data is rarely read after 30 days, and Standard-IA is roughly 45% cheaper for storage at the same durability and the same retrieval speed. Hence a lifecycle rule that transitions objects on day 30.  
Why A is not selected: S3 Glacier Deep Archive returns an object after hours. That breaks the requirement to keep the data immediately accessible.  
Why C is not selected: S3 One Zone-IA keeps data in a single Availability Zone: 99.5% availability versus 99.9% for Standard-IA, and losing the zone means losing the data. That fails the "same resiliency" requirement.  
Why D is not selected: The same single-zone problem applies here, plus moving everything immediately also hits the 25% of data that is still read frequently, which would then incur retrieval charges.

---

357\. A gaming company is moving its public scoreboard from a data center to the AWS Cloud. The company uses Amazon EC2 Windows Server instances behind an Application Load Balancer to host its dynamic application. The company needs a highly available storage solution for the application. The application consists of static files and dynamic server-side code.  
Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Store the static files on Amazon S3. Use Amazon CloudFront to cache objects at the edge.  
B. Store the static files on Amazon S3. Use Amazon ElastiCache to cache objects at the edge.  
C. Store the server-side code on Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS). Mount the EFS volume on each EC2 instance to share the files.  
D. Store the server-side code on Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. Mount the FSx for Windows File Server volume on each EC2 instance to share the files.  
E. Store the server-side code on a General Purpose SSD (gp2) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Mount the EBS volume on each EC2 instance to share the files.  
Answer: AD  
Explanation: The application splits into two parts, and each needs its own storage. The static files go into S3 and are served through CloudFront with caching at edge locations (A). The server-side code has to be shared across all the instances, and those instances run Windows Server — which calls for an SMB share, meaning Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, mounted on each instance (D).  
Why B is not selected: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache within a Region; it doesn't cache objects at edge locations and doesn't serve static files.  
Why C is not selected: EFS speaks the NFS protocol and is built for Linux — it isn't a native access method for Windows instances.  
Why E is not selected: A gp2 volume attaches within a single Availability Zone and isn't designed to be mounted by multiple instances at once: no shared access and no high availability.

---

358\. A social media company runs its application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB).  
The ALB is the origin for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The application has more than a billion images stored in an Amazon S3 bucket and processes thousands of images each second. The company wants to resize the images dynamically and serve appropriate formats to clients.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Install an external image management library on an EC2 instance. Use the image management library to process the images.  
B. Create a CloudFront origin request policy. Use the policy to automatically resize images and to serve the appropriate format based on the User-Agent HTTP header in the request.  
C. Use a [email protected] function with an external image management library. Associate the [email protected] function with the CloudFront behaviors that serve the images.  
D. Create a CloudFront response headers policy. Use the policy to automatically resize images and to serve the appropriate format based on the User-Agent HTTP header in the request.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Resizing images and switching formats on the fly, at a rate of thousands of requests per second, is best done at the edge. A Lambda@Edge function with an image-processing library attaches to the CloudFront cache behavior that serves the images: it receives the request, generates the needed variant, and returns it, with the result then cached. No servers of your own to run.  
Why A is not selected: A library running on an EC2 instance means a fleet you'd have to scale to thousands of requests per second and operate.  
Why B is not selected: An origin request policy controls which headers and parameters are forwarded to the origin. It doesn't transform images.  
Why D is not selected: A response headers policy adds headers to the response and doesn't change the content either.

---

359\. A hospital needs to store patient records in an Amazon S3 bucket. The hospital’s compliance team must ensure that all protected health information (PHI) is encrypted in transit and at rest. The compliance team must administer the encryption key for data at rest.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create a public SSL/TLS certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Associate the certificate with Amazon S3. Configure default encryption for each S3 bucket to use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). Assign the compliance team to manage the KMS keys.  
B. Use the aws:SecureTransport condition on S3 bucket policies to allow only encrypted connections over HTTPS (TLS). Configure default encryption for each S3 bucket to use server-side encryption with S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Assign the compliance team to manage the SSE-S3 keys.  
C. Use the aws:SecureTransport condition on S3 bucket policies to allow only encrypted connections over HTTPS (TLS). Configure default encryption for each S3 bucket to use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). Assign the compliance team to manage the KMS keys.  
D. Use the aws:SecureTransport condition on S3 bucket policies to allow only encrypted connections over HTTPS (TLS). Use Amazon Macie to protect the sensitive data that is stored in Amazon S3. Assign the compliance team to manage Macie.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The requirements break down into three parts. "Encrypted in transit" means enforcing HTTPS with an aws:SecureTransport condition in the bucket policy (otherwise TLS is available but not mandatory). "Encrypted at rest" means default encryption on the bucket. "The compliance team must administer the encryption key" is the deciding detail — only a KMS key can be administered, since it has a key policy, rotation, a usage log, and revocable access. SSE-S3 offers none of that: the service manages those keys itself.  
Why A is not selected: An ACM certificate can't be attached to S3: the service serves data over HTTPS using its own certificate. There's also no mechanism here to enforce TLS.  
Why B is not selected: SSE-S3 doesn't let anyone "administer keys": they aren't visible, carry no policy, and can't be revoked. The compliance team's requirement isn't met.  
Why D is not selected: Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data but doesn't encrypt it. The requirement for encryption at rest is left unaddressed.

---

360\. A company uses Amazon API Gateway to run a private gateway with two REST APIs in the same VPC. The BuyStock RESTful web service calls the CheckFunds RESTful web service to ensure that enough funds are available before a stock can be purchased. The company has noticed in the VPC flow logs that the BuyStock RESTful web service calls the CheckFunds RESTful web service over the internet instead of through the VPC. A solutions architect must implement a solution so that the APIs communicate through the VPC.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the FEWEST changes to the code?  
A. Add an X-API-Key header in the HTTP header for authorization.  
B. Use an interface endpoint.  
C. Use a gateway endpoint.  
D. Add an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue between the two REST APIs.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: A private API in API Gateway is reachable from inside a VPC only through an interface endpoint: it creates a network interface with a private address and a DNS record, so one service calling another travels over the private network. No code changes are needed — the API's name just needs to resolve to the private address.  
Why A is not selected: An API key relates to authorization and has no effect on the network path.  
Why C is not selected: A gateway endpoint exists only for S3 and DynamoDB; there is no such endpoint type for API Gateway.  
Why D is not selected: A queue between the services changes the interaction model from synchronous to asynchronous, which means rewriting code, and it doesn't fix the network path anyway.

---

361\. A company hosts a multiplayer gaming application on AWS. The company wants the application to read data with sub-millisecond latency and run one-time queries on historical data.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use Amazon RDS for data that is frequently accessed. Run a periodic custom script to export the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.  
B. Store the data directly in an Amazon S3 bucket. Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy to move older data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive for long-term storage. Run one-time queries on the data in Amazon S3 by using Amazon Athena.  
C. Use Amazon DynamoDB with DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for data that is frequently accessed. Export the data to an Amazon S3 bucket by using DynamoDB table export. Run one-time queries on the data in Amazon S3 by using Amazon Athena.  
D. Use Amazon DynamoDB for data that is frequently accessed. Turn on streaming to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to read the data from Kinesis Data Streams. Store the records in an Amazon S3 bucket.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The requirements call for sub-millisecond reads and one-time queries on historical data, with the least operational overhead. DynamoDB with a DAX cache delivers microsecond-level response times for frequently accessed data, the built-in table export moves data to S3 without writing a single line of code, and Athena runs the one-time queries against the exported data.  
Why A is not selected: RDS cannot deliver sub-millisecond response times, and a custom export script adds extra code to write and maintain.  
Why B is not selected: Reading directly from S3 takes tens of milliseconds, and retrieving from S3 Glacier Deep Archive takes hours — the requirement is not met.  
Why D is not selected: The Kinesis Data Streams and Kinesis Data Firehose combination works, but it adds extra components compared with the built-in export, and without a cache it won't deliver sub-millisecond response times.

---

362\. A company uses a payment processing system that requires messages for a particular payment ID to be received in the same order that they were sent. Otherwise, the payments might be processed incorrectly.  
Which actions should a solutions architect take to meet this requirement? (Choose two.)  
A. Write the messages to an Amazon DynamoDB table with the payment ID as the partition key.  
B. Write the messages to an Amazon Kinesis data stream with the payment ID as the partition key.  
C. Write the messages to an Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached cluster with the payment ID as the key.  
D. Write the messages to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Set the message attribute to use the payment ID.  
E. Write the messages to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue. Set the message group to use the payment ID.  
Answer: BE  
Explanation: Order must be preserved within a single payment ID. Both correct options use this ID as the partitioning key: an SQS FIFO queue with the payment ID as the message group ID preserves order within the group and processes each message exactly once (E), while a Kinesis data stream using the same value as the partition key places all records for a given payment into a single shard, where order is guaranteed (B).  
Why A is not selected: A DynamoDB table stores data, but it is not a message queue with guaranteed processing order.  
Why C is not selected: Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached is an in-memory cache with no data persistence and no ordering guarantees.  
Why D is not selected: A standard SQS queue can deliver messages out of order, and a message attribute has no effect on ordering.

---

363\. A company is building a game system that needs to send unique events to separate leaderboard, matchmaking, and authentication services concurrently. The company needs an AWS event-driven system that guarantees the order of the events.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Amazon EventBridge event bus  
B. Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) FIFO topics  
C. Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) standard topics  
D. Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queues  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Events must fan out to multiple recipients while preserving order. SNS FIFO topics do both: they deliver to multiple subscribers while preserving the sequence within a message group and preventing duplicates.  
Why A is not selected: An EventBridge event bus fans events out to multiple targets, but it does not guarantee delivery order.  
Why C is not selected: A standard SNS topic likewise does not preserve message order.  
Why D is not selected: An SQS FIFO queue preserves order, but each queue has a single consumer, so it can't fan out concurrently to three services.

---

364\. A hospital is designing a new application that gathers symptoms from patients. The hospital has decided to use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) and Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) in the architecture.  
A solutions architect is reviewing the infrastructure design. Data must be encrypted at rest and in transit. Only authorized personnel of the hospital should be able to access the data.  
Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Turn on server-side encryption on the SQS components. Update the default key policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals.  
B. Turn on server-side encryption on the SNS components by using an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Apply a key policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals.  
C. Turn on encryption on the SNS components. Update the default key policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals. Set a condition in the topic policy to allow only encrypted connections over TLS.  
D. Turn on server-side encryption on the SQS components by using an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Apply a key policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals. Set a condition in the queue policy to allow only encrypted connections over TLS.  
E. Turn on server-side encryption on the SQS components by using an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Apply an IAM policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals. Set a condition in the queue policy to allow only encrypted connections over TLS.  
Answer: BD  
Explanation: Data flows through both SNS and SQS, so both links need to be protected, not just one. Server-side encryption is turned on for each using an AWS KMS customer managed key — only this key type lets you edit the key policy and restrict which principals are allowed to encrypt and decrypt messages. On top of that, the queue policy (and the topic policy) gets an aws:SecureTransport condition so that only TLS connections are accepted. The key nuance: access to a KMS key is governed primarily by the key's own policy — without a grant there, no IAM policy can provide access on its own.  
Why A is not selected: The phrase "default key policy" refers to an AWS managed key, whose policy cannot be edited. This makes it impossible to restrict the set of principals, and there's no TLS requirement here either.  
Why C is not selected: The same problem applies to the default key policy for SNS: it can't be changed, so restricting access this way isn't achievable.  
Why E is not selected: This gets the mechanism wrong: access to a KMS key is granted by the key policy, and an IAM policy only supplements it. Restricting access "through an IAM policy alone" does not protect the key from other principals in the account.

---

365\. A company runs a web application that is backed by Amazon RDS. A new database administrator caused data loss by accidentally editing information in a database table. To help recover from this type of incident, the company wants the ability to restore the database to its state from 5 minutes before any change within the last 30 days.  
Which feature should the solutions architect include in the design to meet this requirement?  
A. Read replicas  
B. Manual snapshots  
C. Automated backups  
D. Multi-AZ deployments  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Restoring to any point within the last 30 days, accurate to within a few minutes, is provided by RDS automated backups: they continuously capture transaction logs, and the retention period can be configured for up to 35 days.  
Why A is not selected: Read replicas replicate every change, including erroneous ones, so the corrupted data ends up there too.  
Why B is not selected: Manual snapshots are discrete points in time; they don't let you restore to "five minutes before an arbitrary change."  
Why D is not selected: A Multi-AZ deployment protects against infrastructure failure, but it also replicates erroneous changes.

---

366\. A company’s web application consists of an Amazon API Gateway API in front of an AWS Lambda function and an Amazon DynamoDB database. The Lambda function handles the business logic, and the DynamoDB table hosts the data. The application uses Amazon Cognito user pools to identify the individual users of the application. A solutions architect needs to update the application so that only users who have a subscription can access premium content.  
Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Enable API caching and throttling on the API Gateway API.  
B. Set up AWS WAF on the API Gateway API. Create a rule to filter users who have a subscription.  
C. Apply fine-grained IAM permissions to the premium content in the DynamoDB table.  
D. Implement API usage plans and API keys to limit the access of users who do not have a subscription.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Subscribers need to be separated from everyone else at the entry point, without rewriting the business logic. API Gateway offers a ready-made mechanism for this: a usage plan with API keys — a key is issued to each subscriber and tied to a plan with quotas and throttling limits, and a request without a valid key is rejected by the gateway itself. No changes to the Lambda function or the DynamoDB table are needed. If access needed to be differentiated based on Cognito user attributes instead, the next step would be a Lambda authorizer, but that means writing code.  
Why A is not selected: API caching and throttling manage load and cost, but they don't distinguish a subscriber from a regular user.  
Why B is not selected: AWS WAF filters on request properties — IP addresses, headers, patterns. It has no knowledge of whether a user has paid for a subscription.  
Why C is not selected: Fine-grained IAM permissions on DynamoDB items apply when a client accesses the table directly using its own credentials. Here, a Lambda function running under its own role sits between the user and the table.

---

367\. A company is using Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to route requests to its UDP-based application for users around the world. The application is hosted on redundant servers in the company's on-premises data centers in the United States, Asia, and Europe. The company’s compliance requirements state that the application must be hosted on premises. The company wants to improve the performance and availability of the application.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Configure three Network Load Balancers (NLBs) in the three AWS Regions to address the on-premises endpoints. Create an accelerator by using AWS Global Accelerator, and register the NLBs as its endpoints. Provide access to the application by using a CNAME that points to the accelerator DNS.  
B. Configure three Application Load Balancers (ALBs) in the three AWS Regions to address the on-premises endpoints. Create an accelerator by using AWS Global Accelerator, and register the ALBs as its endpoints. Provide access to the application by using a CNAME that points to the accelerator DNS.  
C. Configure three Network Load Balancers (NLBs) in the three AWS Regions to address the on-premises endpoints. In Route 53, create a latency-based record that points to the three NLBs, and use it as an origin for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Provide access to the application by using a CNAME that points to the CloudFront DNS.  
D. Configure three Application Load Balancers (ALBs) in the three AWS Regions to address the on-premises endpoints. In Route 53, create a latency-based record that points to the three ALBs, and use it as an origin for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Provide access to the application by using a CNAME that points to the CloudFront DNS.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The application stays in the company's own data centers, runs over UDP, and both performance and availability need to improve. AWS Global Accelerator takes in traffic at the edge location closest to each user, routes it over the AWS global network backbone, and can direct it to the on-premises sites when they're registered as IP-address targets through a Network Load Balancer in each Region. An NLB is chosen because the traffic is UDP, and an ALB only handles HTTP. Failover away from a failed site happens at the accelerator level, without waiting for DNS record TTLs to expire.  
Why B is not selected: An Application Load Balancer does not support UDP, so it cannot serve this application.  
Why C is not selected: CloudFront does not work with UDP traffic and cannot use a Route 53 record as an origin for it.  
Why D is not selected: This has two errors at once: an ALB doesn't support UDP, and CloudFront isn't applicable to this type of traffic.

---

368\. A solutions architect wants all new users to have specific complexity requirements and mandatory rotation periods for IAM user passwords.  
What should the solutions architect do to accomplish this?  
A. Set an overall password policy for the entire AWS account.  
B. Set a password policy for each IAM user in the AWS account.  
C. Use third-party vendor software to set password requirements.  
D. Attach an Amazon CloudWatch rule to the Create_newuser event to set the password with the appropriate requirements.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: In IAM, a password policy is set once for the entire account: minimum length, required character types, reuse prevention, and password expiration. There is no such thing as an individual password policy per user. The setting applies to all IAM users in the account, including new ones, which is exactly what the requirement calls for.  
Why B is not selected: IAM has no per-user password policy: there is a single policy that applies to the whole account.  
Why C is not selected: Third-party software does not govern IAM user password requirements — that's handled by the service itself.  
Why D is not selected: Reacting to the user-creation event means writing code and a delay — the password already exists by then. The built-in setting solves this proactively instead.

---
