369\. A company has migrated an application to Amazon EC2 Linux instances. One of these EC2 instances runs several 1- hour tasks on a schedule. These tasks were written by different teams and have no common programming language. The company is concerned about performance and scalability while these tasks run on a single instance.  
A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to resolve these concerns.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use AWS Batch to run the tasks as jobs. Schedule the jobs by using Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events).  
B. Convert the EC2 instance to a container. Use AWS App Runner to create the container on demand to run the tasks as jobs.  
C. Copy the tasks into AWS Lambda functions. Schedule the Lambda functions by using Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events).  
D. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the EC2 instance that runs the tasks. Create an Auto Scaling group with the AMI to run multiple copies of the instance.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The tasks are written in different languages, run for an hour each, and need to run in parallel. AWS Batch runs them as jobs in containers, automatically provisions and tears down compute capacity, manages the job queue and retries, and EventBridge handles the scheduling. The languages and runtime environments can stay whatever they already are.  
Why B is not selected: AWS App Runner is designed for web services and APIs, not for scheduled batch jobs.  
Why C is not selected: The tasks run for an hour, but the maximum Lambda function execution time is fifteen minutes; on top of that, not every language is supported.  
Why D is not selected: Running multiple copies of the same machine image doesn't solve the problem of running different jobs in parallel, and it still leaves the instances to be maintained.

---

370\. A company runs a public three-tier web application in a VPC. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The EC2 instances that run in private subnets need to communicate with a license server over the internet. The company needs a managed solution that minimizes operational maintenance.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Provision a NAT instance in a public subnet. Modify each private subnet's route table with a default route that points to the NAT instance.  
B. Provision a NAT instance in a private subnet. Modify each private subnet's route table with a default route that points to the NAT instance.  
C. Provision a NAT gateway in a public subnet. Modify each private subnet's route table with a default route that points to the NAT gateway.  
D. Provision a NAT gateway in a private subnet. Modify each private subnet's route table with a default route that points to the NAT gateway.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: A managed path to the internet is needed for the private subnets. A NAT gateway is created in a public subnet, and the private subnets' route tables send all outbound traffic to it. It's a managed resource: AWS handles its availability and scales it up to tens of gigabits per second on its own.  
Why A is not selected: A NAT instance works, but it's an ordinary EC2 instance: patching, monitoring, scaling, and fault tolerance all fall on the company.  
Why B is not selected: A NAT instance in a private subnet has no internet access and simply cannot work.  
Why D is not selected: A NAT gateway must be located in a public subnet: placed in a private one, it would have no way to send traffic outbound.

---

371\. A company needs to create an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster to host a digital media streaming application. The EKS cluster will use a managed node group that is backed by Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes for storage. The company must encrypt all data at rest by using a customer managed key that is stored in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).  
Which combination of actions will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)  
A. Use a Kubernetes plugin that uses the customer managed key to perform data encryption.  
B. After creation of the EKS cluster, locate the EBS volumes. Enable encryption by using the customer managed key.  
C. Enable EBS encryption by default in the AWS Region where the EKS cluster will be created. Select the customer managed key as the default key.  
D. Create the EKS cluster. Create an IAM role that has a policy that grants permission to the customer managed key. Associate the role with the EKS cluster.  
E. Store the customer managed key as a Kubernetes secret in the EKS cluster. Use the customer managed key to encrypt the EBS volumes.  
Answer: CD  
Explanation: EBS volumes for an EKS node group are created automatically as the group scales, so encryption has to be set up in advance rather than volume by volume. Enabling EBS encryption by default in the Region with the customer managed key selected as the default key means that every new volume, including those created by EKS, is encrypted with that key with no action required on your part (C). The second piece is granting access to the key to whatever creates volumes on your behalf: an IAM role with permissions on the KMS key is associated with the cluster, otherwise the nodes simply fail to come up because they can't access the key (D). The key insight: you cannot turn on encryption for an existing EBS volume — it can only be created encrypted from the start.  
Why A is not selected: A Kubernetes plugin that performs the encryption is an extra component you have to install, update, and troubleshoot yourself. That violates the LEAST operational overhead requirement.  
Why B is not selected: You cannot enable encryption on an EBS volume that already exists — encryption is set at creation time. You would have to take a snapshot, copy it with encryption enabled, and recreate the volumes.  
Why E is not selected: A KMS key cannot be "stored as a Kubernetes secret" — the key material never leaves the service. You work with the key through its API, not by copying it around.

---

372\. A company wants to migrate an Oracle database to AWS. The database consists of a single table that contains millions of geographic information systems (GIS) images that are high resolution and are identified by a geographic code.  
When a natural disaster occurs, tens of thousands of images get updated every few minutes. Each geographic code has a single image or row that is associated with it. The company wants a solution that is highly available and scalable during such events.  
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Store the images and geographic codes in a database table. Use Oracle running on an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance.  
B. Store the images in Amazon S3 buckets. Use Amazon DynamoDB with the geographic code as the key and the image S3 URL as the value.  
C. Store the images and geographic codes in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Configure DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) during times of high load.  
D. Store the images in Amazon S3 buckets. Store geographic codes and image S3 URLs in a database table. Use Oracle running on an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance.  
Answer: D  
Review status: Disputed key (alternative: B)  
Dispute note: examtopics t1 q372 — the community is split: B (S3+DynamoDB) is cheaper and more scalable; the counterargument is that a GIS image doesn't reduce to a single geographic code  
Explanation: Both reasonable options share the same core idea: high-resolution images don't belong in database rows. They get moved out to S3, leaving only the geographic code and a reference in the database. The key picks D — the metadata stays in a relational table in Oracle on RDS Multi-AZ: migration effort is minimal, the application keeps working against the familiar schema, and Multi-AZ provides high availability. The dispute is a fair one: B (S3 plus DynamoDB) is cheaper and handles a burst of tens of thousands of updates per minute better, because DynamoDB scales horizontally while a single RDS instance does not. The counterargument for D: the Oracle license and schema are preserved, and "a single image per geographic code" doesn't necessarily mean the whole data model reduces to a simple key-value lookup.  
Why A is not selected: Storing the images themselves as rows in Oracle on RDS is the most expensive option: you pay for premium database storage, and the update burst runs into the IOPS limit of a single instance.  
Why B is not selected: A strong alternative on both cost and scalability. The key doesn't pick it because of the migration: DynamoDB would require rewriting how the data is accessed, and the question describes migrating an existing Oracle schema.  
Why C is not selected: A DynamoDB item is capped at 400 KB — high-resolution images don't fit. DAX also accelerates reads, while the workload described here is write-heavy.

---

373\. A company has an application that collects data from IoT sensors on automobiles. The data is streamed and stored in Amazon S3 through Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose. The data produces trillions of S3 objects each year. Each morning, the company uses the data from the previous 30 days to retrain a suite of machine learning (ML) models.  
Four times each year, the company uses the data from the previous 12 months to perform analysis and train other ML models. The data must be available with minimal delay for up to 1 year. After 1 year, the data must be retained for archival purposes.  
Which storage solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Use the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year.  
B. Use the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class. Configure S3 Intelligent-Tiering to automatically move objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year.  
C. Use the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year.  
D. Use the S3 Standard storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Standard- Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days, and then to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The access pattern here is known in advance, not random: the last 30 days of data are read every morning, then accessed four more times over the course of the year, and after a year the data is kept only for archival purposes. A known pattern is described most cheaply by an explicit Lifecycle chain: S3 Standard for the first 30 days, then Standard-IA up to a year, then Glacier Deep Archive. Scale matters separately here: trillions of objects make Intelligent-Tiering expensive, since its monitoring fee is charged per object.  
Why A is not selected: Intelligent-Tiering across trillions of objects means a huge monitoring fee, with no benefit to show for it — the access pattern is known ahead of time and can be described with a simple rule.  
Why B is not selected: On top of the monitoring fee, the mechanics here are wrong too: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects into archive tiers based on lack of access, not on a calendar year, and the archive tiers have to be enabled separately.  
Why C is not selected: Standard-IA from day one hits the busiest period hardest: the data is read every morning for the first 30 days, and every one of those reads is billed as an IA retrieval.

---

374\. A company is running several business applications in three separate VPCs within the us-east-1 Region. The applications must be able to communicate between VPCs. The applications also must be able to consistently send hundreds of gigabytes of data each day to a latency-sensitive application that runs in a single on-premises data center.  
A solutions architect needs to design a network connectivity solution that maximizes cost-effectiveness.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Configure three AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections from the data center to AWS. Establish connectivity by configuring one VPN connection for each VPC.  
B. Launch a third-party virtual network appliance in each VPC. Establish an IPsec VPN tunnel between the data center and each virtual appliance.  
C. Set up three AWS Direct Connect connections from the data center to a Direct Connect gateway in us-east-1. Establish connectivity by configuring each VPC to use one of the Direct Connect connections.  
D. Set up one AWS Direct Connect connection from the data center to AWS. Create a transit gateway, and attach each VPC to the transit gateway. Establish connectivity between the Direct Connect connection and the transit gateway.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: There are two requirements: connectivity between the three VPCs, and steady delivery of hundreds of gigabytes a day to a latency-sensitive on-premises site. The cheapest way to get both is a single Direct Connect connection plus a transit gateway: every VPC attaches to the gateway and gets connectivity to the others, and the connection attaches to the same gateway through a Direct Connect gateway. One physical connection instead of three, and no mesh of peerings to manage.  
Why A is not selected: Three Site-to-Site VPN connections run over the internet, so latency is unpredictable and hundreds of gigabytes a day will run into the tunnels' bandwidth limits. They also don't provide connectivity between the VPCs.  
Why B is not selected: Running your own virtual appliances in every VPC means licensing, maintenance, and scaling it all yourself — and it still runs over the internet.  
Why C is not selected: Three separate Direct Connect connections cost three times as much, whereas one connection through a transit gateway serves all three VPCs.

---

375\. An ecommerce company is building a distributed application that involves several serverless functions and AWS services to complete order-processing tasks. These tasks require manual approvals as part of the workflow. A solutions architect needs to design an architecture for the order-processing application. The solution must be able to combine multiple AWS Lambda functions into responsive serverless applications. The solution also must orchestrate data and services that run on Amazon EC2 instances, containers, or on-premises servers.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use AWS Step Functions to build the application.  
B. Integrate all the application components in an AWS Glue job.  
C. Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to build the application.  
D. Use AWS Lambda functions and Amazon EventBridge events to build the application.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: This calls for orchestration with manual approvals, tying together Lambda functions and resources outside them — EC2 instances, containers, and on-premises servers. AWS Step Functions is built for exactly this: a state machine with branching, retries, and a wait-for-callback step for manual approval, with integrations that cover both Lambda and other services.  
Why B is not selected: AWS Glue is an ETL service, not a workflow orchestrator with manual approval steps.  
Why C is not selected: A queue passes messages along, but it doesn't describe a sequence of steps and has no built-in support for waiting on an approval.  
Why D is not selected: Functions tied together with events can work, but you'd have to build all the state tracking, retry logic, and approval-waiting yourself.

---

376\. A company has launched an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Most of the connections to the database come from serverless applications. Application traffic to the database changes significantly at random intervals. At times of high demand, users report that their applications experience database connection rejection errors.  
Which solution will resolve this issue with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create a proxy in RDS Proxy. Configure the users’ applications to use the DB instance through RDS Proxy.  
B. Deploy Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached between the users’ applications and the DB instance.  
C. Migrate the DB instance to a different instance class that has higher I/O capacity. Configure the users’ applications to use the new DB instance.  
D. Configure Multi-AZ for the DB instance. Configure the users’ applications to switch between the DB instances.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Connection-rejected errors during spikes from serverless applications are a classic sign of connection exhaustion. RDS Proxy maintains a connection pool and reuses connections, smoothing out swings in the number of clients, while the application only needs to point at a different endpoint.  
Why B is not selected: ElastiCache for Memcached caches reads and has no effect on the number of database connections, and the application would still need to be changed.  
Why C is not selected: A larger instance class raises the connection limit, but it costs more and doesn't address the underlying cause during sharp spikes.  
Why D is not selected: Multi-AZ improves availability; the standby instance doesn't accept connections, so there's nothing for the application to switch between.

---

377\. A company recently deployed a new auditing system to centralize information about operating system versions, patching, and installed software for Amazon EC2 instances. A solutions architect must ensure all instances provisioned through EC2 Auto Scaling groups successfully send reports to the auditing system as soon as they are launched and terminated.  
Which solution achieves these goals MOST efficiently?  
A. Use a scheduled AWS Lambda function and run a script remotely on all EC2 instances to send data to the audit system.  
B. Use EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks to run a custom script to send data to the audit system when instances are launched and terminated.  
C. Use an EC2 Auto Scaling launch configuration to run a custom script through user data to send data to the audit system when instances are launched and terminated.  
D. Run a custom script on the instance operating system to send data to the audit system. Configure the script to be invoked by the EC2 Auto Scaling group when the instance starts and is terminated.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The report has to go out at the exact moment an instance launches and terminates. EC2 Auto Scaling groups have lifecycle hooks for exactly this: the instance is held in a pending launch or terminate state, the required action runs, and only then does the transition complete. It's the only way to reliably send the data before the instance is removed.  
Why A is not selected: A scheduled function isn't tied to the moment of launch or termination, and a terminated instance can no longer be polled.  
Why C is not selected: User data runs only on first boot — it doesn't fire on instance termination.  
Why D is not selected: An Auto Scaling group doesn't invoke scripts inside the operating system — that's exactly what lifecycle hooks exist for.

---

378\. A company is developing a real-time multiplayer game that uses UDP for communications between the client and servers in an Auto Scaling group. Spikes in demand are anticipated during the day, so the game server platform must adapt accordingly. Developers want to store gamer scores and other non-relational data in a database solution that will scale without intervention.  
Which solution should a solutions architect recommend?  
A. Use Amazon Route 53 for traffic distribution and Amazon Aurora Serverless for data storage.  
B. Use a Network Load Balancer for traffic distribution and Amazon DynamoDB on-demand for data storage.  
C. Use a Network Load Balancer for traffic distribution and Amazon Aurora Global Database for data storage.  
D. Use an Application Load Balancer for traffic distribution and Amazon DynamoDB global tables for data storage.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The two requirements map to two separate services. UDP traffic with sharp spikes calls for a Network Load Balancer in front of the Auto Scaling group: it operates at layer 4, supports UDP, and handles millions of connections without warm-up. Non-relational data (player scores, profiles) that scales without manual intervention calls for DynamoDB in on-demand mode: capacity adjusts automatically, with no capacity planning needed.  
Why A is not selected: Route 53 distributes requests via DNS with no awareness of connection state and with resolver-cache delays, and Aurora Serverless is a relational database, while the data described here is non-relational.  
Why C is not selected: The load balancer choice is right, but Aurora Global Database is again a relational store built for cross-Region replication, not for non-relational data with automatic scaling.  
Why D is not selected: Application Load Balancer doesn't support UDP, and DynamoDB global tables are meant for multi-Region writes, which the requirements don't call for.

---

379\. A company hosts a frontend application that uses an Amazon API Gateway API backend that is integrated with AWS Lambda. When the API receives requests, the Lambda function loads many libraries. Then the Lambda function connects to an Amazon RDS database, processes the data, and returns the data to the frontend application. The company wants to ensure that response latency is as low as possible for all its users with the fewest number of changes to the company's operations.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Establish a connection between the frontend application and the database to make queries faster by bypassing the API.  
B. Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function that handles the requests.  
C. Cache the results of the queries in Amazon S3 for faster retrieval of similar datasets.  
D. Increase the size of the database to increase the number of connections Lambda can establish at one time.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The latency comes from a cold start: the function loads a large number of libraries every time. Provisioned concurrency keeps the required number of instances pre-initialized, so a request lands in an environment that's already warmed up. It changes neither the code nor the architecture — it's just a setting on the function.  
Why A is not selected: Connecting the frontend directly to the database and bypassing the API breaks the architecture and requires exposing the database publicly — that's both a redesign and a security hole.  
Why C is not selected: Caching results in S3 only helps for repeated, identical queries and does nothing to address the library-loading delay.  
Why D is not selected: A larger database raises the connection limit, but the function's initialization time stays the same.

---

380\. A company is migrating its on-premises workload to the AWS Cloud. The company already uses several Amazon EC2 instances and Amazon RDS DB instances. The company wants a solution that automatically starts and stops the EC2 instances and DB instances outside of business hours. The solution must minimize cost and infrastructure maintenance.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Scale the EC2 instances by using elastic resize. Scale the DB instances to zero outside of business hours.  
B. Explore AWS Marketplace for partner solutions that will automatically start and stop the EC2 instances and DB instances on a schedule.  
C. Launch another EC2 instance. Configure a crontab schedule to run shell scripts that will start and stop the existing EC2 instances and DB instances on a schedule.  
D. Create an AWS Lambda function that will start and stop the EC2 instances and DB instances. Configure Amazon EventBridge to invoke the Lambda function on a schedule.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: This comes down to starting and stopping resources on a schedule. A Lambda function calls the necessary APIs, and EventBridge invokes it on a schedule: there are no servers to run, you pay only for the seconds the function executes, and maintenance amounts to a few lines of code.  
Why A is not selected: Elastic resize is an Amazon Redshift feature, and RDS instances cannot be scaled down to zero.  
Why B is not selected: A third-party Marketplace solution means extra cost and vendor dependency for something two native services already handle.  
Why C is not selected: A separate instance running crontab is a machine that runs around the clock and has to be patched and monitored — more expensive and more maintenance.

---

381\. A company hosts a three-tier web application that includes a PostgreSQL database. The database stores the metadata from documents. The company searches the metadata for key terms to retrieve documents that the company reviews in a report each month. The documents are stored in Amazon S3. The documents are usually written only once, but they are updated frequently.  
The reporting process takes a few hours with the use of relational queries. The reporting process must not prevent any document modifications or the addition of new documents. A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to speed up the reporting process.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of change to the application code?  
A. Set up a new Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) cluster that includes a read replica. Scale the read replica to generate the reports.  
B. Set up a new Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster that includes an Aurora Replica. Issue queries to the Aurora Replica to generate the reports.  
C. Set up a new Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance. Configure the reporting module to query the secondary RDS node so that the reporting module does not affect the primary node.  
D. Set up a new Amazon DynamoDB table to store the documents. Use a fixed write capacity to support new document entries. Automatically scale the read capacity to support the reports.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Reports run relational queries that take several hours, and they must not interfere with writes of new documents. Aurora PostgreSQL is compatible with the current database, so it requires minimal code changes, and the Aurora Replica reads from the same shared storage with millisecond-level lag. Reports go to the replica while writes continue on the primary instance.  
Why A is not selected: DocumentDB is compatible with MongoDB: the relational queries would have to be rewritten entirely.  
Why C is not selected: The standby instance in an RDS Multi-AZ configuration is not available for reads — reports cannot be directed to it.  
Why D is not selected: DynamoDB does not run relational queries, and moving the documents there would mean rewriting the application.

---

382\. A company has a three-tier application on AWS that ingests sensor data from its users’ devices. The traffic flows through a Network Load Balancer (NLB), then to Amazon EC2 instances for the web tier, and finally to EC2 instances for the application tier. The application tier makes calls to a database.  
What should a solutions architect do to improve the security of the data in transit?  
A. Configure a TLS listener. Deploy the server certificate on the NLB.  
B. Configure AWS Shield Advanced. Enable AWS WAF on the NLB.  
C. Change the load balancer to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Enable AWS WAF on the ALB.  
D. Encrypt the Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume on the EC2 instances by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The requirement is specific — improve the security of data in transit, not defend against attacks or protect data at rest. A Network Load Balancer can terminate TLS: you create a listener on a TLS port, install a server certificate (typically from ACM) on the load balancer, and traffic from devices to the NLB is encrypted. The segment to the instances can be encrypted further if needed. Keep the distinction clear: TLS protects data in transit, KMS protects data at rest, and WAF and Shield protect against attacks.  
Why B is not selected: Shield Advanced and WAF protect against DDoS and common web attacks, but they encrypt nothing. In addition, WAF cannot be attached to a Network Load Balancer.  
Why C is not selected: Replacing the load balancer with an ALB plus WAF again addresses protection against attacks, not encrypting the channel. Using an ALB by itself does not encrypt traffic.  
Why D is not selected: Encrypting EBS volumes protects data at rest on the instances' disks. Data in transit remains unprotected.

---

383\. A company is planning to migrate a commercial off-the-shelf application from its on-premises data center to AWS.  
The software has a software licensing model using sockets and cores with predictable capacity and uptime requirements. The company wants to use its existing licenses, which were purchased earlier this year.  
Which Amazon EC2 pricing option is the MOST cost-effective?  
A. Dedicated Reserved Hosts  
B. Dedicated On-Demand Hosts  
C. Dedicated Reserved Instances  
D. Dedicated On-Demand Instances  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The licenses are tied to sockets and cores, which means access to the physical host is required — that's Dedicated Hosts, the only EC2 option that exposes and accounts for the server's physical configuration. The workload has predictable capacity and uptime, so reserving the host gives the biggest discount.  
Why B is not selected: Dedicated On-Demand Hosts satisfy the licensing requirement, but paying the full on-demand rate for a predictable, round-the-clock workload is not cost-effective.  
Why C is not selected: Dedicated Instances only guarantee that no other tenants share the underlying hardware — they don't expose the host's sockets and cores, so the license cannot be mapped to them.  
Why D is not selected: The same licensing limitation, plus no reservation discount.

---

384\. A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 Linux instances across multiple Availability Zones. The application needs a storage layer that is highly available and Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX)-compliant. The storage layer must provide maximum data durability and must be shareable across the EC2 instances. The data in the storage layer will be accessed frequently for the first 30 days and will be accessed infrequently after that time.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Use the Amazon S3 Standard storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to move infrequently accessed data to S3 Glacier.  
B. Use the Amazon S3 Standard storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to move infrequently accessed data to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA).  
C. Use the Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) Standard storage class. Create a lifecycle management policy to move infrequently accessed data to EFS Standard-Infrequent Access (EFS Standard-IA).  
D. Use the Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) One Zone storage class. Create a lifecycle management policy to move infrequently accessed data to EFS One Zone-Infrequent Access (EFS One Zone-IA).  
Answer: C  
Explanation: A POSIX-compliant file system is required, shared across instances in different Availability Zones, with maximum durability and lower costs for infrequently read data. That's EFS in the Standard storage class, which stores data across multiple Availability Zones, combined with a lifecycle policy that moves files older than 30 days to EFS Standard-Infrequent Access — the price per gigabyte drops by roughly a factor of ten while keeping the same file system semantics.  
Why A is not selected: S3 is not a POSIX-compliant file system, and Glacier does not provide instant access either.  
Why B is not selected: The S3 Standard-IA class is cheaper, but the underlying problem remains: object storage doesn't fit a use case where the application needs a POSIX file system.  
Why D is not selected: The One Zone class stores data in only a single Availability Zone, while the requirement calls for maximum durability.

---

385\. A solutions architect is creating a new VPC design. There are two public subnets for the load balancer, two private subnets for web servers, and two private subnets for MySQL. The web servers use only HTTPS. The solutions architect has already created a security group for the load balancer allowing port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Company policy requires that each resource has the least access required to still be able to perform its tasks.  
Which additional configuration strategy should the solutions architect use to meet these requirements?  
A. Create a security group for the web servers and allow port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Create a security group for the MySQL servers and allow port 3306 from the web servers security group.  
B. Create a network ACL for the web servers and allow port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Create a network ACL for the MySQL servers and allow port 3306 from the web servers security group.  
C. Create a security group for the web servers and allow port 443 from the load balancer. Create a security group for the MySQL servers and allow port 3306 from the web servers security group.  
D. Create a network ACL for the web servers and allow port 443 from the load balancer. Create a network ACL for the MySQL servers and allow port 3306 from the web servers security group.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Least access means each tier accepts traffic only from its neighboring tier. The web servers allow port 443 not from the whole internet but from the load balancer's security group, and the MySQL servers allow port 3306 from the web servers' security group. Referencing security groups instead of addresses keeps working as the fleet scales.  
Why A is not selected: Allowing port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 directly on the web servers is broader than necessary: they could then be reached by more than just the load balancer.  
Why B is not selected: Network ACLs work on addresses and subnets and cannot reference a security group — this kind of rule cannot be created.  
Why D is not selected: Same mistake: a network ACL cannot accept a security group as either a source or a destination.

---

386\. An ecommerce company is running a multi-tier application on AWS. The front-end and backend tiers both run on Amazon EC2, and the database runs on Amazon RDS for MySQL. The backend tier communicates with the RDS instance. There are frequent calls to return identical datasets from the database that are causing performance slowdowns.  
Which action should be taken to improve the performance of the backend?  
A. Implement Amazon SNS to store the database calls.  
B. Implement Amazon ElastiCache to cache the large datasets.  
C. Implement an RDS for MySQL read replica to cache database calls.  
D. Implement Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream the calls to the database.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The problem is that the same queries repeat frequently. An in-memory ElastiCache cache returns such a dataset in a fraction of a millisecond and removes the repeated load from the database — this is the standard solution for repeated, identical queries.  
Why A is not selected: SNS is a notification service; it cannot be used to store database queries.  
Why C is not selected: A read replica offloads the primary instance, but it is not a cache: every query still runs against the database in full.  
Why D is not selected: Firehose delivers streaming data into storage destinations and has nothing to do with speeding up reads.

---

387\. A new employee has joined a company as a deployment engineer. The deployment engineer will be using AWS CloudFormation templates to create multiple AWS resources. A solutions architect wants the deployment engineer to perform job activities while following the principle of least privilege.  
Which combination of actions should the solutions architect take to accomplish this goal? (Choose two.)  
A. Have the deployment engineer use AWS account root user credentials for performing AWS CloudFormation stack operations.  
B. Create a new IAM user for the deployment engineer and add the IAM user to a group that has the PowerUsers IAM policy attached.  
C. Create a new IAM user for the deployment engineer and add the IAM user to a group that has the AdministratorAccess IAM policy attached.  
D. Create a new IAM user for the deployment engineer and add the IAM user to a group that has an IAM policy that allows AWS CloudFormation actions only.  
E. Create an IAM role for the deployment engineer to explicitly define the permissions specific to the AWS CloudFormation stack and launch stacks using that IAM role.  
Answer: DE  
Explanation: Least privilege for an engineer working with CloudFormation is built from two parts. First: a dedicated IAM user in a group with a policy that allows only CloudFormation actions — the person themselves does not get permission to create resources directly (D). Second: a separate service role that the stack assumes during deployment, defining the specific permissions for the resources being created (E). This way, permissions on the resources belong to the stack, not the person, and can be scoped down to exactly what's needed.  
Why A is not selected: The root account should never be used for day-to-day operations at all: it cannot be restricted with policies and cannot be shared among people.  
Why B is not selected: PowerUsers grants nearly full access to all services except IAM management. That's disproportionately broader than what's needed for deploying stacks.  
Why C is not selected: AdministratorAccess is full access to the entire account — the maximum possible violation of least privilege.

---

388\. A company is deploying a two-tier web application in a VPC. The web tier is using an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group with public subnets that span multiple Availability Zones. The database tier consists of an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in separate private subnets. The web tier requires access to the database to retrieve product information.  
The web application is not working as intended. The web application reports that it cannot connect to the database. The database is confirmed to be up and running. All configurations for the network ACLs, security groups, and route tables are still in their default states.  
What should a solutions architect recommend to fix the application?  
A. Add an explicit rule to the private subnet’s network ACL to allow traffic from the web tier’s EC2 instances.  
B. Add a route in the VPC route table to allow traffic between the web tier’s EC2 instances and the database tier.  
C. Deploy the web tier's EC2 instances and the database tier’s RDS instance into two separate VPCs, and configure VPC peering.  
D. Add an inbound rule to the security group of the database tier’s RDS instance to allow traffic from the web tiers security group.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: All settings are at their default state: the network ACLs allow all traffic, the local route within the VPC already exists, but the default security group does not allow inbound connections from other security groups. So an inbound rule must be added to the database allowing traffic from the web tier's security group on the MySQL port.  
Why A is not selected: The default network ACL already allows all traffic: there's nothing to add a rule for.  
Why B is not selected: The route between subnets in the same VPC is created automatically by the local route entry and cannot be deleted.  
Why C is not selected: Splitting the tiers into separate VPCs and configuring peering is an excessive rebuild when a single rule is all that's missing.

---

389\. A company has a large dataset for its online advertising business stored in an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in a single Availability Zone. The company wants business reporting queries to run without impacting the write operations to the production DB instance.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Deploy RDS read replicas to process the business reporting queries.  
B. Scale out the DB instance horizontally by placing it behind an Elastic Load Balancer.  
C. Scale up the DB instance to a larger instance type to handle write operations and queries.  
D. Deploy the DB instance in multiple Availability Zones to process the business reporting queries.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Reporting queries need to be moved off the primary instance so they don't interfere with writes. An RDS read replica receives an asynchronous copy of the data and takes on the entire reporting load without affecting write operations on the primary database.  
Why B is not selected: A load balancer cannot distribute queries to a database and does not create additional copies of the data.  
Why C is not selected: A larger instance raises the overall ceiling, but heavy reports would still compete with writes for the same resources.  
Why D is not selected: The standby instance in a Multi-AZ configuration does not serve queries: it exists solely for failover.

---

390\. A company hosts a three-tier ecommerce application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). All ecommerce data is stored in an Amazon RDS for MariaDB Multi-AZ DB instance.  
The company wants to optimize customer session management during transactions. The application must store session data durably.  
Which solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Turn on the sticky sessions feature (session affinity) on the ALB.  
B. Use an Amazon DynamoDB table to store customer session information.  
C. Deploy an Amazon Cognito user pool to manage user session information.  
D. Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to store customer session information.  
E. Use AWS Systems Manager Application Manager in the application to manage user session information.  
Answer: AD  
Review status: Disputed key (alternative: BD)  
Dispute note: examtopics t1 q390 — sticky sessions don't store data; ElastiCache Redis is only durable with persistence enabled; part of the community favors BD  
Explanation: There's one requirement: store session data durably, so that replacing an instance in the Auto Scaling group doesn't drop the customer's cart. A durable external session store means DynamoDB or ElastiCache for Redis. The dump key gives AD, and this is the most disputed spot: sticky sessions don't actually store anything — they only pin a client to the same instance, and the session is lost when that instance is replaced. A significant part of the community picks BD, and going strictly by the wording of the requirement — "store session data durably" — that is the stronger answer. Keep in mind: what matters in this question isn't the letter of the key, it's the underlying technique — moving state out of the instances.  
Why B is not selected: Formally this is the strongest of the options: DynamoDB is durable by definition, replicates data across three Availability Zones, and is the standard AWS session store. The dump key didn't pick it, and this is exactly where the dispute lies.  
Why C is not selected: Cognito manages user accounts and authentication tokens, not the cart or transaction state. That's a different layer of the problem.  
Why E is not selected: Systems Manager Application Manager is a console for operating application resources. It is not a user session store in any form.

---

391\. A company needs a backup strategy for its three-tier stateless web application. The web application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group with a dynamic scaling policy that is configured to respond to scaling events. The database tier runs on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The web application does not require temporary local storage on the EC2 instances. The company’s recovery point objective (RPO) is 2 hours.  
The backup strategy must maximize scalability and optimize resource utilization for this environment.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Take snapshots of Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes of the EC2 instances and database every 2 hours to meet the RPO.  
B. Configure a snapshot lifecycle policy to take Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots. Enable automated backups in Amazon RDS to meet the RPO.  
C. Retain the latest Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) of the web and application tiers. Enable automated backups in Amazon RDS and use point-in-time recovery to meet the RPO.  
D. Take snapshots of Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes of the EC2 instances every 2 hours. Enable automated backups in Amazon RDS and use point-in-time recovery to meet the RPO.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The application is stateless and does not need temporary local storage, so taking snapshots of the instance volumes is pointless — it is enough to keep up-to-date AMIs, from which the Auto Scaling group can launch any number of instances. A two-hour recovery point for the data is covered by RDS automated backups with point-in-time recovery.  
Why A is not selected: Instance volume snapshots are unnecessary for a stateless application and just consume resources, and "database snapshots every two hours" duplicate RDS's built-in mechanism.  
Why B is not selected: An EBS snapshot lifecycle policy again backs up something that does not need backing up, and without point-in-time recovery the two-hour RPO is not guaranteed.  
Why D is not selected: This also snapshots unnecessary instance volumes, wasting resources, even though the second half of the option is correct.

---

392\. A company wants to deploy a new public web application on AWS. The application includes a web server tier that uses Amazon EC2 instances. The application also includes a database tier that uses an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance.  
The application must be secure and accessible for global customers that have dynamic IP addresses.  
How should a solutions architect configure the security groups to meet these requirements?  
A. Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from the security group of the web servers.  
B. Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from the IP addresses of the customers. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from the security group of the web servers.  
C. Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from the IP addresses of the customers. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from the IP addresses of the customers.  
D. Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Customers are located worldwide and have dynamic IP addresses, so listing their source addresses is impossible — the web tier must accept HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0. The database, however, stays locked down: its security group allows port 3306 not from IP addresses but by referencing the web servers' security group, so access automatically applies to whatever instances currently belong to that group, and only to them.  
Why B is not selected: You cannot enumerate customer IP addresses since they are dynamic, and global users would simply lose the ability to reach the site.  
Why C is not selected: Same mistake with customer IP addresses, plus the database is opened up by a list of addresses instead of referencing the web servers' security group.  
Why D is not selected: Opening port 3306 to the entire internet is a direct violation of the security requirement.

---

393\. A payment processing company records all voice communication with its customers and stores the audio files in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company needs to capture the text from the audio files. The company must remove from the text any personally identifiable information (PII) that belongs to customers.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Process the audio files by using Amazon Kinesis Video Streams. Use an AWS Lambda function to scan for known PII patterns.  
B. When an audio file is uploaded to the S3 bucket, invoke an AWS Lambda function to start an Amazon Textract task to analyze the call recordings.  
C. Configure an Amazon Transcribe transcription job with PII redaction turned on. When an audio file is uploaded to the S3 bucket, invoke an AWS Lambda function to start the transcription job. Store the output in a separate S3 bucket.  
D. Create an Amazon Connect contact flow that ingests the audio files with transcription turned on. Embed an AWS Lambda function to scan for known PII patterns. Use Amazon EventBridge to start the contact flow when an audio file is uploaded to the S3 bucket.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Two operations are needed: transcribe the speech and strip out personal data. Amazon Transcribe does both in a single job — it has a built-in PII redaction feature for the transcript. A Lambda function triggered by the upload event starts the transcription job, and the output is stored in a separate bucket.  
Why A is not selected: Kinesis Video Streams handles streaming video, not already-recorded audio files, and it does not perform speech recognition.  
Why B is not selected: Textract extracts text from documents and images; it does not understand audio.  
Why D is not selected: Amazon Connect is a contact center for live calls, not a tool for batch-processing already-recorded files; a custom-built PII scanner is also unreliable.

---

394\. A company is running a multi-tier ecommerce web application in the AWS Cloud. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances with an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance. Amazon RDS is configured with the latest generation DB instance with 2,000 GB of storage in a General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. The database performance affects the application during periods of high demand.  
A database administrator analyzes the logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs and discovers that the application performance always degrades when the number of read and write IOPS is higher than 20,000.  
What should a solutions architect do to improve the application performance?  
A. Replace the volume with a magnetic volume.  
B. Increase the number of IOPS on the gp3 volume.  
C. Replace the volume with a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volume.  
D. Replace the 2,000 GB gp3 volume with two 1,000 GB gp3 volumes.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The limit is specific: a single gp3 volume tops out at 16,000 IOPS, while the application is hitting 20,000. The fix is to spread the load across two gp3 volumes and combine them at the database or file system level — the combined limit doubles while the cost per gigabyte stays the same.  
Why A is not selected: A magnetic volume is tens of times slower, so performance would get noticeably worse.  
Why B is not selected: gp3 IOPS can only be raised up to 16,000, which is below the required 20,000, so the limit would still be hit.  
Why C is not selected: An io2 volume does deliver more IOPS, but it costs substantially more, whereas two gp3 volumes meet the requirement more cheaply.

---

395\. An IAM user made several configuration changes to AWS resources in their company's account during a production deployment last week. A solutions architect learned that a couple of security group rules are not configured as desired. The solutions architect wants to confirm which IAM user was responsible for making changes.  
Which service should the solutions architect use to find the desired information?  
A. Amazon GuardDuty  
B. Amazon Inspector  
C. AWS CloudTrail  
D. AWS Config  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The question of "who called which API and when" is always answered with AWS CloudTrail: it logs management-operation API calls along with the caller's identity, time, source address, and request parameters, and the AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress event shows exactly who changed the rules. It's worth remembering the split between services: CloudTrail tells you who did what, Config shows what a resource's configuration looked like and how it changed, GuardDuty flags signs of malicious activity, and Inspector finds vulnerabilities in workloads.  
Why A is not selected: GuardDuty looks for signs of compromise and suspicious behavior. It is not a log of user actions.  
Why B is not selected: Inspector scans instances and images for vulnerabilities and insecure configurations; it does not record who changed a resource.  
Why D is not selected: AWS Config will show that the security group's configuration changed and how, but the answer to "which user did this" lives in CloudTrail.

---

396\. A company has implemented a self-managed DNS service on AWS. The solution consists of the following:  
• Amazon EC2 instances in different AWS Regions  
• Endpoints of a standard accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator The company wants to protect the solution against DDoS attacks.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?  
A. Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced. Add the accelerator as a resource to protect.  
B. Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced. Add the EC2 instances as resources to protect.  
C. Create an AWS WAF web ACL that includes a rate-based rule. Associate the web ACL with the accelerator.  
D. Create an AWS WAF web ACL that includes a rate-based rule. Associate the web ACL with the EC2 instances.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: You need to protect the point where the traffic actually arrives — the static anycast addresses of Global Accelerator. AWS Shield Advanced supports the accelerator as a protected resource, so that's what you add to the subscription: the attack is absorbed at the edge of the AWS global network before it ever reaches the instances. Note that this is a DNS service running over UDP, so WAF is inapplicable in principle — it only filters HTTP.  
Why B is not selected: The instances sit behind the accelerator and don't receive traffic directly; the entry point is what needs protecting. Also, Shield Advanced protects an Elastic IP, not an instance as such.  
Why C is not selected: AWS WAF filters HTTP requests and cannot be attached to Global Accelerator: it is useless for DNS traffic.  
Why D is not selected: WAF cannot be attached to EC2 instances, and it's still inapplicable to DNS traffic.

---

397\. An ecommerce company needs to run a scheduled daily job to aggregate and filter sales records for analytics. The company stores the sales records in an Amazon S3 bucket. Each object can be up to 10 GB in size. Based on the number of sales events, the job can take up to an hour to complete. The CPU and memory usage of the job are constant and are known in advance.  
A solutions architect needs to minimize the amount of operational effort that is needed for the job to run.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Create an AWS Lambda function that has an Amazon EventBridge notification. Schedule the EventBridge event to run once a day.  
B. Create an AWS Lambda function. Create an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API, and integrate the API with the function. Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event that calls the API and invokes the function.  
C. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with an AWS Fargate launch type. Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event that launches an ECS task on the cluster to run the job.  
D. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with an Amazon EC2 launch type and an Auto Scaling group with at least one EC2 instance. Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event that launches an ECS task on the cluster to run the job.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The job runs for up to an hour, so Lambda's fifteen-minute limit rules it out. The CPU and memory requirements are known in advance and constant — a perfect fit for an ECS task on Fargate: a scheduled EventBridge rule launches it once a day, the task runs to completion, and there's no infrastructure to maintain.  
Why A is not selected: A Lambda function is capped at fifteen minutes of execution: an hour-long job would be cut off.  
Why B is not selected: Same execution limit, plus an unnecessary API Gateway layer; on top of that, a synchronous call through an HTTP API is constrained even more tightly.  
Why D is not selected: The EC2 launch type means a continuously running instance in the group that must be maintained, even though the job only runs once a day.

---

398\. A company needs to transfer 600 TB of data from its on-premises network-attached storage (NAS) system to the AWS Cloud. The data transfer must be complete within 2 weeks. The data is sensitive and must be encrypted in transit. The company’s internet connection can support an upload speed of 100 Mbps.  
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Use Amazon S3 multi-part upload functionality to transfer the files over HTTPS.  
B. Create a VPN connection between the on-premises NAS system and the nearest AWS Region. Transfer the data over the VPN connection.  
C. Use the AWS Snow Family console to order several AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices. Use the devices to transfer the data to Amazon S3.  
D. Set up a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection between the company location and the nearest AWS Region. Transfer the data over a VPN connection into the Region to store the data in Amazon S3.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Do the math: 600 TB at 100 Mbps takes over a year to transfer, but the deadline is two weeks. Any option that relies on the existing link is ruled out arithmetically. That leaves physical devices: several Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices move the data in days, encrypt the contents with AWS KMS keys, and don't consume any internet bandwidth. See {{q:215}} for more on transferring data over a network link.  
Why A is not selected: Multipart upload speeds up a single object, but the overall bandwidth stays the same: the deadline still isn't met.  
Why B is not selected: A VPN still rides the same 100 Mbps link, just adding encryption overhead on top.  
Why D is not selected: A 10 Gbps Direct Connect connection would technically be fast enough, but provisioning the physical link usually takes weeks, and its cost is out of proportion to a one-time bulk transfer compared with renting the devices for a single trip.

---

399\. A financial company hosts a web application on AWS. The application uses an Amazon API Gateway Regional API endpoint to give users the ability to retrieve current stock prices. The company’s security team has noticed an increase in the number of API requests. The security team is concerned that HTTP flood attacks might take the application offline.  
A solutions architect must design a solution to protect the application from this type of attack.  
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API Gateway Regional API endpoint with a maximum TTL of 24 hours.  
B. Create a Regional AWS WAF web ACL with a rate-based rule. Associate the web ACL with the API Gateway stage.  
C. Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to monitor the Count metric and alert the security team when the predefined rate is reached.  
D. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with [email protected] in front of the API Gateway Regional API endpoint. Create an AWS Lambda function to block requests from IP addresses that exceed the predefined rate.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: An HTTP flood is a large volume of requests that are valid in form, and the way to cut them off is rate limiting. AWS WAF has a rate-based rule for exactly this: it counts requests from each address over a rolling five-minute window and blocks anyone who exceeds the threshold. A Regional web ACL attaches directly to the API Gateway stage, so no extra components are added to the architecture — hence the minimal operational overhead.  
Why A is not selected: CloudFront with a long TTL helps with repeated requests for cacheable content, but stock quotes are dynamic, and CloudFront by itself provides no rate limiting.  
Why C is not selected: The metric and alarm notify people about the problem, but they don't block any requests.  
Why D is not selected: A custom function that maintains per-address counters means development work and state that has to be maintained, instead of a ready-made WAF rule.

---

400\. A meteorological startup company has a custom web application to sell weather data to its users online. The company uses Amazon DynamoDB to store its data and wants to build a new service that sends an alert to the managers of four internal teams every time a new weather event is recorded. The company does not want this new service to affect the performance of the current application.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?  
A. Use DynamoDB transactions to write new event data to the table. Configure the transactions to notify internal teams.  
B. Have the current application publish a message to four Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topics. Have each team subscribe to one topic.  
C. Enable Amazon DynamoDB Streams on the table. Use triggers to write to a single Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to which the teams can subscribe.  
D. Add a custom attribute to each record to flag new items. Write a cron job that scans the table every minute for items that are new and notifies an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to which the teams can subscribe.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The alert needs to fire on every new record without affecting the existing application. DynamoDB Streams publishes a feed of table changes, a handler sends a message to a single SNS topic, and all four teams subscribe to that topic. The application itself doesn't change at all.  
Why A is not selected: DynamoDB transactions guarantee write atomicity and don't notify anyone.  
Why B is not selected: This requires modifying the application and setting up four topics instead of one — extra work and extra upkeep.  
Why D is not selected: Polling the table every minute for a flag means added latency, constant scanning, and a custom scheduler; on top of that, multiple teams can't all subscribe to a single SQS queue.

---

401\. A company wants to use the AWS Cloud to make an existing application highly available and resilient. The current version of the application resides in the company's data center. The application recently experienced data loss after a database server crashed because of an unexpected power outage.  
The company needs a solution that avoids any single points of failure. The solution must give the application the ability to scale to meet user demand.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Deploy the application servers by using Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Use an Amazon RDS DB instance in a Multi-AZ configuration.  
B. Deploy the application servers by using Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group in a single Availability Zone. Deploy the database on an EC2 instance. Enable EC2 Auto Recovery.  
C. Deploy the application servers by using Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Use an Amazon RDS DB instance with a read replica in a single Availability Zone. Promote the read replica to replace the primary DB instance if the primary DB instance fails.  
D. Deploy the application servers by using Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Deploy the primary and secondary database servers on EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach to create shared storage between the instances.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The single point of failure was the database, and that's the first thing to eliminate. RDS in a Multi-AZ configuration synchronously replicates data to another Availability Zone and fails over automatically, so a power outage in one zone does not result in data loss. The application layer sits in an Auto Scaling group spread across multiple Availability Zones, which provides both fault tolerance and the ability to scale with demand.  
Why B is not selected: A single Availability Zone still leaves a single point of failure in place, and EC2 Auto Recovery protects against neither a zone failure nor the loss of data on the instance's disk.  
Why C is not selected: A read replica operates asynchronously and requires manual promotion during an outage, which means both data loss is possible and recovery time is long.  
Why D is not selected: Multi-Attach works only within a single Availability Zone, so the described setup with databases in different zones is not possible.

---

402\. A company needs to ingest and handle large amounts of streaming data that its application generates. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances and sends data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, which is configured with default settings. Every other day, the application consumes the data and writes the data to an Amazon S3 bucket for business intelligence (BI) processing. The company observes that Amazon S3 is not receiving all the data that the application sends to Kinesis Data Streams.  
What should a solutions architect do to resolve this issue?  
A. Update the Kinesis Data Streams default settings by modifying the data retention period.  
B. Update the application to use the Kinesis Producer Library (KPL) to send the data to Kinesis Data Streams.  
C. Update the number of Kinesis shards to handle the throughput of the data that is sent to Kinesis Data Streams.  
D. Turn on S3 Versioning within the S3 bucket to preserve every version of every object that is ingested in the S3 bucket.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The application pulls data only every other day, but a Kinesis stream retains records for 24 hours by default — anything older is dropped before the consumer arrives. Increasing the retention period (up to 7 days in standard mode, and longer with extended retention) is enough to stop the data loss.  
Why B is not selected: The Kinesis Producer Library improves write efficiency, but it has no effect on how long already-written data is retained.  
Why C is not selected: A shortage of shards shows up as write failures, but here writes succeed and the data is lost later, during the read.  
Why D is not selected: S3 Versioning preserves versions of objects that have already been uploaded to S3 and does nothing to save data that was already removed from the stream.

---

403\. A developer has an application that uses an AWS Lambda function to upload files to Amazon S3 and needs the required permissions to perform the task. The developer already has an IAM user with valid IAM credentials required for Amazon S3.  
What should a solutions architect do to grant the permissions?  
A. Add required IAM permissions in the resource policy of the Lambda function.  
B. Create a signed request using the existing IAM credentials in the Lambda function.  
C. Create a new IAM user and use the existing IAM credentials in the Lambda function.  
D. Create an IAM execution role with the required permissions and attach the IAM role to the Lambda function.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Lambda functions get their permissions through an execution role: the role is assigned to the function, and a policy with the required actions — for example, s3:PutObject on a specific bucket — is attached to that role. At runtime, the function automatically obtains temporary credentials for that role, so nothing needs to be stored in the code. The existing IAM user here is just a distractor: putting a person's keys inside a service's code is an anti-pattern. Don't confuse Lambda's two kinds of policies — the execution role defines what the function is allowed to do, while a resource-based policy defines who is allowed to invoke it.  
Why A is not selected: The function's resource policy defines which services and accounts are allowed to invoke it. It does not grant permission to write to S3.  
Why B is not selected: Signing requests with the existing user's keys means embedding a long-lived secret in the function's code. It would work, but it goes against accepted practice and doesn't solve the permissions-management problem.  
Why C is not selected: A new user and its keys are the same mistake: long-lived credentials in the code instead of temporary credentials from a role.

---

404\. A company has deployed a serverless application that invokes an AWS Lambda function when new documents are uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket. The application uses the Lambda function to process the documents. After a recent marketing campaign, the company noticed that the application did not process many of the documents.  
What should a solutions architect do to improve the architecture of this application?  
A. Set the Lambda function's runtime timeout value to 15 minutes.  
B. Configure an S3 bucket replication policy. Stage the documents in the S3 bucket for later processing.  
C. Deploy an additional Lambda function. Load balance the processing of the documents across the two Lambda functions.  
D. Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Send the requests to the queue. Configure the queue as an event source for Lambda.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: During a traffic spike, direct invocation from S3 runs into the function's concurrency limit, and the excess events are lost, since asynchronous invocations have a limited number of retries. An SQS queue accepts every event, holds it, and hands it to the function at exactly the pace the function can keep up with — no document gets dropped.  
Why A is not selected: A 15-minute runtime timeout doesn't help if the event never reaches the function in the first place.  
Why B is not selected: Replication copies objects into another bucket, but it doesn't perform any processing and doesn't preserve events.  
Why C is not selected: A second function doesn't raise the account's overall concurrency limit and doesn't provide buffering, and Lambda invocations can't be load balanced this way.

---

405\. A solutions architect is designing the architecture for a software demonstration environment. The environment will run on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The system will experience significant increases in traffic during working hours but is not required to operate on weekends.  
Which combination of actions should the solutions architect take to ensure that the system can scale to meet demand? (Choose two.)  
A. Use AWS Auto Scaling to adjust the ALB capacity based on request rate.  
B. Use AWS Auto Scaling to scale the capacity of the VPC internet gateway.  
C. Launch the EC2 instances in multiple AWS Regions to distribute the load across Regions.  
D. Use a target tracking scaling policy to scale the Auto Scaling group based on instance CPU utilization.  
E. Use scheduled scaling to change the Auto Scaling group minimum, maximum, and desired capacity to zero for weekends. Revert to the default values at the start of the week.  
Answer: DE  
Explanation: Load rises during business hours and disappears entirely on weekends. For the workday, a target tracking scaling policy based on average CPU utilization fits well — capacity follows actual demand (D). For weekends, scheduled scaling sets the Auto Scaling group's minimum, desired, and maximum capacity to zero, then restores the previous values at the start of the week (E).  
Why A is not selected: The Application Load Balancer scales automatically as a managed service; its capacity cannot and does not need to be configured.  
Why B is not selected: The internet gateway is a logical construct with no throughput limit, so there's nothing to scale.  
Why C is not selected: Deploying across multiple Regions addresses global availability, not intraday load fluctuations, and it costs considerably more.

---

406\. A solutions architect is designing a two-tiered architecture that includes a public subnet and a database subnet.  
The web servers in the public subnet must be open to the internet on port 443. The Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in the database subnet must be accessible only to the web servers on port 3306.  
Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Create a network ACL for the public subnet. Add a rule to deny outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 3306.  
B. Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to allow traffic from the public subnet CIDR block on port 3306.  
C. Create a security group for the web servers in the public subnet. Add a rule to allow traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443.  
D. Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to allow traffic from the web servers’ security group on port 3306.  
E. Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to deny all traffic except traffic from the web servers’ security group on port 3306.  
Answer: CD  
Explanation: The two-tier design is built on security groups: the web servers open port 443 to the whole internet, since a public site needs to accept visitors (C), and the database allows port 3306 by referencing the web servers' security group (D) — that way access is granted to exactly those instances, regardless of their addresses, and no one else.  
Why A is not selected: Network ACLs operate at the subnet level and aren't needed here; denying outbound traffic on port 3306 would break the web servers' connections to the database.  
Why B is not selected: Allowing traffic by the subnet's address range opens the database to any resource in that subnet, not just the web servers.  
Why E is not selected: Security groups have no deny rules — only what's explicitly allowed is permitted — so a rule like this cannot be created.

---

407\. A company is implementing a shared storage solution for a gaming application that is hosted in the AWS Cloud.  
The company needs the ability to use Lustre clients to access data. The solution must be fully managed.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Create an AWS DataSync task that shares the data as a mountable file system. Mount the file system to the application server.  
B. Create an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway. Create a file share that uses the required client protocol. Connect the application server to the file share.  
C. Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system, and configure it to support Lustre. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.  
D. Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The defining phrase again is Lustre clients. There is exactly one managed file system in AWS that speaks this protocol: Amazon FSx for Lustre. It delivers sub-millisecond latency and throughput in the gigabytes per second, while AWS handles all the operational work. A similar walkthrough appears in {{q:99}}.  
Why A is not selected: DataSync moves data between storage systems and doesn't create a mountable file system.  
Why B is not selected: Storage Gateway serves resources over NFS and SMB; it has no Lustre protocol.  
Why C is not selected: EFS has no mode that supports Lustre — no such configuration exists.

---

408\. A company runs an application that receives data from thousands of geographically dispersed remote devices that use UDP. The application processes the data immediately and sends a message back to the device if necessary. No data is stored.  
The company needs a solution that minimizes latency for the data transmission from the devices. The solution also must provide rapid failover to another AWS Region.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Configure an Amazon Route 53 failover routing policy. Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in each of the two Regions. Configure the NLB to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the data.  
B. Use AWS Global Accelerator. Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in each of the two Regions as an endpoint. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Fargate launch type. Create an ECS service on the cluster. Set the ECS service as the target for the NLProcess the data in Amazon ECS.  
C. Use AWS Global Accelerator. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in each of the two Regions as an endpoint. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Fargate launch type. Create an ECS service on the cluster. Set the ECS service as the target for the ALB. Process the data in Amazon ECS.  
D. Configure an Amazon Route 53 failover routing policy. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in each of the two Regions. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Fargate launch type. Create an ECS service on the cluster. Set the ECS service as the target for the ALB. Process the data in Amazon ECS.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: UDP traffic, minimal latency, and rapid failover to another Region point to Global Accelerator with a Network Load Balancer in each Region. The accelerator ingests packets at the nearest edge location, routes them over the AWS global network backbone, and switches to a healthy Region within seconds, without depending on DNS caching. Serverless processing is provided by ECS on Fargate, registered as the load balancer's target. An ALB is out of the question here by definition — it doesn't support UDP.  
Why A is not selected: Failover through Route 53 is slower because of TTL and resolver caching, and a Network Load Balancer can't invoke a Lambda function as a target.  
Why C is not selected: The Application Load Balancer doesn't support UDP: the devices simply wouldn't be able to send their data.  
Why D is not selected: Neither is the ALB suitable for UDP, nor does DNS-based failover provide a fast, fault-tolerant transition.

---

409\. A solutions architect must migrate a Windows Internet Information Services (IIS) web application to AWS. The application currently relies on a file share hosted in the user's on-premises network-attached storage (NAS). The solutions architect has proposed migrating the IIS web servers to Amazon EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones that are connected to the storage solution, and configuring an Elastic Load Balancer attached to the instances.  
Which replacement to the on-premises file share is MOST resilient and durable?  
A. Migrate the file share to Amazon RDS.  
B. Migrate the file share to AWS Storage Gateway.  
C. Migrate the file share to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.
