D. Migrate the file share to Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS).  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The IIS application runs on Windows and accesses the network share over the SMB protocol. The most resilient and durable replacement is Amazon FSx for Windows File Server in a Multi-AZ configuration: data is replicated synchronously between Availability Zones, Windows ACLs and Active Directory are supported, and instances in every zone mount the same file share.  
Why A is not selected: RDS is a relational database; it cannot serve as a file share.  
Why B is not selected: Storage Gateway is designed for hybrid scenarios and relies on a local virtual machine, which itself becomes a single point of failure. For a workload fully migrated to AWS, it isn't needed.  
Why D is not selected: EFS uses the NFS protocol: for an IIS application on Windows this isn't a native access method, and Windows ACLs aren't supported there.

---

410\. A company is deploying a new application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application writes data to Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. The company needs to ensure that all data that is written to the EBS volumes is encrypted at rest.  
Which solution will meet this requirement?  
A. Create an IAM role that specifies EBS encryption. Attach the role to the EC2 instances.  
B. Create the EBS volumes as encrypted volumes. Attach the EBS volumes to the EC2 instances.  
C. Create an EC2 instance tag that has a key of Encrypt and a value of True. Tag all instances that require encryption at the EBS level.  
D. Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key policy that enforces EBS encryption in the account. Ensure that the key policy is active.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: For EBS volumes, encryption is set at creation time and covers the data on disk, data in transit between the volume and the instance, snapshots, and volumes created from those snapshots. Encryption cannot be turned on for an existing unencrypted volume — instead you take a snapshot, copy it while specifying a KMS key, and create a new volume from the encrypted copy. So the right approach is to create the volumes as encrypted from the start; at the account level, this is conveniently enforced with the EC2 "EBS encryption by default" setting.  
Why A is not selected: An IAM role describes what a principal is allowed to do. It has no property that "encrypts volumes" and has no effect on how volumes are created.  
Why C is not selected: A tag is just a label for tracking and search. On its own it turns nothing on; at most you can build policies around it, but a volume doesn't get encrypted because of a tag.  
Why D is not selected: A KMS key policy defines who is allowed to use the key — it doesn't force encryption of volumes across the account. Enforcement is done through the default EBS encryption setting or an SCP policy with an ec2:Encrypted condition.

---

411\. A company has a web application with sporadic usage patterns. There is heavy usage at the beginning of each month, moderate usage at the start of each week, and unpredictable usage during the week. The application consists of a web server and a MySQL database server running inside the data center. The company would like to move the application to the AWS Cloud, and needs to select a cost-effective database platform that will not require database modifications.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Amazon DynamoDB  
B. Amazon RDS for MySQL  
C. MySQL-compatible Amazon Aurora Serverless  
D. MySQL deployed on Amazon EC2 in an Auto Scaling group  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Load spikes unpredictably, the database can't be changed, and cost matters. MySQL-compatible Aurora Serverless is exactly right here: the application runs unmodified, and capacity scales automatically to handle the surges at the start of each month and week, then scales back down during quiet periods, so the company doesn't pay for peak capacity around the clock.  
Why A is not selected: DynamoDB is a non-relational store: the queries and data model would have to be rewritten.  
Why B is not selected: RDS for MySQL requires choosing an instance class sized for the peak and paying for it continuously, even when there's no load.  
Why D is not selected: A relational database can't be scaled with an EC2 Auto Scaling group: new instances don't share the underlying data.

---

412\. An image-hosting company stores its objects in Amazon S3 buckets. The company wants to avoid accidental exposure of the objects in the S3 buckets to the public. All S3 objects in the entire AWS account need to remain private.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use Amazon GuardDuty to monitor S3 bucket policies. Create an automatic remediation action rule that uses an AWS Lambda function to remediate any change that makes the objects public.  
B. Use AWS Trusted Advisor to find publicly accessible S3 buckets. Configure email notifications in Trusted Advisor when a change is detected. Manually change the S3 bucket policy if it allows public access.  
C. Use AWS Resource Access Manager to find publicly accessible S3 buckets. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to invoke an AWS Lambda function when a change is detected. Deploy a Lambda function that programmatically remediates the change.  
D. Use the S3 Block Public Access feature on the account level. Use AWS Organizations to create a service control policy (SCP) that prevents IAM users from changing the setting. Apply the SCP to the account.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The requirement is that no object in the entire account can ever become public, even if someone misconfigures a policy. The first layer is S3 Block Public Access at the account level: it overrides any public ACLs or bucket policies regardless of their content. The second layer is an SCP that denies the s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock action (and disabling the block on individual buckets), so the setting can't be turned off from inside the account. This is preventive protection, not after-the-fact detection.  
Why A is not selected: GuardDuty analyzes threats and suspicious activity, but it doesn't monitor bucket policies or roll them back.  
Why B is not selected: Trusted Advisor finds public buckets after the fact and sends a notification, while the fix stays manual. The data can end up exposed in the meantime.  
Why C is not selected: Resource Access Manager shares resources across accounts and has nothing to do with finding public buckets.

---

413\. An ecommerce company is experiencing an increase in user traffic. The company’s store is deployed on Amazon EC2 instances as a two-tier web application consisting of a web tier and a separate database tier. As traffic increases, the company notices that the architecture is causing significant delays in sending timely marketing and order confirmation email to users. The company wants to reduce the time it spends resolving complex email delivery issues and minimize operational overhead.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Create a separate application tier using EC2 instances dedicated to email processing.  
B. Configure the web instance to send email through Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES).  
C. Configure the web instance to send email through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS).  
D. Create a separate application tier using EC2 instances dedicated to email processing. Place the instances in an Auto Scaling group.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The problem is email delivery, and the company wants to stop dealing with its complexity. Amazon SES is a managed email service: sender reputation, delivery queues, bounces, and complaints are all handled by the service — the application just calls the API.  
Why A is not selected: A dedicated email tier of EC2 instances leaves all the delivery complexity on the company and adds more infrastructure.  
Why C is not selected: SNS delivers notifications to subscribers, but it isn't a full email-sending tool for customers: no templates, no reputation management.  
Why D is not selected: Same as option A, just with Auto Scaling added: operational overhead doesn't go down, it goes up.

---

414\. A company has a business system that generates hundreds of reports each day. The business system saves the reports to a network share in CSV format. The company needs to store this data in the AWS Cloud in near-real time for analysis.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?  
A. Use AWS DataSync to transfer the files to Amazon S3. Create a scheduled task that runs at the end of each day.  
B. Create an Amazon S3 File Gateway. Update the business system to use a new network share from the S3 File Gateway.  
C. Use AWS DataSync to transfer the files to Amazon S3. Create an application that uses the DataSync API in the automation workflow.  
D. Deploy an AWS Transfer for SFTP endpoint. Create a script that checks for new files on the network share and uploads the new files by using SFTP.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The business system can only write to a network share, it can't be modified, and the data needs to reach the cloud in near-real time. S3 File Gateway presents exactly that kind of network share, but every file saved to it is asynchronously turned into an S3 object — essentially in real time and without writing a single line of automation. The system just points to the new share.  
Why A is not selected: A once-a-day task isn't near-real time: reports would sit and wait until the end of the day.  
Why C is not selected: A custom application calling the DataSync API is code that has to be written and maintained, while the gateway does the same job out of the box.  
Why D is not selected: A script that watches for new files and uploads them over SFTP is once again custom automation with its own failures and retries to manage.

---

415\. A company is storing petabytes of data in Amazon S3 Standard. The data is stored in multiple S3 buckets and is accessed with varying frequency. The company does not know access patterns for all the data. The company needs to implement a solution for each S3 bucket to optimize the cost of S3 usage.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?  
A. Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration with a rule to transition the objects in the S3 bucket to S3 Intelligent- Tiering.  
B. Use the S3 storage class analysis tool to determine the correct tier for each object in the S3 bucket. Move each object to the identified storage tier.  
C. Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration with a rule to transition the objects in the S3 bucket to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.  
D. Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration with a rule to transition the objects in the S3 bucket to S3 One Zone- Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA).  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The discriminator is "MOST operational efficiency" when access patterns are unknown. Intelligent-Tiering needs no analysis and no manual decisions: it monitors access to each object itself and moves it between tiers, with no retrieval fees. A single Lifecycle rule per bucket covers petabytes of data. Keep the caveat in mind: objects smaller than 128 KB never move to the archive tiers and are always billed at the frequent-access tier.  
Why B is not selected: Storage class analysis only produces a report. Moving petabytes of objects based on its results has to be done by hand, and repeated every time the access pattern changes — the most operational overhead of any option.  
Why C is not selected: Glacier Instant Retrieval gives instant access, but charges a noticeable retrieval fee and carries a 90-day minimum storage duration. Some of the petabytes are read frequently, and for those it ends up costing more than Standard.  
Why D is not selected: One Zone-IA reduces fault tolerance to a single zone and charges a retrieval fee — a poor choice for data with an unknown access pattern.

---

416\. A rapidly growing global ecommerce company is hosting its web application on AWS. The web application includes static content and dynamic content. The website stores online transaction processing (OLTP) data in an Amazon RDS database The website’s users are experiencing slow page loads.  
Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to resolve this issue? (Choose two.)  
A. Configure an Amazon Redshift cluster.  
B. Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution.  
C. Host the dynamic web content in Amazon S3.  
D. Create a read replica for the RDS DB instance.  
E. Configure a Multi-AZ deployment for the RDS DB instance.  
Answer: BD  
Explanation: The slow page loads come from two sources. CloudFront speeds up the static content and part of the dynamic content: content is cached at edge locations, and requests travel to the Region over the AWS backbone (B). A read replica for RDS takes the load off the database, absorbing the read queries and freeing up the primary instance for transactions (D).  
Why A is not selected: Redshift is an analytics warehouse and has nothing to do with page-load speed on a transactional site.  
Why C is not selected: Dynamic content by definition can't be hosted in S3: it's generated by the application.  
Why E is not selected: A Multi-AZ configuration improves availability, but the standby instance doesn't serve requests, so it doesn't improve performance.

---

417\. A company uses Amazon EC2 instances and AWS Lambda functions to run its application. The company has VPCs with public subnets and private subnets in its AWS account. The EC2 instances run in a private subnet in one of the VPCs. The Lambda functions need direct network access to the EC2 instances for the application to work.  
The application will run for at least 1 year. The company expects the number of Lambda functions that the application uses to increase during that time. The company wants to maximize its savings on all application resources and to keep network latency between the services low.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan Optimize the Lambda functions’ duration and memory usage and the number of invocations. Connect the Lambda functions to the private subnet that contains the EC2 instances.  
B. Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan Optimize the Lambda functions' duration and memory usage, the number of invocations, and the amount of data that is transferred. Connect the Lambda functions to a public subnet in the same VPC where the EC2 instances run.  
C. Purchase a Compute Savings Plan. Optimize the Lambda functions’ duration and memory usage, the number of invocations, and the amount of data that is transferred. Connect the Lambda functions to the private subnet that contains the EC2 instances.  
D. Purchase a Compute Savings Plan. Optimize the Lambda functions’ duration and memory usage, the number of invocations, and the amount of data that is transferred. Keep the Lambda functions in the Lambda service VPC.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The company needs to save money on both the instances and the functions, and the functions need direct network access to the instances. A Compute Savings Plan covers EC2, Lambda, and Fargate together, giving a discount on all of the application's compute. Direct access comes from connecting the functions to the same private subnet where the instances run — traffic stays inside the VPC with minimal latency.  
Why A is not selected: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan only discounts instances: spending on the growing number of functions stays at full price.  
Why B is not selected: The same limited savings plan, and connecting the functions to a public subnet doesn't bring them any closer to the instances — it just complicates routing.  
Why D is not selected: Staying in the Lambda service VPC means the functions don't get direct network access to the instances in the private subnet.

---

418\. A solutions architect needs to allow team members to access Amazon S3 buckets in two different AWS accounts:  
a development account and a production account. The team currently has access to S3 buckets in the development account by using unique IAM users that are assigned to an IAM group that has appropriate permissions in the account.  
The solutions architect has created an IAM role in the production account. The role has a policy that grants access to an S3 bucket in the production account.  
Which solution will meet these requirements while complying with the principle of least privilege?  
A. Attach the Administrator Access policy to the development account users.  
B. Add the development account as a principal in the trust policy of the role in the production account.  
C. Turn off the S3 Block Public Access feature on the S3 bucket in the production account.  
D. Create a user in the production account with unique credentials for each team member.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Classic cross-account access isn't built by duplicating users — it's built on a role: the target account has a role with permissions on the bucket, and that role's trust policy lists who is allowed to assume it. The role in production already exists, so what's left is to add the development account as a principal in its trust policy (and let users assume the role via sts:AssumeRole on their side). Users keep living in a single account, temporary credentials are issued for the duration of the session, and permissions are limited to what the role's policy grants — that's least privilege.  
Why A is not selected: AdministratorAccess grants full access to the entire development account and does nothing to open up the bucket in production. A direct violation of least privilege.  
Why C is not selected: Turning off Block Public Access exposes the bucket to the outside world and has nothing to do with granting the team access. That's a security regression, not a solution.  
Why D is not selected: Separate users in production mean a second set of long-lived credentials per person that have to be created, rotated, and revoked. A role solves the same problem with temporary credentials.

---

419\. A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and runs multiple Amazon EC2 workloads in the ap- southeast-2 Region. The company has a service control policy (SCP) that prevents any resources from being created in any other Region. A security policy requires the company to encrypt all data at rest.  
An audit discovers that employees have created Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes for EC2 instances without encrypting the volumes. The company wants any new EC2 instances that any IAM user or root user launches in ap-southeast-2 to use encrypted EBS volumes. The company wants a solution that will have minimal effect on employees who create EBS volumes.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. In the Amazon EC2 console, select the EBS encryption account attribute and define a default encryption key.  
B. Create an IAM permission boundary. Attach the permission boundary to the root organizational unit (OU). Define the boundary to deny the ec2:CreateVolume action when the ec2:Encrypted condition equals false.  
C. Create an SCP. Attach the SCP to the root organizational unit (OU). Define the SCP to deny the ec2:CreateVolume action whenthe ec2:Encrypted condition equals false.  
D. Update the IAM policies for each account to deny the ec2:CreateVolume action when the ec2:Encrypted condition equals false.  
E. In the Organizations management account, specify the Default EBS volume encryption setting.  
Answer: CE  
Review status: Disputed key (alternative: AC)  
Dispute note: Option E describes a setting that doesn't exist: default EBS encryption is enabled per account and per region individually (an EC2 setting), not "at the organization's management account" level — the correct pair is A and C  
Explanation: This question is flagged as disputed because of how one option is worded. The intended solution is: a preventive ban on creating unencrypted volumes for everyone, including the root users of member accounts, can only come from an SCP with a condition on ec2:Encrypted equal to false (C) — an IAM policy can simply be rewritten by the account's own administrator, and a permission boundary can't be attached to an organizational unit anyway. The other half is making encryption transparent for employees: default EBS encryption means new volumes are encrypted automatically and nobody hits a denied request. The catch is that this setting is configured per account and per Region individually (option A), while option E, as worded in the answer key, describes it as a setting on the organization's management account, which doesn't exist.  
Why A is not selected: This is actually an accurate description of how default encryption is configured: an account attribute in the EC2 console plus a default KMS key. That's exactly why the pair A and C looks more correct than the dump's answer key.  
Why B is not selected: A permission boundary attaches to a user or a role and caps their maximum permissions. It cannot be attached to an organizational unit.  
Why D is not selected: IAM policies in each account can be changed by that account's own administrator, and they don't apply to the account's root user at all. That gives no preventive guarantee.

---

420\. A company wants to use an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB cluster to simplify time-consuming database administrative tasks for production database workloads. The company wants to ensure that its database is highly available and will provide automatic failover support in most scenarios in less than 40 seconds. The company wants to offload reads off of the primary instance and keep costs as low as possible.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Create one read replica and point the read workload to the read replica.  
B. Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB duster deployment Create two read replicas and point the read workload to the read replicas.  
C. Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Point the read workload to the secondary instances in the Multi-AZ pair.  
D. Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment Point the read workload to the reader endpoint.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The key requirements are failover in under 40 seconds and offloading reads at the lowest possible cost. An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster consists of one primary instance and two standby instances that are also readable at the same time: failover typically completes in around 35 seconds, and all the read traffic can go to the reader endpoint without adding a single extra instance.  
Why A is not selected: A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment takes up to one to two minutes to fail over, and a read replica is yet another instance you pay for.  
Why B is not selected: The cluster choice is right, but the two extra read replicas are redundant: the cluster's nodes are already readable, and the requirement is minimum cost.  
Why C is not selected: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, the standby instance doesn't serve requests.

---

421\. A company runs a highly available SFTP service. The SFTP service uses two Amazon EC2 Linux instances that run with elastic IP addresses to accept traffic from trusted IP sources on the internet. The SFTP service is backed by shared storage that is attached to the instances. User accounts are created and managed as Linux users in the SFTP servers.  
The company wants a serverless option that provides high IOPS performance and highly configurable security. The company also wants to maintain control over user permissions.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create an encrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP service with a public endpoint that allows only trusted IP addresses. Attach the EBS volume to the SFTP service endpoint. Grant users access to the SFTP service.  
B. Create an encrypted Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) volume. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP service with elastic IP addresses and a VPC endpoint that has internet-facing access. Attach a security group to the endpoint that allows only trusted IP addresses. Attach the EFS volume to the SFTP service endpoint. Grant users access to the SFTP service.  
C. Create an Amazon S3 bucket with default encryption enabled. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP service with a public endpoint that allows only trusted IP addresses. Attach the S3 bucket to the SFTP service endpoint. Grant users access to the SFTP service.  
D. Create an Amazon S3 bucket with default encryption enabled. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP service with a VPC endpoint that has internal access in a private subnet. Attach a security group that allows only trusted IP addresses. Attach the S3 bucket to the SFTP service endpoint. Grant users access to the SFTP service.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirements are a serverless service, high I/O performance, finely configurable security, and continued control over user permissions. AWS Transfer Family removes the need for self-managed instances, and the storage is an encrypted EFS file system with familiar POSIX permissions, while the endpoint is deployed inside a VPC with internet-facing access and elastic IP addresses so that a security group can be attached to allow only trusted addresses.  
Why A is not selected: An EBS volume cannot be attached to a Transfer Family service: only S3 and EFS are supported as storage. A public endpoint also does not let you apply a security group.  
Why C is not selected: S3 as the storage backend provides neither familiar POSIX permissions nor the same I/O performance profile, and a public endpoint removes the ability to finely control network access with security groups.  
Why D is not selected: An endpoint in a private subnet with no internet access blocks the trusted sources on the public internet that the scenario explicitly requires.

---

422\. A company is developing a new machine learning (ML) model solution on AWS. The models are developed as independent microservices that fetch approximately 1 GB of model data from Amazon S3 at startup and load the data into memory. Users access the models through an asynchronous API. Users can send a request or a batch of requests and specify where the results should be sent.  
The company provides models to hundreds of users. The usage patterns for the models are irregular. Some models could be unused for days or weeks. Other models could receive batches of thousands of requests at a time.  
Which design should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?  
A. Direct the requests from the API to a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Deploy the models as AWS Lambda functions that are invoked by the NLB.  
B. Direct the requests from the API to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Deploy the models as Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) services that read from an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use AWS App Mesh to scale the instances of the ECS cluster based on the SQS queue size.  
C. Direct the requests from the API into an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Deploy the models as AWS Lambda functions that are invoked by SQS events. Use AWS Auto Scaling to increase the number of vCPUs for the Lambda functions based on the SQS queue size.  
D. Direct the requests from the API into an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Deploy the models as Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) services that read from the queue. Enable AWS Auto Scaling on Amazon ECS for both the cluster and copies of the service based on the queue size.  
Answer: D  
Review status: Low-confidence audit  
Explanation: The workload pattern is extremely uneven: a model can sit idle for weeks and then suddenly receive thousands of requests at once. An SQS queue absorbs and holds everything, while the models run as ECS services that read from it; scaling based on queue length grows both the number of service copies and the cluster capacity. Containers are the right fit because each model loads about a gigabyte of data into memory at startup — in a container this happens once for the lifetime of the task.  
Why A is not selected: A Network Load Balancer cannot invoke Lambda functions as a target, and loading a gigabyte of data on every cold start of the function would devastate latency.  
Why B is not selected: A load balancer in front of services that read from a queue is unnecessary, and App Mesh is a service mesh for routing traffic — it does not handle cluster scaling.  
Why C is not selected: The number of vCPUs for a Lambda function is not adjustable through Auto Scaling (memory is set in the configuration), and a gigabyte-sized model held in memory does not fit well with the Lambda execution model.

---

423\. A solutions architect wants to use the following JSON text as an identity-based policy to grant specific permissions:  
Which IAM principals can the solutions architect attach this policy to? (Choose two.)  
![Exhibit for question 423](images/exhibits/q423.png)  
A. Role  
B. Group  
C. Organization  
D. Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) resource  
E. Amazon EC2 resource  
Answer: AB  
Explanation: This is a question about what an identity-based policy is. Such a policy describes what a principal is allowed to do and can be attached only to IAM principals: a user, a group, or a role. Of the options given, that means role and group. Resources (an EC2 instance, an ECS task, a bucket) cannot have a policy attached directly to them — they get a resource-based policy instead, and compute resources gain permissions through a role. An organization is not a principal either: SCPs are attached to it and its organizational units, but an SCP is a guardrail policy, not an identity-based policy.  
Why C is not selected: An organization in AWS Organizations is not an IAM principal. Service control policies are attached to it, and those set a permissions ceiling rather than grant permissions.  
Why D is not selected: An ECS resource cannot carry an IAM policy: a container gets permissions through the task role (taskRoleArn), as covered in {{q:185}}.  
Why E is not selected: An EC2 instance gets permissions through a role attached via an instance profile. A policy cannot be attached directly to an instance — see {{q:17}}.

---

424\. A company is running a custom application on Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances. The application has frontend nodes that need to run 24 hours a day, 7 days a week and backend nodes that need to run only for a short time based on workload. The number of backend nodes varies during the day.  
The company needs to scale out and scale in more instances based on workload.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Use Reserved Instances for the frontend nodes. Use AWS Fargate for the backend nodes.  
B. Use Reserved Instances for the frontend nodes. Use Spot Instances for the backend nodes.  
C. Use Spot Instances for the frontend nodes. Use Reserved Instances for the backend nodes.  
D. Use Spot Instances for the frontend nodes. Use AWS Fargate for the backend nodes.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Two distinct load profiles call for two different purchasing models. The frontend runs around the clock and is predictable, so Reserved Instances give the deepest discount. The backend spins up briefly, the number of machines varies throughout the day, and interruptions are acceptable — which points to Spot Instances, with discounts of up to 90 percent.  
Why A is not selected: Fargate for the backend nodes costs more than Spot Instances given the same tolerance for interruption.  
Why C is not selected: Spot Instances for an around-the-clock frontend are risky: AWS can reclaim that capacity at any time, and reserving capacity for a variable workload is not cost-effective.  
Why D is not selected: This combines a risky Spot-based frontend with a more expensive Fargate backend for the variable workload.

---

425\. A company uses high block storage capacity to runs its workloads on premises. The company's daily peak input and output transactions per second are not more than 15,000 IOPS. The company wants to migrate the workloads to Amazon EC2 and to provision disk performance independent of storage capacity.  
Which Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume type will meet these requirements MOST cost- effectively?  
A. GP2 volume type  
B. io2 volume type  
C. GP3 volume type  
D. io1 volume type  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The key requirement is provisioning performance independently of storage capacity, at up to 15,000 IOPS peak. That is exactly the gp3 volume profile: a baseline of 3,000 IOPS is included in the price, and IOPS can be raised up to 16,000 independently of volume size. Per gigabyte, gp3 costs less than gp2 and far less than provisioned-IOPS volumes.  
Why A is not selected: gp2 performance is tightly coupled to size — three IOPS per gigabyte — so reaching 15,000 IOPS would require provisioning a 5 TB volume.  
Why B is not selected: io2 meets the requirement but costs considerably more, and it's justified only when you need tens of thousands of IOPS or higher volume durability.  
Why D is not selected: io1 is the previous generation of provisioned-IOPS volumes: it too costs more than gp3 and falls short of io2 on specifications.

---

426\. A company needs to store data from its healthcare application. The application’s data frequently changes. A new regulation requires audit access at all levels of the stored data.  
The company hosts the application on an on-premises infrastructure that is running out of storage capacity. A solutions architect must securely migrate the existing data to AWS while satisfying the new regulation.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS DataSync to move the existing data to Amazon S3. Use AWS CloudTrail to log data events.  
B. Use AWS Snowcone to move the existing data to Amazon S3. Use AWS CloudTrail to log management events.  
C. Use Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration to move the existing data to Amazon S3. Use AWS CloudTrail to log data events.  
D. Use AWS Storage Gateway to move the existing data to Amazon S3. Use AWS CloudTrail to log management events.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The requirements are a secure migration of already-accumulated data and audit access at the level of the data itself. AWS DataSync encrypts the transfer, verifies data integrity, and moves the files into S3, while CloudTrail data event logging records every read and write of an object — exactly what the regulation calls for. Management events do not provide that level of detail.  
Why B is not selected: Snowcone is sized for a few terabytes and a one-time transfer, and a management event log does not capture access to the objects themselves.  
Why C is not selected: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads but is not a tool for migrating an existing data set with integrity verification; the logging half of this option is otherwise correct.  
Why D is not selected: Storage Gateway is a persistent hybrid gateway, not a migration tool, and a management event log does not cover access to the data.

---

427\. A solutions architect is implementing a complex Java application with a MySQL database. The Java application must be deployed on Apache Tomcat and must be highly available.  
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Deploy the application in AWS Lambda. Configure an Amazon API Gateway API to connect with the Lambda functions.  
B. Deploy the application by using AWS Elastic Beanstalk. Configure a load-balanced environment and a rolling deployment policy.  
C. Migrate the database to Amazon ElastiCache. Configure the ElastiCache security group to allow access from the application.  
D. Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. Install a MySQL server on the EC2 instance. Configure the application on the server. Create an AMI. Use the AMI to create a launch template with an Auto Scaling group.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The Java application under Tomcat needs to be carried over as-is, with high availability. Elastic Beanstalk offers a ready-made Tomcat platform: it provisions a load balancer and a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group on its own and manages updates, and a rolling deployment policy rolls out new versions without downtime.  
Why A is not selected: Porting a complex Tomcat application to Lambda means rewriting it from scratch.  
Why C is not selected: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache and cannot replace a relational MySQL database.  
Why D is not selected: Running MySQL on the same instance as the application, inside an Auto Scaling group, produces diverging copies of the data and no real availability.

---

428\. A serverless application uses Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, and Amazon DynamoDB. The Lambda function needs permissions to read and write to the DynamoDB table.  
Which solution will give the Lambda function access to the DynamoDB table MOST securely?  
A. Create an IAM user with programmatic access to the Lambda function. Attach a policy to the user that allows read and write access to the DynamoDB table. Store the access_key_id and secret_access_key parameters as part of the Lambda environment variables. Ensure that other AWS users do not have read and write access to the Lambda function configuration.  
B. Create an IAM role that includes Lambda as a trusted service. Attach a policy to the role that allows read and write access to the DynamoDB table. Update the configuration of the Lambda function to use the new role as the execution role.  
C. Create an IAM user with programmatic access to the Lambda function. Attach a policy to the user that allows read and write access to the DynamoDB table. Store the access_key_id and secret_access_key parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as secure string parameters. Update the Lambda function code to retrieve the secure string parameters before connecting to the DynamoDB table.  
D. Create an IAM role that includes DynamoDB as a trusted service. Attach a policy to the role that allows read and write access from the Lambda function. Update the code of the Lambda function to attach to the new role as an execution role.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The most secure way to grant any AWS service permissions is a role, not long-lived keys. The role must trust the Lambda service (principal lambda.amazonaws.com in its trust policy), carry a policy with the needed actions such as dynamodb:GetItem and PutItem scoped to the specific table, and be assigned to the function as its execution role. The resulting credentials are temporary and rotate automatically, with no secrets in the code or environment variables.  
Why A is not selected: Access keys in environment variables are a long-lived secret, visible to anyone who can read the function's configuration, and rotation is left entirely up to you.  
Why C is not selected: Storing the same keys in Parameter Store only hides them: a compromised key is still valid, whereas a role would provide temporary credentials with no key storage needed at all.  
Why D is not selected: The role needs to trust the Lambda service, not DynamoDB: the trust policy defines who can assume the role. And a role cannot be attached from within the function's code either — it is set in the configuration.

---

429\. The following IAM policy is attached to an IAM group. This is the only policy applied to the group.  
What are the effective IAM permissions of this policy for group members?  
![Exhibit for question 429](images/exhibits/q429.png)  
A. Group members are permitted any Amazon EC2 action within the us-east-1 Region. Statements after the Allow permission are not applied.  
B. Group members are denied any Amazon EC2 permissions in the us-east-1 Region unless they are logged in with multi-factor authentication (MFA).  
C. Group members are allowed the ec2:StopInstances and ec2:TerminateInstances permissions for all Regions when logged in with multi-factor authentication (MFA). Group members are permitted any other Amazon EC2 action.  
D. Group members are allowed the ec2:StopInstances and ec2:TerminateInstances permissions for the us-east-1 Region only when logged in with multi-factor authentication (MFA). Group members are permitted any other Amazon EC2 action within the us-east-1 Region.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Read the two statements together. The first allows any EC2 action, but only within the us-east-1 Region (the ec2:Region condition). The second is an explicit Deny that blocks StopInstances and TerminateInstances whenever the request lacks an MFA indicator (BoolIfExists on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent — a construction that also matches when the key is absent). The net effect: within us-east-1 everything is allowed, but stopping or terminating an instance requires signing in with MFA. Outside that Region there is no permission at all, since the Allow is restricted by its condition.  
Why A is not selected: Policy statements are not "cut off" after the first Allow: all statements are evaluated, and an explicit Deny always overrides an Allow.  
Why B is not selected: The Deny applies only to two actions — stopping and terminating instances — not to all EC2 operations.  
Why C is not selected: The Allow applies only within us-east-1, so "in all Regions" is wrong: in other Regions the group has no permission whatsoever.

---

430\. A manufacturing company has machine sensors that upload .csv files to an Amazon S3 bucket. These .csv files must be converted into images and must be made available as soon as possible for the automatic generation of graphical reports.  
The images become irrelevant after 1 month, but the .csv files must be kept to train machine learning (ML) models twice a year. The ML trainings and audits are planned weeks in advance.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)  
A. Launch an Amazon EC2 Spot Instance that downloads the .csv files every hour, generates the image files, and uploads the images to the S3 bucket.  
B. Design an AWS Lambda function that converts the .csv files into images and stores the images in the S3 bucket. Invoke the Lambda function when a .csv file is uploaded.  
C. Create S3 Lifecycle rules for .csv files and image files in the S3 bucket. Transition the .csv files from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier 1 day after they are uploaded. Expire the image files after 30 days.  
D. Create S3 Lifecycle rules for .csv files and image files in the S3 bucket. Transition the .csv files from S3 Standard to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) 1 day after they are uploaded. Expire the image files after 30 days.  
E. Create S3 Lifecycle rules for .csv files and image files in the S3 bucket. Transition the .csv files from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) 1 day after they are uploaded. Keep the image files in Reduced Redundancy Storage (RRS).  
Answer: BC  
Explanation: The images are needed right after upload — that calls for an event-driven Lambda function triggered when a file appears, with no polling and no idle machines (B). From there, lifecycle policy handles the rest: the images become useless after a month and are simply expired, while the source files are needed only twice a year for planned-in-advance training, so transitioning them to S3 Glacier after just one day gives the cheapest storage that still meets the acceptable retrieval time (C).  
Why A is not selected: An instance that downloads files once an hour violates the "as soon as possible" requirement and adds unnecessary infrastructure.  
Why D is not selected: S3 One Zone-IA costs more than Glacier and keeps data in a single Availability Zone — an unnecessary risk for the sole copy of the training data.  
Why E is not selected: S3 Standard-IA is noticeably more expensive than Glacier, and Reduced Redundancy Storage is deprecated and no longer recommended.

---

431\. A company has developed a new video game as a web application. The application is in a three-tier architecture in a VPC with Amazon RDS for MySQL in the database layer. Several players will compete concurrently online. The game’s developers want to display a top-10 scoreboard in near-real time and offer the ability to stop and restore the game while preserving the current scores.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Set up an Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached cluster to cache the scores for the web application to display.  
B. Set up an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to compute and cache the scores for the web application to display.  
C. Place an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the web application to cache the scoreboard in a section of the application.  
D. Create a read replica on Amazon RDS for MySQL to run queries to compute the scoreboard and serve the read traffic to the web application.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirements are a near-real-time leaderboard and score durability across a stop/restart of the game. ElastiCache for Redis satisfies both: sorted sets compute the top 10 in sub-millisecond time, and Redis's disk persistence and replication let the state be restored after a restart.  
Why A is not selected: Memcached has neither sorted data structures for ranking nor data persistence: the scores would be lost after a restart.  
Why C is not selected: CloudFront caches responses at edge locations, but the leaderboard changes constantly, and a distribution has no ability to compute it.  
Why D is not selected: A read replica would offload traffic, but recalculating the top 10 with a query against a relational database thousands of times per second would still be slow.

---

432\. An ecommerce company wants to use machine learning (ML) algorithms to build and train models. The company will use the models to visualize complex scenarios and to detect trends in customer data. The architecture team wants to integrate its ML models with a reporting platform to analyze the augmented data and use the data directly in its business intelligence dashboards.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use AWS Glue to create an ML transform to build and train models. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to visualize the data.  
B. Use Amazon SageMaker to build and train models. Use Amazon QuickSight to visualize the data.  
C. Use a pre-built ML Amazon Machine Image (AMI) from the AWS Marketplace to build and train models. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to visualize the data.  
D. Use Amazon QuickSight to build and train models by using calculated fields. Use Amazon QuickSight to visualize the data.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirements are both model training and dashboards, with minimal operations. Amazon SageMaker handles model building and hosting, while Amazon QuickSight is the business intelligence service that can call a SageMaker model and surface the enriched data directly in a dashboard.  
Why A is not selected: The AWS Glue ML transform only solves the narrow task of finding duplicate records, and OpenSearch Service is a search engine, not a reporting platform.  
Why C is not selected: A pre-built AMI from the Marketplace means managing your own instances, patching, and upkeep — the opposite of the requirement.  
Why D is not selected: QuickSight calculated fields are formulas; they cannot be used to train machine learning models.

---

433\. A company is running its production and nonproduction environment workloads in multiple AWS accounts. The accounts are in an organization in AWS Organizations. The company needs to design a solution that will prevent the modification of cost usage tags.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create a custom AWS Config rule to prevent tag modification except by authorized principals.  
B. Create a custom trail in AWS CloudTrail to prevent tag modification.  
C. Create a service control policy (SCP) to prevent tag modification except by authorized principals.  
D. Create custom Amazon CloudWatch logs to prevent tag modification.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The requirement is to preventively block modification of cost allocation tags across every account in the organization, except by specific trusted principals. Only an SCP can enforce that boundary: it applies to all principals in member accounts, including their root user, and cannot be bypassed by a local IAM policy. Typically this is written as a Deny on tag:* or on actions like ec2:CreateTags and ec2:DeleteTags, with a condition on the tag key and an exception via aws:PrincipalArn for the roles that are allowed to make the change.  
Why A is not selected: AWS Config compares configuration against a rule and reports noncompliance after the fact. It does not block the operation at call time.  
Why B is not selected: CloudTrail records who called what. It's a log, not an enforcement mechanism.  
Why D is not selected: CloudWatch Logs stores log records. It places no restrictions on what actions can be taken in AWS.

---

434\. A company hosts its application in the AWS Cloud. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Elastic Load Balancer in an Auto Scaling group and with an Amazon DynamoDB table. The company wants to ensure the application can be made available in anotherAWS Region with minimal downtime.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of downtime?  
A. Create an Auto Scaling group and a load balancer in the disaster recovery Region. Configure the DynamoDB table as a global table. Configure DNS failover to point to the new disaster recovery Region's load balancer.  
B. Create an AWS CloudFormation template to create EC2 instances, load balancers, and DynamoDB tables to be launched when needed Configure DNS failover to point to the new disaster recovery Region's load balancer.  
C. Create an AWS CloudFormation template to create EC2 instances and a load balancer to be launched when needed. Configure the DynamoDB table as a global table. Configure DNS failover to point to the new disaster recovery Region's load balancer.  
D. Create an Auto Scaling group and load balancer in the disaster recovery Region. Configure the DynamoDB table as a global table. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to trigger an AWS Lambda function that updates Amazon Route 53 pointing to the disaster recovery load balancer.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The key phrase is "minimal downtime." That means the infrastructure in the disaster recovery Region must already exist beforehand rather than being created after a failure: the Auto Scaling group and load balancer are already deployed, the DynamoDB global table continuously replicates data to both Regions, and a Route 53 record with a failover policy switches traffic based on health checks. Recovery time comes down to the DNS record's TTL.  
Why B is not selected: Deploying a CloudFormation stack only after the failure means minutes or tens of minutes of waiting, plus the DynamoDB table still has to be populated with data. The downtime is inherently longer.  
Why C is not selected: The data side is fine here (global table), but the compute layer is still created from a template at the moment of the disaster, so the failover is slower than the option with an Auto Scaling group already stood up.  
Why D is not selected: The infrastructure exists beforehand, but switching over via a CloudWatch alarm and a Lambda function that updates Route 53 records adds its own delay and extra logic instead of relying on a built-in failover policy with health checks.

---

435\. A company needs to migrate a MySQL database from its on-premises data center to AWS within 2 weeks. The database is 20 TB in size. The company wants to complete the migration with minimal downtime.  
Which solution will migrate the database MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Order an AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) with AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to migrate the database with replication of ongoing changes. Send the Snowball Edge device to AWS to finish the migration and continue the ongoing replication.  
B. Order an AWS Snowmobile vehicle. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) with AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to migrate the database with ongoing changes. Send the Snowmobile vehicle back to AWS to finish the migration and continue the ongoing replication.  
C. Order an AWS Snowball Edge Compute Optimized with GPU device. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) with AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to migrate the database with ongoing changes. Send the Snowball device to AWS to finish the migration and continue the ongoing replication  
D. Order a 1 GB dedicated AWS Direct Connect connection to establish a connection with the data center. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) with AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to migrate the database with replication of ongoing changes.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Twenty terabytes in two weeks with minimal downtime is a classic pairing: the full data load travels on a Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device, while the changes accumulated during transit are caught up by AWS DMS's ongoing replication. Once the replication lag reaches zero, the application is cut over to the new database — the downtime window is measured in minutes. Storage Optimized is chosen because the task is purely about data volume.  
Why B is not selected: Snowmobile is a truck built for tens of petabytes. For 20 TB it is disproportionately expensive and slow to arrange.  
Why C is not selected: The GPU-accelerated device is meant for on-site computation (machine learning, video processing) and costs more. There's no computation needed here.  
Why D is not selected: A dedicated connection makes sense as permanent infrastructure, not as a one-time migration method: provisioning it typically takes longer than two weeks, and you'd be paying for months of port charges.

---

436\. A company moved its on-premises PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company successfully launched a new product. The workload on the database has increased. The company wants to accommodate the larger workload without adding infrastructure.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Buy reserved DB instances for the total workload. Make the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance larger.  
B. Make the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance a Multi-AZ DB instance.  
C. Buy reserved DB instances for the total workload. Add another Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance.  
D. Make the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance an on-demand DB instance.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The condition explicitly rules out adding infrastructure, so the only way to grow is up: scale the existing instance larger. And to make that cost-effective, reserved DB instances are purchased for the steady workload — a discount of over 60% compared to on-demand pricing.  
Why B is not selected: Multi-AZ improves availability but adds no performance: the standby instance doesn't serve requests, yet you'd pay double.  
Why C is not selected: A second DB instance is exactly the kind of added infrastructure the condition rules out.  
Why D is not selected: On-demand pricing is the most expensive option and does nothing to handle the increased workload.

---

437\. A company operates an ecommerce website on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in an Auto Scaling group. The site is experiencing performance issues related to a high request rate from illegitimate external systems with changing IP addresses. The security team is worried about potential DDoS attacks against the website. The company must block the illegitimate incoming requests in a way that has a minimal impact on legitimate users.  
What should a solutions architect recommend?  
A. Deploy Amazon Inspector and associate it with the ALB.  
B. Deploy AWS WAF, associate it with the ALB, and configure a rate-limiting rule.  
C. Deploy rules to the network ACLs associated with the ALB to block the incomingtraffic.  
D. Deploy Amazon GuardDuty and enable rate-limiting protection when configuring GuardDuty.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The offending IP addresses keep changing, so they can't be blocked by static lists — what's needed is a limit on request rate. An AWS WAF rate-based rule attached to the Application Load Balancer counts requests from each address and temporarily blocks anyone who exceeds the threshold, without affecting normal users. The rule can be scoped by path or headers so the limit only applies to the heavy endpoints.  
Why A is not selected: Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities and doesn't operate on load balancer traffic.  
Why C is not selected: Network ACLs apply at the subnet level, have a hard limit on the number of rules, and would require manually maintaining lists of addresses that keep changing.  
Why D is not selected: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity, but it has no rate-limiting capability at all.

---

438\. A company wants to share accounting data with an external auditor. The data is stored in an Amazon RDS DB instance that resides in a private subnet. The auditor has its own AWS account and requires its own copy of the database.  
What is the MOST secure way for the company to share the database with the auditor?  
A. Create a read replica of the database. Configure IAM standard database authentication to grant the auditor access.  
B. Export the database contents to text files. Store the files in an Amazon S3 bucket. Create a new IAM user for the auditor. Grant the user access to the S3 bucket.  
C. Copy a snapshot of the database to an Amazon S3 bucket. Create an IAM user. Share the user's keys with the auditor to grant access to the object in the S3 bucket.  
D. Create an encrypted snapshot of the database. Share the snapshot with the auditor. Allow access to the AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption key.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The auditor needs its own copy of the database in its own account, and it has to be shared as securely as possible. The standard mechanism is an encrypted RDS snapshot: it's shared directly with the specified account, and to let the recipient read it, they're granted access to the KMS key that encrypted the snapshot. The auditor then restores the database on their own side. No exported files, no credentials handed over. Keep in mind the limitation: a snapshot encrypted with the AWS managed default key can't be shared — you need your own customer managed key, as in {{q:349}}.  
Why A is not selected: A read replica stays in your account and your VPC, but the auditor needs its own copy. "IAM standard database authentication" also isn't a real mechanism: what exists is IAM database authentication, and it doesn't solve the problem of handing over a copy.  
Why B is not selected: Exporting to text files loses the schema, indexes, and data types, and it means creating an IAM user for an outside party inside your own account. That's both more work and less secure.  
Why C is not selected: Handing an IAM user's access keys to an external party is a direct violation of basic security practice — those are long-lived credentials that belong inside your account.

---

439\. A solutions architect configured a VPC that has a small range of IP addresses. The number of Amazon EC2 instances that are in the VPC is increasing, and there is an insufficient number of IP addresses for future workloads.  
Which solution resolves this issue with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Add an additional IPv4 CIDR block to increase the number of IP addresses and create additional subnets in the VPC. Create new resources in the new subnets by using the new CIDR.  
B. Create a second VPC with additional subnets. Use a peering connection to connect the second VPC with the first VPC Update the routes and create new resources in the subnets of the second VPC.  
C. Use AWS Transit Gateway to add a transit gateway and connect a second VPC with the first VPUpdate the routes of the transit gateway and VPCs. Create new resources in the subnets of the second VPC.  
D. Create a second VPC. Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection between the first VPC and the second VPC by using a VPN-hosted solution on Amazon EC2 and a virtual private gateway. Update the route between VPCs to the traffic through the VPN. Create new resources in the subnets of the second VPC.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: You can add an additional IPv4 CIDR block to a running VPC — up to four secondary CIDRs on top of the primary. This is done in place, with no downtime and no need to move resources: new subnets are created in the new range, and new instances launch into them. Routing within the VPC across all the blocks works automatically.  
Why B is not selected: A second VPC with peering is a separate network with its own route tables, its own security groups, and ongoing maintenance. The problem can be solved by changing a single setting.  
Why C is not selected: Transit Gateway solves the same problem even more heavily, and at extra cost: attachment charges and per-GB data processing charges.  
Why D is not selected: A homegrown VPN on an EC2 instance between two VPCs is maximum complexity, an extra point of failure, and paying for instances that do nothing useful.

---

440\. A company used an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance during application testing. Before terminating the DB instance at the end of the test cycle, a solutions architect created two backups. The solutions architect created the first backup by using the mysqldump utility to create a database dump. The solutions architect created the second backup by enabling the final DB snapshot option on RDS termination.  
The company is now planning for a new test cycle and wants to create a new DB instance from the most recent backup. The company has chosen a MySQL-compatible edition ofAmazon Aurora to host the DB instance.  
Which solutions will create the new DB instance? (Choose two.)  
A. Import the RDS snapshot directly into Aurora.  
B. Upload the RDS snapshot to Amazon S3. Then import the RDS snapshot into Aurora.  
C. Upload the database dump to Amazon S3. Then import the database dump into Aurora.  
D. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to import the RDS snapshot into Aurora.  
E. Upload the database dump to Amazon S3. Then use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to import the database dump into Aurora.  
Answer: AC  
Explanation: There are two backups of different kinds, and each is migrated its own way. The final RDS for MySQL snapshot can be restored directly into an Aurora MySQL-compatible cluster — this is a standard console operation (A). The dump taken with mysqldump is uploaded to an S3 bucket and imported into Aurora from there (C).  
Why B is not selected: RDS snapshots can't be exported to S3 as a file for later import: restoration happens directly from the snapshot.  
Why D is not selected: DMS works against a running database as its source, not an RDS snapshot: a snapshot isn't a supported DMS source.  
Why E is not selected: Likewise, a dump sitting in an S3 bucket isn't a source DMS can use — importing a dump into Aurora is done through Aurora's own standard procedure.

---

441\. A company hosts a multi-tier web application on Amazon Linux Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. The company observes that the Auto Scaling group launches more On-Demand Instances when the application's end users access high volumes of static web content. The company wants to optimize cost.  
What should a solutions architect do to redesign the application MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Update the Auto Scaling group to use Reserved Instances instead of On-Demand Instances.  
B. Update the Auto Scaling group to scale by launching Spot Instances instead of On-Demand Instances.  
C. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution to host the static web contents from an Amazon S3 bucket.  
D. Create an AWS Lambda function behind an Amazon API Gateway API to host the static website contents.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Instances get added because of the static content they serve — and that is the most expensive kind of work for a compute fleet. Move the static content into an S3 bucket and serve it through CloudFront: caching at edge locations absorbs the overwhelming majority of requests, the instances stop scaling in response to this traffic, and costs drop.  
Why A is not selected: Reserved Instances give a discount, but the fleet still grows under static-content load: you would still pay for the extra instances, just at a lower rate.  
Why B is not selected: Spot Instances are cheaper, but AWS can reclaim them at any time, and the root cause of the fleet growth is not addressed.  
Why D is not selected: A Lambda function behind API Gateway to serve static files is an awkward design that ends up noticeably more expensive than S3 and CloudFront.

---

442\. A company stores several petabytes of data across multiple AWS accounts. The company uses AWS Lake Formation to manage its data lake. The company's data science team wants to securely share selective data from its accounts with the company's engineering team for analytical purposes.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Copy the required data to a common account. Create an IAM access role in that account. Grant access by specifying a permission policy that includes users from the engineering team accounts as trusted entities.  
B. Use the Lake Formation permissions Grant command in each account where the data is stored to allow the required engineering team users to access the data.  
C. Use AWS Data Exchange to privately publish the required data to the required engineering team accounts.  
D. Use Lake Formation tag-based access control to authorize and grant cross-account permissions for the required data to the engineering team accounts.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The data lives across multiple accounts, and it needs to be shared selectively without manual work every time the shared data set changes. Lake Formation addresses this with tag-based access control (LF-TBAC): tags are attached to databases, tables, and columns, and permissions are granted not on specific objects but on tag combinations — including across accounts. When a new table appears with the right tag, engineers automatically get access without any grant changes. No data copies are created in the process.  
Why A is not selected: Copying data into a common account means duplicating petabytes, copies drifting out of sync, and extra storage costs.  
Why B is not selected: Manually granting permissions in each account for every object scales linearly with the number of tables — exactly what tag-based access control eliminates.  
Why C is not selected: AWS Data Exchange is designed for publishing data sets to external subscribers, not for internal access control within a data lake.

---

443\. A company wants to host a scalable web application on AWS. The application will be accessed by users from different geographic regions of the world. Application users will be able to download and upload unique data up to gigabytes in size. The development team wants a cost-effective solution to minimize upload and download latency and maximize performance.  
What should a solutions architect do to accomplish this?  
A. Use Amazon S3 with Transfer Acceleration to host the application.  
B. Use Amazon S3 with CacheControl headers to host the application.  
C. Use Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling and Amazon CloudFront to host the application.  
D. Use Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling and Amazon ElastiCache to host the application.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Users worldwide both upload and download unique files up to several gigabytes in size. Uniqueness matters here: there is nothing to cache, so the win comes not from a cache but from a shorter, more reliable path to the bucket. S3 Transfer Acceleration routes traffic to the nearest edge location and then over the AWS backbone, speeding up both uploads and downloads.  
Why B is not selected: Cache-control headers help with repeated requests for the same objects, but the data here is unique to each user.  
Why C is not selected: CloudFront is optimized for serving and caching content; it does not speed up uploads of unique multi-gigabyte files, and the instance fleet adds cost on top.  
Why D is not selected: An in-memory cache within a single Region has no bearing on transferring gigabyte-sized files or on global latency.

---

444\. A company has hired a solutions architect to design a reliable architecture for its application. The application consists of one Amazon RDS DB instance and two manually provisioned Amazon EC2 instances that run web servers. The EC2 instances are located in a single Availability Zone.  
An employee recently deleted the DB instance, and the application was unavailable for 24 hours as a result. The company is concerned with the overall reliability of its environment.  
What should the solutions architect do to maximize reliability of the application's infrastructure?  
A. Delete one EC2 instance and enable termination protection on the other EC2 instance. Update the DB instance to be Multi-AZ, and enable deletion protection.  
B. Update the DB instance to be Multi-AZ, and enable deletion protection. Place the EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer, and run them in an EC2 Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones.  
C. Create an additional DB instance along with an Amazon API Gateway and an AWS Lambda function. Configure the application to invoke the Lambda function through API Gateway. Have the Lambda function write the data to the two DB instances.  
D. Place the EC2 instances in an EC2 Auto Scaling group that has multiple subnets located in multiple Availability Zones. Use Spot Instances instead of On-Demand Instances. Set up Amazon CloudWatch alarms to monitor the health of the instances Update the DB instance to be Multi-AZ, and enable deletion protection.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Reliability is failing on two fronts, and both need to be addressed. Database: switch to a Multi-AZ configuration plus deletion protection, so the manual-deletion incident cannot repeat. Web tier: put the instances behind a load balancer in an Auto Scaling group spanning multiple Availability Zones, so an instance failure or the loss of an entire zone does not take the application down.  
Why A is not selected: Keeping a single instance with termination protection is a step backward: the failure of that one machine or its zone still means downtime.  
Why C is not selected: Writing to two databases through a custom function is homegrown replication that has to be built and maintained, instead of using the built-in Multi-AZ configuration.  
Why D is not selected: The web tier is improved, but the database is still left without deletion protection or redundancy, so the original cause of the outage is not fixed; Spot Instances can also be reclaimed at any time.

---

445\. A company is storing 700 terabytes of data on a large network-attached storage (NAS) system in its corporate data center. The company has a hybrid environment with a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection.  
After an audit from a regulator, the company has 90 days to move the data to the cloud. The company needs to move the data efficiently and without disruption. The company still needs to be able to access and update the data during the transfer window.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create an AWS DataSync agent in the corporate data center. Create a data transfer task Start the transfer to an Amazon S3 bucket.  
B. Back up the data to AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices. Ship the devices to an AWS data center. Mount a target Amazon S3 bucket on the on-premises file system.  
C. Use rsync to copy the data directly from local storage to a designated Amazon S3 bucket over the Direct Connect connection.  
D. Back up the data on tapes. Ship the tapes to an AWS data center. Mount a target Amazon S3 bucket on the on-premises file system.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Check whether the transfer fits the deadline: 700 TB over a 10 Gbps link takes roughly a week of continuous transfer, and the deadline is 90 days. So the link is sufficient, and physical devices are not needed. AWS DataSync, with an agent in the data center, moves data from the NAS to S3 incrementally, verifies integrity, automatically retries failed transfers, and does not get in the way of ongoing file access: files can still be accessed and updated during the transfer, and rerunning the task catches up on the difference.  
Why B is not selected: Snowball devices are for when the link is not big enough. Here the link is sufficient, and "mount a target S3 bucket on the on-premises file system" describes an operation that does not exist.  
Why C is not selected: rsync at this scale is slow and non-parallel, provides neither service-level integrity checking nor automatic retries, and the scripts would have to be maintained by hand.  
Why D is not selected: Tapes and shipping them are the slowest and least controllable path, and mounting a bucket as a file system still is not possible.

---

446\. A company stores data in PDF format in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company must follow a legal requirement to retain all new and existing data in Amazon S3 for 7 years.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Turn on the S3 Versioning feature for the S3 bucket. Configure S3 Lifecycle to delete the data after 7 years. Configure multi-factor authentication (MFA) delete for all S3 objects.  
B. Turn on S3 Object Lock with governance retention mode for the S3 bucket. Set the retention period to expire after 7 years. Recopy all existing objects to bring the existing data into compliance.  
C. Turn on S3 Object Lock with compliance retention mode for the S3 bucket. Set the retention period to expire after 7 years. Recopy all existing objects to bring the existing data into compliance.  
D. Turn on S3 Object Lock with compliance retention mode for the S3 bucket. Set the retention period to expire after 7 years. Use S3 Batch Operations to bring the existing data into compliance.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: A legal requirement to retain data for 7 years means no one — including an administrator or root — should be able to delete an object. That is S3 Object Lock's compliance retention mode: while the retention period is in force, an object version cannot be deleted or overwritten, and the period itself cannot be shortened. Governance mode does not fit here: anyone with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission can bypass it. The second half of the question concerns existing objects: Object Lock applies to new versions, and bringing millions of existing objects into compliance with the least effort is what S3 Batch Operations does — it applies retention settings in bulk from an S3 Inventory report.  
Why A is not selected: Versioning and MFA Delete make deletion harder, but do not prevent it: an administrator can still remove versions. The lifecycle rule that deletes data after 7 years is solving an unrelated problem here — it protects nothing.  
Why B is not selected: Governance mode can be removed by a user with the corresponding permission, so it does not satisfy the legal requirement. Plus it still requires manually recopying every object.  
Why C is not selected: The retention mode chosen is correct, but "recopy all existing objects" means rewriting the entire data set by hand — scripts, transfer traffic, error handling. S3 Batch Operations accomplishes the same thing as a managed job, so this option loses on the LEAST operational overhead criterion.

---

447\. A company has a stateless web application that runs on AWS Lambda functions that are invoked by Amazon API Gateway. The company wants to deploy the application across multiple AWS Regions to provide Regional failover capabilities.  
What should a solutions architect do to route traffic to multiple Regions?  
A. Create Amazon Route 53 health checks for each Region. Use an active-active failover configuration.  
B. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an origin for each Region. Use CloudFront health checks to route traffic.  
C. Create a transit gateway. Attach the transit gateway to the API Gateway endpoint in each Region. Configure the transit gateway to route requests.  
D. Create an Application Load Balancer in the primary Region. Set the target group to point to the API Gateway endpoint hostnames in each Region.  
Answer: A  
Review status: Corrected key (source: B; reviewed: A)  
Correction note: examtopics t1 q447 — CloudFront has no health checks of its own; Route 53 health checks with active-active failover is the standard pattern for multi-region API Gateway/Lambda setups (AWS Compute Blog)  
Explanation: DNS distributes traffic across Regions: health checks in each Region combined with an active-active failover configuration in Route 53 (A) give both load balancing and automatic removal of a failed Region. This is the standard construct for public regional API Gateway endpoints.  
Why B is not selected: CloudFront does not have health checks in the sense needed here: an origin group fails over based on response error codes, not an independent health check of a Region, and you cannot build active-active distribution across Regions this way.  
Why C is not selected: Transit Gateway routes traffic between VPCs and on-premises networks. API Gateway is a public service endpoint — it cannot be attached to a Transit Gateway.  
Why D is not selected: An ALB cannot target an API Gateway hostname, and the load balancer itself lives in a single Region and becomes a single point of failure — the exact opposite of what is needed.

---

448\. A company has two VPCs named Management and Production. The Management VPC uses VPNs through a customer gateway to connect to a single device in the data center. The Production VPC uses a virtual private gateway with two attached AWS Direct Connect connections. The Management and Production VPCs both use a single VPC peering connection to allow communication between the applications.  
What should a solutions architect do to mitigate any single point of failure in this architecture?  
A. Add a set of VPNs between the Management and Production VPCs.  
B. Add a second virtual private gateway and attach it to the Management VPC.  
C. Add a second set of VPNs to the Management VPC from a second customer gateway device.  
D. Add a second VPC peering connection between the Management VPC and the Production VPC.  
Answer: C
