Explanation: The single point of failure is stated right in the question: the VPN from the Management VPC runs through a single customer gateway device in the data center. The standard AWS fix is a second physical device and a second set of tunnels from it: each Site-to-Site connection already has two tunnels, but both terminate on the same hardware. A second router removes that dependency. Production already has redundancy — two Direct Connect connections.  
Why A is not selected: A VPN between the VPCs does not remove the dependency on the single device in the data center; it just adds a parallel path alongside what peering already covers.  
Why B is not selected: A VPC can have only one virtual private gateway, and the failed element here is not the gateway — it is the equipment on the company's side.  
Why D is not selected: A second peering connection between the same two VPCs cannot be created, and peering itself is a managed, redundant service, not a point of failure.

---

449\. A company runs its application on an Oracle database. The company plans to quickly migrate to AWS because of limited resources for the database, backup administration, and data center maintenance. The application uses third-party database features that require privileged access.  
Which solution will help the company migrate the database to AWS MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. Replace third-party features with cloud services.  
B. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle. Customize the database settings to support third- party features.  
C. Migrate the database to an Amazon EC2 Amazon Machine Image (AMI) for Oracle. Customize the database settings to support third-party features.  
D. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL by rewriting the application code to remove dependency on Oracle APEX.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The application needs third-party database features that require privileged access — standard RDS does not grant that kind of access. Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle keeps managed backups and maintenance while still giving the administrator that access: it is cheaper and faster than managing the database on EC2.  
Why A is not selected: Replacing the third-party features with cloud services means reworking the application, but the company wants to migrate quickly and has limited resources.  
Why C is not selected: Oracle on EC2 gives full access, but it hands the company back all the administration and backup work it is trying to get away from.  
Why D is not selected: Moving to PostgreSQL and rewriting the code is the longest and most expensive path, and directly contradicts the requirement to migrate quickly.

---

450\. A company has a three-tier web application that is in a single server. The company wants to migrate the application to the AWS Cloud. The company also wants the application to align with the AWS Well-Architected Framework and to be consistent with AWS recommended best practices for security, scalability, and resiliency.  
Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose three.)  
A. Create a VPC across two Availability Zones with the application's existing architecture. Host the application with existing architecture on an Amazon EC2 instance in a private subnet in each Availability Zone with EC2 Auto Scaling groups. Secure the EC2 instance with security groups and network access control lists (network ACLs).  
B. Set up security groups and network access control lists (network ACLs) to control access to the database layer. Set up a single Amazon RDS database in a private subnet.  
C. Create a VPC across two Availability Zones. Refactor the application to host the web tier, application tier, and database tier. Host each tier on its own private subnet with Auto Scaling groups for the web tier and application tier.  
D. Use a single Amazon RDS database. Allow database access only from the application tier security group.  
E. Use Elastic Load Balancers in front of the web tier. Control access by using security groups containing references to each layer's security groups.  
F. Use an Amazon RDS database Multi-AZ cluster deployment in private subnets. Allow database access only from application tier security groups.  
Answer: CEF  
Explanation: The Well-Architected Framework calls for tier separation, fault tolerance, and least privilege. The application is split into three tiers, each in its own private subnet across two Availability Zones, with Auto Scaling groups for the web and application tiers (C). A load balancer sits in front of the web tier, and access between tiers is controlled through security groups that reference each other (E). The database is deployed as a Multi-AZ cluster in private subnets and accepts connections only from the application tier's security group (F).  
Why A is not selected: Keeping the original monolithic architecture on instances does not meet the best-practices requirement: the tiers are not separated, and there is no load balancer.  
Why B is not selected: A single database instance is a single point of failure, so the resiliency requirement is not met.  
Why D is not selected: The access rule is correct, but a single database without a Multi-AZ configuration is still a single point of failure.

---

451\. A company is migrating its applications and databases to the AWS Cloud. The company will use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), AWS Direct Connect, and Amazon RDS.  
Which activities will be managed by the company's operational team? (Choose three.)  
A. Management of the Amazon RDS infrastructure layer, operating system, and platforms  
B. Creation of an Amazon RDS DB instance and configuring the scheduled maintenance window  
C. Configuration of additional software components on Amazon ECS for monitoring, patch management, log management, and host intrusion detection  
D. Installation of patches for all minor and major database versions for Amazon RDS  
E. Ensure the physical security of the Amazon RDS infrastructure in the data center  
F. Encryption of the data that moves in transit through Direct Connect  
Answer: BCF  
Explanation: This is a shared responsibility model question. The company's operational team retains what it configures itself: creating the RDS instance and setting the scheduled maintenance window (B), installing and configuring additional software inside ECS containers and on ECS hosts — monitoring, application patch management, log collection, and host intrusion detection (C), and encrypting data in transit over Direct Connect, since Direct Connect itself does not encrypt traffic (F).  
Why A is not selected: The infrastructure layer, operating system, and platform of the managed RDS database are handled by AWS — the customer simply has no access to them.  
Why D is not selected: AWS applies the database engine patches during the maintenance window. The customer only chooses the timing and decides when to apply version upgrades.  
Why E is not selected: Physical security of the data centers is AWS's responsibility — "security of the cloud" itself.

---

452\. A company runs a Java-based job on an Amazon EC2 instance. The job runs every hour and takes 10 seconds to run.  
The job runs on a scheduled interval and consumes 1 GB of memory. The CPU utilization of the instance is low except for short surges during which the job uses the maximum CPU available. The company wants to optimize the costs to run the job.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS App2Container (A2C) to containerize the job. Run the job as an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task on AWS Fargate with 0.5 virtual CPU (vCPU) and 1 GB of memory.  
B. Copy the code into an AWS Lambda function that has 1 GB of memory. Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule to run the code each hour.  
C. Use AWS App2Container (A2C) to containerize the job. Install the container in the existing Amazon Machine Image (AMI). Ensure that the schedule stops the container when the task finishes.  
D. Configure the existing schedule to stop the EC2 instance at the completion of the job and restart the EC2 instance when the next job starts.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The job runs for ten seconds once an hour and needs one gigabyte of memory. A Lambda function with 1 GB of memory, triggered by an EventBridge scheduled rule, is billed only for those ten seconds — roughly two and a half minutes of runtime per day instead of an instance running around the clock.  
Why A is not selected: A Fargate task is billed with a minimum billing increment and includes container startup time, which is noticeably more expensive for a ten-second job.  
Why C is not selected: The instance stays running and is billed regardless of whether the container is actually doing work.  
Why D is not selected: Stopping and starting the instance every hour saves some cost, but the boot time is comparable to the job itself, and managing that cycle adds operational work.

---

453\. A company wants to implement a backup strategy for Amazon EC2 data and multiple Amazon S3 buckets.  
Because of regulatory requirements, the company must retain backup files for a specific time period. The company must not alter the files for the duration of the retention period.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS Backup to create a backup vault that has a vault lock in governance mode. Create the required backup plan.  
B. Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager to create the required automated snapshot policy.  
C. Use Amazon S3 File Gateway to create the backup. Configure the appropriate S3 Lifecycle management.  
D. Use AWS Backup to create a backup vault that has a vault lock in compliance mode. Create the required backup plan.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The regulator requires that the copies cannot be altered or deleted before the retention period ends. AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode makes the lock irreversible: once the cooling-off period ends, no one can remove it, not even the account's root user.  
Why A is not selected: Governance mode also locks changes, but users with a special permission can remove the lock — that is not enough to satisfy a regulatory requirement.  
Why B is not selected: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager takes scheduled volume snapshots, but it does not guarantee immutability and does not cover S3 buckets.  
Why C is not selected: S3 File Gateway is a gateway for accessing S3 over file protocols, not a backup tool; lifecycle rules manage storage classes, not a prohibition on modification.

---

454\. A company has resources across multiple AWS Regions and accounts. A newly hired solutions architect discovers a previous employee did not provide details about the resources inventory. The solutions architect needs to build and map the relationship details of the various workloads across all accounts.  
Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?  
A. Use AWS Systems Manager Inventory to generate a map view from the detailed view report.  
B. Use AWS Step Functions to collect workload details. Build architecture diagrams of the workloads manually.  
C. Use Workload Discovery on AWS to generate architecture diagrams of the workloads.  
D. Use AWS X-Ray to view the workload details. Build architecture diagrams with relationships.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The requirement is not just to list resources but to build a map of the relationships between workloads across multiple accounts and Regions. The purpose-built Workload Discovery on AWS solution does exactly that: it collects data from the accounts and automatically draws architecture diagrams.  
Why A is not selected: Systems Manager Inventory collects software information from managed instances and does not show relationships between services.  
Why B is not selected: Step Functions is a process orchestrator; the data it gathers would still need to be diagrammed manually, making this the most labor-intensive path.  
Why D is not selected: X-Ray traces requests within an instrumented application and does not provide an overall map of account resources.

---

455\. A company uses AWS Organizations. The company wants to operate some of its AWS accounts with different budgets. The company wants to receive alerts and automatically prevent provisioning of additional resources on AWS accounts when the allocated budget threshold is met during a specific period.  
Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose three.)  
A. Use AWS Budgets to create a budget. Set the budget amount under the Cost and Usage Reports section of the required AWS accounts.  
B. Use AWS Budgets to create a budget. Set the budget amount under the Billing dashboards of the required AWS accounts.  
C. Create an IAM user for AWS Budgets to run budget actions with the required permissions.  
D. Create an IAM role for AWS Budgets to run budget actions with the required permissions.  
E. Add an alert to notify the company when each account meets its budget threshold. Add a budget action that selects the IAM identity created with the appropriate config rule to prevent provisioning of additional resources.  
F. Add an alert to notify the company when each account meets its budget threshold. Add a budget action that selects the IAM identity created with the appropriate service control policy (SCP) to prevent provisioning of additional resources.  
Answer: BDF  
Explanation: Both an alert and automatic prevention of resource provisioning are needed once the threshold is reached. In AWS Budgets this takes three steps. The budget is created in the billing console of the required account (B). For the budget to take action on your behalf, it needs an IAM role with the necessary permissions — a role, not a user, because the action is performed by the service itself (D). The budget action itself is to apply an SCP that denies resource creation once the threshold is crossed (F). An alert is configured alongside the action.  
Why A is not selected: Cost and Usage Reports is a detailed export of cost data, not where a budget is defined.  
Why C is not selected: Budget actions are performed by the service assuming a role. An IAM user with long-lived keys is not used for this.  
Why E is not selected: An AWS Config rule flags noncompliance but does not prevent resource creation. The budget action must apply an SCP or IAM policy, not a Config rule.

---

456\. A company runs applications on Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region. The company wants to back up the EC2 instances to a second Region. The company also wants to provision EC2 resources in the second Region and manage the EC2 instances centrally from one AWS account.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Create a disaster recovery (DR) plan that has a similar number of EC2 instances in the second Region. Configure data replication.  
B. Create point-in-time Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots of the EC2 instances. Copy the snapshots to the second Region periodically.  
C. Create a backup plan by using AWS Backup. Configure cross-Region backup to the second Region for the EC2 instances.  
D. Deploy a similar number of EC2 instances in the second Region. Use AWS DataSync to transfer the data from the source Region to the second Region.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The requirement is cross-Region backups plus centralized management from a single account, all done cost-effectively. AWS Backup covers all of it: a backup plan with a copy rule to the second Region, a single console and reporting, and billing only for the storage of the copies. There is no need to keep any running instances in the second Region.  
Why A is not selected: A full fleet copy in the second Region is billed around the clock — the most expensive of these approaches.  
Why B is not selected: Manually copying volume snapshots is possible, but it means building your own automation, with no unified retention plan and no centralized management.  
Why D is not selected: Running instances in the second Region plus continuous synchronization via DataSync costs several times more than a backup plan.

---

457\. A company that uses AWS is building an application to transfer data to a product manufacturer. The company has its own identity provider (IdP). The company wants the IdP to authenticate application users while the users use the application to transfer data. The company must use Applicability Statement 2 (AS2) protocol.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS DataSync to transfer the data. Create an AWS Lambda function for IdP authentication.  
B. Use Amazon AppFlow flows to transfer the data. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task for IdP authentication.  
C. Use AWS Transfer Family to transfer the data. Create an AWS Lambda function for IdP authentication.  
D. Use AWS Storage Gateway to transfer the data. Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool for IdP authentication.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: In AWS, exactly one service supports the AS2 protocol — AWS Transfer Family (alongside SFTP, FTPS, and FTP). Authentication can still be performed by the company's own identity provider: Transfer Family can invoke a Lambda function as a custom identity provider, which validates the user against the external system and returns the permissions and home directory. No servers need to be stood up.  
Why A is not selected: DataSync moves files between storage systems and does not support the AS2 protocol.  
Why B is not selected: AppFlow integrates with SaaS applications through their APIs. AS2 is not among its connectors.  
Why D is not selected: Storage Gateway provides hybrid access to storage, not AS2 data exchange, and Cognito is not an authentication mechanism for this transfer protocol.

---

458\. A solutions architect is designing a RESTAPI in Amazon API Gateway for a cash payback service. The application requires 1 GB of memory and 2 GB of storage for its computation resources. The application will require that the data is in a relational format.  
Which additional combination ofAWS services will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative effort?  
(Choose two.)  
A. Amazon EC2  
B. AWS Lambda  
C. Amazon RDS  
D. Amazon DynamoDB  
E. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Services (Amazon EKS)  
Answer: BC  
Explanation: The workload needs roughly one gigabyte of memory for computation and a relational data store, with minimal administrative effort. AWS Lambda runs the logic behind API Gateway — no servers at all (B), while Amazon RDS stores the data as a managed relational database (C).  
Why A is not selected: EC2 instances require patching, scaling, and monitoring — the most administrative effort of the options.  
Why D is not selected: DynamoDB is not a relational database, and the requirement explicitly calls for a relational data format.  
Why E is not selected: An EKS cluster is the most operationally intensive option listed and is overkill for a single API function.

---

459\. A company uses AWS Organizations to run workloads within multiple AWS accounts. A tagging policy adds department tags to AWS resources when the company creates tags.  
An accounting team needs to determine spending on Amazon EC2 consumption. The accounting team must determine which departments are responsible for the costs regardless ofAWS account. The accounting team has access to AWS Cost Explorer for all AWS accounts within the organization and needs to access all reports from Cost Explorer.  
Which solution meets these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?  
A. From the Organizations management account billing console, activate a user-defined cost allocation tag named department. Create one cost report in Cost Explorer grouping by tag name, and filter by EC2.  
B. From the Organizations management account billing console, activate an AWS-defined cost allocation tag named department. Create one cost report in Cost Explorer grouping by tag name, and filter by EC2.  
C. From the Organizations member account billing console, activate a user-defined cost allocation tag named department. Create one cost report in Cost Explorer grouping by the tag name, and filter by EC2.  
D. From the Organizations member account billing console, activate an AWS-defined cost allocation tag named department. Create one cost report in Cost Explorer grouping by tag name, and filter by EC2.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: For costs to be broken down by department across every account, the tag must become a cost allocation tag. It can only be activated in the organization's management account, from the billing console, and since the company created the tag itself, it is a user-defined tag rather than one AWS applies automatically (which use the aws: prefix). Once activated, Cost Explorer can build a report grouped by that tag and filtered to EC2 — a single report covering the whole organization.  
Why B is not selected: AWS-defined tags are the ones the platform itself creates, using the aws: prefix. The department tag was created by the company, so it is a user-defined tag.  
Why C is not selected: Cost allocation tags cannot be activated from a member account: this must be done in the organization's management account.  
Why D is not selected: This option compounds two errors: the wrong account and the wrong tag type.

---

460\. A company wants to securely exchange data between its software as a service (SaaS) application Salesforce account and Amazon S3. The company must encrypt the data at rest by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed keys (CMKs). The company must also encrypt the data in transit. The company has enabled API access for the Salesforce account.  
A. Create AWS Lambda functions to transfer the data securely from Salesforce to Amazon S3.  
B. Create an AWS Step Functions workflow. Define the task to transfer the data securely from Salesforce to Amazon S3.  
C. Create Amazon AppFlow flows to transfer the data securely from Salesforce to Amazon S3.  
D. Create a custom connector for Salesforce to transfer the data securely from Salesforce to Amazon S3.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The task is to regularly and securely move data from Salesforce to S3, encrypting it with a customer-owned KMS key. Amazon AppFlow was built for exactly this: it has a ready-made Salesforce connector, transfers data over TLS, lets you configure the flow without code, and lets you specify a customer managed KMS key when writing to S3. AppFlow can also route traffic through PrivateLink so it never touches the public internet. Every other option involves building this connector yourself.  
Why A is not selected: Lambda functions mean writing your own integration code against the Salesforce API: authentication, pagination, retries, and handling schema changes. A managed connector does all of this for you.  
Why B is not selected: Step Functions orchestrates steps, but the actual Salesforce calls would still need to be written. An orchestrator does not replace a connector.  
Why D is not selected: A custom connector represents the most development and maintenance effort when a managed service already delivers the same result.

---

461\. A company is developing a mobile gaming app in a single AWS Region. The app runs on multiple Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The company stores the app data in Amazon DynamoDB. The app communicates by using TCP traffic and UDP traffic between the users and the servers. The application will be used globally. The company wants to ensure the lowest possible latency for all users.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS Global Accelerator to create an accelerator. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) behind an accelerator endpoint that uses Global Accelerator integration and listening on the TCP and UDP ports. Update the Auto Scaling group to register instances on the ALB.  
B. Use AWS Global Accelerator to create an accelerator. Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) behind an accelerator endpoint that uses Global Accelerator integration and listening on the TCP and UDP ports. Update the Auto Scaling group to register instances on the NLB.  
C. Create an Amazon CloudFront content delivery network (CDN) endpoint. Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) behind the endpoint and listening on the TCP and UDP ports. Update the Auto Scaling group to register instances on the NLB. Update CloudFront to use the NLB as the origin.  
D. Create an Amazon CloudFront content delivery network (CDN) endpoint. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) behind the endpoint and listening on the TCP and UDP ports. Update the Auto Scaling group to register instances on the ALB. Update CloudFront to use the ALB as the origin.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The traffic is both TCP and UDP, which means the load balancer must be a network-level one — an Application Load Balancer works with HTTP only. The lowest latency globally comes from Global Accelerator: the player enters the AWS network at the nearest edge location and then travels over the AWS backbone to the Region where the NLB sits with the Auto Scaling group's instances registered.  
Why A is not selected: ALB does not support UDP: part of the game traffic simply would not get through.  
Why C is not selected: CloudFront works only with HTTP and HTTPS, so it cannot serve TCP on a non-standard port or UDP.  
Why D is not selected: This has two errors at once: CloudFront is not applicable to this kind of traffic, and ALB does not support UDP.

---

462\. A company has an application that processes customer orders. The company hosts the application on an Amazon EC2 instance that saves the orders to an Amazon Aurora database. Occasionally when traffic is high the workload does not process orders fast enough.  
What should a solutions architect do to write the orders reliably to the database as quickly as possible?  
A. Increase the instance size of the EC2 instance when traffic is high. Write orders to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS). Subscribe the database endpoint to the SNS topic.  
B. Write orders to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer to read from the SQS queue and process orders into the database.  
C. Write orders to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS). Subscribe the database endpoint to the SNS topic. Use EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer to read from the SNS topic.  
D. Write orders to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue when the EC2 instance reaches CPU threshold limits. Use scheduled scaling of EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer to read from the SQS queue and process orders into the database.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: During a traffic spike, orders arrive faster than a single instance can write them. An SQS queue accepts orders instantly and holds them until they're processed, so nothing is lost, and the Auto Scaling group reads from the queue and scales based on queue length — processing speeds up exactly when it's needed.  
Why A is not selected: Manually increasing instance size can't keep up with spikes, and subscribing the database endpoint to an SNS topic isn't possible: SNS can't write to a database.  
Why C is not selected: SNS delivers messages immediately and doesn't buffer them: it doesn't smooth out the spike, and subscribing the database to the topic is still not possible.  
Why D is not selected: Scheduled scaling doesn't react to unpredictable spikes, and switching to the queue only after a CPU threshold is reached means some orders are already lost.

---

463\. An IoT company is releasing a mattress that has sensors to collect data about a user’s sleep. The sensors will send data to an Amazon S3 bucket. The sensors collect approximately 2 MB of data every night for each mattress. The company must process and summarize the data for each mattress. The results need to be available as soon as possible. Data processing will require 1 GB of memory and will finish within 30 seconds.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Use AWS Glue with a Scala job  
B. Use Amazon EMR with an Apache Spark script  
C. Use AWS Lambda with a Python script  
D. Use AWS Glue with a PySpark job  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The task is tiny: two megabytes of data, a gigabyte of memory, thirty seconds of runtime, triggered by an event. This is a textbook fit for a Lambda function: it fits within both the memory limit and the time limit, is billed per second, and starts immediately after the file is uploaded.  
Why A is not selected: An AWS Glue job is billed for a minimum of one DPU-hour and takes minutes to start — overkill and expensive for thirty seconds of processing.  
Why B is not selected: An EMR cluster running Spark for two megabytes of data is a mismatch of scale, plus it means constantly running infrastructure.  
Why D is not selected: The same Glue, just with PySpark: the same minimum billing rates and the same startup time.

---

464\. A company hosts an online shopping application that stores all orders in an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Single- AZ DB instance. Management wants to eliminate single points of failure and has asked a solutions architect to recommend an approach to minimize database downtime without requiring any changes to the application code.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Convert the existing database instance to a Multi-AZ deployment by modifying the database instance and specifying the Multi-AZ option.  
B. Create a new RDS Multi-AZ deployment. Take a snapshot of the current RDS instance and restore the new Multi-AZ deployment with the snapshot.  
C. Create a read-only replica of the PostgreSQL database in another Availability Zone. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted record sets to distribute requests across the databases.  
D. Place the RDS for PostgreSQL database in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group with a minimum group size of two. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted record sets to distribute requests across instances.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The single point of failure is the Single-AZ instance, and it's eliminated by turning on Multi-AZ right in the settings of the existing instance. AWS creates a standby copy in another Availability Zone and replicates data synchronously; on failover the endpoint name stays the same, so the application code doesn't need to change. The switch happens in place, with no migration.  
Why B is not selected: A snapshot-based approach works, but it means extra downtime for the restore and a change of endpoint, and the result is the same as simply modifying the setting.  
Why C is not selected: A read replica is not a tool for write fault tolerance, and Route 53 weighted records would send part of the requests to a read-only replica: the application would break the moment it tries to write.  
Why D is not selected: RDS is a managed service — its instances are not placed in an EC2 Auto Scaling group. No such configuration exists.

---

465\. A company is developing an application to support customer demands. The company wants to deploy the application on multiple Amazon EC2 Nitro-based instances within the same Availability Zone. The company also wants to give the application the ability to write to multiple block storage volumes in multiple EC2 Nitro-based instances simultaneously to achieve higher application availability.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use General Purpose SSD (gp3) EBS volumes with Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach  
B. Use Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) EBS volumes with Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi- Attach  
C. Use Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) EBS volumes with Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach  
D. Use General Purpose SSD (gp2) EBS volumes with Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Simultaneous writes from multiple instances to a single volume is the Multi-Attach feature, and it's supported only by Provisioned IOPS volumes: io1 and io2. Of the options given, io2 qualifies, and the instances must be Nitro-based and in the same Availability Zone, which the scenario already states.  
Why A is not selected: gp3 volumes don't support Multi-Attach: this configuration simply can't be created.  
Why B is not selected: st1 volumes, on magnetic disks, also don't support Multi-Attach.  
Why D is not selected: gp2 has no Multi-Attach support.

---

466\. A company designed a stateless two-tier application that uses Amazon EC2 in a single Availability Zone and an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance. New company management wants to ensure the application is highly available.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?  
A. Configure the application to use Multi-AZ EC2 Auto Scaling and create an Application Load Balancer  
B. Configure the application to take snapshots of the EC2 instances and send them to a different AWS Region  
C. Configure the application to use Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to feed requests to the application  
D. Configure Amazon Route 53 rules to handle incoming requests and create a Multi-AZ Application Load Balancer  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The only weak point here is the web tier: the database is already Multi-AZ, but the EC2 instances sit in a single Availability Zone. The application is stateless, so it's enough to stretch the Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones and put an Application Load Balancer in front of it — it distributes requests and excludes unhealthy targets, while the group restores the needed instance count if a zone fails.  
Why B is not selected: Snapshots to another Region are backup, not high availability: restoring from them takes time and manual action.  
Why C is not selected: Latency-based routing makes sense when there are multiple deployed locations. Here there's only one location, and this policy adds no redundancy at all.  
Why D is not selected: A load balancer operates across multiple Availability Zones by definition, but without an Auto Scaling group spread across those zones it has nowhere to route traffic if a zone fails.

---

467\. A company uses AWS Organizations. A member account has purchased a Compute Savings Plan. Because of changes in the workloads inside the member account, the account no longer receives the full benefit of the Compute Savings Plan commitment. The company uses less than 50% of its purchased compute power.  
A. Turn on discount sharing from the Billing Preferences section of the account console in the member account that purchased the Compute Savings Plan.  
B. Turn on discount sharing from the Billing Preferences section of the account console in the company's Organizations management account.  
C. Migrate additional compute workloads from another AWS account to the account that has the Compute Savings Plan.  
D. Sell the excess Savings Plan commitment in the Reserved Instance Marketplace.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: In an organization with consolidated billing, discounts from Savings Plans and Reserved Instances are shared across all accounts by default: an unused commitment in one account automatically covers matching usage in other accounts. This is controlled by the discount sharing switch (RI/SP sharing), located in the billing settings of the organization's management account — a member account cannot change this setting. Turning on sharing is exactly how you put the purchased commitment to full use without migrating workloads.  
Why A is not selected: The discount sharing setting is available only in the organization's management account. There's no such switch in a member account.  
Why C is not selected: Migrating workloads between accounts is a project with downtime and risk, for something a single billing setting already solves.  
Why D is not selected: The Reserved Instance Marketplace only sells standard EC2 Reserved Instances. Savings Plans cannot be resold.

---

468\. A company is developing a microservices application that will provide a search catalog for customers. The company must use REST APIs to present the frontend of the application to users. The REST APIs must access the backend services that the company hosts in containers in private VPC subnets.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Design a WebSocket API by using Amazon API Gateway. Host the application in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) in a private subnet. Create a private VPC link for API Gateway to access Amazon ECS.  
B. Design a REST API by using Amazon API Gateway. Host the application in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) in a private subnet. Create a private VPC link for API Gateway to access Amazon ECS.  
C. Design a WebSocket API by using Amazon API Gateway. Host the application in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) in a private subnet. Create a security group for API Gateway to access Amazon ECS.  
D. Design a REST API by using Amazon API Gateway. Host the application in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) in a private subnet. Create a security group for API Gateway to access Amazon ECS.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Users need a REST API, and the backend runs in containers in private subnets. A REST-type API Gateway connects to them through a private VPC link: a link is created to a Network Load Balancer in front of the ECS service, and traffic flows over the internal network with no public addresses.  
Why A is not selected: A WebSocket API is meant for persistent, bidirectional connections, and the requirement explicitly calls for REST.  
Why C is not selected: Both the API type is wrong, and a security group doesn't give API Gateway network access into a private subnet — a VPC link is required for that.  
Why D is not selected: The API type is correct, but you can't connect to a private subnet through a security group — a VPC link is specifically required.

---

469\. A company stores raw collected data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The data is used for several types of analytics on behalf of the company's customers. The type of analytics requested determines the access pattern on the S3 objects.  
The company cannot predict or control the access pattern. The company wants to reduce its S3 costs.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use S3 replication to transition infrequently accessed objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA)  
B. Use S3 Lifecycle rules to transition objects from S3 Standard to Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard- IA)  
C. Use S3 Lifecycle rules to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 Intelligent-Tiering  
D. Use S3 Inventory to identify and transition objects that have not been accessed from S3 Standard to S3 Intelligent-Tiering  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The key phrase is "cannot predict or control the access pattern": the pattern is set by the customer, depending on the type of analytics they order. Anything that requires guessing an object's age or paying retrieval fees works against you here. Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between tiers on its own, based on actual access, and charges no retrieval fee, so an unexpected analytics request doesn't turn into a surprise bill.  
Why A is not selected: Replication copies objects into another bucket rather than changing the storage class of existing ones. With this setup you pay for two copies instead of saving.  
Why B is not selected: Transitioning to Standard-IA by age assumes that after N days the object really does stop being read. The requirement explicitly says this can't be predicted, and every access to IA will be charged.  
Why D is not selected: S3 Inventory is a report — it doesn't move objects; moving them would still be the job of a Lifecycle rule. On top of that, manually analyzing access patterns duplicates what Intelligent-Tiering already does automatically.

---

470\. A company has applications hosted on Amazon EC2 instances with IPv6 addresses. The applications must initiate communications with other external applications using the internet. However the company’s security policy states that any external service cannot initiate a connection to the EC2 instances.  
What should a solutions architect recommend to resolve this issue?  
A. Create a NAT gateway and make it the destination of the subnet's route table  
B. Create an internet gateway and make it the destination of the subnet's route table  
C. Create a virtual private gateway and make it the destination of the subnet's route table  
D. Create an egress-only internet gateway and make it the destination of the subnet's route table  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The addresses are IPv6, outbound connections are needed, inbound connections are prohibited. This is exactly what an egress-only internet gateway is for: it allows traffic initiated from inside and returns responses over the connection's state, but doesn't let anything be opened from outside.  
Why A is not selected: A NAT gateway works only with IPv4; it doesn't apply to IPv6.  
Why B is not selected: A regular internet gateway is bidirectional: external services would be able to initiate a connection to the instances.  
Why C is not selected: A virtual private gateway is the attachment point for VPN and Direct Connect — it has nothing to do with internet egress.

---

471\. A company is creating an application that runs on containers in a VPC. The application stores and accesses data in an Amazon S3 bucket. During the development phase, the application will store and access 1 TB of data in Amazon S3 each day. The company wants to minimize costs and wants to prevent traffic from traversing the internet whenever possible.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering for the S3 bucket  
B. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for the S3 bucket  
C. Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Associate this endpoint with all route tables in the VPC  
D. Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC. Associate this endpoint with all route tables in the VPC  
Answer: C  
Explanation: There are two requirements here: keep traffic off the public internet, and avoid unnecessary cost at 1 TB per day. A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 adds a route to the VPC's route tables, so traffic to S3 travels over the AWS internal network — and, crucially, the endpoint itself is free, with no charge for the gigabytes that pass through it. An interface endpoint is also private, but it is billed hourly per Availability Zone plus per gigabyte processed: at 1 TB a day that adds up to a meaningful sum. Remember the distinction: the gateway endpoint exists only for S3 and DynamoDB and costs nothing, while every other service is reached only through an interface endpoint.  
Why A is not selected: A storage class changes storage cost, not the traffic path. The requirement to keep data off the internet is not met.  
Why B is not selected: Transfer Acceleration does the opposite: it routes traffic through the global network of edge locations and charges extra for it. That is both more expensive and not private.  
Why D is not selected: An interface endpoint does solve the privacy requirement, but it is billed hourly plus per gigabyte, so at 1 TB a day it loses to the free gateway endpoint. On top of that, an interface endpoint is created in subnets with security groups rather than being "associated with route tables" — that association is exactly how the gateway endpoint works.

---

472\. A company has a mobile chat application with a data store based in Amazon DynamoDB. Users would like new messages to be read with as little latency as possible. A solutions architect needs to design an optimal solution that requires minimal application changes.  
Which method should the solutions architect select?  
A. Configure Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for the new messages table. Update the code to use the DAX endpoint.  
B. Add DynamoDB read replicas to handle the increased read load. Update the application to point to the read endpoint for the read replicas.  
C. Double the number of read capacity units for the new messages table in DynamoDB. Continue to use the existing DynamoDB endpoint.  
D. Add an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cache to the application stack. Update the application to point to the Redis cache endpoint instead of DynamoDB.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The requirement is minimal read latency for new messages with minimal application changes. DAX is DynamoDB's built-in in-memory cache, serving data in microseconds; it's compatible with the same API, so the change amounts to swapping the endpoint address for the DAX cluster endpoint.  
Why B is not selected: DynamoDB has no read replicas: read scaling is done through capacity, global tables, or DAX.  
Why C is not selected: Doubling the read capacity units removes throttling, but response time stays in the millisecond range — there is no latency improvement.  
Why D is not selected: A Redis cache would deliver low latency, but it requires its own cache-loading and invalidation logic in the code, meaning substantial application changes.

---

473\. A company hosts a website on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The website serves static content. Website traffic is increasing, and the company is concerned about a potential increase in cost.  
A. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution to cache state files at edge locations  
B. Create an Amazon ElastiCache cluster. Connect the ALB to the ElastiCache cluster to serve cached files  
C. Create an AWS WAF web ACL and associate it with the ALB. Add a rule to the web ACL to cache static files  
D. Create a second ALB in an alternative AWS Region. Route user traffic to the closest Region to minimize data transfer costs  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The site serves static content and traffic is growing, so costs are being incurred both for data transfer out of the Region and for the instances handling repeated requests. CloudFront addresses both: files are cached at edge locations, so repeat requests never reach the load balancer or the instances, and data transfer out of CloudFront is cheaper than transferring directly out of EC2. It also reduces latency for users far from the origin.  
Why B is not selected: ElastiCache is a cache for application data (sessions, query results), not for serving files to clients. The load balancer has no way to serve content out of ElastiCache.  
Why C is not selected: AWS WAF filters requests and caches nothing — it has no such capability.  
Why D is not selected: A second load balancer in another Region means a second copy of the infrastructure, and it does not reduce the cost of serving static content.

---

474\. A company has multiple VPCs across AWS Regions to support and run workloads that are isolated from workloads in other Regions. Because of a recent application launch requirement, the company’s VPCs must communicate with all other VPCs across all Regions.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of administrative effort?  
A. Use VPC peering to manage VPC communication in a single Region. Use VPC peering across Regions to manage VPC communications.  
B. Use AWS Direct Connect gateways across all Regions to connect VPCs across regions and manage VPC communications.  
C. Use AWS Transit Gateway to manage VPC communication in a single Region and Transit Gateway peering across Regions to manage VPC communications.  
D. Use AWS PrivateLink across all Regions to connect VPCs across Regions and manage VPC communications  
Answer: C  
Explanation: There are multiple VPCs across Regions, all of them need connectivity to each other, and administrative overhead must be minimized. Transit Gateway acts as a central router within a Region: each VPC connects through a single attachment, and the number of connections grows linearly. Between Regions, the gateways connect through transit gateway peering. The number of objects to configure is minimal, and routing is managed in the gateway's route tables.  
Why A is not selected: A mesh of peering connections grows quadratically: for n networks you need n times (n minus one) divided by two connections, and every route table ends up with an entry for each partner. That's hard to administer, and peering does not support transitive routing.  
Why B is not selected: Direct Connect gateway is for connecting an on-premises location to a VPC — it does not provide VPC-to-VPC connectivity.  
Why D is not selected: PrivateLink publishes a single service through an endpoint and gives one-way access to it, not full network connectivity between all the VPCs.

---

475\. A company is designing a containerized application that will use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS).  
The application needs to access a shared file system that is highly durable and can recover data to another AWS Region with a recovery point objective (RPO) of 8 hours. The file system needs to provide a mount target m each Availability Zone within a Region.  
A solutions architect wants to use AWS Backup to manage the replication to another Region.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with a Multi-AZ deployment  
B. Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP with a Multi-AZ deployment  
C. Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with the Standard storage class  
D. Amazon FSx for OpenZFS  
Answer: C  
Explanation: There are three requirements: a file system with a mount target in every Availability Zone, high durability, and replication to another Region via AWS Backup with an RPO of 8 hours. Amazon EFS with the Standard storage class satisfies all of them: data is stored across multiple Availability Zones, mount targets are created in every zone, and AWS Backup can copy EFS backups to another Region on a schedule.  
Why A is not selected: FSx for Windows File Server uses the SMB protocol, and in a Multi-AZ deployment it has a single active endpoint rather than a mount target in every zone.  
Why B is not selected: FSx for NetApp ONTAP in a Multi-AZ deployment likewise has a single active endpoint for access, not a separate mount target in each Availability Zone.  
Why D is not selected: FSx for OpenZFS deploys in a single Availability Zone, so the availability requirement is not met.

---

476\. A company is expecting rapid growth in the near future. A solutions architect needs to configure existing users and grant permissions to new users on AWS. The solutions architect has decided to create IAM groups. The solutions architect will add the new users to IAM groups based on department.  
Which additional action is the MOST secure way to grant permissions to the new users?  
A. Apply service control policies (SCPs) to manage access permissions  
B. Create IAM roles that have least privilege permission. Attach the roles to the IAM groups  
C. Create an IAM policy that grants least privilege permission. Attach the policy to the IAM groups  
D. Create IAM roles. Associate the roles with a permissions boundary that defines the maximum permissions  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Permissions in IAM are granted through policies, and groups exist precisely so a policy can be attached once for an entire department. A new hire joins the group and automatically picks up the right permission set, and a policy change applies to everyone at once. A role doesn't fit here: a role can't be attached to a group — it's assumed, not inherited through group membership. Least privilege comes from the content of the policy itself: only the actions needed on the resources needed.  
Why A is not selected: SCPs are an organization-level tool that caps the maximum permissions available in accounts. They don't grant anything, so new users would still end up with no permissions.  
Why B is not selected: A role cannot be attached to an IAM group: a role is assumed by a principal through AssumeRole, not inherited through group membership.  
Why D is not selected: A permissions boundary sets a ceiling on what a user or role can be granted, but it doesn't grant any permissions by itself. Without a policy, no permissions actually appear.

---

477\. A group requires permissions to list an Amazon S3 bucket and delete objects from that bucket. An administrator has created the following IAM policy to provide access to the bucket and applied that policy to the group. The group is not able to delete objects in the bucket. The company follows least-privilege access rules.  
Which statement should a solutions architect add to the policy to correct bucket access?  
![Exhibit for question 477](images/exhibits/q477.png)  
A. ![Option A for question 477](images/exhibits/q477-A.png)  
B. ![Option B for question 477](images/exhibits/q477-B.png)  
C. ![Option C for question 477](images/exhibits/q477-C.png)  
D. ![Option D for question 477](images/exhibits/q477-D.png)  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The mistake in the original policy is a classic one: actions on objects and actions on the bucket require different ARNs. s3:ListBucket applies to the bucket itself (arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name), while s3:DeleteObject applies to the objects inside it (arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/*). The policy only specifies the bucket ARN, which is why deletion doesn't work. Exactly one permission needs to be added — s3:DeleteObject on arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/* — and nothing beyond that, since the company follows least privilege.  
Why A is not selected: The s3:*Object wildcard grants GetObject, PutObject, RestoreObject, and other actions the group never asked for. The ARN is correct, but the permissions go beyond what's needed.  
Why B is not selected: s3:* is literally every S3 operation on the bucket's objects. Of the options given, this is the most severe violation of least privilege.  
Why C is not selected: The action is correct, but the ARN "arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name*" is still bucket-level scope (and, incidentally, covers every bucket whose name starts the same way). It doesn't cover the objects inside the bucket, so deletion still won't work.

---

478\. A law firm needs to share information with the public. The information includes hundreds of files that must be publicly readable. Modifications or deletions of the files by anyone before a designated future date are prohibited.  
Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?  
A. Upload all files to an Amazon S3 bucket that is configured for static website hosting. Grant read-only IAM permissions to any AWS principals that access the S3 bucket until the designated date.  
B. Create a new Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Versioning enabled. Use S3 Object Lock with a retention period in accordance with the designated date. Configure the S3 bucket for static website hosting. Set an S3 bucket policy to allow read-only access to the objects.  
C. Create a new Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Versioning enabled. Configure an event trigger to run an AWS Lambda function in case of object modification or deletion. Configure the Lambda function to replace the objects with the original versions from a private S3 bucket.  
D. Upload all files to an Amazon S3 bucket that is configured for static website hosting. Select the folder that contains the files. Use S3 Object Lock with a retention period in accordance with the designated date. Grant read-only IAM permissions to any AWS principals that access the S3 bucket.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The two requirements pull in opposite directions: the files must be publicly readable, yet unmodifiable until a set date. Public read access comes from a bucket policy granting s3:GetObject to anonymous requests (typically paired with static website hosting), while immutability comes from S3 Object Lock with a retention period set to the target date, layered on top of versioning. One key detail rules out half the options: anonymous readers' access is governed by a bucket policy, not IAM permissions — the public has no AWS accounts to grant anything to.  
Why A is not selected: IAM permissions apply only to AWS principals, and "the public" isn't one: the files would either stay inaccessible or become accessible through some other mechanism entirely. And there's no protection against modification here at all.  
Why C is not selected: A function that restores the object from a backup after it's been modified is a reaction after the fact. The requirement is that modification be impossible in the first place.  
Why D is not selected: Object Lock is enabled at the bucket level (and requires versioning) — you can't select a "folder" and protect just that. Plus it repeats the same IAM-permissions mistake for anonymous readers.

---

479\. A company is making a prototype of the infrastructure for its new website by manually provisioning the necessary infrastructure. This infrastructure includes an Auto Scaling group, an Application Load Balancer and an Amazon RDS database. After the configuration has been thoroughly validated, the company wants the capability to immediately deploy the infrastructure for development and production use in two Availability Zones in an automated fashion.  
What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS Systems Manager to replicate and provision the prototype infrastructure in two Availability Zones  
B. Define the infrastructure as a template by using the prototype infrastructure as a guide. Deploy the infrastructure with AWS CloudFormation.  
C. Use AWS Config to record the inventory of resources that are used in the prototype infrastructure. Use AWS Config to deploy the prototype infrastructure into two Availability Zones.  
D. Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk and configure it to use an automated reference to the prototype infrastructure to automatically deploy new environments in two Availability Zones.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: A manually built prototype needs to become a repeatable deployment. AWS CloudFormation describes the whole infrastructure as a template: the Auto Scaling group, the load balancer, and the database are all created in one operation, and identical development and production environments are deployed from the same template with different parameters.  
Why A is not selected: Systems Manager manages resources that already exist and does not describe infrastructure as code.  
Why C is not selected: AWS Config records configuration state and checks compliance, but it doesn't create anything.  
Why D is not selected: Elastic Beanstalk deploys applications using its own platform templates and cannot replicate arbitrary existing infrastructure.

---

480\. A business application is hosted on Amazon EC2 and uses Amazon S3 for encrypted object storage. The chief information security officer has directed that no application traffic between the two services should traverse the public internet.  
Which capability should the solutions architect use to meet the compliance requirements?  
A. AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS)  
B. VPC endpoint  
C. Private subnet  
D. Virtual private gateway  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirement is framed around the network path: traffic between EC2 and S3 must not travel over the public internet. Only a VPC endpoint changes that path — for S3 this is typically the free gateway endpoint, which adds a route to the route table pointing at the service's prefix inside the AWS network. Encryption, subnet type, and gateways to an on-premises network have no effect on this path. Access is also commonly further restricted using the aws:SourceVpce condition in the bucket policy.  
Why A is not selected: KMS encrypts the objects but doesn't change the packet's path: the encrypted data would still travel over S3's public endpoint.  
Why C is not selected: An instance in a private subnet without an endpoint reaches S3 through a NAT gateway — that is, over the internet. A private subnet by itself doesn't satisfy the requirement.  
Why D is not selected: A virtual private gateway is the connection point for a VPC to an on-premises network over VPN or Direct Connect. It has nothing to do with requests to S3.

---

481\. A company hosts a three-tier web application in the AWS Cloud. A Multi-AZAmazon RDS for MySQL server forms the database layer Amazon ElastiCache forms the cache layer. The company wants a caching strategy that adds or updates data in the cache when a customer adds an item to the database. The data in the cache must always match the data in the database.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Implement the lazy loading caching strategy  
B. Implement the write-through caching strategy  
C. Implement the adding TTL caching strategy  
D. Implement the AWS AppConfig caching strategy  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirement is stated literally: data must land in the cache at the moment of writing, and the cache contents must always match the database. That's the write-through strategy — on every write, the application updates both the database and the cache, so stale values never occur.  
Why A is not selected: Lazy loading only puts data into the cache after a read miss, so between the write and the first read, the cache lags behind the database.  
Why C is not selected: A TTL limits how long a discrepancy can persist, but it doesn't eliminate it and doesn't update the cache when data is added.  
Why D is not selected: AWS AppConfig distributes application configuration parameters and is not a data caching strategy.

---

482\. A company wants to migrate 100 GB of historical data from an on-premises location to an Amazon S3 bucket. The company has a 100 megabits per second (Mbps) internet connection on premises. The company needs to encrypt the data in transit to the S3 bucket. The company will store new data directly in Amazon S3.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use the s3 sync command in the AWS CLI to move the data directly to an S3 bucket  
B. Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data from the on-premises location to an S3 bucket  
C. Use AWS Snowball to move the data to an S3 bucket  
D. Set up an IPsec VPN from the on-premises location to AWS. Use the s3 cp command in the AWS CLI to move the data directly to an S3 bucket  
Answer: B  
Review status: Disputed key (alternative: A)  
Dispute note: 100 GB over a 100 Mbps link takes roughly 2.5 hours with a plain aws s3 sync over TLS, with no deployed component at all; DataSync requires standing up and maintaining an agent, but in return it verifies integrity and retries failed transfers on its own — "least operational overhead" cuts both ways here  
Explanation: This question is flagged as disputed: both reasonable options satisfy the requirements, and everything hinges on how you read "least operational overhead." The math says the link is fast enough: 100 GB over a 100 Mbps connection takes roughly 2.5 hours, so an offline transfer isn't needed. In-transit encryption comes from TLS, which both approaches provide. The corrected key selects AWS DataSync: the agent splits the transfer into parallel streams, retries failed chunks, and verifies data integrity on its own. The case for aws s3 sync is that it's a single command with no deployed component at all, whereas DataSync means standing up and running an agent for a one-time job. The practical rule of thumb: reach for DataSync for recurring or large transfers that need verification, and for the CLI for a one-off copy of tens to hundreds of gigabytes.  
Why A is not selected: A strong alternative: the aws s3 sync command runs over HTTPS, uses multipart upload, and requires nothing to be deployed. Its weak point is that it lacks DataSync's built-in integrity checking and automatic retries.  
Why C is not selected: AWS Snowball is an offline transfer method for 100 GB of data that would move over the network in a couple of hours anyway. Ordering, waiting for, copying to, and shipping back a device is disproportionate effort.  
Why D is not selected: An IPsec VPN adds a second layer of encryption on top of the already-secured TLS connection to S3 and requires setting up and maintaining a tunnel. It's an extra component with no payoff.

---

483\. A company containerized a Windows job that runs on .NET 6 Framework under a Windows container. The company wants to run this job in the AWS Cloud. The job runs every 10 minutes. The job’s runtime varies between 1 minute and 3 minutes.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Create an AWS Lambda function based on the container image of the job. Configure Amazon EventBridge to invoke the function every 10 minutes.  
B. Use AWS Batch to create a job that uses AWS Fargate resources. Configure the job scheduling to run every 10 minutes.  
C. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate to run the job. Create a scheduled task based on the container image of the job to run every 10 minutes.  
D. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate to run the job. Create a standalone task based on the container image of the job. Use Windows task scheduler to run the job every 10 minutes.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The job is short, runs every ten minutes, and is packaged as a Windows container. Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate supports Windows containers and lets you create a scheduled task: the container spins up, runs for one to three minutes, and terminates, so you pay only for that runtime and there are no servers to manage.  
Why A is not selected: AWS Lambda cannot run Windows containers: only Linux-based images are supported.  
Why B is not selected: AWS Batch on Fargate resources does not support Windows containers, so the job would not run.  
Why D is not selected: Windows Task Scheduler runs inside the operating system, and with the Fargate launch type there's simply no underlying machine for it to live on.

---

484\. A company wants to move from many standalone AWS accounts to a consolidated, multi-account architecture. The company plans to create many new AWS accounts for different business units. The company needs to authenticate access to these AWS accounts by using a centralized corporate directory service.  
Which combination of actions should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Create a new organization in AWS Organizations with all features turned on. Create the new AWS accounts in the organization.  
B. Set up an Amazon Cognito identity pool. Configure AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) to accept Amazon Cognito authentication.  
C. Configure a service control policy (SCP) to manage the AWS accounts. Add AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) to AWS Directory Service.  
D. Create a new organization in AWS Organizations. Configure the organization's authentication mechanism to use AWS Directory Service directly.  
E. Set up AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) in the organization. Configure IAM Identity Center, and integrate it with the company's corporate directory service.  
Answer: AE  
Explanation: This is a two-part task. First, move to a multi-account architecture: create an organization in AWS Organizations with all features enabled so SCPs and centralized management become available, and create the new accounts inside it (A). Second, provide single sign-on through the existing corporate directory: that's AWS IAM Identity Center, connected to the company's directory as the identity source, with permission sets assigned to accounts (E). Users sign in with their corporate credentials and receive temporary roles in the appropriate accounts.  
Why B is not selected: Amazon Cognito is meant for application end users, not employees. IAM Identity Center does not accept Cognito as a corporate identity source.  
Why C is not selected: An SCP governs restrictions, not authentication, and "add IAM Identity Center to AWS Directory Service" gets the order backwards: the directory is connected to Identity Center as its identity source, not the other way around.  
Why D is not selected: The organization itself has no authentication mechanism: sign-in is configured in IAM Identity Center, while Organizations is responsible for account structure and policies.

---

485\. A company is looking for a solution that can store video archives in AWS from old news footage. The company needs to minimize costs and will rarely need to restore these files. When the files are needed, they must be available in a maximum of five minutes.  
What is the MOST cost-effective solution?  
A. Store the video archives in Amazon S3 Glacier and use Expedited retrievals.  
B. Store the video archives in Amazon S3 Glacier and use Standard retrievals.  
C. Store the video archives in Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA).  
D. Store the video archives in Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA).  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Two numbers settle this: access is rare, and the retrieval time cannot exceed five minutes. Instant-access classes (IA) satisfy the timing requirement but are expensive for data that sits idle for years, while S3 Glacier Deep Archive can't meet a five-minute window. That leaves S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval with Expedited retrievals: an expedited retrieval returns the archive in 1–5 minutes, versus 3–5 hours for a standard retrieval. You pay the expedited retrieval cost only when you actually need the data, while storage the rest of the time is billed at the archive rate.  
Why B is not selected: A Standard retrieval from S3 Glacier takes 3–5 hours, which violates the "maximum of five minutes" requirement.  
Why C is not selected: S3 Standard-IA returns objects instantly, but its storage cost is roughly three times that of S3 Glacier. Given the requirement to minimize cost and the rarity of restores, that's paying a premium for speed needed maybe once a year.  
Why D is not selected: S3 One Zone-IA is cheaper than S3 Standard-IA, but its storage cost is still higher than S3 Glacier's, and it keeps only a single copy in one Availability Zone — a questionable trade-off for a news footage archive.

---

486\. A company is building a three-tier application on AWS. The presentation tier will serve a static website The logic tier is a containerized application. This application will store data in a relational database. The company wants to simplify deployment and to reduce operational costs.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use Amazon S3 to host static content. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate for compute power. Use a managed Amazon RDS cluster for the database.  
B. Use Amazon CloudFront to host static content. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with Amazon EC2 for compute power. Use a managed Amazon RDS cluster for the database.  
C. Use Amazon S3 to host static content. Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with AWS Fargate for compute power. Use a managed Amazon RDS cluster for the database.  
D. Use Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances to host static content. Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with Amazon EC2 for compute power. Use a managed Amazon RDS cluster for the database.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The requirements are simple deployment and low operational costs. S3 hosts the static content with no servers involved at all; ECS on Fargate runs the logic tier's containers without any nodes to manage; a managed RDS cluster stores the data. Every tier is chosen so there's no infrastructure left to maintain.  
Why B is not selected: CloudFront doesn't store content by itself — it needs an origin — and running ECS on EC2 instances brings node management back into the picture.  
Why C is not selected: Amazon EKS requires managing a Kubernetes cluster and costs more than ECS for the same workload — added complexity with no upside.  
Why D is not selected: Hosting static content on Reserved Instances is the most expensive and labor-intensive of these options.

---

487\. A company seeks a storage solution for its application. The solution must be highly available and scalable. The solution also must function as a file system be mountable by multiple Linux instances in AWS and on premises through native protocols, and have no minimum size requirements. The company has set up a Site-to-Site VPN for access from its on-premises network to its VPC.  
Which storage solution meets these requirements?  
A. Amazon FSx Multi-AZ deployments  
B. Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach volumes  
C. Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with multiple mount targets  
D. Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with a single mount target and multiple access points  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Gathering the requirements: a file system that can be mounted with native tools both from AWS and from the on-premises network over the already-configured VPN, with no minimum size, that's scalable and highly available. That's Amazon EFS with mount targets in multiple Availability Zones: each mount target serves clients in its own zone, and the on-premises Linux servers mount the file system over NFS through the tunnel.  
Why A is not selected: The Amazon FSx family is built for SMB, Lustre, ONTAP, or OpenZFS, and as described it doesn't satisfy the requirement to mount natively from Linux instances with no minimum size.  
Why B is not selected: Amazon EBS Multi-Attach attaches a volume to multiple instances only within a single Availability Zone and requires a cluster-aware file system, and such a volume isn't reachable from the on-premises network at all.  
Why D is not selected: A single mount target means clients in other zones all route through that one target, turning its zone into a single point of failure. Access points manage permissions, but they don't replace mount targets.

---

488\. A 4-year-old media company is using the AWS Organizations all features feature set to organize its AWS accounts.  
According to the company's finance team, the billing information on the member accounts must not be accessible to anyone, including the root user of the member accounts.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Add all finance team users to an IAM group. Attach an AWS managed policy named Billing to the group.  
B. Attach an identity-based policy to deny access to the billing information to all users, including the root user.  
C. Create a service control policy (SCP) to deny access to the billing information. Attach the SCP to the root organizational unit (OU).  
D. Convert from the Organizations all features feature set to the Organizations consolidated billing feature set.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: This is a strict requirement: billing information must be inaccessible to anyone in member accounts, including their root user. IAM policies are powerless here — they have no effect on an account's root user. The only mechanism that can constrain a member account's root user is a service control policy attached to the organization's root or the relevant OU: it sets a permissions ceiling for every principal in the account. The SCP would deny actions such as aws-portal:* (or account:GetAccountInformation and related billing operations).  
Why A is not selected: The AWS managed Billing policy grants access, and the requirement is the opposite — to block it. It also has no effect on member accounts' root users.  
Why B is not selected: An identity-based policy does not apply to the root user: only an SCP from the organization can restrict root.  
Why D is not selected: Switching to the consolidated billing feature set strips the organization of SCPs and other governance tools, making the situation worse rather than solving the problem.

---

489\. An ecommerce company runs an application in the AWS Cloud that is integrated with an on-premises warehouse solution. The company uses Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to send order messages to an on- premises HTTPS endpoint so the warehouse application can process the orders. The local data center team has detected that some of the order messages were not received.  
A solutions architect needs to retain messages that are not delivered and analyze the messages for up to 14 days.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?  
A. Configure an Amazon SNS dead letter queue that has an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream target with a retention period of 14 days.  
B. Add an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue with a retention period of 14 days between the application and Amazon SNS.  
C. Configure an Amazon SNS dead letter queue that has an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) target with a retention period of 14 days.  
D. Configure an Amazon SNS dead letter queue that has an Amazon DynamoDB target with a TTL attribute set for a retention period of 14 days.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Undelivered SNS messages are routed to a dead-letter queue — and that target is always an SQS queue attached to the subscription. SQS's retention period can be set up to 14 days, giving plenty of time to analyze the messages afterward. No code needs to be written at all — it's just a subscription setting.  
Why A is not selected: An SNS dead-letter queue target can only be an SQS queue; a Kinesis Data Stream is not supported in that role.  
Why B is not selected: A queue placed in front of the topic doesn't help: the messages are lost between SNS and the on-premises endpoint, which is downstream of the topic.  
Why D is not selected: A DynamoDB table also cannot serve as the target of an SNS dead-letter queue.

---

490\. A gaming company uses Amazon DynamoDB to store user information such as geographic location, player data, and leaderboards. The company needs to configure continuous backups to an Amazon S3 bucket with a minimal amount of coding. The backups must not affect availability of the application and must not affect the read capacity units (RCUs) that are defined for the table.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Use an Amazon EMR cluster. Create an Apache Hive job to back up the data to Amazon S3.  
B. Export the data directly from DynamoDB to Amazon S3 with continuous backups. Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table.  
C. Configure Amazon DynamoDB Streams. Create an AWS Lambda function to consume the stream and export the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.  
D. Create an AWS Lambda function to export the data from the database tables to Amazon S3 on a regular basis. Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: DynamoDB has a built-in table export to S3 that runs on top of continuous backups, so it requires point-in-time recovery to be turned on. The export reads from the backup, not from the live table, so it consumes no read capacity units and has no effect on application availability. No code is required.
