A. Run the Amazon CloudWatch agent in the existing EKS cluster. View the metrics and logs in the CloudWatch console.  
B. Run AWS App Mesh in the existing EKS cluster. View the metrics and logs in the App Mesh console.  
C. Configure AWS CloudTrail to capture data events. Query CloudTrail by using Amazon OpenSearch Service.  
D. Configure Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights in the existing EKS cluster. View the metrics and logs in the CloudWatch console.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: What is needed is collecting, aggregating, and summarizing the cluster's metrics and logs in one place. Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights does this natively for EKS: it collects metrics at the cluster, node, pod, and container level, pulls in logs, and builds ready-made dashboards in the CloudWatch console.  
Why A is not selected: The CloudWatch agent collects node-level metrics and logs, but it does not aggregate them by Kubernetes object and does not provide ready-made summaries.  
Why B is not selected: App Mesh manages traffic between services; it does not perform centralized collection of cluster metrics and logs.  
Why C is not selected: CloudTrail records AWS API calls, not what is happening inside the application within the cluster.

---

616\. A company has deployed its newest product on AWS. The product runs in an Auto Scaling group behind a Network Load Balancer. The company stores the product’s objects in an Amazon S3 bucket.  
The company recently experienced malicious attacks against its systems. The company needs a solution that continuously monitors for malicious activity in the AWS account, workloads, and access patterns to the S3 bucket.  
The solution must also report suspicious activity and display the information on a dashboard.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Configure Amazon Macie to monitor and report findings to AWS Config.  
B. Configure Amazon Inspector to monitor and report findings to AWS CloudTrail.  
C. Configure Amazon GuardDuty to monitor and report findings to AWS Security Hub.  
D. Configure AWS Config to monitor and report findings to Amazon EventBridge.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The requirement is continuous monitoring for suspicious activity across the account, workloads, and access to the bucket, with findings surfaced on a dashboard. That is GuardDuty: it analyzes CloudTrail, S3 data event logs, DNS logs, and VPC Flow Logs to detect anomalies and known malicious patterns. Findings are natively sent to AWS Security Hub, which serves as the unified dashboard. The distinction: GuardDuty detects, Security Hub aggregates and evaluates compliance.  
Why A is not selected: Macie looks for sensitive data, and AWS Config tracks resource configuration: neither one is a malicious-activity monitor.  
Why B is not selected: Inspector looks for vulnerabilities, and CloudTrail is an API call log, not a findings dashboard.  
Why D is not selected: AWS Config tracks configuration compliance and does not detect attacks or anomalous access.

---

617\. A company wants to migrate an on-premises data center to AWS. The data center hosts a storage server that stores data in an NFS-based file system. The storage server holds 200 GB of data. The company needs to migrate the data without interruption to existing services. Multiple resources in AWS must be able to access the data by using the NFS protocol.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)  
A. Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system.  
B. Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system.  
C. Create an Amazon S3 bucket to receive the data.  
D. Manually use an operating system copy command to push the data into the AWS destination.  
E. Install an AWS DataSync agent in the on-premises data center. Use a DataSync task between the on- premises location and AWS.  
Answer: BE  
Explanation: The target storage needs to serve data over NFS to multiple AWS resources - that is Amazon EFS (B). Migrating without interrupting existing services is what AWS DataSync does: an agent is deployed in the data center and transfers the data incrementally while verifying integrity, without disrupting operations on the source server (E). Two hundred gigabytes moves quickly over any reasonable connection.  
Why A is not selected: FSx for Lustre is built for high-performance computing, costs significantly more, and uses a different protocol.  
Why C is not selected: S3 does not serve data over the NFS protocol: the requirement explicitly names the protocol.  
Why D is not selected: Manually copying with an operating system command gives you no integrity verification, no incremental transfer, and no protection against interruption.

---

618\. A company wants to use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server for its Amazon EC2 instances that have an SMB file share mounted as a volume in the us-east-1 Region. The company has a recovery point objective (RPO) of 5 minutes for planned system maintenance or unplanned service disruptions. The company needs to replicate the file system to the us-west-2 Region. The replicated data must not be deleted by any user for 5 years.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create an FSx for Windows File Server file system in us-east-1 that has a Single-AZ 2 deployment type. Use AWS Backup to create a daily backup plan that includes a backup rule that copies the backup to us-west-2. Configure AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode for a target vault in us-west-2. Configure a minimum duration of 5 years.  
B. Create an FSx for Windows File Server file system in us-east-1 that has a Multi-AZ deployment type. Use AWS Backup to create a daily backup plan that includes a backup rule that copies the backup to us-west-2. Configure AWS Backup Vault Lock in governance mode for a target vault in us-west-2. Configure a minimum duration of 5 years.  
C. Create an FSx for Windows File Server file system in us-east-1 that has a Multi-AZ deployment type. Use AWS Backup to create a daily backup plan that includes a backup rule that copies the backup to us-west-2. Configure AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode for a target vault in us-west-2. Configure a minimum duration of 5 years.  
D. Create an FSx for Windows File Server file system in us-east-1 that has a Single-AZ 2 deployment type. Use AWS Backup to create a daily backup plan that includes a backup rule that copies the backup to us-west-2. Configure AWS Backup Vault Lock in governance mode for a target vault in us-west-2. Configure a minimum duration of 5 years.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: A five-minute RPO for both planned maintenance and unplanned disruptions is achieved with a Multi-AZ deployment: FSx synchronously replicates data to a second Availability Zone and fails over automatically. Cross-region copies are produced by a scheduled AWS Backup plan, and five-year immutability comes from Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode - in that mode, no one, including the account owner, can shorten or remove the retention period.  
Why A is not selected: A Single-AZ configuration does not deliver a five-minute RPO if the Availability Zone fails.  
Why B is not selected: Governance mode lets users with sufficient permissions remove the lock and delete copies, and the requirement states that no one should be able to delete the data.  
Why D is not selected: This option has both problems at once: a single Availability Zone instead of two, and a lock mode that can be overridden.

---

619\. A solutions architect is designing a security solution for a company that wants to provide developers with individual AWS accounts through AWS Organizations, while also maintaining standard security controls. Because the individual developers will have AWS account root user-level access to their own accounts, the solutions architect wants to ensure that the mandatory AWS CloudTrail configuration that is applied to new developer accounts is not modified.  
Which action meets these requirements?  
A. Create an IAM policy that prohibits changes to CloudTrail. and attach it to the root user.  
B. Create a new trail in CloudTrail from within the developer accounts with the organization trails option enabled.  
C. Create a service control policy (SCP) that prohibits changes to CloudTrail, and attach it the developer accounts.  
D. Create a service-linked role for CloudTrail with a policy condition that allows changes only from an Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in the management account.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Developers get root-user access in their own accounts, which means they can bypass or change any IAM policy within the account. The only mechanism that also constrains the root user of a member account is a service control policy attached to the accounts or their OUs: it denies actions like cloudtrail:StopLogging, DeleteTrail, UpdateTrail, and similar. This is typically combined with an organization trail created from the management account, which member accounts cannot modify.  
Why A is not selected: An IAM policy cannot be attached to the root user, and IAM policies do not apply to it anyway. That is exactly why SCPs exist.  
Why B is not selected: An organization trail is created in the management account, not "from within the developer accounts." And the mere presence of a trail does not prevent someone from disabling it without an SCP in place.  
Why D is not selected: A service-linked role lets a service take action on your behalf. It cannot restrict what the root user does.

---

620\. A company is planning to deploy a business-critical application in the AWS Cloud. The application requires durable storage with consistent, low-latency performance.  
Which type of storage should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?  
A. Instance store volume  
B. Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached cluster  
C. Provisioned IOPS SSD Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume  
D. Throughput Optimized HDD Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The requirements are durable storage with consistently low latency. A Provisioned IOPS EBS volume delivers a guaranteed number of operations per second with predictable latency, and the data is replicated within the Availability Zone and survives an instance stop.  
Why A is not selected: Instance store is ephemeral: data disappears when the instance stops, and durability is explicitly required.  
Why B is not selected: Memcached is an in-memory cache with no data persistence: it does not qualify as durable storage.  
Why D is not selected: Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volumes are optimized for high sequential throughput, not for consistently low latency on random operations.

---

621\. An online photo-sharing company stores its photos in an Amazon S3 bucket that exists in the us-west-1 Region.  
The company needs to store a copy of all new photos in the us-east-1 Region.  
Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational effort?  
A. Create a second S3 bucket in us-east-1. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy photos from the existing S3 bucket to the second S3 bucket.  
B. Create a cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) configuration of the existing S3 bucket. Specify us-east-1 in the CORS rule's AllowedOrigin element.  
C. Create a second S3 bucket in us-east-1 across multiple Availability Zones. Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to save photos into the second S3 bucket.  
D. Create a second S3 bucket in us-east-1. Configure S3 event notifications on object creation and update events to invoke an AWS Lambda function to copy photos from the existing S3 bucket to the second S3 bucket.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The task is to keep a copy of every new object in another region with the least effort. That is exactly what S3 Cross-Region Replication exists for: it is turned on with a rule on the source bucket (versioning is required), copies new objects asynchronously, retries automatically on failures, and can replicate metadata, tags, and encryption status. There is no code and no monitoring to build - the service manages the state. Keep in mind the limitation: replication applies only to objects created after it is enabled; existing objects have to be copied separately with S3 Batch Replication.  
Why B is not selected: CORS controls which websites a browser is allowed to let access the bucket from JavaScript. It does not copy any data between regions.  
Why C is not selected: A Lifecycle rule can change storage class and delete objects within a single bucket. It cannot copy objects to another bucket.  
Why D is not selected: The "S3 event plus Lambda" combination technically works, but it is your own code: error handling, retries, concurrency limits, and invocation costs. By the LEAST operational effort criterion, it loses to built-in replication.

---

622\. A company is creating a new web application for its subscribers. The application will consist of a static single page and a persistent database layer. The application will have millions of users for 4 hours in the morning, but the application will have only a few thousand users during the rest of the day. The company's data architects have requested the ability to rapidly evolve their schema.  
Which solutions will meet these requirements and provide the MOST scalability? (Choose two.)  
A. Deploy Amazon DynamoDB as the database solution. Provision on-demand capacity.  
B. Deploy Amazon Aurora as the database solution. Choose the serverless DB engine mode.  
C. Deploy Amazon DynamoDB as the database solution. Ensure that DynamoDB auto scaling is enabled.  
D. Deploy the static content into an Amazon S3 bucket. Provision an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as the origin.  
E. Deploy the web servers for static content across a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances in Auto Scaling groups. Configure the instances to periodically refresh the content from an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) volume.  
Answer: CD  
Review status: Disputed key (alternative: AD)  
Dispute note: When jumping from thousands to millions of users, on-demand capacity (A) scales instantly, while auto scaling provisioning lags behind sharp spikes  
Explanation: There are two requirements here, met by two different picks. For the static page, it is S3 plus CloudFront (D): serving from edge locations scales without any effort on your part. For the database, "rapidly evolve their schema" means no rigid schema, which points to DynamoDB rather than the relational Aurora. What is left is picking a capacity mode: the answer key goes with C (provisioned with auto scaling), while the community debates in favor of A (on-demand). The case for A: millions of users arrive in a wave, and provisioned auto scaling raises capacity in steps that can lag behind a sharp spike. The case for C: the load is predictable - the same window every morning - and provisioning against a known profile is cheaper.  
Why A is not selected: A strong alternative: on-demand absorbs the spike instantly and needs no configuration. The key favored provisioned because the load pattern in the question repeats predictably, making it cheaper to plan capacity for.  
Why B is not selected: Aurora is a relational database with a fixed schema. The requirement to "rapidly evolve their schema" points in exactly the opposite direction.  
Why E is not selected: A fleet of EC2 instances that periodically pulls static content from EFS is the heaviest to operate and the least scalable way to serve a single static page. S3 with CloudFront achieves the same thing with no servers at all.

---

623\. A company uses Amazon API Gateway to manage its REST APIs that third-party service providers access. The company must protect the REST APIs from SQL injection and cross-site scripting attacks.  
What is the MOST operationally efficient solution that meets these requirements?  
A. Configure AWS Shield.  
B. Configure AWS WAF.  
C. Set up API Gateway with an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Configure AWS Shield in CloudFront.  
D. Set up API Gateway with an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Configure AWS WAF in CloudFront.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: SQL injection and XSS are filtered by AWS WAF, and API Gateway is supported directly: a regional web ACL is associated with the API stage. No additional components are needed - hence "most operationally efficient." The options involving CloudFront add an unnecessary layer (useful when the API is edge-optimized or needs caching and global distribution), and Shield handles DDoS, not injection attacks.  
Why A is not selected: AWS Shield protects against availability attacks and does not inspect request content for injections.  
Why C is not selected: CloudFront is added without a need for it, and Shield again is not the right service for SQL injection.  
Why D is not selected: This would work, but CloudFront is an unnecessary component here: WAF attaches directly to API Gateway, which is simpler to operate.

---

624\. A company wants to provide users with access to AWS resources. The company has 1,500 users and manages their access to on-premises resources through Active Directory user groups on the corporate network. However, the company does not want users to have to maintain another identity to access the resources. A solutions architect must manage user access to the AWS resources while preserving access to the on-premises resources.  
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Create an IAM user for each user in the company. Attach the appropriate policies to each user.  
B. Use Amazon Cognito with an Active Directory user pool. Create roles with the appropriate policies attached.  
C. Define cross-account roles with the appropriate policies attached. Map the roles to the Active Directory groups.  
D. Configure Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) 2 0-based federation. Create roles with the appropriate policies attached Map the roles to the Active Directory groups.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Fifteen hundred employees already live in Active Directory, and they cannot be given a second set of credentials. The standard answer is SAML 2.0 federation: the corporate directory (via ADFS or IAM Identity Center) acts as the identity provider, roles with the appropriate policies are created in AWS, and Active Directory groups are mapped to those roles. The user signs in with their corporate password, receives temporary role credentials, and keeps access to on-premises resources at the same time.  
Why A is not selected: Fifteen hundred IAM users means a second set of credentials and manual upkeep - exactly what needs to be avoided.  
Why B is not selected: Cognito is meant for application end users, not for employee access to the AWS console and APIs. And an "Active Directory-based user pool" is not the right mechanism.  
Why C is not selected: Cross-account roles address access between AWS accounts, but they do not let employees sign in with their corporate credentials: an identity provider is needed.

---

625\. A company is hosting a website behind multiple Application Load Balancers. The company has different distribution rights for its content around the world. A solutions architect needs to ensure that users are served the correct content without violating distribution rights.  
Which configuration should the solutions architect choose to meet these requirements?  
A. Configure Amazon CloudFront with AWS WAF.  
B. Configure Application Load Balancers with AWS WAF  
C. Configure Amazon Route 53 with a geolocation policy  
D. Configure Amazon Route 53 with a geoproximity routing policy  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Distribution rights are tied to countries, so users need to be routed to different content based on their location. In Route 53 that is a geolocation routing policy: records are mapped to a continent, country, or US state, and the request goes to the load balancer authorized to serve that region. Do not confuse this with geoproximity: that policy routes based on geographic distance with a configurable bias and does not guarantee alignment with legal boundaries.  
Why A is not selected: CloudFront with WAF can block countries, but the task is not to block - it is to serve different content to different countries, and routing does that more precisely.  
Why B is not selected: WAF on the load balancers again blocks rather than distributes users to the right destinations.  
Why D is not selected: Geoproximity is based on distance to the resource, not the user's country: a user near a border could easily land on the wrong load balancer.

---

626\. A company stores its data on premises. The amount of data is growing beyond the company's available capacity.  
The company wants to migrate its data from the on-premises location to an Amazon S3 bucket. The company needs a solution that will automatically validate the integrity of the data after the transfer.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Order an AWS Snowball Edge device. Configure the Snowball Edge device to perform the online data transfer to an S3 bucket  
B. Deploy an AWS DataSync agent on premises. Configure the DataSync agent to perform the online data transfer to an S3 bucket.  
C. Create an Amazon S3 File Gateway on premises Configure the S3 File Gateway to perform the online data transfer to an S3 bucket  
D. Configure an accelerator in Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration on premises. Configure the accelerator to perform the online data transfer to an S3 bucket.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: There are two requirements: an online transfer, and automatic integrity verification after the transfer. DataSync does both: the on-premises agent reads the source storage, transfers the data to S3 over multiple TLS-encrypted threads, and on completion compares source and destination checksums, reporting any discrepancies in the task report. Neither File Gateway nor Transfer Acceleration performs this kind of verification. Keep the distinction clear: DataSync is transfer with verification, Storage Gateway is ongoing hybrid access, and the Snow Family is offline shipping for when the network link is not enough.  
Why A is not selected: Snowball Edge is an offline device that is physically shipped to AWS; you cannot "perform an online transfer" with it. The option contradicts itself.  
Why C is not selected: S3 File Gateway is built for ongoing file-based access to S3 objects with a local cache, not for a one-time migration with integrity verification.  
Why D is not selected: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads through edge locations. It does not perform any automatic checksum verification after the transfer.

---

627\. A company wants to migrate two DNS servers to AWS. The servers host a total of approximately 200 zones and receive 1 million requests each day on average. The company wants to maximize availability while minimizing the operational overhead that is related to the management of the two servers.  
What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?  
A. Create 200 new hosted zones in the Amazon Route 53 console Import zone files.  
B. Launch a single large Amazon EC2 instance Import zone tiles. Configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms and notifications to alert the company about any downtime.  
C. Migrate the servers to AWS by using AWS Server Migration Service (AWS SMS). Configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms and notifications to alert the company about any downtime.  
D. Launch an Amazon EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones. Import zone files. Set the desired capacity to 1 and the maximum capacity to 3 for the Auto Scaling group. Configure scaling alarms to scale based on CPU utilization.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The task is hosting DNS zones, not administering servers. Route 53 is a managed service with a 100% availability SLA, so the 200 zones are simply created in it and populated by importing zone files. There is no more patching, scaling, or monitoring of your own servers to do, and a million requests a day is a perfectly ordinary load for it.  
Why B is not selected: A single EC2 instance is the same single point of failure as before, just now in the cloud. Downtime alerts do not substitute for actual availability.  
Why C is not selected: AWS SMS migrates virtual machines as-is: the DNS servers would still exist, along with all the operational burden that comes with them.  
Why D is not selected: An Auto Scaling group of DNS servers requires synchronizing zones across instances and scales based on CPU utilization, which has little to do with DNS load. Complexity goes up with no gain over a managed service.

---

628\. A global company runs its applications in multiple AWS accounts in AWS Organizations. The company's applications use multipart uploads to upload data to multiple Amazon S3 buckets across AWS Regions. The company wants to report on incomplete multipart uploads for cost compliance purposes.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Configure AWS Config with a rule to report the incomplete multipart upload object count.  
B. Create a service control policy (SCP) to report the incomplete multipart upload object count.  
C. Configure S3 Storage Lens to report the incomplete multipart upload object count.  
D. Create an S3 Multi-Region Access Point to report the incomplete multipart upload object count.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: What is needed is a report on incomplete multipart uploads across many buckets, accounts, and regions at once. S3 Storage Lens does this natively: it aggregates metrics organization-wide (when connected to AWS Organizations), and among its metrics are the count and size of incomplete multipart uploads, along with a breakdown by their age. From there, what is found gets addressed with a Lifecycle rule using AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload - see {{q:326,725}}.  
Why A is not selected: AWS Config tracks resource configuration, not bucket contents. It does not count incomplete uploads.  
Why B is not selected: An SCP denies actions. Reporting is not its function.  
Why D is not selected: A Multi-Region Access Point routes requests to buckets across regions and does not produce any upload statistics.

---

629\. A company runs a production database on Amazon RDS for MySQL. The company wants to upgrade the database version for security compliance reasons. Because the database contains critical data, the company wants a quick solution to upgrade and test functionality without losing any data.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create an RDS manual snapshot. Upgrade to the new version of Amazon RDS for MySQL.  
B. Use native backup and restore. Restore the data to the upgraded new version of Amazon RDS for MySQL.  
C. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to replicate the data to the upgraded new version of Amazon RDS for MySQL.  
D. Use Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments to deploy and test production changes.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The requirement is to upgrade the version, verify functionality, and lose no data, with minimal effort. RDS Blue/Green Deployments creates a full copy of the database on the new version, keeps it in sync through replication, and lets you test it. The switchover takes about a minute and is done with a single command, and rollback stays available because the old environment remains in place.  
Why A is not selected: A snapshot is just a safety net: an in-place upgrade still means downtime and no way to test the new version under load beforehand.  
Why B is not selected: Native backup and restore requires manual steps, causes noticeable downtime, and does not let you validate functionality ahead of time.  
Why C is not selected: A DMS task would have to be configured and maintained manually - the same end result, but with significantly more effort.

---

630\. A solutions architect is creating a data processing job that runs once daily and can take up to 2 hours to complete.  
If the job is interrupted, it has to restart from the beginning.  
How should the solutions architect address this issue in the MOST cost-effective manner?  
A. Create a script that runs locally on an Amazon EC2 Reserved Instance that is triggered by a cron job.  
B. Create an AWS Lambda function triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.  
C. Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) Fargate task triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.  
D. Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task running on Amazon EC2 triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The job runs once a day, can take up to two hours, and cannot tolerate interruption. That rules out interruptible capacity, and Lambda's fifteen-minute limit does not fit either. An ECS task on Fargate, triggered by an EventBridge scheduled event, is billed only for the actual two hours and requires no continuously running instance.  
Why A is not selected: A Reserved Instance is billed around the clock, even though it only runs two hours a day.  
Why B is not selected: The Lambda function execution limit is fifteen minutes, and the job runs up to two hours.  
Why D is not selected: The EC2 launch type means an instance that runs - and is billed - outside the job's execution window.

---

631\. A social media company wants to store its database of user profiles, relationships, and interactions in the AWS Cloud. The company needs an application to monitor any changes in the database. The application needs to analyze the relationships between the data entities and to provide recommendations to users.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use Amazon Neptune to store the information. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to process changes in the database.  
B. Use Amazon Neptune to store the information. Use Neptune Streams to process changes in the database.  
C. Use Amazon Quantum Ledger Database (Amazon QLDB) to store the information. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to process changes in the database.  
D. Use Amazon Quantum Ledger Database (Amazon QLDB) to store the information. Use Neptune Streams to process changes in the database.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Profiles, relationships, and interactions are graph data, which points to Amazon Neptune. Its built-in Neptune Streams capability can track changes in the database: the change log is published by the database itself, with no need for additional services or ingestion code.  
Why A is not selected: The database choice is correct, but Kinesis Data Streams would have to be populated manually — an extra pipeline instead of a built-in stream.  
Why C is not selected: QLDB is a ledger with an immutable transaction history; it isn't designed to analyze relationships between entities.  
Why D is not selected: Both the database choice is wrong, and Neptune Streams doesn't apply to QLDB.

---

632\. A company is creating a new application that will store a large amount of data. The data will be analyzed hourly and will be modified by several Amazon EC2 Linux instances that are deployed across multiple Availability Zones.  
The needed amount of storage space will continue to grow for the next 6 months.  
Which storage solution should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?  
A. Store the data in Amazon S3 Glacier. Update the S3 Glacier vault policy to allow access to the application instances.  
B. Store the data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Mount the EBS volume on the application instances.  
C. Store the data in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the file system on the application instances.  
D. Store the data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Provisioned IOPS volume shared between the application instances.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The data is modified by several Linux instances across multiple Availability Zones, and the storage need will keep growing over months. Amazon EFS solves all of this at once: it mounts over NFS on every instance in every zone, supports concurrent writes, and grows automatically with no capacity planning.  
Why A is not selected: Glacier is an archive with retrieval times measured in minutes to hours; you can't modify data stored there.  
Why B is not selected: An EBS volume lives in a single Availability Zone and attaches to one instance, and you'd have to resize it manually.  
Why D is not selected: Even a Provisioned IOPS volume in Multi-Attach mode is limited to a single Availability Zone and requires a cluster-aware file system: instances in another zone can't attach to it.

---

633\. A company manages an application that stores data on an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance.  
Increases in traffic are causing performance problems. The company determines that database queries are the primary reason for the slow performance.  
What should a solutions architect do to improve the application's performance?  
A. Serve read traffic from the Multi-AZ standby replica.  
B. Configure the DB instance to use Transfer Acceleration.  
C. Create a read replica from the source DB instance. Serve read traffic from the read replica.  
D. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose between the application and Amazon RDS to increase the concurrency of database requests.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Read queries are slow, so they need to be offloaded from the primary instance. An RDS read replica is created from the source instance and takes all the read traffic, leaving writes to the primary.  
Why A is not selected: The standby instance in a Multi-AZ deployment doesn't serve requests: it exists only for failover.  
Why B is not selected: Transfer Acceleration is an Amazon S3 feature; it has nothing to do with RDS.  
Why D is not selected: Firehose delivers streaming data to storage destinations and doesn't increase the concurrency of database requests.

---

634\. A company collects 10 GB of telemetry data daily from various machines. The company stores the data in an Amazon S3 bucket in a source data account.  
The company has hired several consulting agencies to use this data for analysis. Each agency needs read access to the data for its analysts. The company must share the data from the source data account by choosing a solution that maximizes security and operational efficiency.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Configure S3 global tables to replicate data for each agency.  
B. Make the S3 bucket public for a limited time. Inform only the agencies.  
C. Configure cross-account access for the S3 bucket to the accounts that the agencies own.  
D. Set up an IAM user for each analyst in the source data account. Grant each user access to the S3 bucket.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The data must stay in the source account while several external agencies get read access to it. The standard mechanism is cross-account access: a bucket policy (or a role that the agencies' accounts assume) grants the needed accounts s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket permissions on the relevant prefix. No copies are made, the accounts stay on the agencies' side, and access can be revoked with a single policy edit. That's both maximum security and minimum operational effort.  
Why A is not selected: "S3 global tables" doesn't exist — global tables are a DynamoDB feature. Even replication would mean copies of the data outside your control.  
Why B is not selected: A public bucket exposes the data to the entire internet, not just the agencies. "For a limited time" changes nothing: during that window anyone, including crawlers, can download the data.  
Why D is not selected: An IAM user per analyst in your own account means outside people holding long-lived credentials inside your perimeter, plus ongoing work provisioning and revoking accounts.

---

635\. A company uses Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP in its primary AWS Region for CIFS and NFS file shares.  
Applications that run on Amazon EC2 instances access the file shares. The company needs a storage disaster recovery (DR) solution in a secondary Region. The data that is replicated in the secondary Region needs to be accessed by using the same protocols as the primary Region.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create an AWS Lambda function to copy the data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Replicate the S3 bucket to the secondary Region.  
B. Create a backup of the FSx for ONTAP volumes by using AWS Backup. Copy the volumes to the secondary Region. Create a new FSx for ONTAP instance from the backup.  
C. Create an FSx for ONTAP instance in the secondary Region. Use NetApp SnapMirror to replicate data from the primary Region to the secondary Region.  
D. Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) volume. Migrate the current data to the volume. Replicate the volume to the secondary Region.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Data must be accessible in the secondary Region using the same CIFS and NFS protocols as the primary Region, so the secondary Region needs an FSx for ONTAP file system too. The standard, lowest-effort replication between them is NetApp SnapMirror: it's built into ONTAP, runs on a snapshot-based schedule, transfers only changes, and lets you quickly promote the target volume to read-write during a disaster.  
Why A is not selected: A custom copy function to S3 is code you have to write and maintain, and more importantly, S3 doesn't serve data over CIFS or NFS.  
Why B is not selected: Backups via AWS Backup give a much longer recovery time: during a disaster you'd have to create the file system from a backup instead of failing over to one that's already running.  
Why D is not selected: EFS doesn't support the CIFS protocol, so the requirement for identical access isn't met.

---

636\. A development team is creating an event-based application that uses AWS Lambda functions. Events will be generated when files are added to an Amazon S3 bucket. The development team currently has Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) configured as the event target from Amazon S3.  
What should a solutions architect do to process the events from Amazon S3 in a scalable way?  
A. Create an SNS subscription that processes the event in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) before the event runs in Lambda.  
B. Create an SNS subscription that processes the event in Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) before the event runs in Lambda  
C. Create an SNS subscription that sends the event to Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Configure the SOS queue to trigger a Lambda function.  
D. Create an SNS subscription that sends the event to AWS Server Migration Service (AWS SMS). Configure the Lambda function to poll from the SMS event.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: An SNS topic delivers events immediately and, if the handler fails, drops them after a few retries. To make processing scalable and lossless, an SQS queue sits between SNS and the function: it absorbs bursts, holds messages, provides retries and a dead-letter queue, and the function reads from it in batches.  
Why A is not selected: Intermediate processing in ECS adds infrastructure and doesn't solve the problem of buffering events.  
Why B is not selected: Same issue with EKS: an extra cluster instead of a simple queue.  
Why D is not selected: AWS SMS is a server migration service; it can't act as an event target.

---

637\. A solutions architect is designing a new service behind Amazon API Gateway. The request patterns for the service will be unpredictable and can change suddenly from 0 requests to over 500 per second. The total size of the data that needs to be persisted in a backend database is currently less than 1 GB with unpredictable future growth.  
Data can be queried using simple key-value requests.  
Which combination ofAWS services would meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. AWS Fargate  
B. AWS Lambda  
C. Amazon DynamoDB  
D. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling  
E. MySQL-compatible Amazon Aurora  
Answer: BC  
Explanation: Load swings from zero to over 500 requests per second, the dataset is under a gigabyte and grows unpredictably, and access is by key. That calls for services that scale instantly and from zero: AWS Lambda as the compute behind API Gateway (B) and Amazon DynamoDB as the key-value store (C). Neither capacity nor servers need to be planned.  
Why A is not selected: Fargate scales, but tasks take seconds to start and are billed for runtime: for a workload that swings between zero and 500 requests, Lambda fits better.  
Why D is not selected: An EC2 Auto Scaling group reacts on the order of minutes, and it still keeps a minimum number of instances running when idle.  
Why E is not selected: Aurora requires choosing an instance class and is billed continuously, whereas the access pattern needed here is simple key-value.

---

638\. A company collects and shares research data with the company's employees all over the world. The company wants to collect and store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket and process the data in the AWS Cloud. The company will share the data with the company's employees. The company needs a secure solution in the AWS Cloud that minimizes operational overhead.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use an AWS Lambda function to create an S3 presigned URL. Instruct employees to use the URL.  
B. Create an IAM user for each employee. Create an IAM policy for each employee to allow S3 access. Instruct employees to use the AWS Management Console.  
C. Create an S3 File Gateway. Create a share for uploading and a share for downloading. Allow employees to mount shares on their local computers to use S3 File Gateway.  
D. Configure AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoints. Select the custom identity provider options. Use AWS Secrets Manager to manage the user credentials Instruct employees to use Transfer Family.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Files need to be distributed to employees worldwide without creating an AWS account for each one or standing up infrastructure. A presigned URL solves this: the application (here, a Lambda function) signs the link with its own permissions, the link is valid for a limited time, and it grants access to exactly one object. Employees need only a browser. Useful limit to remember: a URL signed with long-term credentials is valid for at most 7 days, while one signed with temporary credentials is valid no longer than those credentials themselves.  
Why B is not selected: An IAM user and a separate policy for every employee worldwide is ongoing administrative work: provisioning, revoking, rotating keys, and untangling permissions.  
Why C is not selected: S3 File Gateway is a component you have to deploy and maintain, and employees would have to mount network shares. That's overkill for distributing files to remote users.  
Why D is not selected: Transfer Family with a custom identity provider adds both an hourly endpoint charge and integration work to build. For simply handing out files, that's unnecessary complexity.

---

639\. A company is building a new furniture inventory application. The company has deployed the application on a fleet ofAmazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The EC2 instances run behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in their VPC.  
A solutions architect has observed that incoming traffic seems to favor one EC2 instance, resulting in latency for some requests.  
What should the solutions architect do to resolve this issue?  
A. Disable session affinity (sticky sessions) on the ALB  
B. Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer  
C. Increase the number of EC2 instances in each Availability Zone  
D. Adjust the frequency of the health checks on the ALB's target group  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Traffic skewing toward a single target with an otherwise healthy load balancer is usually explained by session affinity: a client that lands on one instance keeps returning to it via a cookie, so distribution stops being even. Disabling sticky sessions restores the standard round-robin algorithm and evens out the load.  
Why B is not selected: A Network Load Balancer distributes by flow and doesn't fix the affinity problem, while giving up HTTP-layer features.  
Why C is not selected: More instances won't help if traffic keeps going to the same target anyway.  
Why D is not selected: Health check frequency affects how fast a failure is detected, not how requests are distributed.

---

640\. A company has an application workflow that uses an AWS Lambda function to download and decrypt files from Amazon S3. These files are encrypted using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys. A solutions architect needs to design a solution that will ensure the required permissions are set correctly.  
Which combination of actions accomplish this? (Choose two.)  
A. Attach the kms:decrypt permission to the Lambda function’s resource policy  
B. Grant the decrypt permission for the Lambda IAM role in the KMS key's policy  
C. Grant the decrypt permission for the Lambda resource policy in the KMS key's policy.  
D. Create a new IAM policy with the kms:decrypt permission and attach the policy to the Lambda function.  
E. Create a new IAM role with the kms:decrypt permission and attach the execution role to the Lambda function.  
Answer: BE  
Explanation: Access to a KMS key is always checked on two sides, and that's exactly what this question is testing. On the principal side: the function's execution role must have kms:Decrypt — the policy is attached to the role, and the role is assigned to the function (E). On the resource side: that same role must be explicitly allowed in the key policy (B). Remove either half and the function gets an AccessDeniedException when it tries to decrypt the object. Compare with {{q:550}} — the same pairing applies there for Lambda environment variables.  
Why A is not selected: A function's resource policy controls who can invoke it. It doesn't grant permissions to work with a KMS key.  
Why C is not selected: In a key policy, permissions are granted to a principal — a role or an account. "Allow the function's resource policy" is a construct that doesn't exist in KMS.  
Why D is not selected: An IAM policy can't be attached to a function: it's attached to the execution role, and the role is then assigned to the function. The option describes an operation that doesn't exist.

---

641\. A company wants to monitor its AWS costs for financial review. The cloud operations team is designing an architecture in the AWS Organizations management account to query AWS Cost and Usage Reports for all member accounts. The team must run this query once a month and provide a detailed analysis of the bill.  
Which solution is the MOST scalable and cost-effective way to meet these requirements?  
A. Enable Cost and Usage Reports in the management account. Deliver reports to Amazon Kinesis. Use Amazon EMR for analysis.  
B. Enable Cost and Usage Reports in the management account. Deliver the reports to Amazon S3 Use Amazon Athena for analysis.  
C. Enable Cost and Usage Reports for member accounts. Deliver the reports to Amazon S3 Use Amazon Redshift for analysis.  
D. Enable Cost and Usage Reports for member accounts. Deliver the reports to Amazon Kinesis. Use Amazon QuickSight tor analysis.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The Cost and Usage Report is a highly detailed cost export, and it must be enabled in the organization's management account, since only there can you see usage across all member accounts. Reports are delivered to S3 in Parquet format partitioned by month, and running SQL queries against them once a month is a natural fit for Athena: you pay only for bytes scanned and maintain no infrastructure. That makes it both the most scalable and the cheapest option for a monthly review.  
Why A is not selected: Kinesis is meant for streaming data, while the CUR is delivered as files in S3. An EMR cluster for a monthly report is unnecessary expense.  
Why C is not selected: Enabling reports in each member account produces scattered exports instead of one unified view, and a persistent Redshift cluster costs more than Athena for once-a-month queries.  
Why D is not selected: Again, per-account reports, and again Kinesis used for the wrong purpose. QuickSight also builds visualizations on top of a data source rather than replacing one.

---

642\. A company wants to run a gaming application on Amazon EC2 instances that are part of an Auto Scaling group in the AWS Cloud. The application will transmit data by using UDP packets. The company wants to ensure that the application can scale out and in as traffic increases and decreases.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Attach a Network Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.  
B. Attach an Application Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.  
C. Deploy an Amazon Route 53 record set with a weighted policy to route traffic appropriately.  
D. Deploy a NAT instance that is configured with port forwarding to the EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The key word is UDP. Of the AWS load balancers, only the Network Load Balancer works with UDP: it operates at layer 4, supports TCP, UDP, and TLS, and attaches to the Auto Scaling group as a target group. The group scales freely in both directions, and the load balancer distributes packets across healthy instances.  
Why B is not selected: An Application Load Balancer only understands HTTP and HTTPS: it can't handle the game's UDP packets.  
Why C is not selected: A Route 53 weighted policy hands out addresses via DNS without checking load or instantly removing failed instances. That's name distribution, not load balancing.  
Why D is not selected: A NAT instance with port forwarding is a homegrown setup, a single point of failure, and manual upkeep every time the group's membership changes.

---

643\. A company runs several websites on AWS for its different brands. Each website generates tens of gigabytes of web traffic logs each day. A solutions architect needs to design a scalable solution to give the company's developers the ability to analyze traffic patterns across all the company's websites. This analysis by the developers will occur on demand once a week over the course of several months. The solution must support queries with standard SQL.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Store the logs in Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena tor analysis.  
B. Store the logs in Amazon RDS. Use a database client for analysis.  
C. Store the logs in Amazon OpenSearch Service. Use OpenSearch Service for analysis.  
D. Store the logs in an Amazon EMR cluster Use a supported open-source framework for SQL-based analysis.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The logs sit in S3 at tens of gigabytes per day, and they're analyzed once a week. Athena runs standard SQL queries directly against the objects in the bucket and is billed by the amount of data scanned: nothing is charged between queries, and there's no infrastructure at all.  
Why B is not selected: Loading the logs into RDS means a continuously running instance and growing storage — expensive for analysis done once a week.  
Why C is not selected: OpenSearch Service keeps a cluster running around the clock and is built for search and observability, not one-off SQL queries.  
Why D is not selected: An EMR cluster also runs and is billed continuously, and requires administration.

---

644\. An international company has a subdomain for each country that the company operates in. The subdomains are formatted as example.com, country1.example.com, and country2.example.com. The company's workloads are behind an Application Load Balancer. The company wants to encrypt the website data that is in transit.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Use the AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) console to request a public certificate for the apex top domain example com and a wildcard certificate for *.example.com.  
B. Use the AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) console to request a private certificate for the apex top domain example.com and a wildcard certificate for *.example.com.  
C. Use the AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) console to request a public and private certificate for the apex top domain example.com.  
D. Validate domain ownership by email address. Switch to DNS validation by adding the required DNS records to the DNS provider.  
E. Validate domain ownership for the domain by adding the required DNS records to the DNS provider.  
Answer: AE  
Explanation: Certificates are needed for the domain itself and all its country subdomains, along with proof of ownership. A public certificate requested in ACM for example.com and the wildcard *.example.com covers both the apex and all subdomains (A). Domain ownership is validated by adding the required DNS records at the DNS provider — a method that also supports automatic certificate renewal (E).  
Why B is not selected: A private certificate is issued by your own certificate authority and isn't trusted by public visitors' browsers.  
Why C is not selected: A certificate for the apex domain alone doesn't cover country1.example.com and similar subdomains.  
Why D is not selected: Validating by email and then switching to DNS validation is an unnecessary extra step; going straight to DNS validation is enough.

---

645\. A company is required to use cryptographic keys in its on-premises key manager. The key manager is outside of the AWS Cloud because of regulatory and compliance requirements. The company wants to manage encryption and decryption by using cryptographic keys that are retained outside of the AWS Cloud and that support a variety of external key managers from different vendors.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use AWS CloudHSM key store backed by a CloudHSM cluster.  
B. Use an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) external key store backed by an external key manager.  
C. Use the default AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) managed key store.  
D. Use a custom key store backed by an AWS CloudHSM cluster.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirement is rare and very specific: keys must physically stay in the company's own key manager outside AWS, and multiple vendors must be supported. That describes an AWS KMS external key store (XKS): KMS acts as a facade while the external key manager performs the cryptographic operations through the XKS proxy, and the key material never enters AWS. Distinguish the three options: the default KMS key store keeps keys in AWS; a custom key store backed by CloudHSM keeps keys in your own CloudHSM cluster but still inside AWS; an external key store keeps keys outside the cloud entirely.  
Why A is not selected: CloudHSM runs inside AWS: the cluster is deployed in your VPC, but that's still the cloud, and the requirement is to keep keys outside it.  
Why C is not selected: The default KMS key store means keys live inside the AWS service. That directly contradicts the requirement.  
Why D is not selected: A custom key store backed by CloudHSM still keeps keys in the cloud and additionally requires deploying and maintaining an HSM cluster — maximum operational overhead.

---

646\. A solutions architect needs to host a high performance computing (HPC) workload in the AWS Cloud. The workload will run on hundreds of Amazon EC2 instances and will require parallel access to a shared file system to enable distributed processing of large datasets. Datasets will be accessed across multiple instances simultaneously. The workload requires access latency within 1 ms. After processing has completed, engineers will need access to the dataset for manual postprocessing.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) as a shared file system. Access the dataset from Amazon EFS.  
B. Mount an Amazon S3 bucket to serve as the shared file system. Perform postprocessing directly from the S3 bucket.  
C. Use Amazon FSx for Lustre as a shared file system. Link the file system to an Amazon S3 bucket for postprocessing.  
D. Configure AWS Resource Access Manager to share an Amazon S3 bucket so that it can be mounted to all instances for processing and postprocessing.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Hundreds of instances, parallel access to a shared dataset, and sub-millisecond latency point to Amazon FSx for Lustre. The file system links to an S3 bucket, so source data is loaded from there and results are exported back, letting engineers work through postprocessing at their own pace after the compute cluster has been shut down.  
Why A is not selected: EFS provides neither sub-millisecond latency nor the throughput hundreds of compute nodes need.  
Why B is not selected: S3 doesn't mount as a file system through standard means and doesn't provide the latency required for parallel access.  
Why D is not selected: AWS RAM shares resources between accounts and does nothing to turn a bucket into a mountable file system.

---

647\. A gaming company is building an application with Voice over IP capabilities. The application will serve traffic to users across the world. The application needs to be highly available with an automated failover across AWS Regions. The company wants to minimize the latency of users without relying on IP address caching on user devices.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS Global Accelerator with health checks.  
B. Use Amazon Route 53 with a geolocation routing policy.  
C. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that includes multiple origins.  
D. Create an Application Load Balancer that uses path-based routing.  
Answer: A  
Review status: Corrected key (source: C; reviewed: A)  
Correction note: VoIP runs over UDP — CloudFront only works with HTTP/HTTPS. Global Accelerator is explicitly named by AWS as the solution for VoIP and fast cross-region failover (GA FAQ, examtopics t1 q647)  
Explanation: VoIP means UDP, and the requirement to avoid relying on IP address caching on client devices rules out DNS-based solutions. Global Accelerator (A) provides two static anycast IP addresses, works with UDP, routes traffic over the AWS backbone, and fails over between Regions within seconds based on health checks.  
Why B is not selected: Route 53 is DNS: the client caches the response, and if a Region fails it keeps sending traffic to the dead address until the TTL expires. Geolocation routing also picks a Region by geography rather than actual latency.  
Why C is not selected: CloudFront only serves HTTP and HTTPS. Voice traffic over UDP can't pass through it.  
Why D is not selected: An ALB operates within a single Region and only handles HTTP/HTTPS — no cross-Region failover and no UDP.

---

648\. A weather forecasting company needs to process hundreds of gigabytes of data with sub-millisecond latency. The company has a high performance computing (HPC) environment in its data center and wants to expand its forecasting capabilities.  
A solutions architect must identify a highly available cloud storage solution that can handle large amounts of sustained throughput. Files that are stored in the solution should be accessible to thousands of compute instances that will simultaneously access and process the entire dataset.  
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Use Amazon FSx for Lustre scratch file systems.  
B. Use Amazon FSx for Lustre persistent file systems.  
C. Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with Bursting Throughput mode.  
D. Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with Provisioned Throughput mode.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirements are sub-millisecond latency, sustained high throughput, high availability, and simultaneous access from thousands of compute nodes. That's Amazon FSx for Lustre in persistent mode: it replicates data within the Availability Zone and automatically replaces failed components, which scratch mode does not do.  
Why A is not selected: Scratch file systems don't replicate data and don't recover from a server failure, so the high-availability requirement isn't met.  
Why C is not selected: EFS in Bursting Throughput mode provides neither that level of sustained throughput nor sub-millisecond latency.  
Why D is not selected: EFS Provisioned Throughput solves the throughput-stability issue, but an NFS file system's latency is still measured in milliseconds, not fractions of one.

---

649\. An ecommerce company runs a PostgreSQL database on premises. The database stores data by using high IOPS Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) block storage. The daily peak I/O transactions per second do not exceed 15,000 IOPS. The company wants to migrate the database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and provision disk IOPS performance independent of disk storage capacity.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Configure the General Purpose SSD (gp2) EBS volume storage type and provision 15,000 IOPS.  
B. Configure the Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1) EBS volume storage type and provision 15,000 IOPS.  
C. Configure the General Purpose SSD (gp3) EBS volume storage type and provision 15,000 IOPS.  
D. Configure the EBS magnetic volume type to achieve maximum IOPS.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Same requirement as in {{q:425}}: provision performance independently of capacity, with a daily peak up to 15,000 IOPS. A gp3 volume lets you set IOPS independently of size, up to 16,000, so 15,000 fits comfortably, and its per-gigabyte cost is lower than gp2's and notably lower than Provisioned IOPS volumes.  
Why A is not selected: gp2 ties performance to size at a ratio of three IOPS per gigabyte: reaching 15,000 IOPS would require provisioning — and paying for — 5 TB.  
Why B is not selected: io1 covers the requirement but costs significantly more than gp3 and is overkill at 15,000 IOPS.  
Why D is not selected: Magnetic volumes deliver on the order of hundreds of IOPS: the requirement can't be met at all.

---

650\. A company wants to migrate its on-premises Microsoft SQL Server Enterprise edition database to AWS. The company's online application uses the database to process transactions. The data analysis team uses the same production database to run reports for analytical processing. The company wants to reduce operational overhead by moving to managed services wherever possible.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Migrate to Amazon RDS for Microsoft SOL Server. Use read replicas for reporting purposes  
B. Migrate to Microsoft SQL Server on Amazon EC2. Use Always On read replicas for reporting purposes  
C. Migrate to Amazon DynamoDB. Use DynamoDB on-demand replicas for reporting purposes  
D. Migrate to Amazon Aurora MySQL. Use Aurora read replicas for reporting purposes  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The company wants to move to managed services while keeping SQL Server, and to offload reporting from the production database. Amazon RDS for SQL Server supports read replicas that analytics can be pointed at, while AWS handles patching, backups, and fault tolerance. The application and its queries stay unchanged.  
Why B is not selected: SQL Server on EC2 instances remains entirely the company's responsibility to operate: operational overhead isn't reduced.  
Why C is not selected: DynamoDB is a non-relational store: migrating means rewriting all the application logic, and it has no such thing as "on-demand replicas."  
Why D is not selected: Aurora MySQL is incompatible with SQL Server: this would require schema conversion and rewriting queries.

---

651\. A company stores a large volume of image files in an Amazon S3 bucket. The images need to be readily available for the first 180 days. The images are infrequently accessed for the next 180 days. After 360 days, the images need to be archived but must be available instantly upon request. After 5 years, only auditors can access the images. The auditors must be able to retrieve the images within 12 hours. The images cannot be lost during this process.  
A developer will use S3 Standard storage for the first 180 days. The developer needs to configure an S3 Lifecycle rule.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Transition the objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) after 180 days. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 360 days, and S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 5 years.  
B. Transition the objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) after 180 days. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 360 days, and S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 5 years.  
C. Transition the objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 180 days, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 360 days, and S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 5 years.  
D. Transition the objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 180 days, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 360 days, and S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 5 years.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Read the requirements as a timeline and pick a storage class for each segment. The first 180 days: Standard. The next 180 days, access is infrequent, but the data "cannot be lost," so Standard-IA, not One Zone-IA. After 360 days, it's archived but "available instantly upon request" — that's exactly the definition of Glacier Instant Retrieval. After 5 years, only auditors need access with a 12-hour window — that matches Glacier Deep Archive's standard retrieval. Remember the difference between the three Glacier tiers: Instant Retrieval is milliseconds, Flexible Retrieval is minutes to hours, and Deep Archive is 12 hours and the cheapest of the three.  
Why A is not selected: One Zone-IA keeps a single copy in one Availability Zone, and the requirement explicitly forbids losing the images.  
Why B is not selected: Same single-zone problem, plus Glacier Flexible Retrieval doesn't return the object instantly after 360 days.  
Why D is not selected: The storage classes for durability are chosen correctly, but Glacier Flexible Retrieval on the segment after 360 days returns the object in minutes to hours, while instant access is required.

---

652\. A company has a large data workload that runs for 6 hours each day. The company cannot lose any data while the process is running. A solutions architect is designing an Amazon EMR cluster configuration to support this critical data workload.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Configure a long-running cluster that runs the primary node and core nodes on On-Demand Instances and the task nodes on Spot Instances.  
B. Configure a transient cluster that runs the primary node and core nodes on On-Demand Instances and the task nodes on Spot Instances.  
C. Configure a transient cluster that runs the primary node on an On-Demand Instance and the core nodes and task nodes on Spot Instances.  
D. Configure a long-running cluster that runs the primary node on an On-Demand Instance, the core nodes on Spot Instances, and the task nodes on Spot Instances.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The workload runs six hours a day, so the cluster should exist only for that window — a transient cluster terminates as soon as its jobs finish and isn't billed for the other eighteen hours. Data can't be lost, so the primary node and the core nodes, which hold HDFS data, run on On-Demand Instances, while the task nodes, which store nothing, run on Spot Instances, delivering the savings.  
Why A is not selected: A long-running cluster is billed around the clock, even though the workload only runs a quarter of the day.  
Why C is not selected: Spot core nodes hold HDFS data: their reclamation means data loss, which the requirement explicitly forbids.  
Why D is not selected: This combines both drawbacks — a cluster that keeps running plus data sitting on Spot nodes.

---

653\. A company maintains an Amazon RDS database that maps users to cost centers. The company has accounts in an organization in AWS Organizations. The company needs a solution that will tag all resources that are created in a specific AWS account in the organization. The solution must tag each resource with the cost center ID of the user who created the resource.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Move the specific AWS account to a new organizational unit (OU) in Organizations from the management account. Create a service control policy (SCP) that requires all existing resources to have the correct cost center tag before the resources are created. Apply the SCP to the new OU.  
B. Create an AWS Lambda function to tag the resources after the Lambda function looks up the appropriate cost center from the RDS database. Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule that reacts to AWS CloudTrail events to invoke the Lambda function.  
C. Create an AWS CloudFormation stack to deploy an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to look up the appropriate cost center from the RDS database and to tag resources. Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule to invoke the CloudFormation stack.  
D. Create an AWS Lambda function to tag the resources with a default value. Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule that reacts to AWS CloudTrail events to invoke the Lambda function when a resource is missing the cost center tag.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: A tag value needs to be set based on who created the resource, and that value lives in an external database. No declarative policy can do this: an SCP or tag policy can require a tag to be present or restrict its allowed values, but neither can compute a value by looking up the creator. This calls for an event-driven handler: an EventBridge rule catches CloudTrail events for resource creation, and a Lambda function looks up the creator's cost center in the RDS database and applies the tag.  
Why A is not selected: An SCP can require a tag to be present at creation time (using the aws:RequestTag condition), but it can't populate a value from an external database. And a policy can't require a tag on resources that already exist, either.  
Why C is not selected: A CloudFormation stack is a way to deploy the function, not a way to schedule its execution. And running on a schedule is too late anyway: the resource is already created without a tag.  
Why D is not selected: A default tag value doesn't solve the problem: what's needed is the actual cost center of the creating user, otherwise cost allocation is meaningless.

---

654\. A company recently migrated its web application to the AWS Cloud. The company uses an Amazon EC2 instance to run multiple processes to host the application. The processes include an Apache web server that serves static content. The Apache web server makes requests to a PHP application that uses a local Redis server for user sessions.  
The company wants to redesign the architecture to be highly available and to use AWS managed solutions.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk to host the static content and the PHP application. Configure Elastic Beanstalk to deploy its EC2 instance into a public subnet. Assign a public IP address.  
B. Use AWS Lambda to host the static content and the PHP application. Use an Amazon API Gateway REST API to proxy requests to the Lambda function. Set the API Gateway CORS configuration to respond to the domain name. Configure Amazon ElastiCache for Redis to handle session information.  
C. Keep the backend code on the EC2 instance. Create an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster that has Multi- AZ enabled. Configure the ElastiCache for Redis cluster in cluster mode. Copy the frontend resources to Amazon S3. Configure the backend code to reference the EC2 instance.  
D. Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an Amazon S3 endpoint to an S3 bucket that is configured to host the static content. Configure an Application Load Balancer that targets an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) service that runs AWS Fargate tasks for the PHP application. Configure the PHP application to use an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster that runs in multiple Availability Zones.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Each component is replaced with a managed equivalent. Static content moves into an S3 bucket and is served through CloudFront. The PHP application becomes Fargate tasks running in ECS behind an Application Load Balancer, so no servers remain. Sessions move into an ElastiCache for Redis cluster deployed across multiple Availability Zones, so they now survive the failure of any single node.  
Why A is not selected: Elastic Beanstalk manages the deployment, but a single machine in a public subnet with a public IP address is neither highly available nor secure.  
Why B is not selected: Serving static content through a Lambda function and API Gateway is inefficient and costly, and the PHP application would need to be rewritten to run on Lambda.  
Why C is not selected: The code stays on a single EC2 instance — the single point of failure remains, so the high-availability requirement isn't met.

---

655\. A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group that has a target group. The company designed the application to work with session affinity (sticky sessions) for a better user experience.  
The application must be available publicly over the internet as an endpoint. A WAF must be applied to the endpoint for additional security. Session affinity (sticky sessions) must be configured on the endpoint.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Create a public Network Load Balancer. Specify the application target group.  
B. Create a Gateway Load Balancer. Specify the application target group.  
C. Create a public Application Load Balancer. Specify the application target group.  
D. Create a second target group. Add Elastic IP addresses to the EC2 instances.  
E. Create a web ACL in AWS WAF. Associate the web ACL with the endpoint  
Answer: CE  
Explanation: Two requirements both point to the same load balancer type. Sticky sessions via cookies are supported by the Application Load Balancer (C) — it operates at the HTTP layer and can issue a cookie that binds a client to a target. AWS WAF also attaches to an ALB, not to an NLB, so a web ACL is created and associated with this public load balancer (E). One solution satisfies both requirements.  
Why A is not selected: A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4: it doesn't issue cookies, and WAF can't attach to it.  
Why B is not selected: A Gateway Load Balancer is designed for inserting traffic-inspection appliances, not for publishing a web application.  
Why D is not selected: A second target group and Elastic IP addresses on the instances provide neither session affinity nor a way to attach WAF.

---

656\. A company runs a website that stores images of historical events. Website users need the ability to search and view images based on the year that the event in the image occurred. On average, users request each image only once or twice a year. The company wants a highly available solution to store and deliver the images to users.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Store images in Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS). Use a web server that runs on Amazon EC2.  
B. Store images in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS). Use a web server that runs on Amazon EC2.  
C. Store images in Amazon S3 Standard. Use S3 Standard to directly deliver images by using a static website.  
D. Store images in Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA). Use S3 Standard-IA to directly deliver images by using a static website.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Each image is requested only once or twice a year, but access still needs to be instant and reliable. The S3 Standard-Infrequent Access class is built exactly for this: storage costs roughly half of Standard, availability and latency are the same, and only a small retrieval fee applies. The site can be served straight from the bucket as a static website, with no server at all.  
Why A is not selected: EBS volumes plus a continuously running instance is the most expensive setup, and it's also limited to a single Availability Zone.  
Why B is not selected: EFS with a web server on an instance costs more for both storage and compute, with no benefit over a static website.  
Why C is not selected: Standard works, but with such infrequent access the storage overpay is significant, and cost is named as the deciding requirement.

---

657\. A company has multiple AWS accounts in an organization in AWS Organizations that different business units use.  
The company has multiple offices around the world. The company needs to update security group rules to allow new office CIDR ranges or to remove old CIDR ranges across the organization. The company wants to centralize the management of security group rules to minimize the administrative overhead that updating CIDR ranges requires.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Create VPC security groups in the organization's management account. Update the security groups when a CIDR range update is necessary.  
B. Create a VPC customer managed prefix list that contains the list of CIDRs. Use AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share the prefix list across the organization. Use the prefix list in the security groups across the organization.  
C. Create an AWS managed prefix list. Use an AWS Security Hub policy to enforce the security group update across the organization. Use an AWS Lambda function to update the prefix list automatically when the CIDR ranges change.  
D. Create security groups in a central administrative AWS account. Create an AWS Firewall Manager common security group policy for the whole organization. Select the previously created security groups as primary groups in the policy.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Office CIDR ranges change, and rewriting rules across every security group in every account is too costly. A customer-managed prefix list is a named list of CIDRs that's referenced in a security group rule instead of listing addresses directly; when the list changes, the rules update automatically. AWS RAM lets you share that list across the organization, so it's maintained in one place and used everywhere. There's no charge for the list itself, hence the most cost-effective option.  
Why A is not selected: Security groups don't work across accounts and VPCs: ones created in the management account won't apply to resources in other accounts.  
Why C is not selected: AWS managed prefix lists are maintained by AWS itself (for its own service ranges) — you can't add office networks to them. Security Hub also doesn't apply changes; it assesses compliance.
