Why D is not selected: Firewall Manager can propagate common security groups, but it's a paid service that requires Security Hub and policy setup. For simply changing a list of addresses, a prefix list is simpler and cheaper.

---

658\. A company uses an on-premises network-attached storage (NAS) system to provide file shares to its high performance computing (HPC) workloads. The company wants to migrate its latency-sensitive HPC workloads and its storage to the AWS Cloud. The company must be able to provide NFS and SMB multi-protocol access from the file system.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST latency? (Choose two.)  
A. Deploy compute optimized EC2 instances into a cluster placement group.  
B. Deploy compute optimized EC2 instances into a partition placement group.  
C. Attach the EC2 instances to an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system.  
D. Attach the EC2 instances to an Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file system.  
E. Attach the EC2 instances to an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system.  
Answer: AE  
Explanation: There are two separate requirements, solved at two different levels. Multi-protocol access over NFS and SMB from a single file system is provided only by Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP (E). Minimum network latency between compute nodes comes from a cluster placement group: instances are packed into a single rack in one Availability Zone for maximum throughput and minimum latency between them (A).  
Why B is not selected: A partition placement group deliberately spreads instances across different hardware sets for fault tolerance — that increases, not decreases, latency between nodes.  
Why C is not selected: FSx for Lustre is very fast, but it uses the Lustre protocol and serves data over neither NFS nor SMB.  
Why D is not selected: FSx for OpenZFS supports NFS but not SMB, so the multi-protocol access requirement isn't met.

---

659\. A company is relocating its data center and wants to securely transfer 50 TB of data to AWS within 2 weeks. The existing data center has a Site-to-Site VPN connection to AWS that is 90% utilized.  
Which AWS service should a solutions architect use to meet these requirements?  
A. AWS DataSync with a VPC endpoint  
B. AWS Direct Connect  
C. AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized  
D. AWS Storage Gateway  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The link is already 90 percent utilized, and 50 TB needs to move in two weeks — the remaining bandwidth is nowhere near enough, and pushing it would also hurt production traffic. So the data has to travel physically: Snowball Edge Storage Optimized carries tens of terabytes, encrypts its contents with AWS KMS keys, and uses none of the company's network at all.  
Why A is not selected: DataSync is still limited by the same congested VPN link: it can't speed up the transfer.  
Why B is not selected: A dedicated Direct Connect connection typically takes weeks to provision and costs as much as permanent infrastructure, while this is a one-time job on a two-week deadline.  
Why D is not selected: Storage Gateway is built for ongoing hybrid access to data in the cloud, not a one-time bulk migration, and it runs over that same congested link.

---

660\. A company hosts an application on Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group. Application peak hours occur at the same time each day. Application users report slow application performance at the start of peak hours. The application performs normally 2-3 hours after peak hours begin. The company wants to ensure that the application works properly at the start of peak hours.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Configure an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic properly to the instances.  
B. Configure a dynamic scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to launch new instances based on memory utilization.  
C. Configure a dynamic scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to launch new instances based on CPU utilization.  
D. Configure a scheduled scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to launch new instances before peak hours.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Peak hours arrive at the same time every day, but metric-based dynamic scaling reacts after the fact — which is exactly why the application only recovers two to three hours into the peak. A scheduled scaling policy adds capacity ahead of time, before the peak begins, and the problem goes away.  
Why A is not selected: A load balancer distributes traffic but doesn't add the capacity that's missing.  
Why B is not selected: Reacting to a memory metric is still a reaction after the fact, with the same lag.  
Why C is not selected: Same issue with a CPU metric: scaling only starts after performance has already degraded.

---

661\. A company runs applications on AWS that connect to the company's Amazon RDS database. The applications scale on weekends and at peak times of the year. The company wants to scale the database more effectively for its applications that connect to the database.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use Amazon DynamoDB with connection pooling with a target group configuration for the database. Change the applications to use the DynamoDB endpoint.  
B. Use Amazon RDS Proxy with a target group for the database. Change the applications to use the RDS Proxy endpoint.  
C. Use a custom proxy that runs on Amazon EC2 as an intermediary to the database. Change the applications to use the custom proxy endpoint.  
D. Use an AWS Lambda function to provide connection pooling with a target group configuration for the database. Change the applications to use the Lambda function.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The applications scale in bursts, and each new instance opens its own connections to the database. RDS Proxy is a managed connection pool: it reuses connections and smooths out spikes, and the applications only need to point to its endpoint instead of the database endpoint.  
Why A is not selected: DynamoDB is a different database; it doesn't provide connection pooling for RDS, and switching to it would mean rewriting the application.  
Why C is not selected: A custom proxy on EC2 is infrastructure you have to provision for high availability, patch, and scale yourself.  
Why D is not selected: A Lambda function acting as a proxy adds another moving part and custom code instead of a ready-made managed service.

---

662\. A company uses AWS Cost Explorer to monitor its AWS costs. The company notices that Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage and snapshot costs increase every month. However, the company does not purchase additional EBS storage every month. The company wants to optimize monthly costs for its current storage usage.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs to monitor the storage utilization of Amazon EBS. Use Amazon EBS Elastic Volumes to reduce the size of the EBS volumes.  
B. Use a custom script to monitor space usage. Use Amazon EBS Elastic Volumes to reduce the size of the EBS volumes.  
C. Delete all expired and unused snapshots to reduce snapshot costs.  
D. Delete all nonessential snapshots. Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager to create and manage the snapshots according to the company's snapshot policy requirements.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The symptom is that snapshot costs grow month over month even though no new volumes are being purchased: old snapshots are piling up because nothing is removing them. The solution has two steps: a one-time cleanup of unneeded snapshots, plus a process — Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager creates snapshots on a schedule and deletes them automatically according to a retention policy. After that, the snapshot volume stops growing without anyone having to intervene, unlike a one-time cleanup.  
Why A is not selected: Monitoring volume utilization and shrinking volumes solves a different problem; besides, Elastic Volumes can only increase a volume's size, not decrease it.  
Why B is not selected: A custom script adds development work and still doesn't address the snapshot problem — snapshots are what's growing.  
Why C is not selected: A one-time cleanup removes the symptom, but the situation repeats next month: there's still no policy governing snapshot creation and retention.

---

663\. A company is developing a new application on AWS. The application consists of an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster, an Amazon S3 bucket that contains assets for the application, and an Amazon RDS for MySQL database that contains the dataset for the application. The dataset contains sensitive information. The company wants to ensure that only the ECS cluster can access the data in the RDS for MySQL database and the data in the S3 bucket.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create a new AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key to encrypt both the S3 bucket and the RDS for MySQL database. Ensure that the KMS key policy includes encrypt and decrypt permissions for the ECS task execution role.  
B. Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) AWS managed key to encrypt both the S3 bucket and the RDS for MySQL database. Ensure that the S3 bucket policy specifies the ECS task execution role as a user.  
C. Create an S3 bucket policy that restricts bucket access to the ECS task execution role. Create a VPC endpoint for Amazon RDS for MySQL. Update the RDS for MySQL security group to allow access from only the subnets that the ECS cluster will generate tasks in.  
D. Create a VPC endpoint for Amazon RDS for MySQL. Update the RDS for MySQL security group to allow access from only the subnets that the ECS cluster will generate tasks in. Create a VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Update the S3 bucket policy to allow access from only the S3 VPC endpoint.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The requirement is that only the ECS cluster can access the data in the database and the bucket, meaning what needs restricting is the network and authorization path, not encryption. For the database, that's a security group that allows connections only from the subnets the ECS tasks run in. For the bucket, it's a VPC endpoint plus a bucket policy with a condition that requests come only through that endpoint (aws:SourceVpce). Encryption doesn't help with this requirement: it protects data from outsiders, but it doesn't stop anyone with network access and valid credentials from connecting.  
Why A is not selected: Encrypting with a KMS key doesn't restrict database connections: any client that reaches RDS with the correct password gets the decrypted data. This is an access problem, not a storage problem.  
Why B is not selected: An AWS managed key's policy can't be edited, and 'specify the role as a user' doesn't describe any working access-restriction mechanism.  
Why C is not selected: Restricting the bucket to the ECS task execution role misses the target: that role is used by the ECS agent to pull images and send logs, while the application in the container runs under the task role. A policy written this way would end up blocking the application itself.

---

664\. A company has a web application that runs on premises. The application experiences latency issues during peak hours. The latency issues occur twice each month. At the start of a latency issue, the application's CPU utilization immediately increases to 10 times its normal amount.  
The company wants to migrate the application to AWS to improve latency. The company also wants to scale the application automatically when application demand increases. The company will use AWS Elastic Beanstalk for application deployment.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Configure an Elastic Beanstalk environment to use burstable performance instances in unlimited mode. Configure the environment to scale based on requests.  
B. Configure an Elastic Beanstalk environment to use compute optimized instances. Configure the environment to scale based on requests.  
C. Configure an Elastic Beanstalk environment to use compute optimized instances. Configure the environment to scale on a schedule.  
D. Configure an Elastic Beanstalk environment to use burstable performance instances in unlimited mode. Configure the environment to scale on predictive metrics.  
Answer: A  
Review status: Corrected key (source: D; reviewed: A); Low-confidence audit  
Correction note: Predictive scaling learns from recurring daily and weekly patterns, and a spike that occurs twice a month doesn't qualify as such a pattern — the forecast won't catch it. An instant 10x jump in CPU from a low baseline load is handled by burstable instances in unlimited mode, and an irregular spike needs to be handled reactively, based on actual requests, rather than by forecast  
Explanation: Baseline load is low, but the spike drives CPU to ten times normal and happens irregularly. A burstable instance in unlimited mode immediately supplies the CPU needed and doesn't throttle (A), and reacting to an unpredictable spike needs to happen based on actual demand — request count.  
Why B is not selected: Scaling on requests is correct here, but compute optimized instances keep expensive, constant CPU capacity on standby for a spike that happens only twice a month. For a workload that's 'almost always quiet, occasionally sharp,' burstable unlimited delivers the same result more cheaply.  
Why C is not selected: Scheduled scaling requires knowing the timing of the spike in advance. Here only the frequency is known — twice a month, with no fixed schedule.  
Why D is not selected: Predictive scaling learns from recurring daily and weekly patterns. An event that happens twice a month isn't such a pattern, so the forecast won't catch it — which is exactly the mistake in the original answer key.

---

665\. A company has customers located across the world. The company wants to use automation to secure its systems and network infrastructure. The company's security team must be able to track and audit all incremental changes to the infrastructure.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS Organizations to set up the infrastructure. Use AWS Config to track changes.  
B. Use AWS CloudFormation to set up the infrastructure. Use AWS Config to track changes.  
C. Use AWS Organizations to set up the infrastructure. Use AWS Service Catalog to track changes.  
D. Use AWS CloudFormation to set up the infrastructure. Use AWS Service Catalog to track changes.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Two requirements: infrastructure is provisioned through automation, and every change to it can be tracked and audited. The first is CloudFormation: infrastructure is defined as code, deployed repeatably, and templates are versioned. The second is AWS Config: it maintains a configuration history for every resource, shows what changed and when, and can check compliance against rules. Don't confuse Config with CloudTrail: Config answers 'what did the resource look like and how did it change,' while CloudTrail answers 'who called which API.'  
Why A is not selected: AWS Organizations manages accounts and policies, but it doesn't provision infrastructure within accounts.  
Why C is not selected: Service Catalog distributes approved products for deployment, but it doesn't track a history of resource configuration changes.  
Why D is not selected: The infrastructure part is correct, but Service Catalog still isn't a change-auditing tool — that role belongs to AWS Config.

---

666\. A startup company is hosting a website for its customers on an Amazon EC2 instance. The website consists of a stateless Python application and a MySQL database. The website serves only a small amount of traffic. The company is concerned about the reliability of the instance and needs to migrate to a highly available architecture.  
The company cannot modify the application code.  
Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to achieve high availability for the website?  
(Choose two.)  
A. Provision an internet gateway in each Availability Zone in use.  
B. Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance.  
C. Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB, and enable DynamoDB auto scaling.  
D. Use AWS DataSync to synchronize the database data across multiple EC2 instances.  
E. Create an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic to an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances that are distributed across two Availability Zones.  
Answer: BE  
Explanation: There are two weak points, and both need to be addressed. The database moves to an RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ instance: the engine stays the same, so no code changes are needed, and a synchronous replica in another Availability Zone provides fault tolerance (B). The application is stateless, so it's enough to put it in an Auto Scaling group spread across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer (E).  
Why A is not selected: A VPC has a single internet gateway that works across all Availability Zones: you can't create one per zone, and it has nothing to do with availability anyway.  
Why C is not selected: DynamoDB is a non-relational data store: an application built for MySQL would have to be rewritten, which the requirement rules out.  
Why D is not selected: DataSync copies files between storage locations and can't keep a live database consistent across multiple instances.

---

667\. A company is moving its data and applications to AWS during a multiyear migration project. The company wants to securely access data on Amazon S3 from the company's AWS Region and from the company's on-premises location. The data must not traverse the internet. The company has established an AWS Direct Connect connection between its Region and its on-premises location.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create gateway endpoints for Amazon S3. Use the gateway endpoints to securely access the data from the Region and the on-premises location.  
B. Create a gateway in AWS Transit Gateway to access Amazon S3 securely from the Region and the on- premises location.  
C. Create interface endpoints for Amazon S3. Use the interface endpoints to securely access the data from the Region and the on-premises location.  
D. Use an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key to access the data securely from the Region and the on-premises location.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The key requirement is accessing S3 both from the company's Region and from its on-premises location over Direct Connect, without traversing the internet. The distinction that matters is between the two endpoint types: a gateway endpoint works only through VPC route tables and isn't reachable from an on-premises network, while an interface endpoint is a network interface with a private IP in your subnet that you can reach over Direct Connect or VPN. So the hybrid scenario calls specifically for an interface endpoint (PrivateLink). The trade-off is an hourly charge per endpoint per Availability Zone plus a per-GB processing charge, which the free gateway endpoint doesn't have.  
Why A is not selected: A gateway endpoint is reachable only by resources inside the VPC: it works as a route in the route table, and a request coming from on-premises over Direct Connect never reaches it.  
Why B is not selected: Transit Gateway connects VPCs and on-premises networks to each other, but it isn't an access point for S3.  
Why D is not selected: A KMS key encrypts data and has no effect on the network path: without an endpoint, the request still goes to the service's public endpoint.

---

668\. A company created a new organization in AWS Organizations. The organization has multiple accounts for the company's development teams. The development team members use AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign- On) to access the accounts. For each of the company's applications, the development teams must use a predefined application name to tag resources that are created.  
A solutions architect needs to design a solution that gives the development team the ability to create resources only if the application name tag has an approved value.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create an IAM group that has a conditional Allow policy that requires the application name tag to be specified for resources to be created.  
B. Create a cross-account role that has a Deny policy for any resource that has the application name tag.  
C. Create a resource group in AWS Resource Groups to validate that the tags are applied to all resources in all accounts.  
D. Create a tag policy in Organizations that has a list of allowed application names.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The requirement is that resources can only be created with a tag value from an approved list. AWS Organizations has a dedicated tool for exactly this: a tag policy. It defines the allowed tag keys and values and applies across every account in the organization, and with enforcement turned on it blocks resource-creation operations that use a noncompliant tag. This is a declarative setting with no code and no per-account policy edits.  
Why A is not selected: An IAM group with a tag condition could require the tag to be present, but it can't restrict the allowed values organization-wide, and here users sign in through Identity Center rather than belonging to IAM groups.  
Why B is not selected: Denying everything tagged with the application name is the opposite of the goal: the requirement is to allow creation when the correct value is used.  
Why C is not selected: Resource Groups groups together resources that already exist for bulk operations. It can't validate or restrict anything.

---

669\. A company runs its databases on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The company wants a secure solution to manage the master user password by rotating the password every 30 days.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use Amazon EventBridge to schedule a custom AWS Lambda function to rotate the password every 30 days.  
B. Use the modify-db-instance command in the AWS CLI to change the password.  
C. Integrate AWS Secrets Manager with Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL to automate password rotation.  
D. Integrate AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL to automate password rotation.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: RDS has built-in integration with Secrets Manager for the master user password: once enabled, RDS creates the secret itself, encrypts it with a KMS key, and sets up rotation on a schedule — for example, every 30 days. No function, no schedule, and no code to write, which is exactly what LEAST operational overhead calls for. Applications retrieve the password from the secret via a role rather than from configuration.  
Why A is not selected: A custom scheduled function means code, permissions, error handling, and monitoring — exactly the work the built-in integration removes.  
Why B is not selected: The CLI command changes the password manually, meaning a person has to do it every 30 days, and it doesn't address securely storing the new password.  
Why D is not selected: Parameter Store has no built-in rotation and no integration with RDS for changing the master password.

---

670\. A company performs tests on an application that uses an Amazon DynamoDB table. The tests run for 4 hours once a week. The company knows how many read and write operations the application performs to the table each second during the tests. The company does not currently use DynamoDB for any other use case. A solutions architect needs to optimize the costs for the table.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Choose on-demand mode. Update the read and write capacity units appropriately.  
B. Choose provisioned mode. Update the read and write capacity units appropriately.  
C. Purchase DynamoDB reserved capacity for a 1-year term.  
D. Purchase DynamoDB reserved capacity for a 3-year term.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The company already knows the number of read and write operations per second the application performs, and the table is only needed four hours a week. Provisioned mode lets you set capacity units to exactly what the tests require and lower them afterward — with known load, that's cheaper than paying per request.  
Why A is not selected: On-demand mode doesn't use capacity units at all, so that configuration isn't possible.  
Why C is not selected: A one-year reserved capacity commitment assumes continuous use, while the table only runs a few hours a week.  
Why D is not selected: A three-year commitment makes the same problem worse: the paid-for capacity would sit idle almost all the time.

---

671\. A company runs its applications on Amazon EC2 instances. The company performs periodic financial assessments of its AWS costs. The company recently identified unusual spending.  
The company needs a solution to prevent unusual spending. The solution must monitor costs and notify responsible stakeholders in the event of unusual spending.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use an AWS Budgets template to create a zero spend budget.  
B. Create an AWS Cost Anomaly Detection monitor in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console.  
C. Create AWS Pricing Calculator estimates for the current running workload pricing details.  
D. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor costs and to identify unusual spending.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirement is to catch unusual spending, not just cross a fixed threshold. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection builds a model of normal spending by service, account, and tag, and reports deviations along with an estimated size and likely cause; recipients are configured through a subscription (email or an SNS topic). That's what sets it apart from AWS Budgets, where a person sets the threshold and there's no assessment of what's 'unusual.'  
Why A is not selected: A zero-spend budget alerts on any spending at all. For a running production environment it turns into constant noise.  
Why C is not selected: Pricing Calculator estimates the future cost of a configuration during planning and performs no monitoring at all.  
Why D is not selected: CloudWatch exposes an estimated-charges metric, but it doesn't detect anomalies or explain them — it isn't a cost-analysis tool.

---

672\. A marketing company receives a large amount of new clickstream data in Amazon S3 from a marketing campaign.  
The company needs to analyze the clickstream data in Amazon S3 quickly. Then the company needs to determine whether to process the data further in the data pipeline.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create external tables in a Spark catalog. Configure jobs in AWS Glue to query the data.  
B. Configure an AWS Glue crawler to crawl the data. Configure Amazon Athena to query the data.  
C. Create external tables in a Hive metastore. Configure Spark jobs in Amazon EMR to query the data.  
D. Configure an AWS Glue crawler to crawl the data. Configure Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics to use SQL to query the data.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The data already sits in S3, and the goal is to take a quick look at it to decide whether a further pipeline is worth building. An AWS Glue crawler determines the schema itself and populates the catalog, after which Athena runs standard SQL queries with no server to manage — minimal effort and no infrastructure.  
Why A is not selected: External tables in a Spark catalog with Glue jobs mean writing jobs instead of just running a query.  
Why C is not selected: A Hive metastore and an EMR cluster mean deploying and maintaining a cluster just for a one-time look at the data.  
Why D is not selected: Kinesis Data Analytics analyzes streams, and the data here has already landed in a bucket.

---

673\. A company runs an SMB file server in its data center. The file server stores large files that the company frequently accesses for up to 7 days after the file creation date. After 7 days, the company needs to be able to access the files with a maximum retrieval time of 24 hours.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS DataSync to copy data that is older than 7 days from the SMB file server to AWS.  
B. Create an Amazon S3 File Gateway to increase the company's storage space. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days.  
C. Create an Amazon FSx File Gateway to increase the company's storage space. Create an Amazon S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the data after 7 days.  
D. Configure access to Amazon S3 for each user. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the data to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 7 days.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Recent files need to stay quickly accessible, while anything older than seven days only needs to be retrievable within 24 hours — that points directly at S3 Glacier Deep Archive, where standard retrieval takes about twelve hours and costs less than any other storage class. S3 File Gateway gives on-premises applications the familiar SMB share they expect, caching recent files locally, while a lifecycle rule moves objects to the archive after seven days.  
Why A is not selected: DataSync copies data but doesn't give on-premises clients transparent access to what's been moved, and it doesn't manage a lifecycle.  
Why C is not selected: FSx File Gateway caches access to FSx file systems; the data doesn't become S3 objects, so S3 lifecycle rules don't apply to it.  
Why D is not selected: Giving users direct access to S3 changes the familiar workflow, and Glacier Flexible Retrieval costs more than Deep Archive even though the 24-hour window allows the cheapest class to be chosen.

---

674\. A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The application uses a database that runs on an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The application performs slowly when traffic increases. The database experiences a heavy read load during periods of high traffic.  
Which actions should a solutions architect take to resolve these performance issues? (Choose two.)  
A. Turn on auto scaling for the DB instance.  
B. Create a read replica for the DB instance. Configure the application to send read traffic to the read replica.  
C. Convert the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Configure the application to send read traffic to the standby DB instance.  
D. Create an Amazon ElastiCache cluster. Configure the application to cache query results in the ElastiCache cluster.  
E. Configure the Auto Scaling group subnets to ensure that the EC2 instances are provisioned in the same Availability Zone as the DB instance.  
Answer: BD  
Explanation: The database is suffering specifically from read load, so it needs to be addressed on two fronts at once. A read replica takes all of the read traffic off the primary instance (B), while an ElastiCache cluster eliminates repeated round trips to the database for the same results entirely (D). Together they remove the bottleneck during traffic spikes.  
Why A is not selected: RDS Storage Auto Scaling applies to storage capacity, not compute power.  
Why C is not selected: A Multi-AZ standby instance doesn't serve queries — you can't read from it.  
Why E is not selected: Placing the instances in the same Availability Zone as the database saves milliseconds of network latency but reduces fault tolerance and doesn't solve the heavy-read problem.

---

675\. A company uses Amazon EC2 instances and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes to run an application. The company creates one snapshot of each EBS volume every day to meet compliance requirements.  
The company wants to implement an architecture that prevents the accidental deletion of EBS volume snapshots.  
The solution must not change the administrative rights of the storage administrator user.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative effort?  
A. Create an IAM role that has permission to delete snapshots. Attach the role to a new EC2 instance. Use the AWS CLI from the new EC2 instance to delete snapshots.  
B. Create an IAM policy that denies snapshot deletion. Attach the policy to the storage administrator user.  
C. Add tags to the snapshots. Create retention rules in Recycle Bin for EBS snapshots that have the tags.  
D. Lock the EBS snapshots to prevent deletion.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The requirement includes an unusual constraint: the storage administrator's permissions can't change. That rules out deny policies, so the protection has to live on the resource itself. EBS snapshots support a lock: a snapshot is placed in governance or compliance mode for a set period, and it can't be deleted even by someone with full permissions. This is configured as a property of the snapshot, which is also why it takes the least administrative effort.  
Why A is not selected: A separate instance and CLI access don't prohibit anything: the administrator can still delete the snapshot with their existing permissions.  
Why B is not selected: A deny policy changes the storage administrator's permissions, which the requirement explicitly forbids.  
Why C is not selected: Recycle Bin lets you recover a deleted snapshot within a retention window, but it doesn't prevent the deletion in the first place. The requirement is specifically about prevention.

---

676\. A company's application uses Network Load Balancers, Auto Scaling groups, Amazon EC2 instances, and databases that are deployed in an Amazon VPC. The company wants to capture information about traffic to and from the network interfaces in near real time in its Amazon VPC. The company wants to send the information to Amazon OpenSearch Service for analysis.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create a log group in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Configure VPC Flow Logs to send the log data to the log group. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to stream the logs from the log group to OpenSearch Service.  
B. Create a log group in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Configure VPC Flow Logs to send the log data to the log group. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream the logs from the log group to OpenSearch Service.  
C. Create a trail in AWS CloudTrail. Configure VPC Flow Logs to send the log data to the trail. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to stream the logs from the trail to OpenSearch Service.  
D. Create a trail in AWS CloudTrail. Configure VPC Flow Logs to send the log data to the trail. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream the logs from the trail to OpenSearch Service.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: VPC Flow Logs are written to a CloudWatch Logs log group, and the simplest way to deliver them from there to OpenSearch Service in near real time is a subscription to Kinesis Data Firehose: it's a managed delivery stream with a built-in OpenSearch destination, buffering, and retries. There's no consumer code to write.  
Why A is not selected: Kinesis Data Streams is just transport; writing to OpenSearch from it requires your own consumer application, which you'd have to build and operate.  
Why C is not selected: CloudTrail records API calls and can't serve as a destination for VPC flow logs.  
Why D is not selected: Same mistake, with CloudTrail again cast as the destination for flow logs.

---

677\. A company is developing an application that will run on a production Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster. The EKS cluster has managed node groups that are provisioned with On-Demand Instances.  
The company needs a dedicated EKS cluster for development work. The company will use the development cluster infrequently to test the resiliency of the application. The EKS cluster must manage all the nodes.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Create a managed node group that contains only Spot Instances.  
B. Create two managed node groups. Provision one node group with On-Demand Instances. Provision the second node group with Spot Instances.  
C. Create an Auto Scaling group that has a launch configuration that uses Spot Instances. Configure the user data to add the nodes to the EKS cluster.  
D. Create a managed node group that contains only On-Demand Instances.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The cluster is for infrequent resiliency testing, EKS itself needs to manage the nodes, and above all cost matters. A managed node group made up entirely of Spot Instances gives up to a 90 percent discount, and EKS provisions and replaces the nodes itself, including when spot capacity is reclaimed. For resiliency testing, interruptions are even a bonus.  
Why B is not selected: Adding an On-Demand node group increases cost unnecessarily: the environment is for testing and used infrequently.  
Why C is not selected: A self-managed Auto Scaling group that adds nodes via user data means self-managed nodes, while the requirement is for EKS to manage the nodes.  
Why D is not selected: On-Demand Instances only is the most expensive option, even though interruptions are acceptable here.

---

678\. A company stores sensitive data in Amazon S3. A solutions architect needs to create an encryption solution. The company needs to fully control the ability of users to create, rotate, and disable encryption keys with minimal effort for any data that must be encrypted.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use default server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3) to store the sensitive data.  
B. Create a customer managed key by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Use the new key to encrypt the S3 objects by using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS).  
C. Create an AWS managed key by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Use the new key to encrypt the S3 objects by using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS).  
D. Download S3 objects to an Amazon EC2 instance. Encrypt the objects by using customer managed keys. Upload the encrypted objects back into Amazon S3.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirement is full control over creating, rotating, and disabling encryption keys with minimal effort. That's an exact description of a customer managed key in KMS: you create the key, write its key policy, turn on automatic annual rotation or rotate on demand, can disable the key or schedule it for deletion, and every use is visible in CloudTrail. From there the bucket is configured for SSE-KMS with that key, and encryption happens automatically.  
Why A is not selected: SSE-S3 gives you no ability to create, disable, or manage rotation: the service fully owns the keys, and you never even see them.  
Why C is not selected: An AWS managed key can't be disabled, deleted, or have its key policy edited. And 'creating' an AWS managed key isn't even possible — services create them automatically.  
Why D is not selected: Manually downloading objects, encrypting them on an instance, and re-uploading them is the most effort possible, and it has to be repeated for every new object.

---

679\. A company wants to back up its on-premises virtual machines (VMs) to AWS. The company's backup solution exports on-premises backups to an Amazon S3 bucket as objects. The S3 backups must be retained for 30 days and must be automatically deleted after 30 days.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose three.)  
A. Create an S3 bucket that has S3 Object Lock enabled.  
B. Create an S3 bucket that has object versioning enabled.  
C. Configure a default retention period of 30 days for the objects.  
D. Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to protect the objects for 30 days.  
E. Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to expire the objects after 30 days.  
F. Configure the backup solution to tag the objects with a 30-day retention period  
Answer: ACE  
Explanation: There are two requirements pulling in opposite directions: copies must be retained for exactly 30 days (i.e., they can't be deleted early), and they must be deleted automatically once that period passes. S3 Object Lock handles the first: the bucket is created with Object Lock enabled (A), and objects get a default retention period of 30 days (C). An S3 Lifecycle rule handles the second, expiring objects after 30 days (E): once the retention period ends, the objects become deletable, and the rule removes them. One key detail: Object Lock can only be enabled when the bucket is created, and it automatically turns on versioning.  
Why B is not selected: Versioning by itself protects nothing: an object version can still be deleted. Object Lock also turns on versioning automatically, so enabling it separately isn't needed.  
Why D is not selected: A Lifecycle rule can transition and delete objects, but it can't protect them from deletion. Protection is Object Lock's job.  
Why F is not selected: A tag noting a retention period is just metadata. On its own it doesn't prevent or trigger anything.

---

680\. A solutions architect needs to copy files from an Amazon S3 bucket to an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system and another S3 bucket. The files must be copied continuously. New files are added to the original S3 bucket consistently. The copied files should be overwritten only if the source file changes.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create an AWS DataSync location for both the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system. Create a task for the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system. Set the transfer mode to transfer only data that has changed.  
B. Create an AWS Lambda function. Mount the file system to the function. Set up an S3 event notification to invoke the function when files are created and changed in Amazon S3. Configure the function to copy files to the file system and the destination S3 bucket.  
C. Create an AWS DataSync location for both the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system. Create a task for the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system. Set the transfer mode to transfer all data.  
D. Launch an Amazon EC2 instance in the same VPC as the file system. Mount the file system. Create a script to routinely synchronize all objects that changed in the origin S3 bucket to the destination S3 bucket and the mounted file system.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Files need to be copied continuously, only changed files should be re-copied, and operational overhead needs to be minimal. AWS DataSync supports both S3 and EFS as destinations, tasks can run on a schedule, and the 'transfer only data that has changed' mode compares metadata and only rewrites an object when the source has actually changed. No custom code is needed at all.  
Why B is not selected: A Lambda function with the file system mounted means custom code, error handling, retries, and execution-time limits for large files.  
Why C is not selected: Transferring all data every run rewrites the entire dataset each time: the requirement is to overwrite a file only when the source has changed.  
Why D is not selected: An instance running its own script is maximum operational overhead: the machine has to be maintained and the script kept up.

---

681\. A company uses Amazon EC2 instances and stores data on Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes.  
The company must ensure that all data is encrypted at rest by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).  
The company must be able to control rotation of the encryption keys.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create a customer managed key. Use the key to encrypt the EBS volumes.  
B. Use an AWS managed key to encrypt the EBS volumes. Use the key to configure automatic key rotation.  
C. Create an external KMS key with imported key material. Use the key to encrypt the EBS volumes.  
D. Use an AWS owned key to encrypt the EBS volumes.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The phrase "must be able to control rotation of the encryption keys" rules out everything except a customer managed key: only with it can you enable automatic annual rotation, trigger on-demand rotation, disable the key, and edit its policy. EBS volumes are encrypted with this key at creation, and everything after that is transparent to the instances. It helps to keep the hierarchy in mind: AWS owned keys are invisible and unmanageable, AWS managed keys are visible but their policy and rotation are outside your control, and customer managed keys give you full control.  
Why B is not selected: AWS managed keys rotate automatically once a year, and this cannot be configured. The requirement to control rotation is not met.  
Why C is not selected: Imported key material does not support automatic rotation: you would have to import new material yourself. That's maximum operational overhead.  
Why D is not selected: An AWS owned key doesn't even appear in your account: no policy, no usage log, no rotation control. EBS volumes cannot be encrypted with this type of key.

---

682\. A company needs a solution to enforce data encryption at rest on Amazon EC2 instances. The solution must automatically identify noncompliant resources and enforce compliance policies on findings.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?  
A. Use an IAM policy that allows users to create only encrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. Use AWS Config and AWS Systems Manager to automate the detection and remediation of unencrypted EBS volumes.  
B. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to manage access to encrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. Use AWS Lambda and Amazon EventBridge to automate the detection and remediation of unencrypted EBS volumes.  
C. Use Amazon Macie to detect unencrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. Use AWS Systems Manager Automation rules to automatically encrypt existing and new EBS volumes.  
D. Use Amazon inspector to detect unencrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. Use AWS Systems Manager Automation rules to automatically encrypt existing and new EBS volumes.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The requirement isn't just to turn on encryption but to put a process in place: block the creation of unencrypted resources and find any that already exist. The first part is handled by an IAM policy with an ec2:Encrypted condition that denies creating unencrypted volumes. The second part is handled by the AWS Config managed rule encrypted-volumes, which continuously evaluates resources, combined with automatic remediation through a Systems Manager Automation document. Both services are fully managed with no custom code to maintain — hence the LEAST administrative overhead. General pattern: "detect noncompliant resources and remediate" on the exam almost always means AWS Config plus SSM Automation.  
Why B is not selected: KMS manages access to keys but doesn't search for noncompliant resources. Pairing Lambda with EventBridge means writing your own code where a ready-made Config rule already exists.  
Why C is not selected: Macie classifies sensitive data in S3. It doesn't inspect EBS volumes at all.  
Why D is not selected: Inspector looks for vulnerabilities and insecure configurations in workloads, not whether a volume is encrypted. Also, an existing volume can't be encrypted "in place" — you need a snapshot and a new volume.

---

683\. A company is migrating its multi-tier on-premises application to AWS. The application consists of a single-node MySQL database and a multi-node web tier. The company must minimize changes to the application during the migration. The company wants to improve application resiliency after the migration.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Migrate the web tier to Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer.  
B. Migrate the database to Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind a Network Load Balancer.  
C. Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployment.  
D. Migrate the web tier to an AWS Lambda function.  
E. Migrate the database to an Amazon DynamoDB table.  
Answer: AC  
Explanation: Application changes must be minimal, while resiliency needs to improve. The web tier moves as-is onto EC2 instances, but now in an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer: the code doesn't change, and a node or Availability Zone failure stops being a problem (A). The MySQL database moves to an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployment — same engine, same protocol, but with automatic failover (C).  
Why B is not selected: A database behind a Network Load Balancer in an Auto Scaling group doesn't work: MySQL nodes don't scale by adding copies without replication.  
Why D is not selected: Moving the web tier to Lambda functions means rewriting the application, which the requirement says to avoid.  
Why E is not selected: Switching to DynamoDB means changing the data model and rewriting queries.

---

684\. A company wants to migrate its web applications from on premises to AWS. The company is located close to the eu-central-1 Region. Because of regulations, the company cannot launch some of its applications in eu-central-1.  
The company wants to achieve single-digit millisecond latency.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Deploy the applications in eu-central-1. Extend the company’s VPC from eu-central-1 to an edge location in Amazon CloudFront.  
B. Deploy the applications in AWS Local Zones by extending the company's VPC from eu-central-1 to the chosen Local Zone.  
C. Deploy the applications in eu-central-1. Extend the company’s VPC from eu-central-1 to the regional edge caches in Amazon CloudFront.  
D. Deploy the applications in AWS Wavelength Zones by extending the company’s VPC from eu-central-1 to the chosen Wavelength Zone.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Some applications can't run in the region itself, but users near eu-central-1 need single-digit millisecond latency. AWS Local Zones are AWS sites in major cities that you extend your existing VPC into: compute runs physically closer to users while remaining part of your network.  
Why A is not selected: You can't extend a VPC to a CloudFront edge location: there's no compute of yours there.  
Why C is not selected: CloudFront regional edge caches are part of the content delivery network, not a place to run applications.  
Why D is not selected: Wavelength Zones sit inside mobile network operators' networks and are meant for 5G device traffic, not regular corporate users.

---

685\. A company’s ecommerce website has unpredictable traffic and uses AWS Lambda functions to directly access a private Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company wants to maintain predictable database performance and ensure that the Lambda invocations do not overload the database with too many connections.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Point the client driver at an RDS custom endpoint. Deploy the Lambda functions inside a VPC.  
B. Point the client driver at an RDS proxy endpoint. Deploy the Lambda functions inside a VPC.  
C. Point the client driver at an RDS custom endpoint. Deploy the Lambda functions outside a VPC.  
D. Point the client driver at an RDS proxy endpoint. Deploy the Lambda functions outside a VPC.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The database is private, and the number of concurrent functions spikes with traffic — connections run out quickly. RDS Proxy maintains a connection pool and reuses connections, so database performance stays predictable. To reach the private database, the functions are deployed inside the VPC.  
Why A is not selected: A custom endpoint only routes requests to selected instances and doesn't manage a connection pool.  
Why C is not selected: Here both the endpoint is wrong and the functions are outside the VPC, so they can't reach the private database.  
Why D is not selected: The proxy is chosen correctly, but functions outside the VPC still can't reach the private endpoint.

---

686\. A company is creating an application. The company stores data from tests of the application in multiple on- premises locations.  
The company needs to connect the on-premises locations to VPCs in an AWS Region in the AWS Cloud. The number of accounts and VPCs will increase during the next year. The network architecture must simplify the administration of new connections and must provide the ability to scale.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?  
A. Create a peering connection between the VPCs. Create a VPN connection between the VPCs and the on- premises locations.  
B. Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. On the instance, include VPN software that uses a VPN connection to connect all VPCs and on-premises locations.  
C. Create a transit gateway. Create VPC attachments for the VPC connections. Create VPN attachments for the on-premises connections.  
D. Create an AWS Direct Connect connection between the on-premises locations and a central VPC. Connect the central VPC to other VPCs by using peering connections.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The key phrases are "the number of accounts and VPCs will increase" and "simplify connecting new ones." A transit gateway is built as a hub-and-spoke: each new VPC is added with a single attachment, each new site with a VPN attachment, and routing is configured centrally in the gateway's route tables. Nothing needs to be reconfigured in the networks that are already connected.  
Why A is not selected: VPC peering connections grow quadratically and provide no transit: connecting a new site to all the networks through them requires editing every route table.  
Why B is not selected: A homegrown VPN on an EC2 instance means your own software, your own patching, limited throughput, and a single point of failure.  
Why D is not selected: A central VPC with peering connections runs into the same limitation: transit routing through peering doesn't work, so the other VPCs won't be able to see the company's sites.

---

687\. A company that uses AWS needs a solution to predict the resources needed for manufacturing processes each month. The solution must use historical values that are currently stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company has no machine learning (ML) experience and wants to use a managed service for the training and predictions.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Deploy an Amazon SageMaker model. Create a SageMaker endpoint for inference.  
B. Use Amazon SageMaker to train a model by using the historical data in the S3 bucket.  
C. Configure an AWS Lambda function with a function URL that uses Amazon SageMaker endpoints to create predictions based on the inputs.  
D. Configure an AWS Lambda function with a function URL that uses an Amazon Forecast predictor to create a prediction based on the inputs.  
E. Train an Amazon Forsecast predictor by using the historical data in the S3 bucket.  
Answer: DE  
Review status: Corrected key (source: BD; reviewed: DE)  
Correction note: The key mixes training in SageMaker (B) with prediction via a Forecast predictor (D) — an incompatible pairing; given no ML experience, the consistent combination is DE (train a Forecast predictor + a Lambda function that uses that predictor)  
Explanation: The company has no ML experience, so it needs a service that both trains and predicts on its own. Amazon Forecast trains on the historical data in S3 (E), and a Lambda function with a function URL calls the ready-made predictor to return a forecast (D). The pair is consistent: training and inference happen in the same service.  
Why A is not selected: Deploying a SageMaker model and an inference endpoint is ML engineer work: choosing an algorithm, features, tuning. That directly contradicts the "no ML experience" condition.  
Why B is not selected: Training in SageMaker requires the same expertise. In the dump key, this option was also paired with calling a Forecast predictor — an inconsistent pair: train in one service, predict in another.  
Why C is not selected: A Lambda function calling a SageMaker endpoint inherits the same problem: the endpoint first has to be obtained by training a model manually.

---

688\. A company manages AWS accounts in AWS Organizations. AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) and AWS Control Tower are configured for the accounts. The company wants to manage multiple user permissions across all the accounts.  
The permissions will be used by multiple IAM users and must be split between the developer and administrator teams. Each team requires different permissions. The company wants a solution that includes new users that are hired on both teams.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create individual users in IAM Identity Center for each account. Create separate developer and administrator groups in IAM Identity Center. Assign the users to the appropriate groups. Create a custom IAM policy for each group to set fine-grained permissions.  
B. Create individual users in IAM Identity Center for each account. Create separate developer and administrator groups in IAM Identity Center. Assign the users to the appropriate groups. Attach AWS managed IAM policies to each user as needed for fine-grained permissions.  
C. Create individual users in IAM Identity Center. Create new developer and administrator groups in IAM Identity Center. Create new permission sets that include the appropriate IAM policies for each group. Assign the new groups to the appropriate accounts. Assign the new permission sets to the new groups. When new users are hired, add them to the appropriate group.  
D. Create individual users in IAM Identity Center. Create new permission sets that include the appropriate IAM policies for each user. Assign the users to the appropriate accounts. Grant additional IAM permissions to the users from within specific accounts. When new users are hired, add them to IAM Identity Center and assign them to the accounts.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: In IAM Identity Center, permissions aren't granted to individual users but through a permission set assigned to a group on an account. The pattern is: create groups (developers and administrators), create a permission set with the needed policies for each group, and assign the groups to the relevant accounts. A new hire is simply added to a group and immediately gets access to all the required accounts with the right permissions. That's the minimum operational overhead as the team grows.  
Why A is not selected: There's no need to create users "for each account": in Identity Center there's one user, and access to accounts is granted through assignments. A custom policy per group isn't the right mechanism either — permissions are described in a permission set.  
Why B is not selected: Same mistake with per-account users, plus attaching policies to individual users instead of a permission set adds more manual work with each hire.  
Why D is not selected: Assigning a permission set to each user individually and handing out extra permissions inside accounts breaks consistency and requires manual action for every new hire.

---

689\. A company wants to standardize its Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume encryption strategy. The company also wants to minimize the cost and configuration effort required to operate the volume encryption check.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Write API calls to describe the EBS volumes and to confirm the EBS volumes are encrypted. Use Amazon EventBridge to schedule an AWS Lambda function to run the API calls.  
B. Write API calls to describe the EBS volumes and to confirm the EBS volumes are encrypted. Run the API calls on an AWS Fargate task.  
C. Create an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy that requires the use of tags on EBS volumes. Use AWS Cost Explorer to display resources that are not properly tagged. Encrypt the untagged resources manually.  
D. Create an AWS Config rule for Amazon EBS to evaluate if a volume is encrypted and to flag the volume if it is not encrypted.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Checking "is this volume encrypted" is exactly what AWS Config managed rules exist for. The encrypted-volumes rule evaluates every EBS volume on creation and change, flags noncompliant ones, and keeps a history — and you pay for configuration evaluations, not for infrastructure running around the clock. No code, no schedule. This can be extended with automatic remediation via SSM Automation and a preventive deny in an SCP — see {{q:682,419}}.  
Why A is not selected: Custom API calls in a scheduled function mean code, permissions, handling paginated results, and gaps between runs. Config does the same thing as a service.  
Why B is not selected: A Fargate task adds a container image on top of that, which has to be built and updated. Even more work for the same check.  
Why C is not selected: Tags have nothing to do with encryption, and Cost Explorer shows spending, not the encryption state of volumes.

---

690\. A company regularly uploads GB-sized files to Amazon S3. After the company uploads the files, the company uses a fleet of Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to transcode the file format. The company needs to scale throughput when the company uploads data from the on-premises data center to Amazon S3 and when the company downloads data from Amazon S3 to the EC2 instances.  
Which solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Use the S3 bucket access point instead of accessing the S3 bucket directly.  
B. Upload the files into multiple S3 buckets.  
C. Use S3 multipart uploads.  
D. Fetch multiple byte-ranges of an object in parallel.  
E. Add a random prefix to each object when uploading the files.  
Answer: CD  
Explanation: Throughput needs to increase in both directions, and S3 has two standard techniques for that. On upload — multipart upload (C): the file is split into parts, the parts go to S3 in parallel, and total speed stops being limited by a single TCP connection (AWS recommends it for files over 100 MB and requires it above 5 GB). On download — parallel byte-range requests using the Range header (D): the object is pulled by multiple threads at once. Both techniques also improve robustness: a failed part is retried instead of the whole file.  
Why A is not selected: An access point is a named entry point with its own policy, useful for splitting permissions between teams. It doesn't affect throughput.  
Why B is not selected: Spreading files across multiple buckets doesn't increase speed: S3 scales by prefix within a bucket automatically, and extra buckets only add management overhead.  
Why E is not selected: A random prefix is outdated advice from when S3 performance depended on key distribution. Today S3 supports at least 3,500 write and 5,500 read requests per second per prefix and scales automatically, and for a single large file the technique is useless anyway.

---

691\. A solutions architect is designing a shared storage solution for a web application that is deployed across multiple Availability Zones. The web application runs on Amazon EC2 instances that are in an Auto Scaling group. The company plans to make frequent changes to the content. The solution must have strong consistency in returning the new content as soon as the changes occur.  
Which solutions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Use AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI) block storage that is mounted to the individual EC2 instances.  
B. Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the EFS file system on the individual EC2 instances.  
C. Create a shared Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Mount the EBS volume on the individual EC2 instances.  
D. Use AWS DataSync to perform continuous synchronization of data between EC2 hosts in the Auto Scaling group.  
E. Create an Amazon S3 bucket to store the web content. Set the metadata for the Cache-Control header to no- cache. Use Amazon CloudFront to deliver the content.  
Answer: BE  
Explanation: The requirement is shared access from multiple Availability Zones with strong consistency — new content must be visible immediately. Amazon EFS, mounted on all instances in the group, meets this (B). The second working option is to store content in S3 and serve it through CloudFront, setting the Cache-Control header to no-cache so edge locations check back with the origin every time (E); S3 itself provides strong read-after-write consistency.  
Why A is not selected: Volume Gateway is meant for hybrid access from an on-premises site and serves block volumes over iSCSI: it doesn't provide shared access for instances across different Availability Zones.  
Why C is not selected: A shared EBS volume is limited to a single Availability Zone and requires a cluster file system; that doesn't work for an Auto Scaling group spanning multiple zones.  
Why D is not selected: DataSync runs periodic copy tasks, not continuous synchronization between nodes, so it won't provide strong consistency.

---

692\. A company is deploying an application in three AWS Regions using an Application Load Balancer. Amazon Route 53 will be used to distribute traffic between these Regions.  
Which Route 53 configuration should a solutions architect use to provide the MOST high-performing experience?  
A. Create an A record with a latency policy.  
B. Create an A record with a geolocation policy.  
C. Create a CNAME record with a failover policy.  
D. Create a CNAME record with a geoproximity policy.  
Answer: B  
Review status: Disputed key (alternative: A)  
Dispute note: "MOST high-performing" points to the latency routing policy (A); geolocation routes based on the user's geography, not actual latency  
Explanation: The discriminating phrase is MOST high-performing, meaning the lowest actual latency for the user. In Route 53, that's what latency-based routing does: the service measures latency to the regions and sends the client to wherever the response is actually fastest. The dump key points to geolocation, and that's its weak point: geolocation routes by the user's country or continent, not by measured latency; the geographically closest region isn't always the fastest one. On the real exam, when the wording is about performance, pick the latency policy; geolocation is the right choice when the question is about content localization or country-based legal restrictions.  
Why A is not selected: This is the answer that matches the question's wording: latency-based routing sends the request to the region with the lowest measured latency. This is exactly where the dispute with the dump key lies.  
Why C is not selected: Failover is for disaster recovery switching, not performance, and it serves a "primary — secondary" pair, not three equal regions. Also, a CNAME can't be created at the zone apex.  
Why D is not selected: Geoproximity routes by geographic distance with an adjustable bias — that's still not measured latency, and it requires a traffic flow policy. Also, an ALB at the zone apex needs an alias A record, not a CNAME.

---

693\. A company has a web application that includes an embedded NoSQL database. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The instances run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group in a single Availability Zone.  
A recent increase in traffic requires the application to be highly available and for the database to be eventually consistent.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer. Maintain the embedded NoSQL database with its replication service on the EC2 instances.  
B. Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer. Migrate the embedded NoSQL database to Amazon DynamoDB by using AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS).  
C. Modify the Auto Scaling group to use EC2 instances across three Availability Zones. Maintain the embedded NoSQL database with its replication service on the EC2 instances.  
D. Modify the Auto Scaling group to use EC2 instances across three Availability Zones. Migrate the embedded NoSQL database to Amazon DynamoDB by using AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS).  
Answer: D  
Explanation: There are two weak points: a single Availability Zone and a database embedded in the instances. The Auto Scaling group is stretched across three Availability Zones, and the embedded NoSQL database is migrated to DynamoDB using AWS DMS. DynamoDB is fully managed, replicates across zones, and provides eventual consistency by default — exactly what the requirement calls for — while the operational burden of self-managed replication disappears.  
Why A is not selected: Swapping the load balancer changes nothing: the instances are still in a single zone, and the database's own replication still has to be maintained manually.  
Why B is not selected: The load balancer is swapped for no reason (the application is web-based, so an ALB is appropriate), and the main problem — a single Availability Zone — remains.  
Why C is not selected: The zones are fixed, but the embedded database's own replication on the instances is still entirely on the team's shoulders: maximum operational overhead.

---

694\. A company is building a shopping application on AWS. The application offers a catalog that changes once each month and needs to scale with traffic volume. The company wants the lowest possible latency from the application. Data from each user's shopping cart needs to be highly available. User session data must be available even if the user is disconnected and reconnects.  
What should a solutions architect do to ensure that the shopping cart data is preserved at all times?  
A. Configure an Application Load Balancer to enable the sticky sessions feature (session affinity) for access to the catalog in Amazon Aurora.  
B. Configure Amazon ElastiCache for Redis to cache catalog data from Amazon DynamoDB and shopping cart data from the user's session.  
C. Configure Amazon OpenSearch Service to cache catalog data from Amazon DynamoDB and shopping cart data from the user's session.  
D. Configure an Amazon EC2 instance with Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage for the catalog and shopping cart. Configure automated snapshots.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirements are minimal latency and cart data that survives even when the connection drops. ElastiCache for Redis solves both: the catalog, which changes once a month, is cached in memory and served in sub-millisecond time, while cart and session data live outside the web servers, so a user reconnecting loses nothing. Redis also supports replication and data persistence.  
Why A is not selected: Sticky sessions tie a user to a specific server: if it fails, the cart is lost, and database latency stays the same.  
Why C is not selected: OpenSearch is a search engine, not a session cache: latency is higher, and it isn't designed for storing shopping carts.  
Why D is not selected: A single instance with an EBS volume is a single point of failure, and snapshots only restore data to the moment they were taken.

---

695\. A company is building a microservices-based application that will be deployed on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). The microservices will interact with each other. The company wants to ensure that the application is observable to identify performance issues in the future.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Configure the application to use Amazon ElastiCache to reduce the number of requests that are sent to the microservices.  
B. Configure Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights to collect metrics from the EKS clusters. Configure AWS X-Ray to trace the requests between the microservices.  
C. Configure AWS CloudTrail to review the API calls. Build an Amazon QuickSight dashboard to observe the microservice interactions.  
D. Use AWS Trusted Advisor to understand the performance of the application.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Observability for microservices comes from metrics plus tracing. Container Insights collects metrics and logs from the EKS cluster, while AWS X-Ray traces each request's path through all the microservices, showing exactly where time is being lost. Together they give the full picture.  
Why A is not selected: A cache reduces the number of requests but doesn't solve the problem of finding bottlenecks: it doesn't add any observability.  
Why C is not selected: CloudTrail records calls to AWS APIs, not interactions between the microservices themselves.  
Why D is not selected: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations about account configuration and doesn't analyze application performance.

---

696\. A company needs to provide customers with secure access to its data. The company processes customer data and stores the results in an Amazon S3 bucket.  
All the data is subject to strong regulations and security requirements. The data must be encrypted at rest. Each customer must be able to access only their data from their AWS account. Company employees must not be able to access the data.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Provision an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate for each customer. Encrypt the data client-side. In the private certificate policy, deny access to the certificate for all principals except an IAM role that the customer provides.  
B. Provision a separate AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key for each customer. Encrypt the data server-side. In the S3 bucket policy, deny decryption of data for all principals except an IAM role that the customer provides.  
C. Provision a separate AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key for each customer. Encrypt the data server-side. In each KMS key policy, deny decryption of data for all principals except an IAM role that the customer provides.  
D. Provision an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate for each customer. Encrypt the data client-side. In the public certificate policy, deny access to the certificate for all principals except an IAM role that the customer provides.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The key idea: access to decryption is controlled by the KMS key policy, not the bucket policy. If each customer has their own key, and that key's policy allows only the customer's role to use it, then neither another customer nor a company employee can decrypt the objects — even with permission to read the bucket, they'd get AccessDenied on kms:Decrypt. That's exactly the separation required: the company stores and processes the data but can't read it. A separate key per customer also gives you cryptographic erasure: destroy the key, and the customer's data can no longer be recovered.  
Why A is not selected: ACM certificates are for TLS, not for encrypting data at rest, and there's no "certificate policy" that denies access to principals.  
Why B is not selected: A bucket policy governs S3 API calls but not KMS operations: you can't deny decryption there. An employee with permission to read the object and access to the key would still get the plaintext data.  
Why D is not selected: The same mistake with certificates as in option A, plus a public certificate doesn't contain any secret material for encrypting customer data at all.

---

697\. A solutions architect creates a VPC that includes two public subnets and two private subnets. A corporate security mandate requires the solutions architect to launch all Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet. However, when the solutions architect launches an EC2 instance that runs a web server on ports 80 and 443 in a private subnet, no external internet traffic can connect to the server.  
What should the solutions architect do to resolve this issue?  
A. Attach the EC2 instance to an Auto Scaling group in a private subnet. Ensure that the DNS record for the website resolves to the Auto Scaling group identifier.  
B. Provision an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB) in a public subnet. Add the EC2 instance to the target group that is associated with the ALEnsure that the DNS record for the website resolves to the ALB.  
C. Launch a NAT gateway in a private subnet. Update the route table for the private subnets to add a default route to the NAT gateway. Attach a public Elastic IP address to the NAT gateway.  
D. Ensure that the security group that is attached to the EC2 instance allows HTTP traffic on port 80 and HTTPS traffic on port 443. Ensure that the DNS record for the website resolves to the public IP address of the EC2 instance.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Instances must stay in private subnets, and internet traffic still has to reach them somehow. The standard approach is an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in the public subnets: it accepts requests and forwards them to the instances over the internal network. The site's DNS name points to the load balancer.  
Why A is not selected: An Auto Scaling group has no address or name that a DNS record can point to.  
Why C is not selected: A NAT gateway handles outbound connections and must sit in a public subnet; inbound traffic doesn't pass through it.  
Why D is not selected: An instance in a private subnet has no public address, and giving it one would violate the security requirement.

---

698\. A company is deploying a new application to Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with an AWS Fargate cluster. The application needs a storage solution for data persistence. The solution must be highly available and fault tolerant. The solution also must be shared between multiple application containers.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes in the same Availability Zones where EKS worker nodes are placed. Register the volumes in a StorageClass object on an EKS cluster. Use EBS Multi-Attach to share the data between containers.  
B. Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Register the file system in a StorageClass object on an EKS cluster. Use the same file system for all containers.  
C. Create an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Register the volume in a StorageClass object on an EKS cluster. Use the same volume for all containers.  
D. Create Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file systems in the same Availability Zones where EKS worker nodes are placed. Register the file systems in a StorageClass object on an EKS cluster. Create an AWS Lambda function to synchronize the data between file systems.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Fargate does not provide access to the underlying nodes, so the storage must be network-attached and shared between containers.
