B. Store the large data as objects in an Amazon S3 bucket. In a DynamoDB table, create an item that has an attribute that points to the S3 URL of the data.  
C. Split all incoming large data into a collection of items that have the same partition key. Write the data to a DynamoDB table in a single operation by using the BatchWriteItem API operation.  
D. Create an AWS Lambda function that uses gzip compression to compress the large objects as they are written to a DynamoDB table.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: DynamoDB's item size limit is 400 KB, and the data already reaches 700 KB and keeps growing. The standard pattern for this: store the object itself in S3, and keep an item in the table with an attribute pointing to it. This removes both the current limit and the future growth problem.  
Why A is not selected: Splitting data between two databases creates two storage models and a permanent filtering code path — maximum complexity.  
Why C is not selected: Splitting an object into items requires custom slicing and reassembly logic, and BatchWriteItem is limited to sixteen megabytes and twenty-five items.  
Why D is not selected: Compression only pushes the limit back: the data keeps growing, and there's no guarantee a compressed object will fit under 400 KB.

---

820\. A company is migrating a legacy application from an on-premises data center to AWS. The application relies on hundreds of cron jobs that run between 1 and 20 minutes on different recurring schedules throughout the day.  
The company wants a solution to schedule and run the cron jobs on AWS with minimal refactoring. The solution must support running the cron jobs in response to an event in the future.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create a container image for the cron jobs. Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to create a recurring schedule. Run the cron job tasks as AWS Lambda functions.  
B. Create a container image for the cron jobs. Use AWS Batch on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with a scheduling policy to run the cron jobs.  
C. Create a container image for the cron jobs. Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to create a recurring schedule. Run the cron job tasks on AWS Fargate.  
D. Create a container image for the cron jobs. Create a workflow in AWS Step Functions that uses a Wait state to run the cron jobs at a specified time. Use the RunTask action to run the cron job tasks on AWS Fargate.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Hundreds of jobs running one to twenty minutes, almost no code changes allowed, and both a schedule and future event-driven triggering are needed. The jobs are packaged into containers and run as Fargate tasks, while Amazon EventBridge Scheduler sets both recurring schedules and one-time runs at a specified moment. Fargate removes the execution time limit.  
Why A is not selected: Some jobs run up to twenty minutes, which exceeds the Lambda function's fifteen-minute limit.  
Why B is not selected: AWS Batch is built for queues of batch jobs and doesn't provide a convenient scheduler with future-event triggering for hundreds of different schedules.  
Why D is not selected: A Wait state in Step Functions can be adapted, but building hundreds of workflows instead of schedules is noticeably more work.

---

821\. A company uses Salesforce. The company needs to load existing data and ongoing data changes from Salesforce to Amazon Redshift for analysis. The company does not want the data to travel over the public internet.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?  
A. Establish a VPN connection from the VPC to Salesforce. Use AWS Glue DataBrew to transfer data.  
B. Establish an AWS Direct Connect connection from the VPC to Salesforce. Use AWS Glue DataBrew to transfer data.  
C. Create an AWS PrivateLink connection in the VPC to Salesforce. Use Amazon AppFlow to transfer data.  
D. Create a VPC peering connection to Salesforce. Use Amazon AppFlow to transfer data.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The source is the Salesforce SaaS application, the destination is Redshift, traffic must not travel over the public internet, and development effort should be minimal. Amazon AppFlow has a ready-made Salesforce connector, handles both the initial load and picking up changes on a schedule or by event, and privacy is provided by the AWS PrivateLink option: the flow travels over the AWS internal network.  
Why A is not selected: You can't build a VPN connection to Salesforce the way you would to a regular network, and Glue DataBrew is a data-prep tool, not a SaaS integration mechanism.  
Why B is not selected: Direct Connect links AWS to the company's own premises; there's no way to extend it to someone else's SaaS service.  
Why D is not selected: VPC peering can only be created between VPCs within AWS. Salesforce is an external service and has no VPC of its own to peer with.

---

822\. A company recently migrated its application to AWS. The application runs on Amazon EC2 Linux instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. The application stores data in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system that uses EFS Standard-Infrequent Access storage. The application indexes the company's files. The index is stored in an Amazon RDS database.  
The company needs to optimize storage costs with some application and services changes.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Create an Amazon S3 bucket that uses an Intelligent-Tiering lifecycle policy. Copy all files to the S3 bucket. Update the application to use Amazon S3 API to store and retrieve files.  
B. Deploy Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file shares. Update the application to use CIFS protocol to store and retrieve files.  
C. Deploy Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file system shares. Update the application to use the new mount point to store and retrieve files.  
D. Create an Amazon S3 bucket that uses S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Copy all files to the S3 bucket. Update the application to use Amazon S3 API to store and retrieve files as standard retrievals.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The scenario explicitly allows changing the application, so moving from a file system to object storage is on the table. S3 costs several times less per gigabyte than EFS, and Intelligent-Tiering itself moves objects between tiers based on actual access frequency — no rules, no retrieval charges, and no risk that an infrequently read file won't be available instantly.  
Why B is not selected: FSx for Windows File Server is also file storage, and it costs more than EFS: costs would rise, not fall.  
Why C is not selected: FSx for OpenZFS is again a file system priced at EFS level or higher; there's no savings.  
Why D is not selected: Glacier Flexible Retrieval is cheaper to store, but standard retrieval takes hours, while the application indexes and serves files: that delay is unacceptable.

---

823\. A robotics company is designing a solution for medical surgery. The robots will use advanced sensors, cameras, and AI algorithms to perceive their environment and to complete surgeries.  
The company needs a public load balancer in the AWS Cloud that will ensure seamless communication with backend services. The load balancer must be capable of routing traffic based on the query strings to different target groups. The traffic must also be encrypted.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use a Network Load Balancer with a certificate attached from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Use query parameter-based routing.  
B. Use a Gateway Load Balancer. Import a generated certificate in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Attach the certificate to the load balancer. Use HTTP path-based routing.  
C. Use an Application Load Balancer with a certificate attached from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Use query parameter-based routing.  
D. Use a Network Load Balancer. Import a generated certificate in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Attach the certificate to the load balancer. Use query parameter-based routing.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The discriminator is routing based on the query string. Only an Application Load Balancer can parse an HTTP request and pick a target group by query string, header, path, or method — it's a layer-7 load balancer. Encryption is provided by a TLS listener with a certificate from ACM, which is free and auto-renewing. A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and knows nothing about the request's content.  
Why A is not selected: An NLB doesn't parse HTTP: it has no query-parameter-based routing.  
Why B is not selected: A Gateway Load Balancer is built for inserting network security appliances into the traffic path and doesn't do HTTP routing.  
Why D is not selected: Same mistake with the NLB, plus importing a certificate into IAM is an outdated approach: ACM issues and manages certificates for load balancers.

---

824\. A company has an application that runs on a single Amazon EC2 instance. The application uses a MySQL database that runs on the same EC2 instance. The company needs a highly available and automatically scalable solution to handle increased traffic.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Deploy the application to EC2 instances that run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Create an Amazon Redshift cluster that has multiple MySQL-compatible nodes.  
B. Deploy the application to EC2 instances that are configured as a target group behind an Application Load Balancer. Create an Amazon RDS for MySQL cluster that has multiple instances.  
C. Deploy the application to EC2 instances that run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Create an Amazon Aurora Serverless MySQL cluster for the database layer.  
D. Deploy the application to EC2 instances that are configured as a target group behind an Application Load Balancer. Create an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster that uses the MySQL connector.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: There are two weak points: a single machine handling everything, and the database living inside it. The application moves into an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and the database moves into an Aurora Serverless cluster compatible with MySQL: the same engine, capacity adjusts automatically as traffic grows, and data is stored across multiple Availability Zones.  
Why A is not selected: Redshift is an analytics warehouse, not a transactional database, and it has no such thing as "MySQL-compatible nodes."  
Why B is not selected: A target group without an Auto Scaling group doesn't provide automatic growth in instance count — the scalability requirement isn't met.  
Why D is not selected: Redis is a cache, not a database, and it has no "MySQL connector" at all: there's nowhere to store the data.

---

825\. A company is planning to migrate data to an Amazon S3 bucket. The data must be encrypted at rest within the S3 bucket. The encryption key must be rotated automatically every year.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Migrate the data to the S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). Use the built-in key rotation behavior of SSE-S3 encryption keys.  
B. Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Enable automatic key rotation. Set the S3 bucket's default encryption behavior to use the customer managed KMS key. Migrate the data to the S3 bucket.  
C. Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Set the S3 bucket's default encryption behavior to use the customer managed KMS key. Migrate the data to the S3 bucket. Manually rotate the KMS key every year.  
D. Use customer key material to encrypt the data. Migrate the data to the S3 bucket. Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key without key material. Import the customer key material into the KMS key. Enable automatic key rotation.  
Answer: A  
Review status: Disputed key (alternative: B)  
Dispute note: Contradiction within the bank: question {{q:202}} is phrased identically, but there the key is B (KMS CMK). SSE-S3 requires fewer steps, but its rotation period isn't documented as annual — both keys can't be correct at the same time  
Explanation: This is the same text as question {{q:202}}, but the dump's key is the opposite answer — which is why both questions are flagged as disputed. The case for SSE-S3: the service manages and rotates its own keys, there's nothing to configure or maintain, and that's literally "least operational overhead." The case against it: SSE-S3's annual rotation cadence isn't documented anywhere, whereas a KMS key's automatic rotation runs every 365 days and is verifiable through CloudTrail records. If the question mentions "compliance" or requires proving the rotation period to an auditor, choose KMS; if the emphasis is purely on minimal effort, choose SSE-S3.  
Why B is not selected: A strong alternative, and the key for question {{q:202}}: a customer managed key with automatic rotation gives a verifiable yearly cycle. It costs more and requires setting up a key policy — hence the dispute over "least operational overhead."  
Why C is not selected: Manual rotation means a yearly task for a human, whereas KMS achieves the exact same result by simply enabling automatic rotation.  
Why D is not selected: Imported key material is the most labor-intensive option, and automatic rotation isn't supported for it in KMS: new material has to be imported by hand.

826\. A company is migrating applications from an on-premises Microsoft Active Directory that the company manages to AWS. The company deploys the applications in multiple AWS accounts. The company uses AWS Organizations to manage the accounts centrally.  
The company's security team needs a single sign-on solution across all the company's AWS accounts. The company must continue to manage users and groups that are in the on-premises Active Directory.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create an Enterprise Edition Active Directory in AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory. Configure the Active Directory to be the identity source for AWS IAM Identity Center.  
B. Enable AWS IAM Identity Center. Configure a two-way forest trust relationship to connect the company's self-managed Active Directory with IAM Identity Center by using AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory.  
C. Use AWS Directory Service and create a two-way trust relationship with the company's self-managed Active Directory.  
D. Deploy an identity provider (IdP) on Amazon EC2. Link the IdP as an identity source within AWS IAM Identity Center.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Same scenario as question {{q:28}}: users stay in self-managed Active Directory, but sign-in must work across every account in the organization. The solution is IAM Identity Center together with AWS Managed Microsoft AD, with a two-way trust established between it and the on-premises forest. Identity Center uses the directory as its identity source, and account access is granted by assigning a permission set to AD groups.  
Why A is not selected: Creating another directory in the cloud and declaring it the source means standing up a second set of users: the requirement is to keep managing them in the on-premises Active Directory.  
Why C is not selected: Directory Service by itself doesn't provide single sign-on across the organization's accounts — that's Identity Center's job.  
Why D is not selected: A self-hosted identity provider on EC2 is infrastructure you'd have to build and maintain, whereas the Identity Center plus Managed AD combination is a standard pattern.

---

827\. A company is planning to deploy its application on an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 cluster. The application will receive large amounts of traffic. The company wants to optimize the storage performance of the cluster as the load on the application increases.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Configure the cluster to use the Aurora Standard storage configuration.  
B. Configure the cluster storage type as Provisioned IOPS.  
C. Configure the cluster storage type as General Purpose.  
D. Configure the cluster to use the Aurora I/O-Optimized storage configuration.  
Answer: D  
Review status: Corrected key (source: C; reviewed: D)  
Correction note: Aurora has only two storage types — Standard and I/O-Optimized; General Purpose/Provisioned IOPS don't apply to an Aurora cluster  
Explanation: An Aurora cluster has exactly two storage configurations: Standard and I/O-Optimized. Under heavy, sustained I/O load, I/O-Optimized delivers predictable performance and pricing (D): I/O operations are included in the price.  
Why A is not selected: Standard is the default configuration, where every I/O operation is billed separately. Under growing load, that's exactly what you're trying to move away from.  
Why B is not selected: Provisioned IOPS is an EBS volume type that applies to RDS, not to an Aurora cluster. Aurora has no volumes for you to manage.  
Why C is not selected: General Purpose is also an EBS volume type from the RDS world. The concept doesn't apply to Aurora, and the trap here relies on conflating these terms.

---

828\. A financial services company that runs on AWS has designed its security controls to meet industry standards. The industry standards include the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS).  
The company's third-party auditors need proof that the designed controls have been implemented and are functioning correctly. The company has hundreds of AWS accounts in a single organization in AWS Organizations.  
The company needs to monitor the current state of the controls across accounts.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Designate one account as the Amazon Inspector delegated administrator account from the Organizations management account. Integrate Inspector with Organizations to discover and scan resources across all AWS accounts. Enable Inspector industry standards for NIST and PCI DSS.  
B. Designate one account as the Amazon GuardDuty delegated administrator account from the Organizations management account. In the designated GuardDuty administrator account, enable GuardDuty to protect all member accounts. Enable GuardDuty industry standards for NIST and PCI DSS.  
C. Configure an AWS CloudTrail organization trail in the Organizations management account. Designate one account as the compliance account. Enable CloudTrail security standards for NIST and PCI DSS in the compliance account.  
D. Designate one account as the AWS Security Hub delegated administrator account from the Organizations management account. In the designated Security Hub administrator account, enable Security Hub for all member accounts. Enable Security Hub standards for NIST and PCI DSS.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The task is to continuously show the state of NIST and PCI DSS controls across hundreds of accounts and present that to auditors. That's exactly what AWS Security Hub exists for: it aggregates findings, ships ready-made check packs for industry standards, and produces a compliance score. A delegated Security Hub administrator is designated for the organization, after which the service is turned on automatically for all member accounts. Keep the distinction clear: Security Hub is for standards compliance, GuardDuty for threat detection, Inspector for vulnerabilities, and Config for configuration state.  
Why A is not selected: Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities and insecure network paths. It has no check packs for NIST or PCI DSS.  
Why B is not selected: GuardDuty looks for signs of compromise in logs and traffic. It doesn't evaluate compliance of controls against standards.  
Why C is not selected: CloudTrail records API calls. No "security standards" get enabled in it.

---

829\. A company uses an Amazon S3 bucket as its data lake storage platform. The S3 bucket contains a massive amount of data that is accessed randomly by multiple teams and hundreds of applications. The company wants to reduce the S3 storage costs and provide immediate availability for frequently accessed objects.  
What is the MOST operationally efficient solution that meets these requirements?  
A. Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition objects to the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class.  
B. Store objects in Amazon S3 Glacier. Use S3 Select to provide applications with access to the data.  
C. Use data from S3 storage class analysis to create S3 Lifecycle rules to automatically transition objects to the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class.  
D. Transition objects to the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class. Create an AWS Lambda function to transition objects to the S3 Standard storage class when they are accessed by an application.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: A data lake with hundreds of applications accessing objects randomly is the definition of an unpredictable access pattern. There's no way to guess the age at which an object goes cold, and paying a retrieval fee for every unexpected access is unwelcome. S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between the frequent and infrequent tiers on its own, based on actual access, charges no retrieval fee, and returns data instantly from both tiers. One Lifecycle rule on the bucket, and the service runs on its own after that.  
Why B is not selected: Glacier doesn't provide immediate availability, and S3 Select is no longer supported for queries against Glacier archives. Random access from hundreds of applications simply doesn't work on an archival tier.  
Why C is not selected: Storage class analysis produces a report that a person then turns into rules by hand, and with random access, moving to Standard-IA means paying a fee for every unexpected read. That's both more manual work and a risk of overpaying.  
Why D is not selected: A scheme with a Lambda function that moves objects back to Standard on access is a homemade copy of Intelligent-Tiering: custom code, a delay on first access, and a charge for every transition between classes.

---

830\. A company has 5 TB of datasets. The datasets consist of 1 million user profiles and 10 million connections. The user profiles have connections as many-to-many relationships. The company needs a performance efficient way to find mutual connections up to five levels.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store the datasets. Use Amazon Athena to perform SQL JOIN queries to find connections.  
B. Use Amazon Neptune to store the datasets with edges and vertices. Query the data to find connections.  
C. Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store the datasets. Use Amazon QuickSight to visualize connections.  
D. Use Amazon RDS to store the datasets with multiple tables. Perform SQL JOIN queries to find connections.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: A million profiles and ten million many-to-many connections, and the requirement is to find mutual connections up to five levels deep. That's a graph problem, and Amazon Neptune solves it: vertices and edges, graph traversal in predictable time, with no repeated table joins.  
Why A is not selected: A five-level traversal in Athena turns into five sequential joins over terabytes of data — slow and expensive.  
Why C is not selected: QuickSight visualizes data that's already been computed, but it doesn't perform the graph traversal itself.  
Why D is not selected: In a relational database, that kind of traversal needs recursive joins, and at ten million connections performance collapses.

---

831\. A company needs a secure connection between its on-premises environment and AWS. This connection does not need high bandwidth and will handle a small amount of traffic. The connection should be set up quickly.  
What is the MOST cost-effective method to establish this type of connection?  
A. Implement a client VPN.  
B. Implement AWS Direct Connect.  
C. Implement a bastion host on Amazon EC2.  
D. Implement an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: No bandwidth needed, little traffic, and it has to go up fast and cheap — that's a description of AWS Site-to-Site VPN. An IPsec tunnel is configured in hours, encrypts traffic between the site and the VPC, is billed hourly, and costs far less than a dedicated connection.  
Why A is not selected: Client VPN connects individual users to a VPC and is billed per connection and per hour of endpoint uptime. The task here is to link network to network.  
Why B is not selected: Direct Connect takes weeks to provision and is expensive because of the port and cross-connect fees. For light traffic, that's overpaying.  
Why C is not selected: A bastion host gives administrative access to individual machines, not secure connectivity between networks.

---

832\. A company has an on-premises SFTP file transfer solution. The company is migrating to the AWS Cloud to scale the file transfer solution and to optimize costs by using Amazon S3. The company's employees will use their credentials for the on-premises Microsoft Active Directory (AD) to access the new solution. The company wants to keep the current authentication and file access mechanisms.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Configure an S3 File Gateway. Create SMB file shares on the file gateway that use the existing Active Directory to authenticate.  
B. Configure an Auto Scaling group with Amazon EC2 instances to run an SFTP solution. Configure the group to scale up at 60% CPU utilization.  
C. Create an AWS Transfer Family server with SFTP endpoints. Choose the AWS Directory Service option as the identity provider. Use AD Connector to connect the on-premises Active Directory.  
D. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint. Configure the endpoint to use the AWS Directory Service option as the identity provider to connect to the existing Active Directory.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Both the current Active Directory-based authentication and the SFTP access method need to be preserved, while files are stored in S3. An AWS Transfer Family server with an SFTP endpoint takes its identity provider from AWS Directory Service, and AD Connector provides the link to the on-premises domain — it proxies authentication requests to the existing directory without copying any accounts.  
Why A is not selected: S3 File Gateway serves resources over SMB, while employees work over SFTP: the access method would change.  
Why B is not selected: A self-managed fleet of instances running an SFTP server is exactly the operational burden the requirement asks to avoid.  
Why D is not selected: Picking AWS Directory Service as the identity provider isn't enough by itself: without AD Connector or a domain trust, there's no connection to the on-premises directory. That's the difference from the correct option.

---

833\. A company is designing an event-driven order processing system. Each order requires multiple validation steps after the order is created. An idempotent AWS Lambda function performs each validation step. Each validation step is independent from the other validation steps. Individual validation steps need only a subset of the order event information.  
The company wants to ensure that each validation step Lambda function has access to only the information from the order event that the function requires. The components of the order processing system should be loosely coupled to accommodate future business changes.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue for each validation step. Create a new Lambda function to transform the order data to the format that each validation step requires and to publish the messages to the appropriate SQS queues. Subscribe each validation step Lambda function to its corresponding SQS queue.  
B. Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Subscribe the validation step Lambda functions to the SNS topic. Use message body filtering to send only the required data to each subscribed Lambda function.  
C. Create an Amazon EventBridge event bus. Create an event rule for each validation step. Configure the input transformer to send only the required data to each target validation step Lambda function.  
D. Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Create a new Lambda function to subscribe to the SQS queue and to transform the order data to the format that each validation step requires. Use the new Lambda function to perform synchronous invocations of the validation step Lambda functions in parallel on separate threads.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Each handler needs its own slice of the order data, and coupling needs to stay loose. An EventBridge event bus provides a rule per validation step, and the input transformer rewrites the event before invoking the target, handing the function only the fields it needs. Adding a new step just means adding a new rule, with no change to the source.  
Why A is not selected: A queue per step plus a transformer function is custom routing code and an extra component.  
Why B is not selected: SNS filtering decides whether to deliver a message or not, but it can't strip out individual fields: a subscriber receives the whole event.  
Why D is not selected: A shared queue with a dispatcher function brings back tight coupling: the distribution logic ends up back in custom code.

---

834\. A company is migrating a three-tier application to AWS. The application requires a MySQL database. In the past, the application users reported poor application performance when creating new entries. These performance issues were caused by users generating different real-time reports from the application during working hours.  
Which solution will improve the performance of the application when it is moved to AWS?  
A. Import the data into an Amazon DynamoDB table with provisioned capacity. Refactor the application to use DynamoDB for reports.  
B. Create the database on a compute optimized Amazon EC2 instance. Ensure compute resources exceed the on-premises database.  
C. Create an Amazon Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ DB cluster with multiple read replicas. Configure the application to use the reader endpoint for reports.  
D. Create an Amazon Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ DB cluster. Configure the application to use the backup instance of the cluster as an endpoint for the reports.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The cause of the problem is stated directly: reports running during business hours interfere with creating new records. An Aurora MySQL cluster in a Multi-AZ configuration with multiple read replicas fixes this by splitting the load — reports go to the reader endpoint, which distributes them across the replicas, while writes stay on the primary instance.  
Why A is not selected: DynamoDB requires rewriting the application and is a poor fit for ad hoc reports, which are relational by nature.  
Why B is not selected: A more powerful machine speeds everything up at once, but the contention between reports and writes remains, and database maintenance still falls on the company.  
Why D is not selected: Aurora has no "backup instance" available for queries: reads are served specifically by the replicas through the reader endpoint.

---

835\. A company is expanding a secure on-premises network to the AWS Cloud by using an AWS Direct Connect connection. The on-premises network has no direct internet access. An application that runs on the on-premises network needs to use an Amazon S3 bucket.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Create a public virtual interface (VIF). Route the AWS traffic over the public VIF.  
B. Create a VPC and a NAT gateway. Route the AWS traffic from the on-premises network to the NAT gateway.  
C. Create a VPC and an Amazon S3 interface endpoint. Route the AWS traffic from the on-premises network to the S3 interface endpoint.  
D. Create a VPC peering connection between the on-premises network and Direct Connect. Route the AWS traffic over the peering connection.  
Answer: C  
Review status: Disputed key (alternative: A)  
Dispute note: A public VIF is cheaper and is the standard way to access S3 over Direct Connect; an interface endpoint is billed hourly plus data transfer  
Explanation: The site has no internet access, only Direct Connect, and S3 access needs to be as cheap as possible. The key picks C: a VPC with an interface endpoint for S3 — traffic from the data center travels over a private VIF into the VPC and on to S3, never leaving the AWS network. The cost angle is disputable: an interface endpoint is billed hourly per Availability Zone plus per gigabyte processed, whereas a public VIF (option A) gives access to AWS public endpoints directly over Direct Connect with no internet involved and no hourly endpoint fee. By the MOST cost-effective criterion, A looks stronger; by the "nothing public in the network" criterion, C does.  
Why A is not selected: A strong, and by cost the better, alternative: a public VIF gives access to S3 through Direct Connect with no internet exposure and no hourly endpoint charge. The one objection is that it uses the service's public addresses, which doesn't fit every company's policy.  
Why B is not selected: A NAT gateway sends traffic to the internet, which the site doesn't have, and it charges per gigabyte processed. Routing through the internet directly contradicts the scenario.  
Why D is not selected: VPC peering connects two VPCs. There's no mechanism to peer a VPC with an on-premises network or with Direct Connect directly.

---

836\. A company serves its website by using an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances in a single AWS Region.  
The website does not require a database.  
The company is expanding, and the company's engineering team deploys the website to a second Region. The company wants to distribute traffic across both Regions to accommodate growth and for disaster recovery purposes. The solution should not serve traffic from a Region in which the website is unhealthy.  
Which policy or resource should the company use to meet these requirements?  
A. An Amazon Route 53 simple routing policy  
B. An Amazon Route 53 multivalue answer routing policy  
C. An Application Load Balancer in one Region with a target group that specifies the EC2 instance IDs from both Regions  
D. An Application Load Balancer in one Region with a target group that specifies the IP addresses of the EC2 instances from both Regions  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Two sites in different Regions, traffic needs to be split, and an unhealthy Region shouldn't get any of it. Route 53 multivalue answer returns several addresses at once, but each record is tied to its own health check, and unhealthy ones are excluded from the answer. That delivers both load distribution and protection against a Region going down.  
Why A is not selected: A simple routing policy doesn't support health checks: it would keep returning the address of a failed Region right alongside the working one.  
Why C is not selected: A target group registers targets by instance ID only within its own VPC — instances from another Region can't be added to it.  
Why D is not selected: Registering by IP address does allow addresses outside the VPC, but that traffic would travel over inter-Region peering or the internet, with a single point of failure in the first Region's load balancer. If that Region goes down, everything goes down with it.

---

837\. A company runs its applications on Amazon EC2 instances that are backed by Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS). The EC2 instances run the most recent Amazon Linux release. The applications are experiencing availability issues when the company's employees store and retrieve files that are 25 GB or larger. The company needs a solution that does not require the company to transfer files between EC2 instances. The files must be available across many EC2 instances and across multiple Availability Zones.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Migrate all the files to an Amazon S3 bucket. Instruct the employees to access the files from the S3 bucket.  
B. Take a snapshot of the existing EBS volume. Mount the snapshot as an EBS volume across the EC2 instances. Instruct the employees to access the files from the EC2 instances.  
C. Mount an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system across all the EC2 instances. Instruct the employees to access the files from the EC2 instances.  
D. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) from the EC2 instances. Configure new EC2 instances from the AMI that use an instance store volume. Instruct the employees to access the files from the EC2 instances.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Files must be available to many instances across different Availability Zones, without copying between machines and without reworking the access method. Amazon EFS mounts over NFS on all the instances at once, stores data across multiple zones, and has no limit on individual file size — large files of 25 GB or more are handled natively.  
Why A is not selected: S3 is object storage accessed through an API: employees and applications would have to change how they work with files.  
Why B is not selected: A snapshot is restored as a separate volume, which attaches to a single instance in a single Availability Zone. There's no shared access, and copies immediately diverge.  
Why D is not selected: Instance store is ephemeral and local to each machine: data isn't shared and is lost when the instance stops.

---

838\. A company is running a highly sensitive application on Amazon EC2 backed by an Amazon RDS database.  
Compliance regulations mandate that all personally identifiable information (PII) be encrypted at rest.  
Which solution should a solutions architect recommend to meet this requirement with the LEAST amount of changes to the infrastructure?  
A. Deploy AWS Certificate Manager to generate certificates. Use the certificates to encrypt the database volume.  
B. Deploy AWS CloudHSM, generate encryption keys, and use the keys to encrypt database volumes.  
C. Configure SSL encryption using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys to encrypt database volumes.  
D. Configure Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) encryption and Amazon RDS encryption with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys to encrypt instance and database volumes.  
Answer: D  
Review status: Corrected key (source: C; reviewed: D)  
Correction note: The dump's key, C, describes SSL, i.e., encryption in transit, even though the requirement is encryption at rest; option D covers both storage layers: the instance's EBS volumes and RDS storage, both encrypted with KMS keys  
Explanation: The dump's key (option C) was corrected during the audit: it proposes "SSL encryption with KMS keys for the database volumes," but SSL protects data in transit, while the requirement is specifically about encryption at rest. The data lives in two places: the EBS volumes of the EC2 instances and RDS storage. So encryption is enabled for both EBS and RDS, both with KMS keys. The infrastructure changes are minimal: for EBS it's enough to create volumes encrypted (or turn on default encryption at the account level), and for RDS it means restoring the instance from an encrypted snapshot copy, as covered in {{q:121}}.  
Why A is not selected: ACM issues TLS certificates for securing connections. They can't be used to encrypt database volumes.  
Why B is not selected: CloudHSM gives you full control over encryption, but it requires deploying and maintaining an HSM cluster. That's disproportionate for a "least amount of changes" requirement when KMS achieves the same result through configuration.  
Why C is not selected: This was the original dump key: SSL protects data in transit, while the question is about data at rest. The phrase "SSL encryption with KMS keys for the volumes" conflates two different mechanisms.

---

839\. A company runs an AWS Lambda function in private subnets in a VPC. The subnets have a default route to the internet through an Amazon EC2 NAT instance. The Lambda function processes input data and saves its output as an object to Amazon S3.  
Intermittently, the Lambda function times out while trying to upload the object because of saturated traffic on the NAT instance's network. The company wants to access Amazon S3 without traversing the internet.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Replace the EC2 NAT instance with an AWS managed NAT gateway.  
B. Increase the size of the EC2 NAT instance in the VPC to a network optimized instance type.  
C. Provision a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPUpdate the route tables of the subnets accordingly.  
D. Provision a transit gateway. Place transit gateway attachments in the private subnets where the Lambda function is running.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The problem is that all traffic to S3 goes through the NAT and runs into its bandwidth limit. The right fix is a gateway endpoint for S3 with a route added to the private subnets' route tables: traffic to the buckets stops going through the NAT and never reaches the internet at all, the bandwidth constraint disappears, and there's no charge for the endpoint itself.  
Why A is not selected: A managed NAT gateway scales better than an instance, but traffic still travels over the internet and is still billed by gigabytes processed. The requirement to avoid the internet isn't met.  
Why B is not selected: A larger NAT instance only pushes the saturation point back and doesn't change the route through the internet.  
Why D is not selected: A transit gateway connects networks to each other; S3 can't be attached to it, and it has no effect on the route to the bucket.

---

840\. A news company that has reporters all over the world is hosting its broadcast system on AWS. The reporters send live broadcasts to the broadcast system. The reporters use software on their phones to send live streams through the Real Time Messaging Protocol (RTMP).  
A solutions architect must design a solution that gives the reporters the ability to send the highest quality streams.  
The solution must provide accelerated TCP connections back to the broadcast system.  
What should the solutions architect use to meet these requirements?  
A. Amazon CloudFront  
B. AWS Global Accelerator  
C. AWS Client VPN  
D. Amazon EC2 instances and AWS Elastic IP addresses  
Answer: B  
Explanation: What needs accelerating is specifically the TCP connections from reporters worldwide to the broadcast system. Global Accelerator accepts the connection at the nearest edge location and carries it onward over the AWS backbone: a shorter path, less loss and jitter, and fixed addresses. For RTMP streams, which run over TCP, that's exactly what's needed.  
Why A is not selected: CloudFront is optimized for delivering and caching content to viewers, not for ingesting incoming streams from sources.  
Why C is not selected: Client VPN gives secure network access but doesn't accelerate the network path and provides no fixed anycast addresses.  
Why D is not selected: Instances with Elastic IP addresses receive traffic over the ordinary internet: no path acceleration appears.

---

841\. A company uses Amazon EC2 instances and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) to run its self-managed database. The company has 350 TB of data spread across all EBS volumes. The company takes daily EBS snapshots and keeps the snapshots for 1 month. The daily change rate is 5% of the EBS volumes.  
Because of new regulations, the company needs to keep the monthly snapshots for 7 years. The company needs to change its backup strategy to comply with the new regulations and to ensure that data is available with minimal administrative effort.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Keep the daily snapshot in the EBS snapshot standard tier for 1 month. Copy the monthly snapshot to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive with a 7-year retention period.  
B. Continue with the current EBS snapshot policy. Add a new policy to move the monthly snapshot to Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive with a 7-year retention period.  
C. Keep the daily snapshot in the EBS snapshot standard tier for 1 month. Keep the monthly snapshot in the standard tier for 7 years. Use incremental snapshots.  
D. Keep the daily snapshot in the EBS snapshot standard tier. Use EBS direct APIs to take snapshots of all the EBS volumes every month. Store the snapshots in an Amazon S3 bucket in the Infrequent Access tier for 7 years.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Daily snapshots are already working correctly — they're incremental and kept for a month. For seven-year retention of the monthly copies, there's a standard tier called EBS Snapshots Archive: a snapshot is moved into the archive and costs roughly three-quarters less than standard storage. It's managed through a lifecycle policy, meaning no manual work.  
Why A is not selected: EBS snapshots can't be directly copied into Glacier Deep Archive: these are different services, and no such operation exists.  
Why C is not selected: Keeping monthly snapshots in the standard tier for seven years would cost several times more than the archive tier.  
Why D is not selected: The EBS direct APIs allow reading snapshot blocks, but exporting 350 TB every month with your own tooling means both huge cost and maximum manual effort.

---

842\. A company runs an application on several Amazon EC2 instances that store persistent data on an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. The company needs to replicate the data to another AWS Region by using an AWS managed service solution.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Use the EFS-to-EFS backup solution to replicate the data to an EFS file system in another Region.  
B. Run a nightly script to copy data from the EFS file system to an Amazon S3 bucket. Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication on the S3 bucket.  
C. Create a VPC in another Region. Establish a cross-Region VPC peer. Run a nightly rsync to copy data from the original Region to the new Region.  
D. Use AWS Backup to create a backup plan with a rule that takes a daily backup and replicates it to another Region. Assign the EFS file system resource to the backup plan.  
Answer: D  
Review status: Corrected key (source: A; reviewed: D)  
Correction note: "EFS-to-EFS backup" is a legacy AWS Solutions offering built on CloudFormation, not a managed service; cross-region EFS replication is handled by AWS Backup  
Explanation: Cross-Region replication of EFS data is needed, using a managed service. AWS Backup (D) handles the schedule, retention, and cross-Region copy of the backup, and the file system is simply assigned to the plan.  
Why A is not selected: "EFS-to-EFS backup" is a legacy AWS Solutions CloudFormation deployment — a set of resources you deploy and maintain yourself. It isn't a managed service.  
Why B is not selected: A nightly script into S3 plus CRR means custom code, a schedule, and monitoring on your side, plus a change in data model: files become objects.  
Why C is not selected: rsync over VPC peering is an entirely self-built solution: your own instance, your own retries, your own integrity checks.

---

843\. An ecommerce company is migrating its on-premises workload to the AWS Cloud. The workload currently consists of a web application and a backend Microsoft SQL database for storage.  
The company expects a high volume of customers during a promotional event. The new infrastructure in the AWS Cloud must be highly available and scalable.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?  
A. Migrate the web application to two Amazon EC2 instances across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for Microsoft SQL Server with read replicas in both Availability Zones.  
B. Migrate the web application to an Amazon EC2 instance that runs in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Migrate the database to two EC2 instances across separate AWS Regions with database replication.  
C. Migrate the web application to Amazon EC2 instances that run in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ deployment.  
D. Migrate the web application to three Amazon EC2 instances across three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Migrate the database to three EC2 instances across three Availability Zones.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Availability, scalability, and minimal administration are all required. The web tier moves into an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer — it can absorb the promotional surge — and the SQL Server database moves into managed RDS in a Multi-AZ configuration with automatic failover.  
Why A is not selected: Two fixed instances don't scale for a surge, and read replicas aren't a substitute for a Multi-AZ configuration when it comes to fault tolerance.  
Why B is not selected: A database on EC2 instances across separate Regions means self-managed replication and maximum administration.  
Why D is not selected: Three static instances and a database spread across three EC2 machines give neither automatic scaling nor a managed database.

---

844\. A company has an on-premises business application that generates hundreds of files each day. These files are stored on an SMB file share and require a low-latency connection to the application servers. A new company policy states all application-generated files must be copied to AWS. There is already a VPN connection to AWS.  
The application development team does not have time to make the necessary code modifications to move the application to AWS.  
Which service should a solutions architect recommend to allow the application to copy files to AWS?  
A. Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)  
B. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server  
C. AWS Snowball  
D. AWS Storage Gateway  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The application can't be rewritten, it writes to an SMB share and needs low latency, and connectivity to AWS already exists. AWS Storage Gateway in file gateway mode is installed on premises, presents the application with the familiar SMB share it expects, and at the same time stores every file as an object in S3: the company policy is satisfied, the code doesn't change, and latency is governed by the local cache.  
Why A is not selected: EFS uses the NFS protocol and lives in the cloud: wrong protocol, and latency over the VPN would be noticeable.  
Why B is not selected: FSx for Windows File Server speaks SMB, but it lives in the cloud: every operation would cross the tunnel, and the low-latency requirement isn't met.  
Why C is not selected: Snowball is a device for a one-time bulk transfer, while files are generated daily and need continuous copying.

---

845\. A company has 15 employees. The company stores employee start dates in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The company wants to send an email message to each employee on the day of the employee's work anniversary.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?  
A. Create a script that scans the DynamoDB table and uses Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to send email messages to employees when necessary. Use a cron job to run this script every day on an Amazon EC2 instance.  
B. Create a script that scans the DynamoDB table and uses Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to send email messages to employees when necessary. Use a cron job to run this script every day on an Amazon EC2 instance.  
C. Create an AWS Lambda function that scans the DynamoDB table and uses Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to send email messages to employees when necessary. Schedule this Lambda function to run every day.  
D. Create an AWS Lambda function that scans the DynamoDB table and uses Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to send email messages to employees when necessary. Schedule this Lambda function to run every day.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The task is tiny and runs once a day. A scheduled Lambda function scans a fifteen-row table and sends emails through SNS, which has a built-in email delivery protocol. No servers, no scheduler of your own.  
Why A is not selected: A cron script on an EC2 instance means a machine running around the clock for a couple of seconds of work a day.  
Why B is not selected: Same unnecessary machine, and on top of that SQS doesn't send emails: it's a message queue.  
Why D is not selected: The schedule is right, but you can't send an email through an SQS queue — that needs SNS or SES.

---

846\. A company’s application is running on Amazon EC2 instances within an Auto Scaling group behind an Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) load balancer. Based on the application's history, the company anticipates a spike in traffic during a holiday each year. A solutions architect must design a strategy to ensure that the Auto Scaling group proactively increases capacity to minimize any performance impact on application users.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to scale up the EC2 instances when CPU utilization exceeds 90%.  
B. Create a recurring scheduled action to scale up the Auto Scaling group before the expected period of peak demand.  
C. Increase the minimum and maximum number of EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group during the peak demand period.  
D. Configure an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification to send alerts when there are autoscaling:EC2_INSTANCE_LAUNCH events.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The date of the spike is known in advance — the holiday recurs every year. A recurring scheduled action increases the Auto Scaling group's capacity ahead of the expected peak, so the instances are already in place before the users arrive. That's exactly the proactive scaling the scenario calls for.  
Why A is not selected: A CPU-utilization alarm only fires after users have already felt the slowdown — that's a reaction, not preparation.  
Why C is not selected: Manually adjusting the limits for the peak period requires someone to do it by hand every year.  
Why D is not selected: Notifications about instance launches only inform the administrator and add no capacity.

---

847\. A company uses Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL databases for its data tier. The company must implement password rotation for the databases.  
Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager. Enable automatic rotation on the secret.  
B. Store the password in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Enable automatic rotation on the parameter.  
C. Store the password in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Write an AWS Lambda function that rotates the password.  
D. Store the password in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Enable automatic rotation on the AWS KMS key.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Rotating a database password is exactly what Secrets Manager does with no code: the secret is stored encrypted with a KMS key, and for RDS PostgreSQL AWS provides a ready-made rotation function that just needs to be turned on with a period set. The application reads the password via GetSecretValue through its role, so the password change is invisible to it. Keep the service boundaries straight: Secrets Manager is for secrets with rotation, Parameter Store for parameters and simple secrets without rotation, and KMS for encryption keys, not passwords.  
Why B is not selected: Parameter Store has no built-in automatic rotation: there's no way to "enable it on the parameter."  
Why C is not selected: A custom rotation function means code, permissions, testing, and maintenance. Secrets Manager achieves the same thing through configuration.  
Why D is not selected: KMS rotates cryptographic keys, not database user passwords. It doesn't solve the task.

---

848\. A company runs its application on Oracle Database Enterprise Edition. The company needs to migrate the application and the database to AWS. The company can use the Bring Your Own License (BYOL) model while migrating to AWS. The application uses third-party database features that require privileged access.  
A solutions architect must design a solution for the database migration.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for Oracle by using native tools. Replace the third-party features with AWS Lambda.  
B. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle by using native tools. Customize the new database settings to support the third-party features.  
C. Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB by using AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS). Customize the new database settings to support the third-party features.  
D. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL by using AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS). Rewrite the application code to remove the dependency on third-party features.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The application uses Oracle features that require privileged access — and standard RDS for Oracle provides no SYS-level privileges or operating system access. Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle was built specifically for cases like this: it's a managed service that still gives access to the underlying operating system and database settings, and it supports the Bring Your Own License model.  
Why A is not selected: Standard RDS for Oracle doesn't offer privileged access, and replacing third-party vendor features with Lambda functions means rewriting the application.  
Why C is not selected: DynamoDB is a non-relational store: migrating from Oracle would mean completely rewriting the data model and queries.  
Why D is not selected: Moving to PostgreSQL with a code rewrite contradicts both the requirement to use the existing license and the requirement for lowest cost.

---

849\. A large international university has deployed all of its compute services in the AWS Cloud. These services include Amazon EC2, Amazon RDS, and Amazon DynamoDB. The university currently relies on many custom scripts to back up its infrastructure. However, the university wants to centralize management and automate data backups as much as possible by using AWS native options.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use third-party backup software with an AWS Storage Gateway tape gateway virtual tape library.  
B. Use AWS Backup to configure and monitor all backups for the services in use.  
C. Use AWS Config to set lifecycle management to take snapshots of all data sources on a schedule.  
D. Use AWS Systems Manager State Manager to manage the configuration and monitoring of backup tasks.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Backups need to be centralized and automated using AWS-native tools. AWS Backup was built exactly for this: it supports EC2, RDS, DynamoDB, and many other services, defines plans with schedules and retention periods, manages the backup vaults, shows the status of every job in one place, and replaces custom scripts.  
Why A is not selected: Third-party software and a virtual tape library aren't AWS-native tools or centralization — they're just carrying the old approach over.  
Why C is not selected: AWS Config tracks configuration compliance and doesn't take scheduled snapshots.  
Why D is not selected: State Manager maintains a desired configuration state on nodes, but it isn't a backup service.

---

850\. A company wants to build a map of its IT infrastructure to identify and enforce policies on resources that pose security risks. The company's security team must be able to query data in the IT infrastructure map and quickly identify security risks.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use Amazon RDS to store the data. Use SQL to query the data to identify security risks.  
B. Use Amazon Neptune to store the data. Use SPARQL to query the data to identify security risks.  
C. Use Amazon Redshift to store the data. Use SQL to query the data to identify security risks.  
D. Use Amazon DynamoDB to store the data. Use PartiQL to query the data to identify security risks.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: An infrastructure map is resources and the relationships between them — a graph. Amazon Neptune stores this kind of data as vertices and edges and lets you query it with graph query languages, including SPARQL, so questions like "which resources are connected to this vulnerable node" are answered with a single query and no infrastructure of your own.  
Why A is not selected: In a relational database, relationships are unwound through repeated table joins: queries become unwieldy and slow.  
Why C is not selected: Redshift is built for analytics over large datasets, not for traversing relationships between objects.  
Why D is not selected: DynamoDB stores items by key; PartiQL doesn't turn it into a graph database, and it can't traverse relationships.

---

851\. A large company wants to provide its globally located developers separate, limited size, managed PostgreSQL databases for development purposes. The databases will be low volume. The developers need the databases only when they are actively working.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Give the developers the ability to launch separate Amazon Aurora instances. Set up a process to shut down Aurora instances at the end of the workday and to start Aurora instances at the beginning of the next workday.  
B. Develop an AWS Service Catalog product that enforces size restrictions for launching Amazon Aurora instances. Give the developers access to launch the product when they need a development database.  
C. Create an Amazon Aurora Serverless cluster. Develop an AWS Service Catalog product to launch databases in the cluster with the default capacity settings. Grant the developers access to the product.  
D. Monitor AWS Trusted Advisor checks for idle Amazon RDS databases. Create a process to terminate identified idle RDS databases.  
Answer: B  
Review status: Disputed key (alternative: C)  
Dispute note: Aurora Serverless scales down during idle periods, which more accurately matches the requirement of "needed only while running"  
Explanation: The key phrases are "only when they are actively working" and "limited size." The cheapest solution is one that isn't billed while idle and still keeps developers from spinning up an arbitrarily large cluster. The key picks B: a Service Catalog product with size restrictions baked in — size stays under control, and developers launch it themselves. The weak point of the key is that a provisioned Aurora instance keeps billing overnight too, and the developers are spread across time zones. Option C adds Aurora Serverless on top of the same Service Catalog approach, and since it scales down on its own when idle, it actually matches the "only needed while working" requirement more precisely.  
Why A is not selected: A manual start/stop schedule doesn't work for developers spread across time zones and puts the whole burden on operations. There's also no size restriction here — anyone can launch a large instance.  
Why C is not selected: A strong alternative: Serverless scales down when idle, so billing tracks actual usage. The objection against it is that "default capacity settings" don't satisfy the requirement to limit the database size.  
Why D is not selected: Trusted Advisor finds idle databases after the fact, and automatic deletion destroys the developer's data instead of just pausing it. That's a reaction to the problem, not a solution.

---

852\. A company is building a web application that serves a content management system. The content management system runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The EC2 instances run in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Users are constantly adding and updating files, blogs, and other website assets in the content management system.  
A solutions architect must implement a solution in which all the EC2 instances share up-to-date website content with the least possible lag time.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Update the EC2 user data in the Auto Scaling group lifecycle policy to copy the website assets from the EC2 instance that was launched most recently. Configure the ALB to make changes to the website assets only in the newest EC2 instance.  
B. Copy the website assets to an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Configure each EC2 instance to mount the EFS file system locally. Configure the website hosting application to reference the website assets that are stored in the EFS file system.  
C. Copy the website assets to an Amazon S3 bucket. Ensure that each EC2 instance downloads the website assets from the S3 bucket to the attached Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Run the S3 sync command once each hour to keep files up to date.  
D. Restore an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshot with the website assets. Attach the EBS snapshot as a secondary EBS volume when a new EC2 instance is launched. Configure the website hosting application to reference the website assets that are stored in the secondary EBS volume.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: All instances need to see the same site content with minimal lag, and users are constantly changing it. A shared Amazon EFS file system mounts on every instance, and a write made on one machine is immediately visible to the others: no synchronization and no lag.  
Why A is not selected: Copying content from the "most recently launched" instance at boot means lag and complete chaos when changes happen concurrently, and the load balancer has no way to route changes to a specific machine.  
Why C is not selected: Syncing once an hour means up to an hour of lag, while the requirement calls for the least possible lag.  
Why D is not selected: An EBS snapshot gives each machine its own copy frozen at the moment the snapshot was taken: changes on one instance are never visible to the others at all.

---

853\. A company's web application consists of multiple Amazon EC2 instances that run behind an Application Load Balancer in a VPC. An Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance contains the data. The company needs the ability to automatically detect and respond to suspicious or unexpected behavior in its AWS environment. The company already has added AWS WAF to its architecture.  
What should a solutions architect do next to protect against threats?  
A. Use Amazon GuardDuty to perform threat detection. Configure Amazon EventBridge to filter for GuardDuty findings and to invoke an AWS Lambda function to adjust the AWS WAF rules.  
B. Use AWS Firewall Manager to perform threat detection. Configure Amazon EventBridge to filter for Firewall Manager findings and to invoke an AWS Lambda function to adjust the AWS WAF web ACL.  
C. Use Amazon Inspector to perform threat detection and to update the AWS WAF rules. Create a VPC network ACL to limit access to the web application.  
D. Use Amazon Macie to perform threat detection and to update the AWS WAF rules. Create a VPC network ACL to limit access to the web application.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: WAF is already in place and filters known attack patterns. The next layer is detecting anomalous behavior across the account and the network, and that's Amazon GuardDuty: it analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and data events to surface reconnaissance, calls to known malicious addresses, and unusual API activity. Automated response is built from standard building blocks: findings flow into EventBridge, and a Lambda function adds the offending IP address to an IP set in the web ACL.  
Why B is not selected: Firewall Manager rolls out WAF, Shield, and Network Firewall policies across accounts. It doesn't do threat detection and doesn't produce findings.  
Why C is not selected: Inspector looks for vulnerabilities in images and instances, not suspicious behavior, and it doesn't update WAF rules.  
Why D is not selected: Macie classifies sensitive data in S3. It has nothing to do with detecting threats in the environment.

---

854\. A company is planning to run a group of Amazon EC2 instances that connect to an Amazon Aurora database. The company has built an AWS CloudFormation template to deploy the EC2 instances and the Aurora DB cluster. The company wants to allow the instances to authenticate to the database in a secure way. The company does not want to maintain static database credentials.  
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?  
A. Create a database user with a user name and password. Add parameters for the database user name and password to the CloudFormation template. Pass the parameters to the EC2 instances when the instances are launched.  
B. Create a database user with a user name and password. Store the user name and password in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Configure the EC2 instances to retrieve the database credentials from Parameter Store.  
C. Configure the DB cluster to use IAM database authentication. Create a database user to use with IAM authentication. Associate a role with the EC2 instances to allow applications on the instances to access the database.  
D. Configure the DB cluster to use IAM database authentication with an IAM user. Create a database user that has a name that matches the IAM user. Associate the IAM user with the EC2 instances to allow applications on the instances to access the database.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The requirement is not to maintain static database credentials. IAM database authentication solves this: IAM authentication is enabled on the Aurora cluster, a database user is created with the rds_iam grant, and the application on the instance calls generate-db-auth-token and connects with that temporary token (valid for 15 minutes). Permission for rds-db:connect comes from the role attached to the instance — so identity comes from the role, and no password ever exists.  
Why A is not selected: Passing a user name and password as template parameters is still static credentials, and they end up in the stack parameters and in the instance configuration.  
Why B is not selected: Parameter Store just stores that same static password, and it still has to be rotated manually. The requirement not to maintain static credentials isn't met.  
Why D is not selected: An IAM user can't be "associated with instances": an instance runs under a role. And with IAM authentication, the database user name isn't required to match the IAM user name.

---

855\. A company wants to configure its Amazon CloudFront distribution to use SSL/TLS certificates. The company does not want to use the default domain name for the distribution. Instead, the company wants to use a different domain name for the distribution.  
Which solution will deploy the certificate without incurring any additional costs?  
A. Request an Amazon issued private certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the us-east-1 Region.  
B. Request an Amazon issued private certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the us-west-1 Region.  
C. Request an Amazon issued public certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the us-east-1 Region.  
D. Request an Amazon issued public certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the us-west-1 Region.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: A custom domain name on CloudFront requires a public certificate, and a public certificate issued by ACM is free. Important detail: the certificate for CloudFront must be located in the us-east-1 Region regardless of where the origins are located.  
Why A is not selected: Private certificates are issued by AWS Private CA, which is a paid service; browsers also don't trust them by default.  
Why B is not selected: Here the certificate is both private and in the wrong Region.  
Why D is not selected: The certificate is public and free, but the Region is wrong: CloudFront only accepts certificates from us-east-1.

---

856\. A company creates operations data and stores the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. For the company's annual audit, an external consultant needs to access an annual report that is stored in the S3 bucket. The external consultant needs to access the report for 7 days.  
The company must implement a solution to allow the external consultant access to only the report.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?  
A. Create a new S3 bucket that is configured to host a public static website. Migrate the operations data to the new S3 bucket. Share the S3 website URL with the external consultant.  
B. Enable public access to the S3 bucket for 7 days. Remove access to the S3 bucket when the external consultant completes the audit.  
C. Create a new IAM user that has access to the report in the S3 bucket. Provide the access keys to the external consultant. Revoke the access keys after 7 days.  
D. Generate a presigned URL that has the required access to the location of the report on the S3 bucket. Share the presigned URL with the external consultant.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The need is to grant one external person access to a single object for a limited time without creating an account for them. That's exactly what a presigned URL is: the link is signed with your permissions and carries an expiration, and the recipient just downloads the file over HTTPS. Nothing needs to be created and later revoked — the link expires on its own. A useful number: a presigned URL signed with long-lived credentials can live for up to 7 days (604,800 seconds), which matches the required duration exactly; a URL signed with a role's temporary credentials stops working as soon as those credentials do.  
Why A is not selected: Moving the operations data into a publicly accessible website bucket exposes the entire dataset to the whole internet for the sake of one report. Maximum risk for minimal benefit.  
Why B is not selected: Public access to the whole bucket for a week is the same mistake: the consultant needs one report, but all of the company's data is exposed.  
Why C is not selected: An IAM user and access keys for an outside person are long-lived credentials that have to be created, delivered over a secure channel, and remembered to be revoked. More work and more risk.

---

857\. A company plans to run a high performance computing (HPC) workload on Amazon EC2 Instances. The workload requires low-latency network performance and high network throughput with tightly coupled node-to-node communication.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Configure the EC2 instances to be part of a cluster placement group.  
B. Launch the EC2 instances with Dedicated Instance tenancy.  
C. Launch the EC2 instances as Spot Instances.  
D. Configure an On-Demand Capacity Reservation when the EC2 instances are launched.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Tightly coupled computation requires minimal latency and high throughput between nodes. A cluster placement group packs instances as close together as possible within a single Availability Zone, delivering low-latency, full-bandwidth networking — the standard solution for high performance computing.  
Why B is not selected: Dedicated tenancy affects which hardware you share, not network latency between nodes.  
Why C is not selected: Spot Instances change the pricing model and can be reclaimed — that has nothing to do with network characteristics.  
Why D is not selected: A capacity reservation guarantees that instances can launch, but not that they're placed close together.

---

858\. A company has primary and secondary data centers that are 500 miles (804.7 km) apart and interconnected with high-speed fiber-optic cable. The company needs a highly available and secure network connection between its data centers and a VPC on AWS for a mission-critical workload. A solutions architect must choose a connection solution that provides maximum resiliency.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Two AWS Direct Connect connections from the primary data center terminating at two Direct Connect locations on two separate devices  
B. A single AWS Direct Connect connection from each of the primary and secondary data centers terminating at one Direct Connect location on the same device  
C. Two AWS Direct Connect connections from each of the primary and secondary data centers terminating at two Direct Connect locations on two separate devices  
D. A single AWS Direct Connect connection from each of the primary and secondary data centers terminating at one Direct Connect location on two separate devices  
Answer: C  
Explanation: AWS's recommended maximum resiliency is achieved when every single point of failure is eliminated: two connections from each data center, terminating at two different Direct Connect locations, ending on different equipment. Then a failure of a router, a Direct Connect location, a cable, or an entire data center doesn't cut off connectivity to the VPC.  
Why A is not selected: The connections only originate from the primary data center: its failure breaks connectivity entirely, and the secondary site is never connected at all.  
Why B is not selected: A single location and a single device is two shared points of failure for both connections at once.  
Why D is not selected: The devices are different, but there's only one location, and only one connection runs from each data center: resiliency falls short of maximum.

---

859\. A company runs several Amazon RDS for Oracle On-Demand DB instances that have high utilization. The RDS DB instances run in member accounts that are in an organization in AWS Organizations.  
The company's finance team has access to the organization's management account and member accounts. The finance team wants to find ways to optimize costs by using AWS Trusted Advisor.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Use the Trusted Advisor recommendations in the management account.  
B. Use the Trusted Advisor recommendations in the member accounts where the RDS DB instances are running.  
C. Review the Trusted Advisor checks for Amazon RDS Reserved Instance Optimization.  
D. Review the Trusted Advisor checks for Amazon RDS Idle DB Instances.  
E. Review the Trusted Advisor checks for compute optimization. Crosscheck the results by using AWS Compute Optimizer.  
Answer: AC  
Explanation: This answer has two parts.
