939\. A company uses an Amazon RDS for MySQL instance. To prepare for end-of-year processing, the company added a read replica to accommodate extra read-only queries from the company's reporting tool. The read replica CPU usage was 60% and the primary instance CPU usage was 60%.  
After end-of-year activities are complete, the read replica has a constant 25% CPU usage. The primary instance still has a constant 60% CPU usage. The company wants to rightsize the database and still provide enough performance for future growth.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Delete the read replica Do not make changes to the primary instance  
B. Resize the read replica to a smaller instance size Do not make changes to the primary instance  
C. Resize the read replica to a larger instance size Resize the primary instance to a smaller instance size  
D. Delete the read replica Resize the primary instance to a larger instance  
Answer: B  
Explanation: After year-end reporting wraps up, the replica is only a quarter loaded while the primary instance is still at sixty percent. That means the replica should be sized down while the primary is left alone: it's under a reasonable load and has headroom for growth.  
Why A is not selected: Deleting the replica sends the reporting queries back to the primary instance and overloads it again.  
Why C is not selected: Sizing the replica up at twenty-five percent utilization wastes money, and sizing the primary down at sixty percent removes its headroom for growth.  
Why D is not selected: Deleting the replica and sizing the primary up is the most expensive path and loses the separation of reads from writes.

---

940\. A company is migrating its databases to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The company is migrating its applications to Amazon EC2 instances. The company wants to optimize costs for long-running workloads.  
Which solution will meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Use On-Demand Instances for the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL workloads. Purchase a 1 year Compute Savings Plan with the No Upfront option for the EC2 instances.  
B. Purchase Reserved Instances for a 1 year term with the No Upfront option for the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL workloads. Purchase a 1 year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with the No Upfront option for the EC2 instances.  
C. Purchase Reserved Instances for a 1 year term with the Partial Upfront option for the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL workloads. Purchase a 1 year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with the Partial Upfront option for the EC2 instances.  
D. Purchase Reserved Instances for a 3 year term with the All Upfront option for the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL workloads. Purchase a 3 year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with the All Upfront option for the EC2 instances.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The workload is long-running and steady, and the goal is minimum cost. The biggest discount comes from the longest commitments with full upfront payment: three-year Reserved Instances for RDS and a three-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with All Upfront for the instances.  
Why A is not selected: On-Demand pricing for RDS is the most expensive mode for a steady workload.  
Why B is not selected: A one-year commitment with no upfront payment gives the smallest discount of all the commitment-based options.  
Why C is not selected: A one-year term with partial upfront saves less than three years with full upfront.

---

941\. A company is using an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster. The company must ensure that Kubernetes service accounts in the EKS cluster have secure and granular access to specific AWS resources by using IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA).  
Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Create an IAM policy that defines the required permissions Attach the policy directly to the IAM role of the EKS nodes.  
B. Implement network policies within the EKS cluster to prevent Kubernetes service accounts from accessing specific AWS services.  
C. Modify the EKS cluster's IAM role to include permissions for each Kubernetes service account. Ensure a one- to-one mapping between IAM roles and Kubernetes roles.  
D. Define an IAM role that includes the necessary permissions. Annotate the Kubernetes service accounts with the Amazon ResourceName (ARN) of the IAM role.  
E. Set up a trust relationship between the IAM roles for the service accounts and an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider.  
Answer: DE  
Explanation: IRSA is built from two halves. First: the EKS cluster has an OIDC provider, and the IAM role must trust exactly that provider — the trust policy names the provider and a condition scoped to a specific service account (E). Second: the Kubernetes service account itself is annotated with that role's ARN, after which pods running under it get temporary credentials via web identity (D). This way permissions are granted precisely to an application, not to the whole node.  
Why A is not selected: Permissions granted to the node's role are available to every pod on that node — the opposite of the granular access IRSA exists to provide.  
Why B is not selected: Kubernetes network policies restrict traffic between pods. They neither grant nor take away AWS API permissions.  
Why C is not selected: The cluster has no single role that permissions for every service account can be folded into: the mapping is done through individual roles via OIDC and annotations.

---

942\. A company regularly uploads confidential data to Amazon S3 buckets for analysis.  
The company's security policies mandate that the objects must be encrypted at rest. The company must automatically rotate the encryption key every year. The company must be able to track key rotation by using AWS CloudTrail. The company also must minimize costs for the encryption key.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C)  
B. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3)  
C. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)  
D. Use server-side encryption with customer managed AWS KMS keys  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The requirements are encryption at rest, automatic rotation exactly once a year, the ability to confirm rotation through CloudTrail, and minimum cost for the key. Rotation you can enable, verify, and see logged is only offered by a customer managed KMS key: it has an automatic rotation toggle (365 days), a history of key material, and CloudTrail entries for every use. The cost is one dollar a month per key plus request charges, which is the lowest price at which all three requirements are satisfied; the only further saving comes from turning on an S3 Bucket Key, as in {{q:1009}}.  
Why A is not selected: With SSE-C the customer manages the key: AWS doesn't store it, doesn't rotate it, and doesn't log its use. No automatic rotation and no CloudTrail trail.  
Why B is not selected: SSE-S3 is free, but the keys are invisible: the rotation period isn't documented, and there are no separate CloudTrail entries for key usage. The audit requirement isn't satisfied.  
Why C is not selected: Naming it without qualification means the AWS managed key (aws/s3): it's free and rotates on its own, but you control neither its policy nor its rotation and can't configure it. The control the scenario requires comes specifically from a customer managed key.

---

943\. A company has migrated several applications to AWS in the past 3 months. The company wants to know the breakdown of costs for each of these applications. The company wants to receive a regular report that includes this information.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Use AWS Budgets to download data for the past 3 months into a .csv file. Look up the desired information.  
B. Load AWS Cost and Usage Reports into an Amazon RDS DB instance. Run SQL queries to get the desired information.  
C. Tag all the AWS resources with a key for cost and a value of the application's name. Activate cost allocation tags. Use Cost Explorerto get the desired information.  
D. Tag all the AWS resources with a key for cost and a value of the application's name. Use the AWS Billing and Cost Management console todownload bills for the past 3 months. Look up the desired information.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: To see spending broken down by application, resources are tagged with the application's name, and that tag is activated as a cost allocation tag in the management account — billing ignores it until activation. After that, Cost Explorer builds a breakdown by tag value and can email a regular report. No extra services or storage needed, which also makes it the cheapest option.  
Why A is not selected: AWS Budgets doesn't export historical spend by application: it watches thresholds.  
Why B is not selected: Loading the CUR into an RDS instance means a continuously running database and writing your own queries — noticeably more expensive and complex than Cost Explorer.  
Why D is not selected: Downloading bills by hand every month is manual work, and without activating the tags no application breakdown appears in the bill at all.

---

944\. An ecommerce company is preparing to deploy a web application on AWS to ensure continuous service for customers. The architecture includes a web application that the company hosts on Amazon EC2 instances, a relational database in Amazon RDS, and static assets that the company stores in Amazon S3.  
The company wants to design a robust and resilient architecture for the application.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Deploy Amazon EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone. Deploy an RDS DB instance in the same Availability Zone. Use Amazon S3 with versioning enabled to store static assets.  
B. Deploy Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Deploy a Multi-AZ RDS DB instance. Use Amazon CloudFront to distribute static assets.  
C. Deploy Amazon EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone. Deploy an RDS DB instance in a second Availability Zone for cross-AZ redundancy. Serve static assets directly from the EC2 instances.  
D. Use AWS Lambda functions to serve the web application. Use Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 for the database. Store static assets in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) One Zone-Infrequent Access (One Zone-IA).  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Resiliency is built at all three layers at once. The web layer: an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones, so a zone failure doesn't stop the application. The database: RDS in a Multi-AZ configuration with automatic failover to the standby. Static content: S3 served through CloudFront, which takes load off the instances and brings content closer to users.  
Why A is not selected: A single Availability Zone for both the instances and the database: a zone failure stops the application entirely. Versioning protects against deletion, not downtime.  
Why C is not selected: The instances are still in one zone, and serving static content directly from them loads down the web layer and goes down along with it.  
Why D is not selected: The EFS One Zone-IA class lives in a single Availability Zone — the weakest link in a design that's supposed to be resilient.

---

945\. An ecommerce company runs several internal applications in multiple AWS accounts. The company uses AWS Organizations to manage its AWS accounts.  
A security appliance in the company's networking account must inspect interactions between applications across AWS accounts.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in the networking account to send traffic to the security appliance. Configure the application accounts to send traffic to the NLB by using an interface VPC endpoint in the application accounts.  
B. Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in the application accounts to send traffic directly to the security appliance.  
C. Deploy a Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) in the networking account to send traffic to the security appliance. Configure the application accounts to send traffic to the GWLB by using an interface GWLB endpoint in the application accounts.  
D. Deploy an interface VPC endpoint in the application accounts to send traffic directly to the security appliance.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The task is to pass traffic between accounts through a network security appliance transparently, without changing the applications. That's exactly what a Gateway Load Balancer was built for: it operates at layer 3, encapsulates traffic in GENEVE, and hands it off to a fleet of inspection appliances while preserving the original addresses. A GWLB endpoint (a flavor of PrivateLink) is created in the application accounts, and routes send traffic through it into the networking account. This is the standard pattern for centralized inspection.  
Why A is not selected: An NLB works at layer 4 and isn't built for transparent inspection: it terminates flows and changes the addressing scheme, while security appliances need the original traffic.  
Why B is not selected: An ALB is an HTTP request load balancer inside the application account. It doesn't provide centralized inspection of cross-account traffic.  
Why D is not selected: A plain interface endpoint publishes a specific service — it doesn't wrap arbitrary traffic for inspection. That specifically requires a GWLB endpoint.

---

946\. A company runs its production workload on an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster that includes six Aurora Replicas. The company wants near-real-time reporting queries from one of its departments to be automatically distributed across three of the Aurora Replicas. Those three replicas have a different compute and memory specification from the rest of the DB cluster.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Create and use a custom endpoint for the workload  
B. Create a three-node cluster clone and use the reader endpoint  
C. Use any of the instance endpoints for the selected three nodes  
D. Use the reader endpoint to automatically distribute the read-only workload  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Reporting queries need to be routed to three specific replicas with a distinct configuration. Aurora has a custom endpoint for exactly this: a defined set of instances is added to it, and requests are balanced only among those. The rest of the cluster never sees the reporting load.  
Why B is not selected: Cloning the cluster creates a separate copy of the data that stops receiving fresh writes: it won't be anywhere close to real time.  
Why C is not selected: A specific instance's endpoint points to exactly one machine: there's no automatic distribution across three replicas.  
Why D is not selected: The reader endpoint spreads requests across every replica in the cluster, including the other three, when only the three selected ones are wanted.

---

947\. A company runs a Node js function on a server in its on-premises data center. The data center stores data in a PostgreSQL database. The company stores the credentials in a connection string in an environment variable on the server. The company wants to migrate its application to AWS and to replace the Node.js application server with AWS Lambda. The company also wants to migrate to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and to ensure that the database credentials are securely managed.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Store the database credentials as a parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store Configure Parameter Store to automatically rotate the secrets every 30 days. Update the Lambda function to retrieve the credentials from the parameter.  
B. Store the database credentials as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure Secrets Manager to automatically rotate the credentials every 30 days. Update the Lambda function to retrieve the credentials from the secret.  
C. Store the database credentials as an encrypted Lambda environment variable. Write a custom Lambda function to rotate the credentials. Schedule the Lambda function to run every 30 days.  
D. Store the database credentials as a key in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Configure automatic rotation for the key. Update the Lambda function to retneve the credentials from the KMS key.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The connection string in the environment variable moves into Secrets Manager: the secret is stored encrypted with a KMS key, the Lambda function retrieves it with a GetSecretValue call under its execution role, and a ready-made AWS rotation function handles rotation for RDS PostgreSQL on a 30-day schedule. No custom code, and no redeploying the function whenever the password changes. A practical detail: the secret value is typically cached in the function's global scope or via the Parameters and Secrets Extension so the API isn't called on every invocation.  
Why A is not selected: Parameter Store stores the parameter encrypted, but it has no built-in automatic rotation — there's no way to "configure it in Parameter Store."  
Why C is not selected: An environment variable means the function has to be updated every time the password changes, and rotation has to be written by hand. That's the most operational effort of the options given.  
Why D is not selected: KMS stores encryption keys, not credentials: you can't retrieve a username and password from it, and rotating the key doesn't change the password in the database.

---

948\. A company wants to replicate existing and ongoing data changes from an on-premises Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. The amount of data to replicate varies throughout each day. The company wants to use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) for data replication. The solution must allocate only the capacity that the replication instance requires.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Configure the AWS DMS replication instance with a Multi-AZ deployment to provision instances across multiple Availability Zones.  
B. Create an AWS DMS Serverless replication task to analyze and replicate the data while provisioning the required capacity.  
C. Use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling to scale the size of the AWS DMS replication instance up or down based on the amount of data toreplicate.  
D. Provision AWS DMS replication capacity by using Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with an AWS Fargate launch type to analyze and replicate the data while provisioning the required capacity.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The volume of changes swings throughout the day, and exactly the needed capacity should be provisioned. That's a description of AWS DMS Serverless: the service assesses the load itself and picks compute units, scaling them up and down as it goes, so you never pay for idle capacity.  
Why A is not selected: A Multi-AZ configuration improves the replication instance's fault tolerance, but the capacity stays fixed.  
Why C is not selected: A DMS replication instance is a managed resource: it can't be placed into an EC2 Auto Scaling group.  
Why D is not selected: DMS can't be run in your own ECS containers: it's a managed service with its own way of provisioning capacity.

---

949\. A company has a multi-tier web application. The application's internal service components are deployed on Amazon EC2 instances. The internal service components need to access third-party software as a service (SaaS) APIs that are hosted on AWS.  
The company needs to provide secure and private connectivity from the application's internal services to the third- party SaaS application. The company needs to ensure that there is minimal public internet exposure.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Implement an AWS Site-to-Site VPN to establish a secure connection with the third-party SaaS provider.  
B. Deploy AWS Transit Gateway to manage and route traffic between the application's VPC and the third-party SaaS provider.  
C. Configure AWS PrivateLink to allow only outbound traffic from the VPC without enabling the third-party SaaS provider to establish.  
D. Use AWS PrivateLink to create a private connection between the application's VPC and the third-party SaaS provider.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The SaaS provider hosts its application on AWS, so it can be reached through AWS PrivateLink: the provider publishes its service behind a Network Load Balancer, the company creates an interface endpoint in its own VPC, and calls go to a private address. Traffic never leaves the AWS network, nothing is opened to the outside, and connections are only ever initiated from the company's side.  
Why A is not selected: Site-to-Site VPN connects a VPC to the company's own network, not to a third party's SaaS application: there's no customer gateway on their end for you to connect to.  
Why B is not selected: A transit gateway routes traffic between your own VPCs and sites, but it doesn't provide access to someone else's published service.  
Why C is not selected: This wording describes the same idea as the correct option but cuts off partway through and doesn't describe a working configuration: PrivateLink has no mode of "outbound traffic only, with no service published by the provider."

---

950\. A solutions architect needs to connect a company's corporate network to its VPC to allow on-premises access to its AWS resources. The solution must provide encryption of all traffic between the corporate network and the VPC at the network layer and the session layer. The solution also must provide security controls to prevent unrestricted access between AWS and the on-premises systems.  
Which solution meets these requirements?  
A. Configure AWS Direct Connect to connect to the VPC. Configure the VPC route tables to allow and deny traffic between AWS and on premises as required.  
B. Create an IAM policy to allow access to the AWS Management Console only from a defined set of corporate IP addresses. Restrict user access based on job responsibility by using an IAM policy and roles.  
C. Configure AWS Site-to-Site VPN to connect to the VPConfigure route table entries to direct traffic from on premises to the VPConfigure instance security groups and network ACLs to allow only required traffic from on premises.  
D. Configure AWS Transit Gateway to connect to the VPC. Configure route table entries to direct traffic from on premises to the VPC. Configure instance security groups and network ACLs to allow only required traffic from on premises.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The requirement of encryption "at the network and session layer" describes IPsec, i.e. AWS Site-to-Site VPN: the tunnel encrypts all traffic between the corporate network and the VPC. The second requirement, preventing unrestricted access, is met with network controls inside the VPC: routes send traffic through the virtual gateway, and security groups plus network ACLs allow only the necessary ports and subnets. Keep this key fact in mind: Direct Connect by itself doesn't encrypt traffic — VPN or MACsec has to be layered on top of it for encryption.  
Why A is not selected: Direct Connect is a dedicated link, but not an encrypted one: the encryption requirement isn't met. Route tables also aren't an access-control mechanism.  
Why B is not selected: IAM policies control access to the AWS API, while this is about a network connection between a data center and a VPC.  
Why D is not selected: A transit gateway connects networks to each other, but it doesn't by itself create an encrypted channel to the corporate network: VPN or Direct Connect is still needed for that.

---

951\. A company has a custom application with embedded credentials that retrieves information from a database in an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB cluster. The company needs to make the application more secure with minimal programming effort. The company has created credentials on the RDS for MySQL database for the application user.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Store the credentials in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Create keys in AWS KMS. Configure the application to load the database credentials from AWS KMS. Enable automatic key rotation  
B. Store the credentials in encrypted local storage. Configure the application to load the database credentials from the local storage. Set up a credentials rotation schedule by creating a cron job.  
C. Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Secrets Manager. Set up a credentials rotation schedule by creating an AWS Lambda function for Secrets Manager.  
D. Store the credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Parameter Store. Set up a credentials rotation schedule in the RDS for MySQL database by using Parameter Store.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The same task as {{q:339}}: remove hardcoded credentials and enable rotation without rewriting the application. Secrets Manager stores the username-password pair encrypted, the application reads it with a single call under its role, and rotation is handled by a ready-made function AWS provides as a template for RDS MySQL — it just needs to be turned on. The application never knows the password changed: it fetches the current secret value every time.  
Why A is not selected: KMS manages encryption keys and doesn't store logins and passwords. Rotating a key doesn't change the credentials in the database.  
Why B is not selected: Local storage plus a cron job means a copy of the secret on every server and hand-rolled synchronization with the database. That's more code and more risk than a managed service.  
Why D is not selected: Parameter Store has no mechanism for rotating database credentials: "configure a rotation schedule through Parameter Store" isn't possible.

---

952\. A company wants to move its application to a serverless solution. The serverless solution needs to analyze existing data and new data by using SQL. The company stores the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The data must be encrypted at rest and replicated to a different AWS Region.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create a new S3 bucket that uses server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region keys (SSE-KMS). Configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR). Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to query the data.  
B. Create a new S3 bucket that uses server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). Configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR). Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use Amazon RDS to query the data.  
C. Configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR) on the existing S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). Use Amazon Athena to query the data.  
D. Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) on the existing S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region keys (SSE-KMS). Use Amazon RDS to query the data.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: A verbatim repeat of question {{q:134}} with the same answer, and a handy check of understanding. Serverless SQL over data in S3 is Athena, so the RDS options are out immediately. From there, pick an encryption scheme compatible with cross-Region replication: a multi-Region KMS key exists in both Regions with the same key material, so replicas can be read in place with no re-encryption and no second key policy to manage.  
Why B is not selected: Amazon RDS is a database server that data has to be loaded into, while the requirement is serverless analysis of data already sitting in S3.  
Why C is not selected: Athena is the right choice, but SSE-S3 means separate, invisible keys in each Region: there's no way to manage them or confirm the replica is protected. The "encryption plus cross-Region replication" combination on the exam is solved with multi-Region KMS keys.  
Why D is not selected: The encryption choice is right, but RDS still isn't a serverless way to run SQL over S3 objects.

---

953\. A company has a web application that has thousands of users. The application uses 8-10 user-uploaded images to generate AI images. Users can download the generated AI images once every 6 hours. The company also has a premium user option that gives users the ability to download the generated AI images anytime.  
The company uses the user-uploaded images to run AI model training twice a year. The company needs a storage solution to store the images.  
Which storage solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Move uploaded images to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive. Move premium user-generated AI images to S3 Standard. Move non-premium user-generated AI images to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA).  
B. Move uploaded images to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive Move all generated AI images to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.  
C. Move uploaded images to Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA). Move premium user- generated AI images to S3 Standard. Move non-premium user-generated AI images to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA).  
D. Move uploaded images to Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA). Move all generated AI images to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: There are three different datasets here with three different access patterns, and the winning solution treats each one differently. The original uploaded images are needed twice a year for model training, with no urgency — the cheapest class, Glacier Deep Archive. Premium users' generated images can be downloaded anytime — S3 Standard. Regular users' generated images are available once every six hours, meaning infrequent reads that still need to be served instantly — Standard-IA. The general lesson: don't pick one storage class for a whole bucket when the scenario lists several distinct data categories.  
Why B is not selected: All generated images go to Glacier Flexible Retrieval, where an object takes minutes to hours to come back. A premium user promised download at any time shouldn't have to wait that long.  
Why C is not selected: One Zone-IA for the source images is both pricier than Deep Archive and riskier: a single copy in one Availability Zone for data touched twice a year is a bad tradeoff.  
Why D is not selected: Two mistakes at once: the source images sit in the pricier, less durable One Zone-IA, and the generated images are in Glacier, from which they can't be served to a user quickly.

---

954\. A company is developing machine learning (ML) models on AWS. The company is developing the ML models as independent microservices. The microservices fetch approximately 1 GB of model data from Amazon S3 at startup and load the data into memory. Users access the ML models through an asynchronous API. Users can send a request or a batch of requests.  
The company provides the ML models to hundreds of users. The usage patterns for the models are irregular. Some models are not used for days or weeks. Other models receive batches of thousands of requests at a time.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Direct the requests from the API to a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Deploy the ML models as AWS Lambda functions that the NLB will invoke. Use auto scaling to scale the Lambda functions based on the traffic that the NLB receives.  
B. Direct the requests from the API to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Deploy the ML models as Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) services that the ALB will invoke. Use auto scaling to scale the ECS cluster instances based on the traffic that the ALB receives.  
C. Direct the requests from the API into an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Deploy the ML models as AWS Lambda functions that SQS events will invoke. Use auto scaling to increase the number of vCPUs for the Lambda functions based on the size of the SQS queue.  
D. Direct the requests from the API into an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Deploy the ML models as Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) services that read from the queue. Use auto scaling for Amazon ECS to scale both the cluster capacity and number of the services based on the size of the SQS queue.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The same scenario as {{q:422}}: irregular load ranging from idle for weeks to thousands of requests at once, an asynchronous interface, and a gigabyte of model data in memory. An SQS queue accepts and holds requests, ECS services read from it, and auto scaling driven by queue length grows both the number of service copies and the cluster's capacity.  
Why A is not selected: A Network Load Balancer can't invoke Lambda functions as a target, and reloading a gigabyte of model data on every cold start is unacceptable.  
Why B is not selected: A load balancer in front of the models makes processing synchronous, whereas the interface is described as asynchronous, and a burst of thousands of requests would cause failures.  
Why C is not selected: The number of vCPUs for a Lambda function isn't something auto scaling adjusts, and a gigabyte-sized model doesn't fit the Lambda execution model well.

---

955\. A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application stores data in an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster.  
The company needs to create a disaster recovery (DR) solution. The acceptable recovery time for the DR solution is up to 30 minutes. The DR solution does not need to support customer usage when the primary infrastructure is healthy.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Deploy the DR infrastructure in a second AWS Region with an ALB and an Auto Scaling group. Set the desired capacity and maximum capacity of the Auto Scaling group to a minimum value. Convert the Aurora MySQL DB cluster to an Aurora global database. Configure Amazon Route 53 for an active-passive failover with ALB endpoints.  
B. Deploy the DR infrastructure in a second AWS Region with an ALUpdate the Auto Scaling group to include EC2 instances from the second Region. Use Amazon Route 53 to configure active-active failover. Convert the Aurora MySQL DB cluster to an Aurora global database.  
C. Back up the Aurora MySQL DB cluster data by using AWS Backup. Deploy the DR infrastructure in a second AWS Region with an ALB. Update the Auto Scaling group to include EC2 instances from the second Region. Use Amazon Route 53 to configure active-active failover. Create an Aurora MySQL DB cluster in the second Region Restore the data from the backup.  
D. Back up the infrastructure configuration by using AWS Backup. Use the backup to create the required infrastructure in a second AWS Region. Set the Auto Scaling group desired capacity to zero. Use Amazon Route 53 to configure active-passive failover. Convert the Aurora MySQL DB cluster to an Aurora global database.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The acceptable recovery time is 30 minutes, and the standby site doesn't need to serve customers while the primary is healthy. That's the pilot light pattern: a load balancer and an Auto Scaling group at minimal capacity are pre-deployed in the second Region, the Aurora cluster is converted into a global database with continuous replication, and Route 53 is set up for active-passive failover based on health checks. During an outage the group scales up and the secondary cluster is promoted to primary — all within the time limit.  
Why B is not selected: An active-active setup serves traffic in the second Region continuously, which the scenario doesn't call for, and it costs noticeably more. An Auto Scaling group also can't span instances across Regions.  
Why C is not selected: Restoring the database from a backup gives an RPO measured in hours, whereas a global database keeps it at seconds. And an Auto Scaling group still can't be cross-Region.  
Why D is not selected: Desired capacity of zero means instances have to boot from scratch during a disaster along with application warm-up, and the infrastructure itself is only created from a configuration backup after the failure happens. Hitting 30 minutes is far from reliable.

---

956\. A company is migrating its data processing application to the AWS Cloud. The application processes several short- lived batch jobs that cannot be disrupted. Data is generated after each batch job is completed. The data is accessed for 30 days and retained for 2 years.  
The company wants to keep the cost of running the application in the AWS Cloud as low as possible.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Migrate the data processing application to Amazon EC2 Spot Instances. Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard. Move the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Instant. Retrieval after 30 days. Set an expiration to delete the data after 2 years.  
B. Migrate the data processing application to Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances. Store the data in Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval. Move the data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days. Set an expiration to delete the data after 2 years.  
C. Deploy Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to run the batch jobs. Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard. Move the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days. Set an expiration to delete the data after 2 years.  
D. Deploy Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances to run the batch jobs. Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard. Move the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days. Set an expiration to delete the data after 2 years.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The first requirement rules out half the options: jobs "cannot be disrupted," and AWS reclaims Spot Instances with only a two-minute warning. So compute has to be On-Demand (which, for short batch jobs, is also cheaper than a reservation since you only pay for actual runtime). Second, the data: 30 days of active access is Standard, then almost two years sitting untouched is Glacier Deep Archive, the cheapest class, plus expiration after 2 years so you stop paying.  
Why A is not selected: Spot Instances get interrupted, and the scenario explicitly forbids interrupting the jobs. Glacier Instant Retrieval for two years of untouched storage is also roughly four times pricier than Deep Archive.  
Why B is not selected: Compute is chosen correctly, but the data is actively read for the first 30 days, and Glacier Instant Retrieval charges per retrieval. It also has a 90-day minimum storage duration, so moving to Deep Archive on day 30 triggers an early-deletion penalty.  
Why C is not selected: The same mistake with Spot, plus Glacier Flexible Retrieval costs more than Deep Archive, and fast access to data older than 30 days isn't required by the scenario.

---

957\. A company needs to design a hybrid network architecture. The company's workloads are currently stored in the AWS Cloud and in on-premises data centers. The workloads require single-digit latencies to communicate. The company uses an AWS Transit Gateway transit gateway to connect multiple VPCs.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)  
A. Establish an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to each VPC.  
B. Associate an AWS Direct Connect gateway with the transit gateway that is attached to the VPCs.  
C. Establish an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to an AWS Direct Connect gateway.  
D. Establish an AWS Direct Connect connection. Create a transit virtual interface (VIF) to a Direct Connect gateway.  
E. Associate AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections with the transit gateway that is attached to the VPCs.  
Answer: BD  
Explanation: Single-digit-millisecond latency rules out the internet and VPN — a dedicated connection is needed. A Direct Connect connection is created with a transit virtual interface to a Direct Connect gateway (D), and that Direct Connect gateway is then associated with the existing transit gateway (B). That single pair of objects gives the site connectivity to every VPC attached to the transit gateway, and adding new networks changes nothing about this setup.  
Why A is not selected: A separate VPN per VPC runs over the internet: latency is unpredictable, and the single-digit-millisecond requirement isn't met.  
Why C is not selected: A VPN connection isn't established directly to a Direct Connect gateway — that construction doesn't exist. A VPN terminates on a virtual private gateway or a transit gateway.  
Why E is not selected: Associating a VPN with a transit gateway is possible, but it's again a path over the internet with unpredictable latency.

---

958\. A global ecommerce company runs its critical workloads on AWS. The workloads use an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance that is configured for a Multi-AZ deployment.  
Customers have reported application timeouts when the company undergoes database failovers. The company needs a resilient solution to reduce failover time.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create an Amazon RDS Proxy. Assign the proxy to the DB instance.  
B. Create a read replica for the DB instance. Move the read traffic to the read replica.  
C. Enable Performance Insights. Monitor the CPU load to identify the timeouts.  
D. Take regular automatic snapshots. Copy the automatic snapshots to multiple AWS Regions.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The timeouts happen right at the moment of the switch: the application is still holding connections to the old primary instance and doesn't learn about the change immediately. RDS Proxy maintains a connection pool and redirects it to the new primary itself, cutting the failover time the application experiences by more than half.  
Why B is not selected: A read replica takes load off the primary instance but has no effect on failover duration.  
Why C is not selected: Performance Insights helps find the bottleneck but doesn't speed anything up on its own.  
Why D is not selected: Copying snapshots to other Regions is a disaster recovery concern, not the speed of failover within a Multi-AZ configuration.

---

959\. A company has multiple Amazon RDS DB instances that run in a development AWS account. All the instances have tags to identify them as development resources. The company needs the development DB instances to run on a schedule only during business hours.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to identify RDS instances that need to be stopped. Create an AWS Lambda function to start and stop the RDS instances.  
B. Create an AWS Trusted Advisor report to identify RDS instances to be started and stopped. Create an AWS Lambda function to start and stop the RDS instances.  
C. Create AWS Systems Manager State Manager associations to start and stop the RDS instances.  
D. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that invokes AWS Lambda functions to start and stop the RDS instances.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The instances are already tagged, and all that's needed is starting and stopping them on a schedule. State Manager associations in Systems Manager do this out of the box: the target is selected by tag, the action and schedule are set through configuration, and there's no custom code at all.  
Why A is not selected: A CloudWatch alarm tracks metrics, not the time of day, and would still require a custom function.  
Why B is not selected: Trusted Advisor gives optimization recommendations, not a list of instances to start and stop on a schedule.  
Why D is not selected: A schedule with functions works, but that's custom code that has to be written and maintained, while State Manager solves the task with configuration alone.

---

960\. A consumer survey company has gathered data for several years from a specific geographic region. The company stores this data in an Amazon S3 bucket in an AWS Region.  
The company has started to share this data with a marketing firm in a new geographic region. The company has granted the firm's AWS account access to the S3 bucket. The company wants to minimize the data transfer costs when the marketing firm requests data from the S3 bucket.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Configure the Requester Pays feature on the company’s S3 bucket.  
B. Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) from the company’s S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm’s S3 buckets.  
C. Configure AWS Resource Access Manager to share the S3 bucket with the marketing firm AWS account.  
D. Configure the company’s S3 bucket to use S3 Intelligent-Tiering Sync the S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm’s S3 buckets.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The same technique as in question {{q:88}}: outbound traffic from S3 is billed to the bucket owner by default, and Requester Pays flips that rule. The marketing firm accesses the bucket under its own account and pays for both the requests and the outbound transfer, while the company continues paying only for storage. The firm already has access — nothing about that needs to change, only the billing. Keep in mind: with Requester Pays every request must be signed and include acknowledgment of paying, and anonymous requests are rejected.  
Why B is not selected: Cross-Region Replication means the company itself pays for cross-Region transfer of every object plus storing the copy. That's a cost increase, not a decrease.  
Why C is not selected: AWS Resource Access Manager can't share S3 buckets — bucket access is granted through a bucket policy or a cross-account role. And even with access granted, the transfer bill would still land on the owner.  
Why D is not selected: The storage class has no effect on outbound transfer cost, and syncing to someone else's bucket is an export paid for by the company.

---

961\. A company uses AWS to host its public ecommerce website. The website uses an AWS Global Accelerator accelerator for traffic from the internet. The Global Accelerator accelerator forwards the traffic to an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that is the entry point for an Auto Scaling group.  
The company recently identified a DDoS attack on the website. The company needs a solution to mitigate future attacks.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST implementation effort?  
A. Configure an AWS WAF web ACL for the Global Accelerator accelerator to block traffic by using rate-based rules  
B. Configure an AWS Lambda function to read the ALB metrics to block attacks by updating a VPC network ACL  
C. Configure an AWS WAF web ACL on the ALB to block traffic by using rate-based rules  
D. Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the Global Accelerator accelerator  
Answer: C  
Review status: Corrected key (source: A; reviewed: C)  
Correction note: AWS WAF doesn't support AWS Global Accelerator as a protected resource (supported resources are CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito, App Runner, and Verified Access), so the web ACL is attached to the ALB behind the accelerator  
Explanation: The dump key was corrected during the audit. Rate limiting is configured with an AWS WAF rule, but a web ACL can't be attached to Global Accelerator: the service isn't among the resource types WAF supports (CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito, App Runner, Verified Access). So the rate-based rule is created on the Application Load Balancer that sits behind the accelerator and receives its traffic. The change is minimal — the architecture stays the same, only a web ACL is added to the existing load balancer.  
Why A is not selected: The original dump key. AWS Global Accelerator isn't a resource a WAF web ACL can attach to, so this configuration isn't possible.  
Why B is not selected: A custom function reading metrics and editing network ACLs means code, a delayed response, and the hard limit on rules in an ACL.  
Why D is not selected: Putting CloudFront in front of Global Accelerator is a significant architectural rework, while the requirement calls for minimal effort.

---

962\. A company uses an Amazon DynamoDB table to store data that the company receives from devices. The DynamoDB table supports a customer-facing website to display recent activity on customer devices. The company configured the table with provisioned throughput for writes and reads.  
The company wants to calculate performance metrics for customer device data on a daily basis. The solution must have minimal effect on the table's provisioned read and write capacity.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use an Amazon Athena SQL query with the Amazon Athena DynamoDB connector to calculate performance metrics on a recurring schedule.  
B. Use an AWS Glue job with the AWS Glue DynamoDB export connector to calculate performance metrics on a recurring schedule.  
C. Use an Amazon Redshift COPY command to calculate performance metrics on a recurring schedule.  
D. Use an Amazon EMR job with an Apache Hive external table to calculate performance metrics on a recurring schedule.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Calculating metrics shouldn't touch the table's provisioned capacity. The DynamoDB export connector in AWS Glue reads data not from the table itself but from an export to S3 produced by the backup mechanism, so no read capacity units are consumed at all.  
Why A is not selected: The Athena connector for DynamoDB scans the table itself and consumes its read capacity.  
Why C is not selected: Redshift's COPY command can't read a DynamoDB table without spending its capacity — it performs a scan.  
Why D is not selected: A Hive external table in EMR also reads the table directly, taking read capacity away from the customer-facing site.

---

963\. A solutions architect is designing the cloud architecture for a new stateless application that will be deployed on AWS. The solutions architect created an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) and launch template for the application.  
Based on the number of jobs that need to be processed, the processing must run in parallel while adding and removing application Amazon EC2 instances as needed. The application must be loosely coupled. The job items must be durably stored.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to send the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Auto Scaling group by using the launch template with the scaling policy set to add and remove EC2 instances based on CPU usage.  
B. Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to hold the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Auto Scaling group by using the launch template with the scaling policy set to add and remove EC2 instances based on network usage.  
C. Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to hold the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Auto Scaling group by using the launch template with the scaling policy set to add and remove EC2 instances based on the number of items in the SQS queue.  
D. Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to send the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Auto Scaling group by using the launch template with the scaling policy set to add and remove EC2 instances based on the number of messages published to the SNS topic.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Jobs need to be stored durably, processed in parallel, and stay loosely coupled. An SQS queue stores jobs durably and decouples the sender from the processors, while an Auto Scaling group grows and shrinks based on the number of messages in the queue — that is, on actual work volume rather than an indirect signal.  
Why A is not selected: SNS doesn't store messages: if there's no ready subscriber, the job is lost, and scaling on CPU doesn't reflect queue length.  
Why B is not selected: The queue choice is right, but scaling on network usage is an indirect signal that may not correlate with the number of jobs at all.  
Why D is not selected: An SNS topic again doesn't provide durable storage of jobs.

---

964\. A global ecommerce company uses a monolithic architecture. The company needs a solution to manage the increasing volume of product data. The solution must be scalable and have a modular service architecture. The company needs to maintain its structured database schemas. The company also needs a storage solution to store product data and product images.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use an Amazon EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group to deploy a containerized application. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute web traffic. Use an Amazon RDS DB instance to store product data and product images.  
B. Use AWS Lambda functions to manage the existing monolithic application. Use Amazon DynamoDB to store product data and product images. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) for event-driven communication between the Lambda functions.  
C. Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with an Amazon EC2 deployment to deploy a containerized application. Use an Amazon Aurora cluster to store the product data. Use AWS Step Functions to manage workflows. Store the product images in Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.  
D. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate to deploy a containerized application. Use Amazon RDS with a Multi-AZ deployment to store the product data. Store the product images in an Amazon S3 bucket.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The requirements are a modular architecture instead of a monolith, keeping the structured database schema, storing images, and minimal operations. ECS on Fargate runs container services with no managed node to look after, RDS in a Multi-AZ configuration preserves the relational schema and provides fault tolerance, and images go into S3, which grows without limit.  
Why A is not selected: EC2 instances have to be patched and scaled by you, and storing images in a relational database is a bad practice that bloats it and drives up cost.  
Why B is not selected: A monolith wrapped inside Lambda functions doesn't become modular, and DynamoDB's 400 KB item size limit makes storing images impossible.  
Why C is not selected: EKS on EC2 instances requires managing nodes, and Glacier Deep Archive takes hours to retrieve an object — unacceptable for product images.

---

965\. A company is migrating an application from an on-premises environment to AWS. The application will store sensitive data in Amazon S3. The company must encrypt the data before storing the data in Amazon S3.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Encrypt the data by using client-side encryption with customer managed keys.  
B. Encrypt the data by using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS).  
C. Encrypt the data by using server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C).  
D. Encrypt the data by using client-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: "The company must encrypt the data before storing the data in Amazon S3" means encryption has to happen on the application side, before it's sent. That's client-side encryption using a key the company controls (typically a customer managed KMS key via envelope encryption, or a key of its own). Every SSE-based option is out by definition: those are performed by the service after the object is received. Compare this with {{q:801}}, which additionally requires keeping the keys entirely outside AWS.  
Why B is not selected: SSE-KMS encrypts the object only after S3 has already received it. The "before storing" requirement isn't met.  
Why C is not selected: With SSE-C the client sends the key along with the request, but S3 is still the one doing the encryption after receiving the plaintext data. The key also travels over the network with every request.  
Why D is not selected: Client-side encryption with keys managed by S3 isn't possible: those keys never leave the service and aren't available to the application.

---

966\. A company wants to create an Amazon EMR cluster that multiple teams will use. The company wants to ensure that each team’s big data workloads can access only the AWS services that each team needs to interact with. The company does not want the workloads to have access to Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2) on the cluster’s underlying EC2 instances.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Configure interface VPC endpoints for each AWS service that the teams need. Use the required interface VPC endpoints to submit the big data workloads.  
B. Create EMR runtime roles. Configure the cluster to use the runtime roles. Use the runtime roles to submit the big data workloads.  
C. Create an EC2 IAM instance profile that has the required permissions for each team. Use the instance profile to submit the big data workloads.  
D. Create an EMR security configuration that has the EnableApplicationScopedIAMRole option set to false. Use the security configuration to submit the big data workloads.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The task is to give each team its own permissions on a shared EMR cluster while keeping jobs from reaching the instance role's credentials through instance metadata. That's EMR runtime roles: a job is submitted specifying a role, EMR runs it as that role, and access to the instance profile from the job's code is blocked. That way the same infrastructure serves teams with different permissions.  
Why A is not selected: Interface endpoints control the traffic path, not what permissions a job has. They can't separate teams by permission.  
Why C is not selected: An instance profile grants the same permissions to every job on the cluster and stays reachable through instance metadata — exactly what needs to be avoided.  
Why D is not selected: Turning off application-scoped roles does the opposite: it reverts job execution back to the shared instance role instead of runtime roles.

---

967\. A solutions architect is designing an application that helps users fill out and submit registration forms. The solutions architect plans to use a two-tier architecture that includes a web application server tier and a worker tier.  
The application needs to process submitted forms quickly. The application needs to process each form exactly once. The solution must ensure that no data is lost.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue between the web application server tier and the worker tier to store and forward form data.  
B. Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API between the web application server tier and the worker tier to store and forward form data.  
C. Use an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue between the web application server tier and the worker tier to store and forward form data.  
D. Use an AWS Step Functions workflow. Create a synchronous workflow between the web application server tier and the worker tier that stores and forwards form data.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Forms need to be processed exactly once with nothing lost. An SQS FIFO queue provides exactly that: the message is stored durably, duplicates within the deduplication window are dropped, and ordering and exactly-once processing are both guaranteed.  
Why B is not selected: An HTTP API forwards the request onward but stores nothing: if the processor is unavailable, the data is lost.  
Why C is not selected: A standard queue guarantees at-least-once delivery, so the same form could be processed twice.  
Why D is not selected: A synchronous workflow ties the tiers together tightly: if the processor is busy or down, the data is lost again.

---

968\. A finance company uses an on-premises search application to collect streaming data from various producers. The application provides real-time updates to search and visualization features.  
The company is planning to migrate to AWS and wants to use an AWS native solution.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use Amazon EC2 instances to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon S3 buckets tor storage. Use Amazon Athena to search the data. Use Amazon Managed Grafana to create visualizations.  
B. Use Amazon EMR to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon Redshift for storage. Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to search the data. Use Amazon QuickSight to create visualizations.  
C. Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon DynamoDB for storage. Use Amazon CloudWatch to create graphical dashboards to search and visualize the data.  
D. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon OpenSearch Service. Use OpenSearch Service to search the data. Use Amazon QuickSight to create visualizations.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The requirements are ingesting streaming data, near-real-time search, and visualization — using AWS-native services. Kinesis Data Streams ingests the streams from the producers, OpenSearch Service indexes them and provides search with real-time updates, and Amazon QuickSight builds the dashboards.  
Why A is not selected: Self-managed instances to ingest the stream is unnecessary operations, and Athena gives queries over data in S3 with a delay, not real-time search.  
Why B is not selected: EMR and Redshift are batch and analytical processing: they don't provide real-time updates.  
Why C is not selected: An EKS cluster for stream ingestion means managing infrastructure, and CloudWatch isn't a search engine for application data.

---

969\. A company currently runs an on-premises application that usesASP.NET on Linux machines. The application is resource-intensive and serves customers directly.  
The company wants to modernize the application to .NET. The company wants to run the application on containers and to scale based on Amazon CloudWatch metrics. The company also wants to reduce the time spent on operational maintenance activities.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use AWS App2Container to containerize the application. Use an AWS CloudFormation template to deploy the application to Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate.  
B. Use AWS App2Container to containerize the application. Use an AWS CloudFormation template to deploy the application to Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on Amazon EC2 instances.  
C. Use AWS App Runner to containerize the application. Use App Runner to deploy the application to Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate.  
D. Use AWS App Runner to containerize the application. Use App Runner to deploy the application to Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) on Amazon EC2 instances.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The application needs to be containerized and run without managing infrastructure. AWS App2Container analyzes the running application and produces an image along with deployment artifacts, including a CloudFormation template, and ECS on Fargate runs the containers with no node to manage, scaling based on CloudWatch metrics.  
Why B is not selected: The EC2 launch type brings node management back: operations don't decrease.  
Why C is not selected: App Runner isn't a tool for containerizing an existing application and doesn't deploy workloads onto ECS: it's a standalone run service.  
Why D is not selected: The same mistake about App Runner's role, and EC2 nodes in EKS again mean managing infrastructure.

---

970\. A company is designing a new internal web application in the AWS Cloud. The new application must securely retrieve and store multiple employee usernames and passwords from an AWS managed service.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Store the employee credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Use AWS CloudFormation and the BatchGetSecretValue API to retrieve usernames and passwords from Parameter Store.  
B. Store the employee credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Use AWS CloudFormation and AWS Batch with the BatchGetSecretValue API to retrieve the usernames and passwords from Secrets Manager.  
C. Store the employee credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Use AWS CloudFormation and AWS Batch with the BatchGetSecretValue API to retrieve the usernames and passwords from Parameter Store.  
D. Store the employee credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Use AWS CloudFormation and the BatchGetSecretValue API to retrieve the usernames and passwords from Secrets Manager.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: What needs to be stored is specifically credentials — username-password pairs — using a managed service with minimal effort. That's Secrets Manager: secrets are encrypted with a KMS key, access is granted through a role, and there's a dedicated BatchGetSecretValue call for reading many secrets in a single request. The presence of that API in the scenario is itself the clue: Parameter Store has no such operation.  
Why A is not selected: Parameter Store has no BatchGetSecretValue call: that API belongs specifically to Secrets Manager. This option describes a combination that doesn't exist.  
Why B is not selected: AWS Batch is a service for running batch compute jobs on containers — it has nothing to do with reading secrets. An unnecessary component in the design.  
Why C is not selected: Two mistakes at once: the store is picked without the needed API, and AWS Batch is added for no reason.

---

971\. A company that is in the ap-northeast-1 Region has a fleet of thousands of AWS Outposts servers. The company has deployed the servers at remote locations around the world. All the servers regularly download new software versions that consist of 100 files. There is significant latency before all servers run the new software versions.  
The company must reduce the deployment latency for new software versions.  
Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create an Amazon S3 bucket in ap-northeast-1. Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution in ap-northeast-1 that includes a CachingDisabled cache policy. Configure the S3 bucket as the origin. Download the software by using signed URLs.  
B. Create an Amazon S3 bucket in ap-northeast-1. Create a second S3 bucket in the us-east-1 Region. Configure replication between the buckets. Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses ap-northeast-1 as the primary origin and us-east-1 as the secondary origin. Download the software by using signed URLs.  
C. Create an Amazon S3 bucket in ap-northeast-1. Configure Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration. Download the software by using the S3 Transfer Acceleration endpoint.  
D. Create an Amazon S3 bucket in ap-northeast-1. Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Configure the S3 bucket as the origin. Download the software by using signed URLs.  
Answer: C  
Review status: Disputed key (alternative: D)  
Dispute note: Repeatedly serving the same files from servers in different regions is what CloudFront caching does; Transfer Acceleration primarily speeds up uploads to S3 and doesn't cache  
Explanation: Thousands of Outposts servers worldwide regularly download the same set of 100 files from a bucket in ap-northeast-1. Identical content, many remote consumers, repeated downloads — that's a textbook CDN problem: CloudFront caches the files at edge locations, so the second and every subsequent server in a region gets them locally. The dump key picks C (S3 Transfer Acceleration), and that's its weak point: Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfer over the AWS backbone, but it caches nothing, so each of the thousands of servers still pulls the file all the way from Tokyo. On the merits, option D is the stronger fit.  
Why A is not selected: The CachingDisabled policy turns off caching, removing the one reason to put CloudFront in front at all. Every request still goes all the way to the origin in ap-northeast-1.  
Why B is not selected: Replicating to a second bucket with origin failover solves a fault-tolerance problem, not latency. It's also doubled storage and extra configuration on top of a "LEAST operational overhead" requirement.  
Why D is not selected: This option addresses the problem on its merits: CloudFront caches the 100 files at edge locations near the servers, and repeat downloads happen locally. This is where the disagreement with the dump key lies.

---

972\. A company currently runs an on-premises stock trading application by using Microsoft Windows Server. The company wants to migrate the application to the AWS Cloud.  
The company needs to design a highly available solution that provides low-latency access to block storage across multiple Availability Zones.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST implementation effort?  
A. Configure a Windows Server cluster that spans two Availability Zones on Amazon EC2 instances. Install the application on both cluster nodes. Use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server as shared storage between the two cluster nodes.  
B. Configure a Windows Server cluster that spans two Availability Zones on Amazon EC2 instances. Install the application on both cluster nodes. Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) General Purpose SSD (gp3) volumes as storage attached to the EC2 instances. Set up application-level replication to sync data from one EBS volume in one Availability Zone to another EBS volume in the second Availability Zone.  
C. Deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. Configure one EC2 instance as active and the second EC2 instance in standby mode. Use an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP Multi-AZ file system to access the data by using Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI) protocol.  
D. Deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. Configure one EC2 instance as active and the second EC2 instance in standby mode. Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volumes as storage attached to the EC2 instances. Set up Amazon EBS level replication to sync data from one io2 volume in one Availability Zone to another io2 volume in the second Availability Zone.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: A Windows Server cluster needs shared storage reachable by both nodes, and the nodes must sit in different Availability Zones. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server takes the least effort here: it supports continuously available shares for clustering, replicates synchronously between zones, and provides high availability on its own. Nothing needs to be written or configured by hand.  
Why B is not selected: Application-level replication between two gp3 volumes is hand-rolled logic, with a risk of divergence and the most implementation work of the options.  
Why C is not selected: An active/standby setup without a cluster provides no automatic failover, and iSCSI access to ONTAP takes more configuration than a ready-made shared folder.  
Why D is not selected: There's no such thing as service-level EBS volume replication across Availability Zones — that capability doesn't exist.

---

973\. A company is designing a web application with an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB).  
The company needs the ALB to receive HTTPS web traffic from the public internet. The ALB must send only HTTPS traffic to the web application servers hosted on the Amazon EC2 instances on port 443. The ALB must perform a health check of the web application servers over HTTPS on port 8443.  
Which combination of configurations of the security group that is associated with the ALB will meet these requirements? (Choose three.)  
A. Allow HTTPS inbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 for port 443.  
B. Allow all outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 for port 443.  
C. Allow HTTPS outbound traffic to the web application instances for port 443.  
D. Allow HTTPS inbound traffic from the web application instances for port 443.  
E. Allow HTTPS outbound traffic to the web application instances for the health check on port 8443.  
F. Allow HTTPS inbound traffic from the web application instances for the health check on port 8443.  
Answer: ACE  
Explanation: This is about the load balancer's own security group, so one inbound rule and two outbound rules are needed. Inbound HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443 is the public internet traffic (A). Outbound HTTPS to the instances on port 443 forwards requests to the application (C). Outbound HTTPS to the instances on port 8443 is the health check (E).  
Why B is not selected: Allowing outbound traffic to the whole internet is excessive: the load balancer only needs to reach its own targets.  
Why D is not selected: An inbound rule from the instances isn't needed: the load balancer initiates the connections to the targets, and the responses are permitted by connection state.  
Why F is not selected: The same applies to health checks: they're outbound, so no inbound rule is needed for them.

---

974\. A company hosts an application on AWS. The application gives users the ability to upload photos and store the photos in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company wants to use Amazon CloudFront and a custom domain name to upload the photo files to the S3 bucket in the eu-west-1 Region.  
Which solution will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create a public certificate in the us-east-1 Region. Use the certificate in CloudFront.  
B. Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create a public certificate in eu-west-1. Use the certificate in CloudFront.  
C. Configure Amazon S3 to allow uploads from CloudFront. Configure S3 Transfer Acceleration.  
D. Configure Amazon S3 to allow uploads from CloudFront origin access control (OAC).  
E. Configure Amazon S3 to allow uploads from CloudFront. Configure an Amazon S3 website endpoint.  
Answer: AD  
Review status: Corrected key (source: BD; reviewed: AD)  
Correction note: The certificate for CloudFront must be issued in us-east-1 regardless of the bucket's region  
Explanation: Two independent requirements. A certificate for a custom domain on CloudFront always comes from ACM in us-east-1 (A) — the bucket's Region doesn't matter. And the ability to write to the bucket through the distribution comes from origin access control (D): CloudFront supports uploads to S3 via OAC.  
Why B is not selected: A certificate issued in eu-west-1 simply won't be visible to CloudFront: the distribution only pulls certificates from us-east-1.  
Why C is not selected: S3 Transfer Acceleration is a separate endpoint for faster uploads straight to S3. It doesn't grant CloudFront write access and isn't needed alongside a distribution.  
Why E is not selected: An S3 website endpoint serves static content over HTTP, doesn't support uploads, and doesn't work with OAC.

---

975\. A weather forecasting company collects temperature readings from various sensors on a continuous basis. An existing data ingestion process collects the readings and aggregates the readings into larger Apache Parquet files. Then the process encrypts the files by using client-side encryption with KMS managed keys (CSE-KMS).  
Finally, the process writes the files to an Amazon S3 bucket with separate prefixes for each calendar day.  
The company wants to run occasional SQL queries on the data to take sample moving averages for a specific calendar day.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Configure Amazon Athena to read the encrypted files. Run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.  
B. Use Amazon S3 Select to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.  
C. Configure Amazon Redshift to read the encrypted files. Use Redshift Spectrum and Redshift query editor v2 to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.  
D. Configure Amazon EMR Serverless to read the encrypted files. Use Apache SparkSQL to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The data already sits in S3 as Parquet, client-side encrypted with a KMS key (CSE-KMS), and queries are only needed occasionally. Amazon Athena reads such files directly: it supports client-side encryption with KMS keys, understands Parquet and prefix-based partitions, and you're billed only for the bytes scanned — a query for a single calendar day scans only that day's prefix. No cluster, no standing infrastructure. Cost tip: columnar format plus partitions plus a partition filter cut the Athena bill by a large factor.  
Why B is not selected: S3 Select works on one object per request and can't read data encrypted on the client side. A moving average across many files can't be computed this way.  
Why C is not selected: Redshift Spectrum requires a Redshift cluster, which is billed continuously, while queries here are only occasional. That's a noticeable overpay for sporadic lookups.  
Why D is not selected: EMR Serverless would work, but it's already the Spark framework with its own configuration and startup cost. For a handful of SQL queries, Athena is simpler and cheaper.

---

976\. A company is implementing a new application on AWS. The company will run the application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones within multiple AWS Regions. The application will be available through the internet. Users will access the application from around the world.  
The company wants to ensure that each user who accesses the application is sent to the EC2 instances that are closest to the user’s location.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Implement an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy. Use an internet-facing Application Load Balancer to distribute the traffic across all Availability Zones within the same Region.  
B. Implement an Amazon Route 53 geoproximity routing policy. Use an internet-facing Network Load Balancer to distribute the traffic across all Availability Zones within the same Region.  
C. Implement an Amazon Route 53 multivalue answer routing policy. Use an internet-facing Application Load Balancer to distribute the traffic across all Availability Zones within the same Region.  
D. Implement an Amazon Route 53 weighted routing policy. Use an internet-facing Network Load Balancer to distribute the traffic across all Availability Zones within the same Region.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The requirement is to route each user to the geographically closest instances. In Route 53, geoproximity is what handles distance: it computes proximity to the coordinates given for each resource and lets you shift the boundaries of influence with the bias parameter. Within a Region, the load balancer already spreads requests across all Availability Zones.  
Why A is not selected: Geolocation routes by the requester's country or continent, not by distance: a user near a border can easily be sent to a far-away Region simply because that's what the rule says for their country.  
Why C is not selected: Multivalue answer returns a random set of healthy records and doesn't account for proximity to the user at all.  
Why D is not selected: A weighted policy splits traffic in set proportions regardless of where the request came from.
