---

977\. A financial services company plans to launch a new application on AWS to handle sensitive financial transactions.  
The company will deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances. The company will use Amazon RDS for MySQL as the database. The company’s security policies mandate that data must be encrypted at rest and in transit.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Configure encryption at rest for Amazon RDS for MySQL by using AWS KMS managed keys. Configure AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) SSL/TLS certificates for encryption in transit.  
B. Configure encryption at rest for Amazon RDS for MySQL by using AWS KMS managed keys. Configure IPsec tunnels for encryption in transit.  
C. Implement third-party application-level data encryption before storing data in Amazon RDS for MySQL. Configure AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) SSL/TLS certificates for encryption in transit.  
D. Configure encryption at rest for Amazon RDS for MySQL by using AWS KMS managed keys. Configure a VPN connection to enable private connectivity to encrypt data in transit.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Both directions need to be covered with minimal effort. At rest: turn on RDS encryption with a KMS key — it covers disks, snapshots, backups, and replicas, and needs no application changes. In transit: TLS, and the public-facing part (the load balancer, the application's domain) is covered by a free ACM certificate with automatic renewal. A useful detail about the database connection itself: ACM doesn't issue a certificate for it — the client has to trust RDS's root certificate from the AWS bundle, as covered in {{q:743}}.  
Why B is not selected: IPsec tunnels to a database inside the VPC is an over-engineered construct that has to be deployed and maintained, while RDS already supports TLS natively.  
Why C is not selected: Third-party application-level encryption means custom development and managing your own keys. That violates the minimal-operational-overhead requirement.  
Why D is not selected: A VPN provides privacy for the channel between networks, but it doesn't encrypt application traffic to the database and doesn't replace TLS. It's also an extra component to operate.

---

978\. A company is migrating its on-premises Oracle database to an Amazon RDS for Oracle database. The company needs to retain data for 90 days to meet regulatory requirements. The company must also be able to restore the database to a specific point in time for up to 14 days.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Create Amazon RDS automated backups. Set the retention period to 90 days.  
B. Create an Amazon RDS manual snapshot every day. Delete manual snapshots that are older than 90 days.  
C. Use the Amazon Aurora Clone feature for Oracle to create a point-in-time restore. Delete clones that are older than 90 days.  
D. Create a backup plan that has a retention period of 90 days by using AWS Backup for Amazon RDS.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: There are two requirements: retain data for 90 days and be able to restore to any point within the last 14 days. RDS automated backups are capped at 35 days, so AWS Backup is needed: the plan sets a 90-day retention period, and continuous backup provides point-in-time restore. Everything is configured through a single plan.  
Why A is not selected: The maximum retention for RDS automated backups is 35 days: 90 days can't be set.  
Why B is not selected: Daily manual snapshots can be kept indefinitely, but they don't provide point-in-time restore, and deleting old ones would have to be automated yourself.  
Why C is not selected: The clone feature belongs to Aurora and doesn't work for RDS for Oracle, and it doesn't substitute for point-in-time restore.

---

979\. A company is developing a new application that uses a relational database to store user data and application configurations. The company expects the application to have steady user growth. The company expects the database usage to be variable and read-heavy, with occasional writes.  
The company wants to cost-optimize the database solution. The company wants to use an AWS managed database solution that will provide the necessary performance.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Deploy the database on Amazon RDS. Use Provisioned IOPS SSD storage to ensure consistent performance for read and write operations.  
B. Deploy the database on Amazon Aurora Serverless to automatically scale the database capacity based on actual usage to accommodate the workload.  
C. Deploy the database on Amazon DynamoDB. Use on-demand capacity mode to automatically scale throughput to accommodate the workload.  
D. Deploy the database on Amazon RDS. Use magnetic storage and use read replicas to accommodate the workload.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The load is variable, mostly reads, with occasional writes; the database needs to be relational and managed; and cost is the priority. Aurora Serverless adjusts capacity to actual usage and scales down during lulls, so you don't pay for peak capacity around the clock, and growth in user count is handled automatically.  
Why A is not selected: Provisioned IOPS storage is billed continuously at peak values, even though the load is variable.  
Why C is not selected: DynamoDB isn't a relational database, and the scenario explicitly calls for a relational model.  
Why D is not selected: Magnetic storage is outdated and slow, and multiple read replicas are billed around the clock regardless of actual load.

---

980\. A company hosts its application on several Amazon EC2 instances inside a VPC. The company creates a dedicated Amazon S3 bucket for each customer to store their relevant information in Amazon S3.  
The company wants to ensure that the application running on EC2 instances can securely access only the S3 buckets that belong to the company’s AWS account.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
![Exhibit for question 980](images/exhibits/q980-1.png)  
![Exhibit for question 980](images/exhibits/q980-2.png)  
A. Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 that is attached to the VPC. Update the IAM instance profile policy to provide access to only the specific buckets that the application needs.  
B. Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet with a security group that allows access to only Amazon S3. Update the route tables to use the NAT Gateway.  
C. Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 that is attached to the VPUpdate the IAM instance profile policy with a Deny action and the following condition key:  
D. Create a NAT Gateway in a public subnet. Update route tables to use the NAT Gateway. Assign bucket policies for all buckets with a Deny action and the following condition key:  
Answer: C  
Explanation: There are many buckets and more are created continuously, so listing them in a policy is endless manual work. A gateway endpoint provides the private route, and the restriction "only our account's buckets" is best expressed not as a list but as a condition: Deny on S3 actions whenever aws:ResourceAccount doesn't match your account ID. That policy is written once and automatically covers every future bucket, while blocking access to buckets belonging to other accounts on the internet.  
Why A is not selected: Listing specific buckets in a policy works, but it needs an edit for every new customer. It loses on operational overhead compared to a condition on the account ID.  
Why B is not selected: A NAT gateway sends traffic out to the internet and is billed per gigabyte, and a security group can't distinguish your account's buckets from anyone else's.  
Why D is not selected: A policy on "all buckets" can't be applied to someone else's buckets the application might try to reach, and NAT again means the internet and transfer charges.

---

981\. A company is building a cloud-based application on AWS that will handle sensitive customer data. The application uses Amazon RDS for the database, Amazon S3 for object storage, and S3 Event Notifications that invoke AWS Lambda for serverless processing.  
The company uses AWS IAM Identity Center to manage user credentials. The development, testing, and operations teams need secure access to Amazon RDS and Amazon S3 while ensuring the confidentiality of sensitive customer data. The solution must comply with the principle of least privilege.  
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use IAM roles with least privilege to grant all the teams access. Assign IAM roles to each team with customized IAM policies defining specific permission for Amazon RDS and S3 object access based on team responsibilities.  
B. Enable IAM Identity Center with an Identity Center directory. Create and configure permission sets with granular access to Amazon RDS and Amazon S3. Assign all the teams to groups that have specific access with the permission sets.  
C. Create individual IAM users for each member in all the teams with role-based permissions. Assign the IAM roles with predefined policies for RDS and S3 access to each user based on user needs. Implement IAM Access Analyzer for periodic credential evaluation.  
D. Use AWS Organizations to create separate accounts for each team. Implement cross-account IAM roles with least privilege. Grant specific permission for RDS and S3 access based on team roles and responsibilities.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The company already uses IAM Identity Center, so team access should be granted through its native mechanism — a permission set assigned to a group for the relevant accounts. Permissions are defined once and reused, new employees get access by being added to a group, and credentials are always temporary. Setting up parallel IAM roles or users per team would duplicate the access model and require maintaining it by hand.  
Why A is not selected: Roles with fine-grained policies are the right idea, but done around the already-configured Identity Center: access assignment and rotation would have to be managed separately.  
Why C is not selected: Individual IAM users are long-lived credentials and manual upkeep, which conflicts with both minimal effort and the presence of Identity Center.  
Why D is not selected: A separate account per team is a heavy restructuring of the landscape just to separate access to two services.

---

982\. A company has an Amazon S3 bucket that contains sensitive data files. The company has an application that runs on virtual machines in an on-premises data center. The company currently uses AWS IAM Identity Center.  
The application requires temporary access to files in the S3 bucket. The company wants to grant the application secure access to the files in the S3 bucket.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create an S3 bucket policy that permits access to the bucket from the public IP address range of the company’s on-premises data center.  
B. Use IAM Roles Anywhere to obtain security credentials in IAM Identity Center that grant access to the S3 bucket. Configure the virtual machines to assume the role by using the AWS CLI.  
C. Install the AWS CLI on the virtual machine. Configure the AWS CLI with access keys from an IAM user that has access to the bucket.  
D. Create an IAM user and policy that grants access to the bucket. Store the access key and secret key for the IAM user in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the application to retrieve the access key and secret key at startup.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The application runs outside AWS, so it has no instance role or task role, and long-lived keys shouldn't be issued. That's exactly what IAM Roles Anywhere exists for: the virtual machines present an X.509 certificate issued by a trusted certificate authority, exchange it for temporary role credentials, and use those to work with S3. No keys are stored anywhere, the lifetime is bounded, and revocation happens by revoking the certificate or the trust.  
Why A is not selected: Allowing a range of public IP addresses isn't authentication: anyone behind the same NAT would get access. Unacceptable for sensitive data.  
Why C is not selected: IAM user keys on a virtual machine are a long-lived secret that has to be distributed and rotated manually. That's exactly what the "temporary access" requirement is meant to avoid.  
Why D is not selected: Secrets Manager just stores those same long-lived keys more neatly: a compromised key stays valid until it's manually revoked.

---

983\. A company hosts its core network services, including directory services and DNS, in its on-premises data center.  
The data center is connected to the AWS Cloud using AWS Direct Connect (DX). Additional AWS accounts are planned that will require quick, cost-effective, and consistent access to these network services.  
What should a solutions architect implement to meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?  
A. Create a DX connection in each new account. Route the network traffic to the on-premises servers.  
B. Configure VPC endpoints in the DX VPC for all required services. Route the network traffic to the on-premises servers.  
C. Create a VPN connection between each new account and the DX VPRoute the network traffic to the on- premises servers.  
D. Configure AWS Transit Gateway between the accounts. Assign DX to the transit gateway and route network traffic to the on-premises servers.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Many new accounts are planned, and each needs access to the directory and DNS services in the data center. A transit gateway is set up once, shared with the accounts via AWS RAM, their VPCs attach to it, and the Direct Connect link is associated with it through a Direct Connect gateway. Each new account is added with a single attachment, giving fast, cheap, and consistent access for all of them.  
Why A is not selected: A separate Direct Connect link per account means months of provisioning and multiplying port costs.  
Why B is not selected: VPC endpoints provide private access to AWS services, not to the directory and DNS servers in the company's data center.  
Why C is not selected: A VPN connection per account means traffic over the internet with unpredictable latency and many constructs to maintain.

---

984\. A company hosts its main public web application in one AWS Region across multiple Availability Zones. The application uses an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group and an Application Load Balancer (ALB).  
A web development team needs a cost-optimized compute solution to improve the company’s ability to serve dynamic content globally to millions of customers.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Configure the existing ALB as the origin.  
B. Use Amazon Route 53 to serve traffic to the ALB and EC2 instances based on the geographic location of each customer.  
C. Create an Amazon S3 bucket with public read access enabled. Migrate the web application to the S3 bucket. Configure the S3 bucket for website hosting.  
D. Use AWS Direct Connect to directly serve content from the web application to the location of each customer.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The content is dynamic, the audience is global, and cost specifically needs to be optimized. CloudFront with the existing load balancer as the origin solves both: TLS terminates at the nearest edge location, the request travels to the Region over the AWS backbone, and outbound traffic from CloudFront is cheaper than outbound traffic straight from the Region. Dynamic content doesn't even need to be cached — the win comes from the network itself and connection reuse.  
Why B is not selected: Geographic routing makes sense when multiple sites are deployed. There's only one Region here, and routing won't make it any closer to the user.  
Why C is not selected: S3 only serves static files: a dynamic application can't be moved there. Public read access is also a poor practice.  
Why D is not selected: Direct Connect is a dedicated link to one specific company site, not a way to deliver content to millions of users worldwide.

---

985\. A company stores user data in AWS. The data is used continuously with peak usage during business hours. Access patterns vary, with some data not being used for months at a time. A solutions architect must choose a cost- effective solution that maintains the highest level of durability while maintaining high availability.  
Which storage solution meets these requirements?  
A. Amazon S3 Standard  
B. Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering  
C. Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive  
D. Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA)  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Three requirements at once: the highest durability, high availability, and a reasonable price under a pattern where part of the data goes untouched for months. Eleven nines of durability are shared by every class except One Zone (which has the same number but in a single zone — losing the zone loses the data), narrowing the choice to Standard, Standard-IA, and Intelligent-Tiering. Since the access pattern isn't known in advance and keeps changing, Intelligent-Tiering wins: tiering happens automatically, there's no retrieval fee, and availability and durability match Standard.  
Why A is not selected: S3 Standard meets the durability and availability requirements, but you pay the full rate for data that sits untouched for months. The scenario also demands cost-effectiveness.  
Why C is not selected: Deep Archive takes up to 12 hours to return an object, while the data is used continuously with a peak during business hours. That's a hard violation of the availability requirement.  
Why D is not selected: One Zone-IA keeps a single copy in one Availability Zone: both "highest level of durability" and high availability are out.

---

986\. A company is testing an application that runs on an Amazon EC2 Linux instance. A single 500 GB Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) General Purpose SSO (gp2) volume is attached to the EC2 instance.  
The company will deploy the application on multiple EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. All instances require access to the data that is stored in the EBS volume. The company needs a highly available and resilient solution that does not introduce significant changes to the application's code.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Provision an EC2 instance that uses NFS server software. Attach a single 500 GB gp2 EBS volume to the instance.  
B. Provision an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. Configure the file system as an SMB file store within a single Availability Zone.  
C. Provision an EC2 instance with two 250 GB Provisioned IOPS SSD EBS volumes.  
D. Provision an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Configure the file system to use General Purpose performance mode.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Data from the EBS volume needs to become available to every instance in the Auto Scaling group, without significant code changes and with resilience to failures. Amazon EFS solves this directly: the file system mounts over NFS on each instance, the application keeps using ordinary paths, and data is stored across multiple Availability Zones. General Purpose performance mode gives the lowest latency and suits most workloads.  
Why A is not selected: A self-managed NFS server on an instance with a single volume is a single point of failure and a machine that has to be maintained.  
Why B is not selected: The application runs on Linux, and SMB confined to a single Availability Zone gives neither the native protocol nor resilience to a zone failure.  
Why C is not selected: EBS volumes stay tied to a single instance and a single zone: no shared access results.

---

987\. A company recently launched a new application for its customers. The application runs on multiple Amazon EC2 instances across two Availability Zones. End users use TCP to communicate with the application.  
The application must be highly available and must automatically scale as the number of users increases.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)  
A. Add a Network Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.  
B. Configure an Auto Scaling group for the EC2 instances.  
C. Add an Application Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.  
D. Manually add more EC2 instances for the application.  
E. Add a Gateway Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.  
Answer: AB  
Explanation: Clients communicate over TCP, so a Network Load Balancer is needed — an Application Load Balancer only understands HTTP and HTTPS (A). Automatic growth as user count rises comes from an Auto Scaling group, which adds instances as needed and removes surplus ones (B).  
Why C is not selected: An Application Load Balancer works at the HTTP layer and doesn't suit arbitrary TCP traffic.  
Why D is not selected: Manually adding instances contradicts the requirement for automatic scaling.  
Why E is not selected: A Gateway Load Balancer is built for passing traffic through virtual network appliances, not for publishing an application.

---

988\. A company is designing the architecture for a new mobile app that uses the AWS Cloud. The company uses organizational units (OUs) in AWS Organizations to manage its accounts. The company wants to tag Amazon EC2 instances with data sensitivity by using values of sensitive and nonsensitive. IAM identities must not be able to delete a tag or create instances without a tag.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)  
A. In Organizations, create a new tag policy that specifies the data sensitivity tag key and the required values. Enforce the tag values for the EC2 instances. Attach the tag policy to the appropriate OU.  
B. In Organizations, create a new service control policy (SCP) that specifies the data sensitivity tag key and the required tag values. Enforce the tag values for the EC2 instances. Attach the SCP to the appropriate OU.  
C. Create a tag policy to deny running instances when a tag key is not specified. Create another tag policy that prevents identities from deleting tags. Attach the tag policies to the appropriate OU.  
D. Create a service control policy (SCP) to deny creating instances when a tag key is not specified. Create another SCP that prevents identities from deleting tags. Attach the SCPs to the appropriate OU.  
E. Create an AWS Config rule to check if EC2 instances use the data sensitivity tag and the specified values. Configure an AWS Lambda function to delete the resource if a noncompliant resource is found.  
Answer: AD  
Explanation: The requirements split into two, and each half is met by a different type of organization policy. Allowed tag values (sensitive and nonsensitive) are described by a tag policy with enforcement turned on for EC2 resources (A). Forbidding instance creation without the tag and forbidding tag deletion are API actions, which are governed by an SCP: Deny on ec2:RunInstances with a Null condition on aws:RequestTag, and Deny on ec2:DeleteTags (D). The key distinction: a tag policy governs tag values, an SCP governs which actions are allowed.  
Why B is not selected: An SCP can't describe the set of allowed tag values as such — that's what a tag policy is for. Conditions can check a specific value, but that doesn't replace managing the value dictionary.  
Why C is not selected: A tag policy doesn't forbid API calls: it can neither block launching an instance nor forbid deleting tags. That's what an SCP does.  
Why E is not selected: An AWS Config rule plus deleting resources with a function is a reaction after the fact and risks losing a needed resource. The requirement calls for prevention.

---

989\. A company runs database workloads on AWS that are the backend for the company's customer portals. The company runs a Multi-AZ database cluster on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.  
The company needs to implement a 30-day backup retention policy. The company currently has both automated RDS backups and manual RDS backups. The company wants to maintain both types of existing RDS backups that are less than 30 days old.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups by using AWS Backup. Manually delete manual backups that are older than 30 days.  
B. Disable RDS automated backups. Delete automated backups and manual backups that are older than 30 days. Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups.  
C. Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups. Manually delete manual backups that are older than 30 days.  
D. Disable RDS automated backups. Delete automated backups and manual backups that are older than 30 days automatically by using AWS CloudFormation. Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: RDS automated backups delete themselves once their retention period expires, so it's enough to set that period to 30 days — no extra cost and no extra services needed. Manual snapshots stick around until deleted, so old ones have to be removed by hand.  
Why A is not selected: AWS Backup is an unnecessary layer here: automated backup retention is configured directly in RDS, and a backup service would add its own cost on top.  
Why B is not selected: Turning off automated backups and deleting everything that exists violates the requirement to keep backups younger than 30 days.  
Why D is not selected: CloudFormation deploys infrastructure, not deleting backups by age; existing backups would again be lost.

---

990\. A company is planning to migrate a legacy application to AWS. The application currently uses NFS to communicate to an on-premises storage solution to store application data. The application cannot be modified to use any other communication protocols other than NFS for this purpose.  
Which storage solution should a solutions architect recommend for use after the migration?  
A. AWS DataSync  
B. Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)  
C. Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)  
D. Amazon EMR File System (Amazon EMRFS)  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The application can only speak the NFS protocol and can't be changed. In AWS, the managed file system that speaks it is Amazon EFS: it mounts on instances as an ordinary network resource, grows automatically, and stores data across multiple Availability Zones.  
Why A is not selected: DataSync moves data between storage systems and isn't storage itself.  
Why B is not selected: EBS volumes provide a block device, not an NFS network resource: the application can't work with it the way it used to.  
Why D is not selected: EMRFS is an access layer to S3 for EMR clusters, not an NFS file system for general-purpose applications.

---

991\. A company uses GPS trackers to document the migration patterns of thousands of sea turtles. The trackers check every 5 minutes to see if a turtle has moved more than 100 yards (91.4 meters). If a turtle has moved, its tracker sends the new coordinates to a web application running on three Amazon EC2 instances that are in multiple Availability Zones in one AWS Region.  
Recently, the web application was overwhelmed while processing an unexpected volume of tracker data. Data was lost with no way to replay the events. A solutions architect must prevent this problem from happening again and needs a solution with the least operational overhead.  
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?  
A. Create an Amazon S3 bucket to store the data. Configure the application to scan for new data in the bucket for processing.  
B. Create an Amazon API Gateway endpoint to handle transmitted location coordinates. Use an AWS Lambda function to process each item concurrently.  
C. Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to store the incoming data. Configure the application to poll for new messages for processing.  
D. Create an Amazon DynamoDB table to store transmitted location coordinates. Configure the application to query the table for new data for processing. Use TTL to remove data that has been processed.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The application drowned in a burst of traffic and the data was lost for good. An SQS queue fixes both problems at once: it absorbs any burst, stores messages durably, and hands them to the application at whatever pace it can keep up with, so unprocessed events stay in the queue instead of disappearing.  
Why A is not selected: Scanning a bucket for new objects is polling with a delay and requires custom logic to track what's already been processed.  
Why B is not selected: A gateway with functions can absorb the burst, but that's reworking ingestion, and this design has no buffer with replay capability.  
Why D is not selected: A table polled for new records again requires custom query logic and provides no buffering for the burst.

---

992\. A company's software development team needs an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ cluster. The RDS cluster will serve as a backend for a desktop client that is deployed on premises. The desktop client requires direct connectivity to the RDS cluster.  
The company must give the development team the ability to connect to the cluster by using the client when the team is in the office.  
Which solution provides the required connectivity MOST securely?  
A. Create a VPC and two public subnets. Create the RDS cluster in the public subnets. Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN with a customer gateway in the company's office.  
B. Create a VPC and two private subnets. Create the RDS cluster in the private subnets. Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN with a customer gateway in the company's office.  
C. Create a VPC and two private subnets. Create the RDS cluster in the private subnets. Use RDS security groups to allow the company's office IP ranges to access the cluster.  
D. Create a VPC and two public subnets. Create the RDS cluster in the public subnets. Create a cluster user for each developer. Use RDS security groups to allow the users to access the cluster.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Maximum security means the database shouldn't be reachable from the internet at all, and the channel should be encrypted. The cluster is placed in private subnets with no public address, and the office connects over Site-to-Site VPN with a customer gateway on its side: access is only possible from the office network, traffic is encrypted, and there's no public endpoint.  
Why A is not selected: A cluster in public subnets gets an internet-reachable endpoint, and having a VPN doesn't cancel that out: the database can still be attacked around the tunnel.  
Why C is not selected: Security groups scoped to the office's addresses restrict the source, but the traffic still travels over the open internet with no network-layer encryption, and office addresses can be spoofed under other network conditions.  
Why D is not selected: Public subnets plus database users is protection only at the account level, with fully open network access. The least secure option.

---

993\. A solutions architect is creating an application that will handle batch processing of large amounts of data. The input data will be held in Amazon S3 and the output data will be stored in a different S3 bucket. For processing, the application will transfer the data over the network between multiple Amazon EC2 instances.  
What should the solutions architect do to reduce the overall data transfer costs?  
A. Place all the EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group.  
B. Place all the EC2 instances in the same AWS Region.  
C. Place all the EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone.  
D. Place all the EC2 instances in private subnets in multiple Availability Zones.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: This is about the charge for data transfer between instances. Traffic between Availability Zones is billed, while traffic within a single zone over private addresses is not. So every instance that exchanges data needs to sit in the same Availability Zone.  
Why A is not selected: An Auto Scaling group manages the instance count and has no effect on transfer billing.  
Why B is not selected: A single Region is necessary but not sufficient: cross-zone traffic within a Region is still billed.  
Why D is not selected: Multiple Availability Zones is exactly what generates the transfer charge.

---

994\. A company hosts a multi-tier web application that uses an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster for storage. The application tier is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances. The company's IT security guidelines mandate that the database credentials be encrypted and rotated every 14 days.  
What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement with the LEAST operational effort?  
A. Create a new AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption key. Use AWS Secrets Manager to create a new secret that uses the KMS key with the appropriate credentials. Associate the secret with the Aurora DB cluster. Configure a custom rotation period of 14 days.  
B. Create two parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: one for the user name as a string parameter and one that uses the SecureString type for the password. Select AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption for the password parameter, and load these parameters in the application tier. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the password every 14 days.  
C. Store a file that contains the credentials in an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encrypted Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the EFS file system in all EC2 instances of the application tier. Restrict the access to the file on the file system so that the application can read the file and that only super users can modify the file. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the key in Aurora every 14 days and writes new credentials into the file.  
D. Store a file that contains the credentials in an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encrypted Amazon S3 bucket that the application uses to load the credentials. Download the file to the application regularly to ensure that the correct credentials are used. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the Aurora credentials every 14 days and uploads these credentials to the file in the S3 bucket.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: A verbatim repeat of question {{q:336}}: encrypt credentials and rotate them every 14 days with the least effort. Secrets Manager handles it all through configuration — the secret is encrypted with a KMS key, attached to the Aurora cluster, the rotation period is set to an arbitrary number of days, and AWS provides the rotation function for supported databases. The other options assemble the same result from custom code and homegrown ways of delivering the password to the instances.  
Why B is not selected: Parameter Store keeps the password encrypted, but rotation has to be written and maintained by hand.  
Why C is not selected: A file on a shared file system plus a custom rotation function adds development work, file permissions, and the risk of the database and the file drifting out of sync.  
Why D is not selected: Periodically downloading the password file leaves a window where the application works with a stale value, and again requires a custom rotation function.

---

995\. A streaming media company is rebuilding its infrastructure to accommodate increasing demand for video content that users consume daily.  
The company needs to process terabyte-sized videos to block some content in the videos. Video processing can take up to 20 minutes.  
The company needs a solution that will scale with demand and remain cost-effective.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use AWS Lambda functions to process videos. Store video metadata in Amazon DynamoDB. Store video content in Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering.  
B. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) and AWS Fargate to implement microservices to process videos. Store video metadata in Amazon Aurora. Store video content in Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering.  
C. Use Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to process videos. Store video content in Amazon S3 Standard. Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) for queuing and to decouple processing tasks.  
D. Deploy a containerized video processing application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) on Amazon EC2. Store video metadata in Amazon RDS in a single Availability Zone. Store video content in Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Video processing takes up to twenty minutes, which exceeds Lambda's fifteen-minute execution limit. Containers are needed instead: ECS on Fargate scales with demand, is billed for the actual runtime of the tasks, and requires no node management. Metadata is stored in Aurora, and the video files themselves go into S3 with Intelligent-Tiering, which automatically cuts the cost of rarely-read content on its own.  
Why A is not selected: Twenty minutes doesn't fit within Lambda's fifteen-minute limit: the job would get cut off.  
Why C is not selected: An EC2 instance fleet has to be maintained and scaled, and a load balancer in front of video-processing tasks isn't needed at all.  
Why D is not selected: EKS on EC2 instances means managing nodes, a database in a single Availability Zone is fragile, and Glacier Deep Archive takes hours to retrieve files.

---

996\. A company runs an on-premises application on a Kubernetes cluster. The company recently added millions of new customers. The company's existing on-premises infrastructure is unable to handle the large number of new customers. The company needs to migrate the on-premises application to the AWS Cloud.  
The company will migrate to an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster. The company does not want to manage the underlying compute infrastructure for the new architecture on AWS.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use a self-managed node to supply compute capacity. Deploy the application to the new EKS cluster.  
B. Use managed node groups to supply compute capacity. Deploy the application to the new EKS cluster.  
C. Use AWS Fargate to supply compute capacity. Create a Fargate profile. Use the Fargate profile to deploy the application.  
D. Use managed node groups with Karpenter to supply compute capacity. Deploy the application to the new EKS cluster.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The cluster needs to stay Kubernetes, and the company doesn't want to manage the compute infrastructure. AWS Fargate on EKS solves this fully: a Fargate profile is created, and pods that match its rules run with no node behind them at all — no patching, no node scaling.  
Why A is not selected: Self-managed nodes are the most work: images, updates, scaling, all done by hand.  
Why B is not selected: Managed node groups simplify life, but EC2 nodes still exist and their lifecycle still needs attention.  
Why D is not selected: Karpenter automates node provisioning, but the nodes still exist — the infrastructure hasn't gone away.

---

997\. A company is launching a new application that requires a structured database to store user profiles, application settings, and transactional data. The database must be scalable with application traffic and must offer backups.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Deploy a self-managed database on Amazon EC2 instances by using open source software. Use Spot Instances for cost optimization. Configure automated backups to Amazon S3.  
B. Use Amazon RDS. Use on-demand capacity mode for the database with General Purpose SSD storage. Configure automatic backups with a retention period of 7 days.  
C. Use Amazon Aurora Serverless for the database. Use serverless capacity scaling. Configure automated backups to Amazon S3.  
D. Deploy a self-managed NoSQL database on Amazon EC2 instances. Use Reserved Instances for cost optimization. Configure automated backups directly to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: The database needs to be structured, scale with traffic, have backups, and be cheap. Aurora Serverless checks every box: a relational model, capacity that adjusts automatically to actual load, and built-in automated backups to AWS storage. You pay almost nothing while idle.  
Why A is not selected: A self-managed database on interruptible instances risks losing the node at any moment, plus all the operations fall on the company.  
Why B is not selected: Amazon RDS has no on-demand capacity mode: the instance class is picked in advance and billed continuously.  
Why D is not selected: A non-relational database conflicts with the structured-schema requirement, and backing up straight to Glacier means slow recovery.

---

998\. A company runs its legacy web application on AWS. The web application server runs on an Amazon EC2 instance in the public subnet of a VPC. The web application server collects images from customers and stores the image files in a locally attached Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. The image files are uploaded every night to an Amazon S3 bucket for backup.  
A solutions architect discovers that the image files are being uploaded to Amazon S3 through the public endpoint.  
The solutions architect needs to ensure that traffic to Amazon S3 does not use the public endpoint.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Create a gateway VPC endpoint for the S3 bucket that has the necessary permissions for the VPC. Configure the subnet route table to use the gateway VPC endpoint.  
B. Move the S3 bucket inside the VPC. Configure the subnet route table to access the S3 bucket through private IP addresses.  
C. Create an Amazon S3 access point for the Amazon EC2 instance inside the VPConfigure the web application to upload by using the Amazon S3 access point.  
D. Configure an AWS Direct Connect connection between the VPC that has the Amazon EC2 instance and Amazon S3 to provide a dedicated network path.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: The requirement is to stop using the public S3 endpoint. A gateway endpoint adds a route to the service's prefix in the subnet's route table, traffic goes through the endpoint inside the AWS network, and the endpoint policy grants permissions on the needed bucket. The nightly upload doesn't need a single line of code changed.  
Why B is not selected: The bucket can't be moved inside the VPC: S3 is a regional service with no addresses in your network.  
Why C is not selected: An access point changes how addressing and access control work, but the call still goes over the public endpoint unless there's a matching VPC endpoint on the network.  
Why D is not selected: Direct Connect connects the company's own site to AWS. The instance is already inside the VPC, so building a dedicated link to it makes no sense.

---

999\. A company is creating a prototype of an ecommerce website on AWS. The website consists of an Application Load Balancer, an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances for web servers, and an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance that runs with the Single-AZ configuration.  
The website is slow to respond during searches of the product catalog. The product catalog is a group of tables in the MySQL database that the company does not update frequently. A solutions architect has determined that the CPU utilization on the DB instance is high when product catalog searches occur.  
What should the solutions architect recommend to improve the performance of the website during searches of the product catalog?  
A. Migrate the product catalog to an Amazon Redshift database. Use the COPY command to load the product catalog tables.  
B. Implement an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to cache the product catalog. Use lazy loading to populate the cache.  
C. Add an additional scaling policy to the Auto Scaling group to launch additional EC2 instances when database response is slow.  
D. Turn on the Multi-AZ configuration for the DB instance. Configure the EC2 instances to throttle the product catalog queries that are sent to the database.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The product catalog changes rarely, and searching it is what loads down the database's CPU. An ElastiCache for Redis cache with lazy loading keeps query results in memory: the first request goes to the database, later ones are served from the cache, and load on the instance drops.  
Why A is not selected: Redshift is built for analytics over large datasets, not fast catalog lookups in a live application.  
Why C is not selected: Adding web servers doesn't help: the bottleneck is the database, and more instances just pile on more pressure against it.  
Why D is not selected: Multi-AZ improves availability, not performance, and throttling queries makes the site worse, not better.

---

1000\. A company currently stores 5 TB of data in on-premises block storage systems. The company's current storage solution provides limited space for additional data. The company runs applications on premises that must be able to retrieve frequently accessed data with low latency. The company requires a cloud-based storage solution.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?  
A. Use Amazon S3 File Gateway. Integrate S3 File Gateway with the on-premises applications to store and directly retrieve files by using the SMB file system.  
B. Use an AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway with cached volumes as iSCSI targets.  
C. Use an AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway with stored volumes as iSCSI targets.  
D. Use an AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway. Integrate Tape Gateway with the on-premises applications to store virtual tapes in Amazon S3.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The existing storage is block-based (iSCSI), space is running out, and hot data needs to be read with low latency. Volume Gateway in cached volumes mode was built for exactly this: the volume is presented to applications as an iSCSI device, the full dataset lives in S3, and a local disk holds a cache of recently used blocks. There's no need to grow local capacity, and the applications don't need to be rewritten. Compare with {{q:307}} — same logic, different wording.  
Why A is not selected: S3 File Gateway serves data over SMB and NFS, i.e. file protocols. The applications work with block volumes over iSCSI, and switching would mean reworking them.  
Why C is not selected: Stored volumes keep the full data copy locally and only snapshot it to AWS. The lack of on-site space is left unsolved.  
Why D is not selected: Tape Gateway emulates a tape library for backup and archiving. It isn't built for everyday low-latency access.

---

1001\. A company operates a food delivery service. Because of recent growth, the company's order processing system is experiencing scaling problems during peak traffic hours. The current architecture includes Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group that collect orders from an application. A second group of EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group fulfills the orders.  
The order collection process occurs quickly, but the order fulfillment process can take longer. Data must not be lost because of a scaling event.  
A solutions architect must ensure that the order collection process and the order fulfillment process can both scale adequately during peak traffic hours.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the CPUUtilization metric for each instance in both Auto Scaling groups. Configure each Auto Scaling group's minimum capacity to meet its peak workload value.  
B. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the CPUUtilization metric for each instance in both Auto Scaling groups. Configure a CloudWatch alarm to invoke an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to create additional Auto Scaling groups on demand.  
C. Provision two Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queues. Use one SQS queue for order collection. Use the second SQS queue for order fulfillment. Configure the EC2 instances to poll their respective queues. Scale the Auto Scaling groups based on notifications that the queues send.  
D. Provision two Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queues. Use one SQS queue for order collection. Use the second SQS queue for order fulfillment. Configure the EC2 instances to poll their respective queues. Scale the Auto Scaling groups based on the number of messages in each queue.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Order collection is fast and fulfillment is slower, so the tiers need to be decoupled with buffers: one SQS queue per stage, so nothing is lost during a burst. The groups then need to scale based on the number of messages in the corresponding queue — a direct measure of the work that's piled up.  
Why A is not selected: Keeping minimum capacity at peak level means paying for peak instance count around the clock and still doesn't protect against data loss.  
Why B is not selected: Spinning up new Auto Scaling groups on a signal is an unworkable, unmanageable scheme with no buffer for the orders in it.  
Why C is not selected: The queues are chosen correctly, but SQS doesn't send notifications about its own state: scaling needs to be driven by the message-count metric.

---

1002\. An online gaming company is transitioning user data storage to Amazon DynamoDB to support the company's growing user base. The current architecture includes DynamoDB tables that contain user profiles, achievements, and in-game transactions.  
The company needs to design a robust, continuously available, and resilient DynamoDB architecture to maintain a seamless gaming experience for users.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Create DynamoDB tables in a single AWS Region. Use on-demand capacity mode. Use global tables to replicate data across multiple Regions.  
B. Use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to cache frequently accessed data. Deploy tables in a single AWS Region and enable auto scaling. Configure Cross-Region Replication manually to additional Regions.  
C. Create DynamoDB tables in multiple AWS Regions. Use on-demand capacity mode. Use DynamoDB Streams for Cross-Region Replication between Regions.  
D. Use DynamoDB global tables for automatic multi-Region replication. Deploy tables in multiple AWS Regions. Use provisioned capacity mode. Enable auto scaling.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Continuous multi-Region availability is achieved with global tables: DynamoDB replicates the data across Regions itself and allows writes in any of them. The gaming service's load is predictable and steady, so provisioned capacity with auto scaling costs less than paying per request.  
Why A is not selected: Tables in a single Region and global tables at the same time is a contradiction: a global table by definition spans multiple Regions.  
Why B is not selected: A cache speeds up reads, but nobody maintains cross-Region replication by hand: that's exactly what global tables exist for.  
Why C is not selected: Homegrown replication built on change streams is code that has to be written and maintained, and on-demand mode is more expensive under steady load.

---

1003\. A company runs its media rendering application on premises. The company wants to reduce storage costs and has moved all data to Amazon S3. The on-premises rendering application needs low-latency access to storage.  
The company needs to design a storage solution for the application. The storage solution must maintain the desired application performance.  
Which storage solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?  
A. Use Mountpoint for Amazon S3 to access the data in Amazon S3 for the on-premises application.  
B. Configure an Amazon S3 File Gateway to provide storage for the on-premises application.  
C. Copy the data from Amazon S3 to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. Configure an Amazon FSx File Gateway to provide storage for the on-premises application.  
D. Configure an on-premises file server. Use the Amazon S3 API to connect to S3 storage. Configure the application to access the storage from the on-premises file server.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The data has already moved to S3, but the local rendering application needs to read it with low latency and without being rewritten against an object API. S3 File Gateway is deployed on-site, presents the bucket as a shared folder over NFS or SMB, and keeps a local cache of hot files: the first read comes from S3, later ones from local disk. You're paying for S3 and a lightweight gateway, not a second full-fledged storage system — hence "most cost-effective."  
Why A is not selected: Mountpoint for Amazon S3 mounts the bucket as a file system, but every read still goes to S3 over the WAN, and it doesn't provide a real local cache of hot data or full POSIX semantics. Latency for on-site rendering would stay high.  
Why C is not selected: Copying data into FSx for Windows File Server means a second paid storage system on top of the S3 you're already paying for, plus a separate gateway. It meets the latency requirement but loses on cost.  
Why D is not selected: A homegrown file server calling the S3 API is development and operations you do yourself: caching, consistency, and fault tolerance would all have to be built by hand.

---

1004\. A company hosts its enterprise resource planning (ERP) system in the us-east-1 Region. The system runs on Amazon EC2 instances. Customers use a public API that is hosted on the EC2 instances to exchange information with the ERP system. International customers report slow API response times from their data centers.  
Which solution will improve response times for the international customers MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Create an AWS Direct Connect connection that has a public virtual interface (VIF) to provide connectivity from each customer's data center to us-east-1. Route customer API requests by using a Direct Connect gateway to the ERP system API.  
B. Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API. Configure the CachingOptimized managed cache policy to provide improved cache efficiency.  
C. Set up AWS Global Accelerator. Configure listeners for the necessary ports. Configure endpoint groups for the appropriate Regions to distribute traffic. Create an endpoint in the group for the API.  
D. Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN to establish dedicated VPN tunnels between Regions and customer networks. Route traffic to the API over the VPN connections.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: The API is public, runs over HTTP, and the complaints about latency come from customers abroad. Putting CloudFront in front of the API solves it two ways: TLS terminates at the nearest edge location and the request continues over the AWS backbone from there, and cacheable responses are returned without touching the Region at all. The key differentiator here is cost: CloudFront has no fixed hourly charge, while Global Accelerator always does.  
Why A is not selected: A dedicated link to every customer's data center is the most expensive and slowest option available, and a public virtual interface doesn't even combine with a Direct Connect gateway.  
Why C is not selected: Global Accelerator would also speed things up and would be the right answer for non-HTTP traffic, but it costs more: a fixed accelerator fee plus a data transfer premium, with no caching at all.  
Why D is not selected: VPN tunnels to every customer's network don't scale, require configuration on each customer's side, and don't speed up a public API.

---

1005\. A company tracks customer satisfaction by using surveys that the company hosts on its website. The surveys sometimes reach thousands of customers every hour. Survey results are currently sent in email messages to the company so company employees can manually review results and assess customer sentiment.  
The company wants to automate the customer survey process. Survey results must be available for the previous 12 months.  
Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST scalable way?  
A. Send the survey results data to an Amazon API Gateway endpoint that is connected to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Create an AWS Lambda function to poll the SQS queue, call Amazon Comprehend for sentiment analysis, and save the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table. Set the TTL for all records to 365 days in the future.  
B. Send the survey results data to an API that is running on an Amazon EC2 instance. Configure the API to store the survey results as a new record in an Amazon DynamoDB table, call Amazon Comprehend for sentiment analysis, and save the results in a second DynamoDB table. Set the TTL for all records to 365 days in the future.  
C. Write the survey results data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use S3 Event Notifications to invoke an AWS Lambda function to read the data and call Amazon Rekognition for sentiment analysis. Store the sentiment analysis results in a second S3 bucket. Use S3 lifecycle policies on each bucket to expire objects after 365 days.  
D. Send the survey results data to an Amazon API Gateway endpoint that is connected to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure the SQS queue to invoke an AWS Lambda function that calls Amazon Lex for sentiment analysis and saves the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table. Set the TTL for all records to 365 days in the future.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: Thousands of responses an hour call for a buffer, and sentiment analysis calls for a ready-made service. API Gateway accepts the results and drops them on an SQS queue, which absorbs the burst; a Lambda function drains the queue and calls Amazon Comprehend for the sentiment score, and the results are kept for the following twelve months.  
Why B is not selected: An API on an EC2 instance is a bottleneck that has to be scaled and maintained by hand.  
Why C is not selected: Amazon Rekognition analyzes images and video — it doesn't determine text sentiment.  
Why D is not selected: Amazon Lex builds conversational bots; it doesn't do sentiment analysis for surveys.

---

1006\. A company uses AWS Systems Manager for routine management and patching of Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances are in an IP address type target group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB).  
New security protocols require the company to remove EC2 instances from service during a patch. When the company attempts to follow the security protocol during the next patch, the company receives errors during the patching window.  
Which combination of solutions will resolve the errors? (Choose two.)  
A. Change the target type of the target group from IP address type to instance type.  
B. Continue to use the existing Systems Manager document without changes because it is already optimized to handle instances that are in an IP address type target group behind an ALB.  
C. Implement the AWSEC2-PatchLoadBalanacerInstance Systems Manager Automation document to manage the patching process.  
D. Use Systems Manager Maintenance Windows to automatically remove the instances from service to patch the instances.  
E. Configure Systems Manager State Manager to remove the instances from service and manage the patching schedule. Use ALB health checks to re-route traffic.  
Answer: CD  
Explanation: The errors happen because instances get patched while still part of the target group. Systems Manager has a ready-made automation document, AWSEC2-PatchLoadBalancerInstance, that takes the instance out from behind the load balancer itself, installs the updates, and puts it back (C); this process is triggered by maintenance windows, which handle taking instances out of service and patching on a schedule (D).  
Why A is not selected: Switching the target type from IP address to instance doesn't fix the problem: the instance still stays in the target group during patching.  
Why B is not selected: It's precisely the current document that causes the errors, so leaving it unchanged isn't an option.  
Why E is not selected: State Manager maintains a desired configuration state, but it doesn't take instances out from behind a load balancer for the duration of patching.

---

1007\. A medical company wants to perform transformations on a large amount of clinical trial data that comes from several customers. The company must extract the data from a relational database that contains the customer data.  
Then the company will transform the data by using a series of complex rules. The company will load the data to Amazon S3 when the transformations are complete.  
All data must be encrypted where it is processed before the company stores the data in Amazon S3. All data must be encrypted by using customer-specific keys.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational effort?  
A. Create one AWS Glue job for each customer. Attach a security configuration to each job that uses server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) to encrypt the data.  
B. Create one Amazon EMR cluster for each customer. Attach a security configuration to each cluster that uses client-side encryption with a custom client-side root key (CSE-Custom) to encrypt the data.  
C. Create one AWS Glue job for each customer. Attach a security configuration to each job that uses client-side encryption with AWS KMS managed keys (CSE-KMS) to encrypt the data.  
D. Create one Amazon EMR cluster for each customer. Attach a security configuration to each cluster that uses server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) to encrypt the data.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Two requirements shape the answer. "Least operational effort" points to AWS Glue: it's managed, serverless ETL, with no clusters to stand up and tear down, unlike EMR. "All data must be encrypted where it is processed" plus "customer-specific keys" points to client-side encryption with KMS keys (CSE-KMS): data is encrypted before it's written, with its own key per customer, and the job's intermediate results are protected too. This is set through a security configuration attached to the Glue job.  
Why A is not selected: SSE-S3 uses keys the service manages — they can't be "customer-specific." And encryption happens only at write time to S3, not during processing.  
Why B is not selected: An EMR cluster per customer means managing clusters instead of serverless jobs, and CSE-Custom requires implementing your own key provider. The most effort of the options.  
Why D is not selected: Again clusters instead of Glue, and SSE-KMS protects objects at rest in S3, not data during processing.

---

1008\. A company hosts a website analytics application on a single Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instance. The analytics application is highly resilient and is designed to run in stateless mode.  
The company notices that the application is showing signs of performance degradation during busy times and is presenting 5xx errors. The company needs to make the application scale seamlessly.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On- Demand Instance. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the load across the two EC2 instances.  
B. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On- Demand Instance. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted routing to distribute the load across the two EC2 instances.  
C. Create an AWS Lambda function to stop the EC2 instance and change the instance type. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to invoke the Lambda function when CPU utilization is more than 75%.  
D. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the web application. Apply the AMI to a launch template. Create an Auto Scaling group that includes the launch template. Configure the launch template to use a Spot Fleet. Attach an Application Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The application is stateless and resilient to failures, so interruptible capacity is a fit. The cheapest setup: build an AMI, put it in a launch template, create an Auto Scaling group on top of a Spot Fleet, and attach an Application Load Balancer. Capacity scales itself, and Spot Instances cost up to 90 percent less than On-Demand; reclamation isn't a concern because there's no state to lose.  
Why A is not selected: Two On-Demand instances is fixed capacity: it still falls short at peak and the company pays for idle capacity during lulls. No real scaling.  
Why B is not selected: The same fixed-capacity drawback, and Route 53 weighted routing also doesn't remove a failed instance instantly the way a load balancer does.  
Why C is not selected: Changing the instance type requires stopping it, i.e. downtime, and still leaves a single machine as a point of failure. That's vertical scaling, not seamless scaling.

---

1009\. A company runs an environment where data is stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The objects are accessed frequently throughout the day. The company has strict da ta encryption requirements for data that is stored in the S3 bucket. The company currently uses AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) for encryption.  
The company wants to optimize costs associated with encrypting S3 objects without making additional calls to AWS KMS.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3).  
B. Use an S3 Bucket Key for server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) on the new objects.  
C. Use client-side encryption with AWS KMS customer managed keys.  
D. Use server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C) stored in AWS KMS.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Objects are read frequently, KMS encryption is mandated by policy, and the cost driver is calls to KMS rather than storage: under SSE-KMS every read or write means a Decrypt or GenerateDataKey call. An S3 Bucket Key solves exactly this: S3 requests one bucket-level key from KMS for a short period and derives per-object keys from it itself, cutting the number of KMS calls — and the bill for them — by roughly 99%. Encryption stays SSE-KMS, and key permissions and logging are preserved.  
Why A is not selected: SSE-S3 is indeed cheaper, but it drops KMS entirely, while the company has strict requirements and key management already built around KMS.  
Why C is not selected: Client-side encryption with KMS keys increases the number of KMS calls and requires reworking the application — the opposite of "without additional calls to KMS."  
Why D is not selected: This combination isn't possible: with SSE-C the client supplies the key with every request, and it's never stored in KMS. It also doesn't save on calls.

---

1010\. A company runs multiple workloads on virtual machines (VMs) in an on-premises data center. The company is expanding rapidly. The on-premises data center is not able to scale fast enough to meet business needs. The company wants to migrate the workloads to AWS.  
The migration is time sensitive. The company wants to use a lift-and-shift strategy for non-critical workloads.  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose three.)  
A. Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to collect data about the VMs.  
B. Use AWS Application Migration Service. Install the AWS Replication Agent on the VMs.  
C. Complete the initial replication of the VMs. Launch test instances to perform acceptance tests on the VMs.  
D. Stop all operations on the VMs. Launch a cutover instance.  
E. Use AWS App2Container (A2C) to collect data about the VMs.  
F. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate the VMs.  
Answer: BCD  
Explanation: A lift-and-shift move on a tight timeline means block-level replication of the virtual machines. The standard tool is AWS Application Migration Service: the Replication Agent is installed on the machines (B), initial replication completes and test instances are launched for acceptance testing (C), and at cutover, work on the source machines stops and the final instance is launched (D). Downtime comes down to minutes.  
Why A is not selected: The Schema Conversion Tool converts database schemas and doesn't collect information about virtual machines.  
Why E is not selected: App2Container packages applications into containers, i.e. changes how they run — that's no longer a lift-and-shift.  
Why F is not selected: DMS migrates database contents, not entire virtual machines.

---

1011\. A company hosts an application in a private subnet. The company has already integrated the application with Amazon Cognito. The company uses an Amazon Cognito user pool to authenticate users.  
The company needs to modify the application so the application can securely store user documents in an Amazon S3 bucket.  
Which combination of steps will securely integrate Amazon S3 with the application? (Choose two.)  
A. Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool to generate secure Amazon S3 access tokens for users when they successfully log in.  
B. Use the existing Amazon Cognito user pool to generate Amazon S3 access tokens for users when they successfully log in.  
C. Create an Amazon S3 VPC endpoint in the same VPC where the company hosts the application.  
D. Create a NAT gateway in the VPC where the company hosts the application. Assign a policy to the S3 bucket to deny any request that is not initiated from Amazon Cognito.  
E. Attach a policy to the S3 bucket that allows access only from the users' IP addresses.  
Answer: AC  
Explanation: Two halves of the task. Permissions: the Cognito user pool confirms identity and issues a token, but that token can't be used to call S3 — an identity pool is needed to exchange it for temporary IAM role credentials scoped to the right bucket prefix (A). Path: the application runs in a private subnet, so calls to S3 go through a VPC endpoint without ever reaching the internet (C). Distinguishing the user pool from the identity pool is the most common source of confusion in Cognito questions.  
Why B is not selected: The user pool issues identity and access tokens for your own application, not AWS credentials. They can't be used to call S3.  
Why D is not selected: A NAT gateway sends traffic out to the internet, contradicting the idea of private access, and there's no such thing as a "request initiated by Cognito" condition in a bucket policy.  
Why E is not selected: Restricting by user IP address doesn't work for mobile or home users and isn't an authorization mechanism at all.

---

1012\. A company has a three-tier web application that processes orders from customers. The web tier consists of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The processing tier consists of EC2 instances. The company decoupled the web tier and processing tier by using Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). The storage layer uses Amazon DynamoDB.  
At peak times, some users report order processing delays and halls. The company has noticed that during these delays, the EC2 instances are running at 100% CPU usage, and the SQS queue fills up. The peak times are variable and unpredictable.  
The company needs to improve the performance of the application.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Use scheduled scaling for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling to scale out the processing tier instances for the duration of peak usage times. Use the CPU Utilization metric to determine when to scale.  
B. Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in front of the DynamoDB backend tier. Use target utilization as a metric to determine when to scale.  
C. Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution to cache the responses for the web tier. Use HTTP latency as a metric to determine when to scale.  
D. Use an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking policy to scale out the processing tier instances. Use the ApproximateNumberOfMessages attribute to determine when to scale.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: The symptom is described precisely: the queue grows while the processing instances sit at 100 percent CPU, and the peaks are unpredictable. That means scaling has to track queue length. A target tracking policy driven by a metric based on ApproximateNumberOfMessages (typically messages per instance) adds processing capacity exactly when messages start piling up, regardless of any schedule.  
Why A is not selected: Scheduled scaling doesn't work with unpredictable peaks, and CPU is already at 100 percent by the time it would trigger — the signal arrives too late.  
Why B is not selected: A cache in front of DynamoDB won't help: the bottleneck is compute processing of the messages, not reading from the database.  
Why C is not selected: CloudFront caches responses at the web tier, but the delays occur at the order-processing tier reading from the queue.

---

1013\. A company's production environment consists of Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday. The instances must run for only 12 hours on Sunday and cannot tolerate interruptions. The company wants to cost-optimize the production environment.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Purchase Scheduled Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.  
B. Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.  
C. Use Spot Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.  
D. Use Spot Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.  
Answer: A  
Source note: Outdated wording: AWS no longer offers Scheduled Reserved Instances to new customers. Within the question's logic, option A remains the only choice with no interruptions for a recurring time window; in practice today the same task is solved by scheduling instance start/stop together with a Savings Plan or On-Demand  
Explanation: Interruptions aren't tolerable, so Spot Instances are ruled out entirely. For running continuously Monday through Saturday, Standard Reserved Instances are purchased, and for the twelve hours on Sunday, Scheduled Reserved Instances — reserved for exactly that recurring window. Worth noting: AWS no longer offers this reservation type to new customers, but within the logic of the question it remains the only interruption-free option for a recurring window.  
Why B is not selected: Convertible Reserved Instances are billed continuously: for twelve hours once a week, that's an almost entirely unused commitment.  
Why C is not selected: Spot Instances can be reclaimed, and the scenario explicitly forbids interruptions.  
Why D is not selected: The same Spot problem here, plus a smaller discount from Convertible Reserved Instances for the steady workload.

---

1014\. A digital image processing company wants to migrate its on-premises monolithic application to the AWS Cloud.  
The company processes thousands of images and generates large files as part of the processing workflow.  
The company needs a solution to manage the growing number of image processing jobs. The solution must also reduce the manual tasks in the image processing workflow. The company does not want to manage the underlying infrastructure of the solution.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the images. Configure Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS).  
B. Use AWS Batch jobs to process the images. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in an Amazon S3 bucket.  
C. Use AWS Lambda functions and Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the images. Store the processed files in Amazon FSx.  
D. Deploy a group of Amazon EC2 instances to process the images. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Image processing is a stream of batch jobs, and the company doesn't want to manage infrastructure. AWS Batch itself provisions and runs the compute resources for the job queue (including on Fargate), AWS Step Functions describes the sequence of steps and removes manual handoffs, and the large result files land in S3, which grows without limit and costs less than file storage systems.  
Why A is not selected: An ECS cluster on interruptible instances still requires managing the compute environment, and SQS only provides a queue, not workflow orchestration.  
Why C is not selected: Lambda functions are limited in time and memory for heavy image processing, and interruptible instances again mean managing your own infrastructure.  
Why D is not selected: A group of EC2 instances is exactly the infrastructure the company doesn't want to manage, and an EBS volume isn't shared across machines and is limited in size.

---

1015\. A company's image-hosting website gives users around the world the ability to up load, view, and download images from their mobile devices. The company currently hosts the static website in an Amazon S3 bucket.  
Because of the website's growing popularity, the website's performance has decreased. Users have reported latency issues when they upload and download images.  
The company must improve the performance of the website.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST implementation effort?  
A. Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the S3 bucket to improve the download performance. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to improve the upload performance.  
B. Configure Amazon EC2 instances of the right sizes in multiple AWS Regions. Migrate the application to the EC2 instances. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the website traffic equally among the EC2 instances. Configure AWS Global Accelerator to address global demand with low latency.  
C. Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the S3 bucket as an origin to improve the download performance. Configure the application to use CloudFront to upload images to improve the upload performance. Create S3 buckets in multiple AWS Regions. Configure replication rules for the buckets to replicate users' data based on the users' location. Redirect downloads to the S3 bucket that is closest to each user's location.
