D. Configure AWS Global Accelerator for the S3 bucket to improve network performance. Create an endpoint for the application to use Global Accelerator instead of the S3 bucket.  
Answer: A  
Explanation: There are two problems — slow downloads and slow uploads — and they're solved with different tools, with minimal effort. CloudFront in front of the bucket speeds up downloads: images are cached at edge locations near the user. S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads: the file is accepted at the nearest edge location and travels to the bucket over the AWS backbone. Both are turned on with configuration, no architecture changes needed.  
Why B is not selected: Moving the site to instances across multiple Regions is a rewrite of the architecture with ongoing cost, while minimal implementation effort is required.  
Why C is not selected: Uploading through CloudFront is inefficient, and buckets in multiple Regions with replication and download redirection is a complex, expensive construction.  
Why D is not selected: Global Accelerator doesn't work with S3 as an endpoint: that configuration doesn't exist.

---

1016\. A company runs an application in a private subnet behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in a VPC. The VPC has a NAT gateway and an internet gateway. The application calls the Amazon S3 API to store objects.  
According to the company's security policy, traffic from the application must not travel across the internet.  
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?  
A. Configure an S3 interface endpoint. Create a security group that allows outbound traffic to Amazon S3.  
B. Configure an S3 gateway endpoint. Update the VPC route table to use the endpoint.  
C. Configure an S3 bucket policy to allow traffic from the Elastic IP address that is assigned to the NAT gateway.  
D. Create a second NAT gateway in the same subnet where the legacy application is deployed. Update the VPC route table to use the second NAT gateway.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: Traffic to S3 must not travel over the internet, and the cheapest solution is needed. An S3 gateway endpoint adds a route to the service's prefix in the VPC route table, traffic stays inside the AWS network, and the endpoint itself carries no charge — neither hourly nor per data processed.  
Why A is not selected: An interface endpoint is also private, but it's billed hourly and per traffic processed, while a gateway endpoint is free.  
Why C is not selected: Allowing the NAT gateway's IP address doesn't change the route: traffic still goes over the internet.  
Why D is not selected: A second NAT gateway just doubles the cost and leaves the same path over the internet.

---

1017\. A company has an application that runs on an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster on Amazon EC2 instances. The application has a UI that uses Amazon DynamoDB and data services that use Amazon S3 as part of the application deployment.  
The company must ensure that the EKS Pods for the UI can access only Amazon DynamoDB and that the EKS Pods for the data services can access only Amazon S3. The company uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).  
Which solution meals these requirements?  
A. Create separate IAM policies for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB access with the required permissions. Attach both IAM policies to the EC2 instance profile. Use role-based access control (RBAC) to control access to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB for the respective EKS Pods.  
B. Create separate IAM policies for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB access with the required permissions. Attach the Amazon S3 IAM policy directly to the EKS Pods for the data services and the DynamoDB policy to the EKS Pods for the UI.  
C. Create separate Kubernetes service accounts for the UI and data services to assume an IAM role. Attach the AmazonS3FullAccess policy to the data services account and the AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess policy to the UI service account.  
D. Create separate Kubernetes service accounts for the UI and data services to assume an IAM role. Use IAM Role for Service Accounts (IRSA) to provide access to the EKS Pods for the UI to Amazon S3 and the EKS Pods for the data services to DynamoDB.  
Answer: D  
Explanation: Pods need distinct permissions rather than the shared node permissions, which calls for IRSA: separate Kubernetes service accounts are created for the UI and the data services, each annotated with its own IAM role's ARN, and the roles trust the cluster's OIDC provider with a condition scoped to a specific service account. That way the UI pod can reach only its DynamoDB table, and the data-services pod only its bucket. Note: the option's wording actually swaps the services (S3 is assigned to the UI, DynamoDB to data services) — that's a typo in the dump; the mechanism itself is described correctly. The same technique is covered in {{q:941,223}}.  
Why A is not selected: Policies on the instance profile grant permissions to every pod on the node at once, and Kubernetes RBAC controls access to the Kubernetes API itself, not to AWS services.  
Why B is not selected: An IAM policy can't be attached to a pod directly: the principal is the role a pod assumes via its service account.  
Why C is not selected: The mechanism is named almost correctly, but the FullAccess managed policies grant full access to the entire service, which conflicts with the requirement for scoped access.

---

1018\. A company needs to give a globally distributed development team secure access to the company's AWS resources in a way that complies with security policies.  
The company currently uses an on-premises Active Directory for internal authentication. The company uses AWS Organizations to manage multiple AWS accounts that support multiple projects.  
The company needs a solution to integrate with the existing infrastructure to provide centralized identity management and access control.  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?  
A. Set up AWS Directory Service to create an AWS managed Microsoft Active Directory on AWS. Establish a trust relationship with the on-premises Active Directory. Use IAM rotes that are assigned to Active Directory groups to access AWS resources within the company's AWS accounts.  
B. Create an IAM user for each developer. Manually manage permissions for each IAM user based on each user's involvement with each project. Enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) as an additional layer of security.  
C. Use AD Connector in AWS Directory Service to connect to the on-premises Active Directory. Integrate AD Connector with AWS IAM Identity Center. Configure permissions sets to give each AD group access to specific AWS accounts and resources.  
D. Use Amazon Cognito to deploy an identity federation solution. Integrate the identity federation solution with the on-premises Active Directory. Use Amazon Cognito to provide access tokens for developers to access AWS accounts and resources.  
Answer: C  
Explanation: Users stay in the on-premises Active Directory, and access is needed across several accounts in the organization. The lightest path is AD Connector: it keeps no copy of the directory and instead proxies authentication requests to your own domain controllers, connecting as an identity source to IAM Identity Center. From there, permission sets are assigned to AD groups for the relevant accounts. No forest trust and no second directory in the cloud need to be stood up — hence the minimal operational overhead.  
Why A is not selected: Managed Microsoft AD with a trust relationship works, but it's an additional directory in the cloud that has to be paid for and maintained, plus setting up a forest trust. More effort than AD Connector.  
Why B is not selected: IAM users for a distributed team means manually managing permissions and long-lived credentials, conflicting with both the requirements and minimal effort.  
Why D is not selected: Cognito is built for application end users, not for employee access to AWS accounts.

---

1019\. A company is developing an application in the AWS Cloud. The application's HTTP API contains critical information that is published in Amazon API Gateway. The critical information must be accessible from only a limited set of trusted IP addresses that belong to the company's internal network.  
Which solution will meet these requirements?  
A. Set up an API Gateway private integration to restrict access to a predefined set of IP addresses.  
B. Create a resource policy for the API that denies access to any IP address that is not specifically allowed.  
C. Directly deploy the API in a private subnet. Create a network ACL. Set up rules to allow the traffic from specific IP addresses.  
D. Modify the security group that is attached to API Gateway to allow inbound traffic from only the trusted IP addresses.  
Answer: B  
Explanation: An API in API Gateway has its own access-restriction mechanism — a resource policy. It denies every address except the listed trusted ones, and the check is performed by the gateway itself before the backend is ever invoked.  
Why A is not selected: A private integration controls how the gateway reaches the backend inside the network — it doesn't restrict client access by IP address.  
Why C is not selected: API Gateway is a managed service; it can't be deployed into your own subnet, and network ACLs don't apply to it.  
Why D is not selected: A security group can't be attached to API Gateway: the service has no network interfaces of yours for inbound traffic to hit.
